title: Effects of salivary amylase gene copy number on metabolic health
abstract: Precision nutrition is the personalization of dietary recommendations based on characteristics such as genetics, the microbiome, lifestyle, environment, and baseline metabolic state. One potential basis for the development of guidelines is the characterization of gene-diet interactions. In this narrative review, we evaluate the published literature reporting associations between salivary amylase gene copy number and metabolic health. The salivary amylase enzyme facilitates starch digestion and is encoded by AMY1 , a gene copy number (CN) variant. Humans have 2–20 copies, and AMY1 CN has been associated with metabolic health conditions such as obesity and insulin resistance. Studies of these associations have conflicting findings. The objectives of this review are to assess the findings from studies testing associations between AMY1 CN and adiposity, glucose metabolism, and gut microbiome composition; to explore possible mechanisms underlying the effects on metabolic health; and to identify knowledge gaps requiring additional research. To identify relevant articles, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, and Centre for Agricultural and Biosciences International for articles focused on AMY1 CN and one or more of the following: body mass index, glucose metabolism, and the microbiome. Key findings are that AMY1 CN has a positive association with postprandial glucose response and that a high AMY1 CN is protective against insulin resistance. AMY1 CN alone does not appear to be an accurate predictor of adiposity, and the relationship is likely convoluted by habitual starch intake, genetic background, and lifestyle factors. Future studies are required to determine how AMY1 CN could be used as a biomarker or to inform precision nutrition protocols to achieve metabolic health outcomes.
body: Despite therapeutic advancements, the incidence of metabolic disorders, such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, has progressively increased in adults and is a major financial burden on healthcare systems. The prevalence of obesity has more than doubled since 1990, with more than 1 billion people experiencing obesity worldwide ( 1 ). In the U.S. alone, obesity incurs over 1.73 trillion dollars in cost annually, equating to almost 10% of GDP ( 2 ). The prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) has increased concurrently with the international diabetes federation estimating that 1 in 8 people will have diabetes by 2045, an increase of 46% ( 3 ). T2D costs the U.S. healthcare system $327 billion in 2017 ( 4 ). Although there are effective pharmaceutical treatments for T2D and obesity, including metformin and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), there are numerous benefits to preventing or reversing these conditions with lifestyle interventions, including dietary changes. Metformin is widely used and well-tolerated by most patients, but gastrointestinal issues are the most frequently reported side effects, affecting up to 21% of patients ( 5–7 ). In some patients, GLP-1 RAs cause gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), especially at higher doses ( 8–12 ). GLP-1 RAs are expensive and often not fully covered by insurance, creating significant access barriers, which is one reason why some eligible patients do not receive these drugs despite guideline recommendations ( 13–15 ). Some patients may turn to compounding pharmacies if commercial products are unaffordable or unavailable due to episodic shortages, which poses concerns about safety and quality ( 16–19 ). Additionally, the use of metformin or GLP-1 RAs to manage diabetes or weight should be thought of by patients as a life-long intervention, with cessation of GLP-1 RAs frequently causing patients to regain weight and metabolic markers to return to previous values ( 20 , 21 ). A portion of the weight lost using GLP-1 RAs is lean mass ( 22 ); GLP1-RAs are commonly associated with micronutrient deficiencies ( 23 ); and there is a limited amount of data regarding the effects of long-term use. Furthermore, no single medication can confer all the benefits of appropriate dietary modification for improving body composition, glucose metabolism, cardiovascular health, and cancer risk. Most patients with prediabetes or obesity prefer lifestyle interventions over medication, citing concerns about drug side effects and dependency ( 24–28 ). However, broad population-based guidelines regarding lifestyle and dietary modifications have had limited success, and personalized approaches, in which dietary recommendations are tailored to the person, are an area of active study. Precision nutrition aims to utilize individual attributes such as health- and diet-related genotypes and gut microbiome composition to tailor dietary advice. Genetic heritability partly accounts for the phenotypic variation in body mass index (40–70%) ( 29 , 30 ) and glucose metabolism (~30–40%) ( 31–33 ). Delineating the mechanisms underlying the interactions between host genotype and dietary intake to influence metabolic health would contribute to the development of precision nutrition protocols. A candidate enzyme involved in starch digestion and previously associated with BMI and glucose metabolism is encoded by the gene copy number variant AMY1 . Dozens of studies have tested associations between salivary amylase gene copy number and metabolic health parameters ( Tables 1 – 3 ; Supplementary Tables S2–S4 ). Amylase is an enzyme that helps mammals digest dietary starch. Salivary amylase is encoded by a gene copy number variant, AMY1 , which has an instructive evolutionary history. Carbohydrate intake influences body weight and blood glucose, so variations in amylase enzyme dosage could affect these outcomes. Variability in the ratio of digestible carbohydrates to dietary fiber that reaches the gut microbiome could further impact metabolic health through the activity of microbial metabolites. In this review, we summarize the physiology, genomic arrangement, and evolutionary history of amylase. Then we discuss reported associations between salivary amylase gene copy number and metabolic health, including studies reporting interactions with starch intake. This review contributes to the foundation for future research directing precision nutrition strategies. Summary of studies reporting associations between AMY1 CN and adiposity. See Supplementary Table S2 for more details. CN = copy number; BMI = body mass index; HOMA-IR = homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance; QUICKI = Quantitative Insulin Sensitivity Check Index; HbA1c = hemoglobin A1c. Summary of studies reporting associations between AMY1 CN and glucose homeostasis. See Supplementary Table S3 for more details. CN = copy number; BMI = body mass index; HOMA-IR = homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance; QUICKI = Quantitative Insulin Sensitivity Check Index; HbA1c = hemoglobin A1c. Summary of studies reporting associations between AMY1 CN and the microbiome. See Supplementary Table S4 for more details. FMT = fecal microbiota transplant; OTU = operational taxonomic unit. Amylase was among the first enzymes discovered and is produced by microbes, plants, and animals ( 34 , 35 ). Amylase breaks down starch and glycogen into simpler sugars, and there are three forms—alpha-amylase, beta-amylase, and gamma-amylase—which target different bonds in a substrate ( 36 ). The amylase genes encoded in the human genome produce alpha-amylases, which are the subject of this review. Salivary glands secrete amylase in the mouth, and the pancreas secretes amylase into the small intestine to help digest dietary starches ( 37 ). Amylase is the most abundant enzyme in human saliva ( 38 ). Other organs contain amylase, but at orders of magnitude lower than the salivary glands and pancreas ( 39 ). Serum amylase is derived primarily from the pancreas and salivary glands and is used to diagnose pancreatitis ( 40 , 41 ). This review focuses on salivary amylase, which is more frequently measured in research studies than serum amylase. Salivary and pancreatic amylase are encoded by two different genes, AMY1 and AMY2 , which have variable copy number in humans. The AMY1 gene encodes the salivary amylase enzyme. The number of gene copies is positively correlated with salivary amylase activity, but additional factors, including stress, caffeine, smoking, and the time of day, affect salivary amylase activity ( 37 , 42 , 43 ). Amylase initiates the breakdown of dietary polysaccharides through the hydrolysis of internal alpha-1,4-glucosidic bonds to release smaller malto-oligosaccharides, maltotriose, maltose, and a small amount of free glucose ( 44 , 45 ). Dietary starch is a form of digestible carbohydrate primarily composed of alpha-1,4-glycosidic-linked glucose moieties, and its digestion is affected by the expression of AMY1 ( 46 , 47 ). Salivary amylase is expressed in the major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, and sublingual) in the oral cavity and increases following ingestion of food to aid in starch degradation ( 48 , 49 ). Mechanical disruption of the food matrix is necessary for increasing enzymatic access, with a reduction in mastication decreasing carbohydrate digestion and absorption ( 46 ). Salivary amylase activity initiated in the oral cavity remains significant past gastric digestion, into the lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract within the food bolus ( Figure 1 ) ( 50 , 51 ). Spatiotemporal expression and activity of amylase throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Salivary amylase is secreted in the oral cavity to begin starch degradation during the oral and esophageal phase. During the gastric phase, the stomach’s acidic pH is buffered by the food bolus, maintaining partial enzymatic activity of salivary amylase throughout. Pancreatic amylase is secreted into the intestinal lumen following gastric emptying to complete starch breakdown to disaccharides with the remaining active salivary amylase. Created in BioRender . Poole, A. ( https://BioRender.com/16im9jj ) is licensed under CC BY 4.0. Pancreatic amylase, encoded by AMY2 , comprises 5–6% of the protein content in pancreatic secretions ( 52 ). It is synthesized by pancreatic acinar cells and secreted into the duodenal lumen through the pancreatic ductal system in response to a combination of vagal nervous signaling and regulatory hormonal peptide release from the small intestine ( 53 , 54 ). It represents the primary amylolytic enzyme during the intestinal phase of digestion. Like salivary amylase, pancreatic amylase is an alpha-amylase, which is specific to internal alpha-1,4-glucosidic bonds. Many animals have pancreatic amylase, but no salivary amylase. Humans have both pancreatic and salivary amylase, encoded by genes located adjacent to each other on chromosome 1. The human amylase locus, located on chromosome 1p21.1, contains the genes AMY1 and AMY2 ( Figure 2 ). The promoter region of AMY1 contains a gamma actin pseudogene disrupted by a retroviral-like element, which is sufficient to direct amylase expression to the parotid gland ( 49 , 55 ). AMY1 and AMY2 are gene copy number (CN) variants. Copy number variants (CNVs) are structural variations in the genome where segments of DNA are present in variable copy numbers between individuals ( 56 ). CNVs can encompass entire genes or regulatory regions, potentially altering gene dosage and affecting gene expression. CNVs are a major source of genetic diversity and can influence phenotypic traits, disease susceptibility, and evolutionary adaptation. Structure of the human AMY1 gene locus. The AMY1 and AMY2 genes are located adjacent to each other on human chromosome 1. AMY1 -specific primers target AMY1A, AMY1B, and AMY1C paralogs to estimate overall AMY1 copy number. The pancreatic amylase gene paralogs AMY2A and AMY2B are shown in yellow and purple, respectively. The nonfunctional pseudogene is depicted in gray. Arrows represent the directionality of the genes. The salivary amylase gene paralogs include AMY1A , AMY1B , and AMY1C . The salivary paralogs exhibit over 99.9% identity at the nucleotide level ( 57 ). Diploid AMY1 CN is typically reported as the sum of the copies of AMY1A , AMY1B , and AMY1C in both haplotypes and ranges from 2 to 20 copies ( 58 ). AMY2 , which encodes pancreatic amylase, is the ancestral copy of the gene from which AMY1 originated, and the paralogs include AMY2A and AMY2B . AMY2A CN ranges from 0 to 6 copies, and AMY2B CN ranges from 2 to 7 copies. There is also a pseudogene ( 58 ), referred to as AMYP1 or AMY2A , an incomplete copy of p AMY2A , which must be avoided when designing primers to quantify the intact copies of the amylase gene. The AMY2 gene paralogs have 94% sequence identity with each other, and the AMY1 gene paralogs are approximately 93% identical to the AMY2 gene paralogs. Not all humans have all AMY1 or AMY2 paralogs, and several groups have characterized the haplotypes of the amylase locus. The haplotypes have different combinations of the AMY1 and AMY2 paralogs, and some haplotypes include duplications of the paralogs. There are at least 30 documented haplotypes ( 59 ). Different populations around the world have different haplotype prevalences. Most people have an even-numbered diploid AMY1 CN because haplotypes tend to have an odd-numbered CN of AMY1 , and the sum of two odd numbers is an even number ( 57 , 60 ). In Europeans, AMY1 CN is correlated with AMY2A CN, so reported associations of AMY1 CN with phenotype in this population could be due to salivary or pancreatic amylase. AMY1 has greater CN variation than AMY2 ( 61 , 62 ). Nonallelic homologous recombination likely has produced AMY1 duplications and deletions, whereas nonrecurrent microhomology-mediated break-induced replication, which occurs less frequently, is responsible for AMY2 CN variation ( 59 ). From mouse to man, amylase gene duplications appear to have occurred as an adaptation to dietary starch intake. Increases in amylase CN arose independently throughout the mammalian lineage, i.e., mice, rats, dogs, pigs, and humans, as suggested by the presence of lineage-specific retrotransposons near amylase genes ( 63 ). The ancestral amylase gene in mammals was pancreatic, and duplications of the amylase gene are found in all species with salivary expression. Thus, duplication of the gene appears to have allowed for a change in genetic architecture, facilitating expression in a different tissue, the salivary glands. Mammals consuming greater amounts of starch in their diet, typically because of domestication by humans or access to human food, have higher amylase CN accompanied by salivary amylase expression. Haplotypes with higher AMY1 , AMY2A, and AMY2B CN are enriched in modern-day human populations with historically agricultural diets compared to populations that historically subsisted via fishing, hunting, and pastoral activities. Estimates have timed the original duplication as having occurred 800,000 to 200,000 years ago ( 59 , 64 ). Subsequently, haplotypes with amylase gene duplications were fixed during selective sweeps at different times during evolutionary history, coinciding with how easily people could access starch. For example, haplotypes with amylase duplications increased in frequency in Eurasians about 12,000 years ago with the development of agriculture in the Crescent Valley. Effects of salivary amylase gene copy number on metabolic health

Precision nutrition is the personalization of dietary recommendations based on characteristics such as genetics, the microbiome, lifestyle, environment, and baseline metabolic state. One potential basis for the development of guidelines is the characterization of gene-diet interactions. In this narrative review, we evaluate the published literature reporting associations between salivary amylase gene copy number and metabolic health. The salivary amylase enzyme facilitates starch digestion and is encoded by AMY1 , a gene copy number (CN) variant. Humans have 2–20 copies, and AMY1 CN has been associated with metabolic health conditions such as obesity and insulin resistance. Studies of these associations have conflicting findings. The objectives of this review are to assess the findings from studies testing associations between AMY1 CN and adiposity, glucose metabolism, and gut microbiome composition; to explore possible mechanisms underlying the effects on metabolic health; and to identify knowledge gaps requiring additional research. To identify relevant articles, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, and Centre for Agricultural and Biosciences International for articles focused on AMY1 CN and one or more of the following: body mass index, glucose metabolism, and the microbiome. Key findings are that AMY1 CN has a positive association with postprandial glucose response and that a high AMY1 CN is protective against insulin resistance. AMY1 CN alone does not appear to be an accurate predictor of adiposity, and the relationship is likely convoluted by habitual starch intake, genetic background, and lifestyle factors. Future studies are required to determine how AMY1 CN could be used as a biomarker or to inform precision nutrition protocols to achieve metabolic health outcomes.

Despite therapeutic advancements, the incidence of metabolic disorders, such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, has progressively increased in adults and is a major financial burden on healthcare systems. The prevalence of obesity has more than doubled since 1990, with more than 1 billion people experiencing obesity worldwide ( 1 ). In the U.S. alone, obesity incurs over 1.73 trillion dollars in cost annually, equating to almost 10% of GDP ( 2 ). The prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) has increased concurrently with the international diabetes federation estimating that 1 in 8 people will have diabetes by 2045, an increase of 46% ( 3 ). T2D costs the U.S. healthcare system $327 billion in 2017 ( 4 ). Although there are effective pharmaceutical treatments for T2D and obesity, including metformin and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), there are numerous benefits to preventing or reversing these conditions with lifestyle interventions, including dietary changes. Metformin is widely used and well-tolerated by most patients, but gastrointestinal issues are the most frequently reported side effects, affecting up to 21% of patients ( 5–7 ). In some patients, GLP-1 RAs cause gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), especially at higher doses ( 8–12 ). GLP-1 RAs are expensive and often not fully covered by insurance, creating significant access barriers, which is one reason why some eligible patients do not receive these drugs despite guideline recommendations ( 13–15 ). Some patients may turn to compounding pharmacies if commercial products are unaffordable or unavailable due to episodic shortages, which poses concerns about safety and quality ( 16–19 ). Additionally, the use of metformin or GLP-1 RAs to manage diabetes or weight should be thought of by patients as a life-long intervention, with cessation of GLP-1 RAs frequently causing patients to regain weight and metabolic markers to return to previous values ( 20 , 21 ). A portion of the weight lost using GLP-1 RAs is lean mass ( 22 ); GLP1-RAs are commonly associated with micronutrient deficiencies ( 23 ); and there is a limited amount of data regarding the effects of long-term use. Furthermore, no single medication can confer all the benefits of appropriate dietary modification for improving body composition, glucose metabolism, cardiovascular health, and cancer risk. Most patients with prediabetes or obesity prefer lifestyle interventions over medication, citing concerns about drug side effects and dependency ( 24–28 ). However, broad population-based guidelines regarding lifestyle and dietary modifications have had limited success, and personalized approaches, in which dietary recommendations are tailored to the person, are an area of active study. Precision nutrition aims to utilize individual attributes such as health- and diet-related genotypes and gut microbiome composition to tailor dietary advice. Genetic heritability partly accounts for the phenotypic variation in body mass index (40–70%) ( 29 , 30 ) and glucose metabolism (~30–40%) ( 31–33 ). Delineating the mechanisms underlying the interactions between host genotype and dietary intake to influence metabolic health would contribute to the development of precision nutrition protocols. A candidate enzyme involved in starch digestion and previously associated with BMI and glucose metabolism is encoded by the gene copy number variant AMY1 . Dozens of studies have tested associations between salivary amylase gene copy number and metabolic health parameters ( Tables 1 – 3 ; Supplementary Tables S2–S4 ). Amylase is an enzyme that helps mammals digest dietary starch. Salivary amylase is encoded by a gene copy number variant, AMY1 , which has an instructive evolutionary history. Carbohydrate intake influences body weight and blood glucose, so variations in amylase enzyme dosage could affect these outcomes. Variability in the ratio of digestible carbohydrates to dietary fiber that reaches the gut microbiome could further impact metabolic health through the activity of microbial metabolites. In this review, we summarize the physiology, genomic arrangement, and evolutionary history of amylase. Then we discuss reported associations between salivary amylase gene copy number and metabolic health, including studies reporting interactions with starch intake. title: Markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein leading to the diagnosis of high-grade endometrial carcinoma during hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance
abstract: Background Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is widely used for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in patients with chronic liver disease. AFP is rarely elevated in endometrial cancer but may be a useful marker of aggressive histologic variants. Case A 70-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis–associated cirrhosis undergoing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance developed a rapid rise in AFP from 5 ng/mL to greater than 13,000 ng/mL. Liver imaging revealed no evidence of HCC. Positron-emission tomography (PET) demonstrated focal uptake in the uterus. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging identified a deeply invasive endometrial mass. Hysteroscopic biopsy revealed high-grade endometrial carcinoma. The patient subsequently underwent total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) with pathology demonstrating a stage IB high-grade endometrial carcinoma with extensive somatic-type glandular yolk sac / fetal-type differentiation and minor carcinosarcoma component (<5%). Serum AFP steadily and rapidly decreased after surgery. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering extrahepatic sources of AFP elevation and demonstrates an unusual presentation of endometrial carcinoma detected during HCC surveillance.
body: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a glycoprotein produced by the yolk sac, liver, and gastrointestinal tract during embryonic development. In adults, AFP levels are typically low, and large elevations are most commonly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and germ cell tumors. AFP is frequently utilized in HCC surveillance for patients with chronic liver disease ( Hanif et al., 2022 ). Mild AFP elevations may occur in benign conditions such as active hepatitis or cirrhosis; however, markedly elevated levels are often suspicious for malignancy. Extrahepatic tumors such as ovarian, testicular, and gastric primaries may produce AFP. Most ovarian and testicular AFP-producing primaries are germ cell tumors, including yolk sac tumors, embryonal carcinoma, and immature teratomas. Sex cord stromal tumors, such as Sertoli Leydig cell tumors, can also secrete AFP, though this is a less common presentation ( Kaczmarek-Borowska et al., 2023 ). Gastric carcinomas producing AFP can be classified in morphologic subtypes, including hepatoid, yolk sac tumor-like, enteroblastic, and common adenocarcinoma type ( Matsumoto et al., 2025 ; Kinjo et al., 2012 ; Arora et al., 2018 ). AFP-producing uterine tumors are uncommon with reports in the literature describing endometrial carcinomas with hepatoid and yolk sac differentiation ( Otani et al., 2021 ; Otani et al., 2022 ; Takeuchi et al., 2006 ; Li et al., 2026 ). We report a case in which marked AFP elevation during routine HCC surveillance ultimately led to the diagnosis of an unusual high-grade endometrial adenocarcinoma with extensive somatic-type glandular yolk sac / fetal-type differentiation in the absence of overt hepatoid differentiation. A 70-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis and metabolic dysfunction associated steatohepatitis (MASH) complicated by cirrhosis and portal hypertension was followed with routine HCC surveillance. Her medical history was also notable for systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's syndrome, autoimmune nephritis, and prior stage cT2N0 squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal treated with chemoradiation in 2021. Family history was notable for maternal grandmother with unknown abdominal cancer. She did not have additional risk factors for endometrial cancer, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, or nulliparity. Her liver disease was medically managed with mycophenolate mofetil with stable hepatic function. Serial elastography demonstrated gradual improvement in hepatic fibrosis, most recently consistent with stage F2 fibrosis in 2025. Between 2019 and 2024, serum AFP levels ranged from 3.0 to 5.4 ng/mL. In September 2025, her AFP increased dramatically to 70 ng/mL. She was asymptomatic with no abdominal or pelvic pain or fullness, postmenopausal bleeding, or vaginal discharge ( Boeckstaens et al., 2020 ). Her screening liver ultrasound did not show any focal liver lesions. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis performed in October 2025 demonstrated cirrhotic liver morphology with a stable, previously known hemangioma and no evidence of new focal liver lesions; the scan was also notable for a fibroid uterus without signs of metastasis or malignancy in the abdomen and pelvis. Repeat laboratory testing demonstrated a rapid increase in AFP to 2411 ng/mL in December 2025 ( Fig. 1 ). Follow up multiphasic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the liver redemonstrated morphologic changes of chronic liver disease without any focal lesion suspicious for hepatocellular carcinoma. Fig. 1 AFP trend over time Scatterplot with AFP trend over time demonstrating dramatic decrease after hysterectomy. Fig. 1 AFP trend over time Scatterplot with AFP trend over time demonstrating dramatic decrease after hysterectomy. Due to the rapid increase in AFP despite negative hepatic imaging, fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography–computed tomography (FDG PET-CT) was performed in December 2025. PET-CT demonstrated no evidence of hepatic malignancy or distant metastases but revealed a posterior uterine body lesion with moderate FDG uptake (SUVmax 3.9) ( Fig. 2 A-B). The etiology of the lesion was indeterminate with differential considerations including a degenerating fibroid versus uterine malignancy. Fig. 2 PET/CT scan and MRI of the pelvis (A) Axial CT and (B) axial fused PET-CT images at the same level in the pelvis demonstrate a focal enhancing uterine mass with marked FDG uptake. (C) Sagittal T2-weighted image demonstrates a 2.6 × 2.3 cm fundal endometrial mass with intermediate T2 signal. (D) Axial post-contrast T1-weighted image demonstrates a hypoenhancing endometrial mass with >50% myometrial invasion. (E) Axial diffusion-weighted imaging shows diffusion restriction within the mass, suspicious for malignancy. (F) Sagittal pre-contrast T1-weighted image shows T1-hyperintense blood products filling the endometrial cavity. Fig. 2 PET/CT scan and MRI of the pelvis (A) Axial CT and (B) axial fused PET-CT images at the same level in the pelvis demonstrate a focal enhancing uterine mass with marked FDG uptake. (C) Sagittal T2-weighted image demonstrates a 2.6 × 2.3 cm fundal endometrial mass with intermediate T2 signal. (D) Axial post-contrast T1-weighted image demonstrates a hypoenhancing endometrial mass with >50% myometrial invasion. (E) Axial diffusion-weighted imaging shows diffusion restriction within the mass, suspicious for malignancy. (F) Sagittal pre-contrast T1-weighted image shows T1-hyperintense blood products filling the endometrial cavity. During Liver Tumor Board review of her imaging, the enhancing lesion in the posterior uterus was noted to be increasing in size, and a pelvic MRI was recommended. At the area of FDG uptake on prior PET-CT, pelvic MRI demonstrated a focal hypoenhancing endometrial mass with deep myometrial invasion, suspicious for endometrial neoplasm. No pelvic lymphadenopathy or extrauterine disease was identified ( Fig. 2 C-F). At this time, she was referred to gynecologic oncology. Additional tumor markers including CA-125, CA 19–9, and carcinoembryonic antigen were obtained with respective values of 16 U/mL, 11 U/mL, and 1.4 ng/mL; these were all within normal limits. Hysteroscopy in February 2026 revealed an atrophic endometrial cavity with a small polypoid lesion in the lower uterine segment. Histopathologic evaluation of the polypoid lesion was consistent with grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium. Subsequently, the patient underwent total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO), sentinel lymph node biopsy, and omental biopsy. Intraoperative evaluation revealed no evidence of metastatic disease. In February 2026, the day prior to surgery, her AFP was notably elevated to 13,022 ng/mL. Because the half-life of AFP is 5 days, serum AFP was drawn weekly to monitor for appropriate decrease in AFP after TAH-BSO ( Adigun et al., 2026 ). One week post-operatively, it declined to 4596 ng/mL, and it continued to downtrend in the weeks following ( Fig. 1 ). Final pathologic examination demonstrated high-grade endometrial adenocarcinoma, extending deep into the myometrium, with less than 1 mm distance from the uterine serosa. While extensive lymphovascular invasion was seen, no disease outside the uterus was identified (FIGO 2009 Stage IB / FIGO 2023 Stage IIC). The carcinoma was composed of solid and glandular architecture with extensive cytoplasmic clearing ( Fig. 3 A). The tumor cells exhibited high grade nuclear features with primitive appearance and brisk mitotic activity ( Fig. 3 B-C), resembling fetal-type endodermal glands. Focal areas of the tumor showed highly atypical stromal cells, associated with extracellular globules, which were consistent with a minor component of homologous sarcomatous transformation (<5%) ( Fig. 3 D). Immunohistochemistry was positive for SALL4, glypican3, and AFP ( Fig. 3 E-F), supporting the somatic-type glandular yolk sac / fetal-type differentiation. When AFP elevation cannot be explained by hepatic pathology, clinicians should consider extrahepatic malignancies and pursue comprehensive diagnostic testing. Markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein leading to the diagnosis of high-grade endometrial carcinoma during hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance

Background Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is widely used for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in patients with chronic liver disease. AFP is rarely elevated in endometrial cancer but may be a useful marker of aggressive histologic variants. Case A 70-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis–associated cirrhosis undergoing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance developed a rapid rise in AFP from 5 ng/mL to greater than 13,000 ng/mL. Liver imaging revealed no evidence of HCC. Positron-emission tomography (PET) demonstrated focal uptake in the uterus. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging identified a deeply invasive endometrial mass. Hysteroscopic biopsy revealed high-grade endometrial carcinoma. The patient subsequently underwent total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) with pathology demonstrating a stage IB high-grade endometrial carcinoma with extensive somatic-type glandular yolk sac / fetal-type differentiation and minor carcinosarcoma component (<5%). Serum AFP steadily and rapidly decreased after surgery. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering extrahepatic sources of AFP elevation and demonstrates an unusual presentation of endometrial carcinoma detected during HCC surveillance.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a glycoprotein produced by the yolk sac, liver, and gastrointestinal tract during embryonic development. In adults, AFP levels are typically low, and large elevations are most commonly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and germ cell tumors. Extrahepatic tumors such as ovarian, testicular, and gastric primaries may produce AFP. Most ovarian and testicular AFP-producing primaries are germ cell tumors, including yolk sac tumors, embryonal carcinoma, and immature teratomas. Sex cord stromal tumors, such as Sertoli Leydig cell tumors, can also secrete AFP, though this is a less common presentation ( Kaczmarek-Borowska et al., 2023 ). Gastric carcinomas producing AFP can be classified in morphologic subtypes, including hepatoid, yolk sac tumor-like, enteroblastic, and common adenocarcinoma type ( Matsumoto et al., 2025 ; Kinjo et al., 2012 ; Arora et al., 2018 ). AFP-producing uterine tumors are uncommon with reports in the literature describing endometrial carcinomas with hepatoid and yolk sac differentiation ( Otani et al., 2021 ; Otani et al., 2022 ; Takeuchi et al., 2006 ; Li et al., 2026 ). We report a case in which marked AFP elevation during routine HCC surveillance ultimately led to the diagnosis of an unusual high-grade endometrial adenocarcinoma with extensive somatic-type glandular yolk sac / fetal-type differentiation in the absence of overt hepatoid differentiation. A 70-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis and metabolic dysfunction associated steatohepatitis (MASH) complicated by cirrhosis and portal hypertension was followed with routine HCC surveillance. She was asymptomatic with no abdominal or pelvic pain or fullness, postmenopausal bleeding, or vaginal discharge ( Boeckstaens et al., 2020 ). title: Innovative Hydrogels: A Novel Approach to Tackle Obesity and Its Associated Health Risks
abstract: Obesity, considered a chronic and multifactorial disease, is one of the most urgent public health challenges, affecting about 13% of the global population. It is strongly associated with comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and certain types of cancer. Conventional management strategies, including lifestyle interventions, pharmacotherapy, and bariatric surgery, often provide limited or short-term benefits that encompass adverse effects or poor adherence depending on the patients’ response. Hence, there is a need for innovative and minimally invasive treatments. In this context, hydrogels have emerged as promising and versatile platforms. Hydrogels are biocompatible three-dimensional polymeric networks that absorb and retain large amounts of water inside their structure. They can be engineered as stimuli-responsive materials in response to environmental changes, including pH, temperature, and enzymes. These capabilities position hydrogels as malleable tools applicable across several obesity-related fields, ranging from controlled drug delivery and gastric volume modulation to the development of nontoxic ingestible systems. Recent advances highlight superabsorbent hydrogels that expand in the stomach to induce satiety; targeted hydrogels that deliver antiobesogenic compounds; and smart hydrogels that integrate nanomaterials to enhance mechanical strength and functionality. This review summarizes the classification of hydrogels, fabrication processes, and principal characteristics required in the biomedical field. The current evidence for hydrogel development as a basis for obesity management is analyzed, focusing on the main results from preclinical and clinical trials. Finally, hydrogels are highlighted as multifunctional and transformative platforms that offer new strategies to overcome the limitations and drawbacks of current obesity treatment therapies.
body: According to the World Health Organization, obesity is defined as an abnormal or excessive accumulation of body fat that poses a risk to health. Obesity represents one of the most serious global health and economic challenges today. Since 1975, the worldwide prevalence of obesity has increased nearly 3-fold, and it is now estimated that about 13% of the global population is affected. Its development is influenced by interactions among biopsychosocial factors, such as genetics, environment, physical inactivity, excessive caloric intake, and the gut microbiome. Obesity is directly linked to increased mortality and morbidity. , Common comorbidities include type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary heart disease, and sleep apnea, all of which represent a significant economic burden for patients and governments. Current treatment approaches include lifestyle changes, pharmacotherapy, medical devices, and bariatric surgery. Although lifestyle changes remain the foundation of obesity management, many individuals find it difficult to maintain long-term success due to adherence challenges and physiological adaptations. , , , In addition, antiobesity medications often show limited efficacy, and several have been withdrawn from the market due to serious adverse effects. Similarly, bariatric surgery, although effective, is a costly and invasive procedure with inherent risks. , , To overcome the limitations of current treatments, researchers have explored the usage of hydrogels. Hydrogels are highly biocompatible three-dimensional polymeric networks capable of retaining a significant fraction of water. These materials stand out for their highly tunable properties, including their swelling behavior and responsiveness to external stimuli. , As a result, hydrogels have been investigated for long-term gastric retention to support body weight control, improve metabolic outcomes, and act as versatile platforms for controlled drug delivery (CDD). The development of edible hydrogels that tolerate stomach acidity represents a promising approach for their oral administration. − Hydrogels have shown promise for obesity treatment through three key mechanisms: satiety induction (SI), CDD, and targeting metabolic pathways (TMP). In SI, these materials are administered orally and are engineered to expand in the stomach and small intestine. By activating gastrointestinal stretch receptors, they promote a feeling of fullness without contributing calories. , In CDD, these same materials function as carriers that encapsulate therapeutic compounds and gradually release them, shielding the drugs from degradation and allowing targeted delivery in response to stimuli such as pH or temperature. , Finally, to target metabolic pathways, hydrogels can stimulate ″fat browning″ to convert energy-storing white fat into energy-burning beige fat, or modulate the gut microbiota to promote beneficial bacteria. , , Hydrogels offer an alternative and multifunctional solution for obesity treatment, overcoming the limitations of current methods, or serving as an aid that enables faster weight loss. This study examines how these biocompatible materials can induce satiety by expanding in a controlled manner within the digestive tract, support CDD to enhance therapeutic effectiveness, and modulate key metabolic pathways to improve physiological responses. Overall, the work seeks to highlight a safer, less invasive, and more effective strategy for obesity treatment. Obesity has been redefined as a chronic and progressive disease, whose assessment goes beyond simple body weight. The most common way to measure it is by calculating the Body Mass Index (BMI), which is obtained by dividing weight by the square of height. Current strategies look beyond weight and instead focus on body composition and fat distribution, especially visceral fat accumulation around the abdomen. Methods such as waist circumference measurements, bioelectrical impedance analysis, and dual-energy X-ray absorption studies provide a clearer idea of how much body fat a person has and how it may affect their health. This comprehensive evaluation is essential because the risk of conditions such as diabetes and hypertension is influenced not only by body weight, but also by its distribution. Accordingly, the updated obesity classification introduces an important distinction between preclinical obesity and clinical obesity. Preclinical obesity is a high-risk condition where extra weight is present but has not yet caused damage to the organs. At this point, the focus is preventive through lifestyle changes. Clinical obesity is diagnosed once the excess weight has already led to problems in the body’s functions, manifesting as different health issues such as sleep apnea or high blood pressure. At this advanced stage, treatment is intensive and may require medical or surgical interventions. A person is considered eligible for bariatric surgery if they have a BMI of 40 or higher. If there is a major obesity-related condition such as uncontrolled diabetes or severe sleep apnea, it may also qualify with a BMI of 35 to 39.9. Individuals with a BMI between 30 and 34.9 who have poorly controlled type 2 diabetes may also qualify. Candidates need a documented history of unsuccessful nonsurgical weight loss efforts and demonstrate a willingness to adhere to lifelong postoperative changes. Altogether, this suggests that obesity is a progressive condition that demands ongoing and personalized management rather than a one-time intervention. Obesity is a multifactorial condition that develops from a long-term imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure. Its development results from a complex interplay between genetic predisposition and an obesogenic environment that encourages high caloric intake and low levels of physical activity. , The main risk factors are physical inactivity and excessive caloric intake. Other key contributors include psychosocial stress, insufficient sleep, and various early influences, such as the intrauterine and postnatal environment. , In a small fraction of cases, obesity has a monogenic origin, a unique genetic dysfunction that is inherited in a Mendelian fashion. These mutations affect key genes that regulate the central melanocortin pathway in the hypothalamus, which controls feeding behavior and induces satiety. Genes most frequently mutated in this pathway include leptin, its receptor, proopiomelanocortin, and the melanocortin 4 receptor. The core mechanism underlying obesity is a disruption in energy balance, in which the body physiologically maintains a higher body weight. This process is further intensified by biological influences such as psychosocial stress, which triggers the release of cortisol, a hormone that promotes fat accumulation, particularly in the visceral region. There are different types of adipose tissue (AT): white adipose tissue (WAT), the primary form of energy storage; brown adipose tissue (BAT), which oxidizes energy to generate heat (thermogenesis); and beige fat, which can emerge within WAT with thermogenic properties. The excessive and dysfunctional accumulation of WAT in the visceral region is key. WAT is metabolically more active and directly releases free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines into the portal circulation, contributing to serious metabolic complications. In addition, the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in these processes. The gut microbiota is the complex community of trillions of microorganisms (including bacteria, viruses, and fungi) residing in the gastrointestinal tract. It plays a fundamental role in obesity by influencing the “energy harvest” from food and regulating the host’s metabolism. Dysbiosis (bacterial imbalance), which can be further exacerbated by stress, increases this energy harvest from indigestible food, fermenting it into short-chain fatty acids that are absorbed and promote lipogenesis (fat production) in the liver. Moreover, the microbiota enhances the activity of enzymes that facilitate triglyceride uptake and storage in adipocytes. This excessive accumulation causes adipose tissue to hypertrophy and become dysfunctional, acting as an altered endocrine organ. This dysfunction triggers a state of low-grade systemic inflammation, which is the pathophysiological link connecting obesity with its most severe comorbidities, such as Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. , Disruptions in energy balance are closely tied to the function and adaptability of AT. Excess accumulation of WAT leads to hypertrophy, resulting in an altered endocrine organ. In contrast, BAT expresses Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1), which allows it to dissipate energy as heat. However, in obesity, BAT undergoes functional decline through a process known as whitening, characterized by mitochondrial depletion and a reduction of its thermogenic capacity. Consequently, a key area of therapeutic investigation is the browning of WAT, in which white fat depots convert into beige adipocytes that share the UCP1-expressing, multilocular characteristics of BAT, effectively tilting the energy balance toward expenditure (see Figure ). Progressive whitening of adipocytes and loss of thermogenic function. Schematic illustration of the transition from a thermogenically active brown adipocyte to a dysfunctional white adipocyte during obesity progression. (1) In the browning stage, adipocytes exhibit multilocular lipid structure, high mitochondrial density, and elevated UCP1 expression, supporting energy expenditure. (2) During early whitening, lipid droplets enlarge while mitochondrial content and UCP1 levels decrease, reflecting a shift toward oxidative metabolism. (3) In advanced whitening, thermogenic gene expression is further suppressed, accompanied by activation of adipogenic pathways and increased lipid storage capacity. (4) The fully whitened adipocyte displays an unilocular lipid droplet, minimal mitochondrial content, and negligible UCP1 expression, characteristics of an energy storage phenotype. The excessive accumulation of dysfunctional WAT drives the endocrine changes and inflammatory pathways that underlie metabolic disease. The hypertrophied AT releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, initiating a state of low-grade systemic inflammation. Additionally, the central control of energy balance is disrupted, with the hypothalamic system losing sensitivity to key hormonal regulators such as leptin, ghrelin, and insulin, , leading to continued hyperphagia. The role of hormonal contraceptives (HCs) introduces an additional patient-specific metabolic factor. While combined oral contraceptives (OCs) are not consistently associated with weight gain, some progestin-only formulations may contribute to increased adiposity. Moreover, HCs can alter glucose and lipid metabolism and increase insulin resistance, particularly in obese individuals. The elevated risk of venous thromboembolism in this population further complicates treatment strategies. Although not a primary focus, these factors highlight the need for nonsystemic and safer therapeutic alternatives, such as hydrogel-based interventions, which can minimize systemic exposure while targeting local or gastrointestinal mechanisms. Obesity management involves a spectrum of therapeutic strategies that differ in mechanism, efficacy, safety, and accessibility. As outlined in Table , lifestyle interventions remain the foundation of treatment and provide important metabolic benefits. However, their long-term success is frequently limited by poor adherence and compensatory physiological mechanisms that favor weight regain. , BMI: Body Mass Index; GLP-1s: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists; PHEN/TPM: Phentermine/Topiramate; USD: United States Dollar. Pharmacological therapies, particularly Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, have established a new benchmark for nonsurgical weight loss, achieving clinically meaningful reductions in body weight and improvements in metabolic parameters. Despite their efficacy, these agents are associated with gastrointestinal side effects (e.g., nausea, vomiting), potential cardiovascular considerations, and high long-term costs, which may limit adherence and accessibility. , Importantly, their mechanism of action is systemic, targeting appetite regulation and metabolic signaling pathways without directly addressing the physical properties of gastric filling or caloric dilution in the gastrointestinal tract. At the other end of the spectrum, bariatric surgery provides the most substantial and sustained weight loss, along with significant resolution of comorbidities. However, its invasive nature, perioperative risks, and high cost restrict its use to patients with severe obesity, limiting its applicability as a population-wide solution. , In this therapeutic landscape, hydrogel-based approaches offer a mechanistically distinct and complementary strategy. Unlike pharmacological treatments that rely on systemic biochemical modulation or surgical interventions that induce irreversible anatomical changes, hydrogels act primarily through local, nonsystemic mechanisms, such as gastric volume expansion, delayed gastric emptying, or targeted delivery within the gastrointestinal tract. This enables satiety induction through mechanical signaling, potentially reducing caloric intake with a favorable safety profile. , Clinically, hydrogel-based systems demonstrate moderate but meaningful weight loss, generally lower than that achieved by GLP-1 receptor agonists but accompanied by improved tolerability, reduced systemic exposure, and fewer severe adverse effects. These characteristics position hydrogels as particularly suitable for early stage intervention, useful for patients with contraindications to pharmacotherapy, or as adjunct therapies that may enhance existing treatment regimens. , Nevertheless, their current limitations include lower efficacy compared to advanced pharmacological agents, dependence on patient adherence (e.g., capsule intake with water), and variability in response to gastrointestinal physiology. Therefore, rather than replacing established treatments, hydrogels are better understood as bridging technologies that fill the gap between lifestyle interventions and more intensive approaches. Overall, the limitations of current therapies (adherence challenges, systemic side effects, high costs, and invasiveness) underscore the need for safe, accessible, and scalable alternatives. Innovative Hydrogels: A Novel Approach to Tackle Obesity and Its Associated Health Risks

Obesity, considered a chronic and multifactorial disease, is one of the most urgent public health challenges, affecting about 13% of the global population. It is strongly associated with comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and certain types of cancer. Conventional management strategies, including lifestyle interventions, pharmacotherapy, and bariatric surgery, often provide limited or short-term benefits that encompass adverse effects or poor adherence depending on the patients’ response. Hence, there is a need for innovative and minimally invasive treatments. In this context, hydrogels have emerged as promising and versatile platforms. Hydrogels are biocompatible three-dimensional polymeric networks that absorb and retain large amounts of water inside their structure. They can be engineered as stimuli-responsive materials in response to environmental changes, including pH, temperature, and enzymes. These capabilities position hydrogels as malleable tools applicable across several obesity-related fields, ranging from controlled drug delivery and gastric volume modulation to the development of nontoxic ingestible systems. Recent advances highlight superabsorbent hydrogels that expand in the stomach to induce satiety; targeted hydrogels that deliver antiobesogenic compounds; and smart hydrogels that integrate nanomaterials to enhance mechanical strength and functionality. This review summarizes the classification of hydrogels, fabrication processes, and principal characteristics required in the biomedical field. The current evidence for hydrogel development as a basis for obesity management is analyzed, focusing on the main results from preclinical and clinical trials. Finally, hydrogels are highlighted as multifunctional and transformative platforms that offer new strategies to overcome the limitations and drawbacks of current obesity treatment therapies.

According to the World Health Organization, obesity is defined as an abnormal or excessive accumulation of body fat that poses a risk to health. Obesity represents one of the most serious global health and economic challenges today. Since 1975, the worldwide prevalence of obesity has increased nearly 3-fold, and it is now estimated that about 13% of the global population is affected. Its development is influenced by interactions among biopsychosocial factors, such as genetics, environment, physical inactivity, excessive caloric intake, and the gut microbiome. Obesity is directly linked to increased mortality and morbidity. , Common comorbidities include type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary heart disease, and sleep apnea, all of which represent a significant economic burden for patients and governments. Current treatment approaches include lifestyle changes, pharmacotherapy, medical devices, and bariatric surgery. Although lifestyle changes remain the foundation of obesity management, many individuals find it difficult to maintain long-term success due to adherence challenges and physiological adaptations. , , , In addition, antiobesity medications often show limited efficacy, and several have been withdrawn from the market due to serious adverse effects. Similarly, bariatric surgery, although effective, is a costly and invasive procedure with inherent risks. , , To overcome the limitations of current treatments, researchers have explored the usage of hydrogels. Hydrogels are highly biocompatible three-dimensional polymeric networks capable of retaining a significant fraction of water. These materials stand out for their highly tunable properties, including their swelling behavior and responsiveness to external stimuli. , As a result, hydrogels have been investigated for long-term gastric retention to support body weight control, improve metabolic outcomes, and act as versatile platforms for controlled drug delivery (CDD). The development of edible hydrogels that tolerate stomach acidity represents a promising approach for their oral administration. − Hydrogels have shown promise for obesity treatment through three key mechanisms: satiety induction (SI), CDD, and targeting metabolic pathways (TMP). In SI, these materials are administered orally and are engineered to expand in the stomach and small intestine. By activating gastrointestinal stretch receptors, they promote a feeling of fullness without contributing calories. , In CDD, these same materials function as carriers that encapsulate therapeutic compounds and gradually release them, shielding the drugs from degradation and allowing targeted delivery in response to stimuli such as pH or temperature. , Finally, to target metabolic pathways, hydrogels can stimulate ″fat browning″ to convert energy-storing white fat into energy-burning beige fat, or modulate the gut microbiota to promote beneficial bacteria. , , Hydrogels offer an alternative and multifunctional solution for obesity treatment, overcoming the limitations of current methods, or serving as an aid that enables faster weight loss. This study examines how these biocompatible materials can induce satiety by expanding in a controlled manner within the digestive tract, support CDD to enhance therapeutic effectiveness, and modulate key metabolic pathways to improve physiological responses. Overall, the work seeks to highlight a safer, less invasive, and more effective strategy for obesity treatment. Obesity has been redefined as a chronic and progressive disease, whose assessment goes beyond simple body weight. The most common way to measure it is by calculating the Body Mass Index (BMI), which is obtained by dividing weight by the square of height. Current strategies look beyond weight and instead focus on body composition and fat distribution, especially visceral fat accumulation around the abdomen. Methods such as waist circumference measurements, bioelectrical impedance analysis, and dual-energy X-ray absorption studies provide a clearer idea of how much body fat a person has and how it may affect their health. This comprehensive evaluation is essential because the risk of conditions such as diabetes and hypertension is influenced not only by body weight, but also by its distribution. Accordingly, the updated obesity classification introduces an important distinction between preclinical obesity and clinical obesity. Preclinical obesity is a high-risk condition where extra weight is present but has not yet caused damage to the organs. At this point, the focus is preventive through lifestyle changes. Clinical obesity is diagnosed once the excess weight has already led to problems in the body’s functions, manifesting as different health issues such as sleep apnea or high blood pressure. At this advanced stage, treatment is intensive and may require medical or surgical interventions. A person is considered eligible for bariatric surgery if they have a BMI of 40 or higher. If there is a major obesity-related condition such as uncontrolled diabetes or severe sleep apnea, it may also qualify with a BMI of 35 to 39.9. Individuals with a BMI between 30 and 34.9 who have poorly controlled type 2 diabetes may also qualify. Candidates need a documented history of unsuccessful nonsurgical weight loss efforts and demonstrate a willingness to adhere to lifelong postoperative changes. Altogether, this suggests that obesity is a progressive condition that demands ongoing and personalized management rather than a one-time intervention. Obesity is a multifactorial condition that develops from a long-term imbalance between energy intake and energy expenditure. Its development results from a complex interplay between genetic predisposition and an obesogenic environment that encourages high caloric intake and low levels of physical activity. , The main risk factors are physical inactivity and excessive caloric intake. Other key contributors include psychosocial stress, insufficient sleep, and various early influences, such as the intrauterine and postnatal environment. , In a small fraction of cases, obesity has a monogenic origin, a unique genetic dysfunction that is inherited in a Mendelian fashion. These mutations affect key genes that regulate the central melanocortin pathway in the hypothalamus, which controls feeding behavior and induces satiety. Genes most frequently mutated in this pathway include leptin, its receptor, proopiomelanocortin, and the melanocortin 4 receptor. The core mechanism underlying obesity is a disruption in energy balance, in which the body physiologically maintains a higher body weight. This process is further intensified by biological influences such as psychosocial stress, which triggers the release of cortisol, a hormone that promotes fat accumulation, particularly in the visceral region. There are different types of adipose tissue (AT): white adipose tissue (WAT), the primary form of energy storage; brown adipose tissue (BAT), which oxidizes energy to generate heat (thermogenesis); and beige fat, which can emerge within WAT with thermogenic properties. The excessive and dysfunctional accumulation of WAT in the visceral region is key. WAT is metabolically more active and directly releases free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines into the portal circulation, contributing to serious metabolic complications. In addition, the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in these processes. The gut microbiota is the complex community of trillions of microorganisms (including bacteria, viruses, and fungi) residing in the gastrointestinal tract. It plays a fundamental role in obesity by influencing the “energy harvest” from food and regulating the host’s metabolism. Dysbiosis (bacterial imbalance), which can be further exacerbated by stress, increases this energy harvest from indigestible food, fermenting it into short-chain fatty acids that are absorbed and promote lipogenesis (fat production) in the liver. Moreover, the microbiota enhances the activity of enzymes that facilitate triglyceride uptake and storage in adipocytes. This excessive accumulation causes adipose tissue to hypertrophy and become dysfunctional, acting as an altered endocrine organ. This dysfunction triggers a state of low-grade systemic inflammation, which is the pathophysiological link connecting obesity with its most severe comorbidities, such as Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. , Disruptions in energy balance are closely tied to the function and adaptability of AT. Excess accumulation of WAT leads to hypertrophy, resulting in an altered endocrine organ. In contrast, BAT expresses Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1), which allows it to dissipate energy as heat. However, in obesity, BAT undergoes functional decline through a process known as whitening, characterized by mitochondrial depletion and a reduction of its thermogenic capacity. Consequently, a key area of therapeutic investigation is the browning of WAT, in which white fat depots convert into beige adipocytes that share the UCP1-expressing, multilocular characteristics of BAT, effectively tilting the energy balance toward expenditure (see Figure ). (1) In the browning stage, adipocytes exhibit multilocular lipid structure, high mitochondrial density, and elevated UCP1 expression, supporting energy expenditure. (2) During early whitening, lipid droplets enlarge while mitochondrial content and UCP1 levels decrease, reflecting a shift toward oxidative metabolism. (3) In advanced whitening, thermogenic gene expression is further suppressed, accompanied by activation of adipogenic pathways and increased lipid storage capacity. (4) The fully whitened adipocyte displays an unilocular lipid droplet, minimal mitochondrial content, and negligible UCP1 expression, characteristics of an energy storage phenotype. The excessive accumulation of dysfunctional WAT drives the endocrine changes and inflammatory pathways that underlie metabolic disease. The hypertrophied AT releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, initiating a state of low-grade systemic inflammation. Additionally, the central control of energy balance is disrupted, with the hypothalamic system losing sensitivity to key hormonal regulators such as leptin, ghrelin, and insulin, , leading to continued hyperphagia. The role of hormonal contraceptives (HCs) introduces an additional patient-specific metabolic factor. While combined oral contraceptives (OCs) are not consistently associated with weight gain, some progestin-only formulations may contribute to increased adiposity. Moreover, HCs can alter glucose and lipid metabolism and increase insulin resistance, particularly in obese individuals. The elevated risk of venous thromboembolism in this population further complicates treatment strategies. Although not a primary focus, these factors highlight the need for nonsystemic and safer therapeutic alternatives, such as hydrogel-based interventions, which can minimize systemic exposure while targeting local or gastrointestinal mechanisms. Pharmacological therapies, particularly Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, have established a new benchmark for nonsurgical weight loss, achieving clinically meaningful reductions in body weight and improvements in metabolic parameters. At the other end of the spectrum, bariatric surgery provides the most substantial and sustained weight loss, along with significant resolution of comorbidities. title: Primary care physician characteristics and potentially inappropriate medications in older adults
abstract: Abstract Background Potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) are a growing public health concern. While research in North America suggests physician characteristics were associated with PIM prescription, their generalizability to other countries remains understudied. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study using a nationwide electronic health record database of primary care clinics in Japan. We analyzed patients aged ≥75 years who visited solo-practice physicians at least quarterly during October 2022 to September 2023. Multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for patient characteristics, was used to examine the association between physician characteristics and PIM prescriptions, defined as at least one medication listed in the Screening Tool for Older Person's Appropriate Prescriptions for Japanese for ≥28 days. Results Among 184 097 patients treated by 1532 physicians, 70 319 (38.2%) received at least one PIM. Approximately two-thirds of PIM prescriptions were concentrated among 20% of the physicians. Younger physicians (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.27; 95% CI, 1.05-1.55), physicians with lower volumes of older patients (aOR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.19-1.61), and physicians in eastern or central Japan were more likely to prescribe PIMs. Conclusions PIM prescriptions were common and concentrated among a subset of physicians, particularly younger and less experienced physicians. Targeted interventions among high prescribers may reduce PIM efficiently.
body: Ensuring medication safety and reducing adverse drug events are critical challenges for older adults in primary care. Prescribing potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs), defined as medications that carry a higher risk of adverse events than benefits for older patients, 1 is a major contributor to such events. 2 Studies have shown that PIMs are frequently prescribed in primary care settings 3 and are associated with increased risk of unfavorable outcomes in older patients, including injuries from falls, 4 hospitalization, 5 death, and increased healthcare costs. 3 A recent meta-analysis found a significant association between PIM prescription and cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality. 6 7 Studies have assessed multifaceted factors related to PIM prescriptions, including patient factors, physician factors, and social and contextual factors. Regarding physician factors, several studies found that physicians who were male, older, practiced alone, and board-certified in internal medicine were more likely to prescribe PIMs. 8 , 9 However, these studies are limited to a small number of patients or a specific region, and comprehensive nationwide data examining this association remains scarce, except for one study conducted using Medicare Part D data in the United States. 9 , 10 Consequently, it remains unclear whether these observed associations reflect physician-level practice patterns that generalize across different healthcare systems or are shaped by country-specific payment structures and policy environments. This underscores the need for large-scale studies in diverse policy contexts to identify physician factors associated with high rates of PIM prescribing, which may inform effective and generalizable interventions to improve medication safety in older adults. 11 Japan provides a unique and informative context regarding PIM prescribers. Similar to the United States, reducing PIM prescriptions is a critical public health issue in Japan, particularly as population aging is more advanced than in most high-income countries. In 2015, the Japan Geriatric Society introduced a clinical practice guideline listing PIMs for older adults (Screening Tool for Older Person's Appropriate Prescriptions for Japanese [STOPP-J]), corresponding to the Beers criteria in the US and the STOPP in Europe. 12 However, while recent evidence in Japan suggests that their use continues to increase, 13 , 14 the association between physician characteristics and PIM prescribing remains understudied. The Japanese healthcare system is characterized by universal health coverage—which covers outpatient care, prescription drugs, and hospitalization costs under a government-regulated fee schedule—and fee-for-service payment in outpatient settings. From physicians' perspective, this universal coverage and fee-for-service system is similar in structure to the traditional Medicare fee schedule and fee-for-service payment for outpatient care in the United States. As Japan is an advanced aging country, generalists and non-geriatric specialists frequently manage older patients with complex conditions in outpatient settings. 15 16 Examining prescriber-level factors associated with PIM prescription in Japan may have important implications beyond a single national context. Many challenges faced by Japan, such as rapid population aging, increasing care complexity, and shortages of geriatric specialists, are increasingly relevant to other high-income countries, including the United States. Therefore, identifying physician characteristics associated with PIM prescribing in Japan may offer insights that may be transferable to other aging healthcare systems and be useful for future strategies to reduce PIM prescriptions. In this context, using a sample of older patients in the nationwide electronic health record (EHR) database linked with claims data in primary care clinics in Japan, we aimed to investigate the association between primary care physicians' characteristics and PIM prescribing. Building on prior literature on healthcare overuse, we hypothesized that PIM prescribing is concentrated among a small number of physicians and associated with physician characteristics, such as age, sex, and board certification. 17 Japan's universal healthcare system is characterized by predominantly privately operated medical institutions, with funding from a mix of social health insurance and patient cost-sharing. By law, all residents must be enrolled in a public health insurance program, which provides uniform coverage, including standardized co-insurance rates (ranging from 10% to 30% depending on age), a cap on out-of-pocket expenses through a catastrophic coverage scheme, and unrestricted access to any medical institution. This open-access model resembles the US Preferred Provider Organization system, though some tertiary hospitals may impose an additional fee for initial visits without a referral. Insurance benefits and fee schedules are regulated by the Japanese government and are consistent across plans. They generally cover all medical services, excluding preventive care—which is funded through general taxation—and long-term care, which is financed by a separate long-term care insurance system. While most inpatient services provided by large acute care hospitals are paid using a per diem bundled payment system called the Diagnosis Procedure Combination (a Japanese adaptation of the US diagnosis-related group model), outpatient care is primarily reimbursed on a fee-for-service model. While these features ensure broad access to healthcare, they also create incentives for providers to increase the number of outpatient visits while shortening the consultation time per patient. This feature, combined with the fact that many PIMs are covered by public insurance without systematic quality or safety monitoring, poses a risk for increasing PIM prescribing in Japan. This cross-sectional study analyzed the Japan Medical Data Survey (JAMDAS) database collected by M3 Inc., a nationwide outpatient EHR database (including data from claims) of primarily primary care clinics in Japan. The JAMDAS database comprises all outpatient visits covered by Japan's public medical insurance system, which includes office, home, nursing home, and telehealth visits. The database recorded approximately 40 million patient visits from October 1, 2022, through September 30, 2023 (hereafter, the study period), accounting for 4% of all primary care visits in Japan. 18 Compared to the government-conducted survey of all physicians, physicians in the JAMDAS were slightly younger and more likely to be female, but the distributions of the practice regions were similar ( 17 Table S1 ). The sex distribution among the patients registered in the JAMDAS is similar to national estimates from the Patient Survey, but they tend to be slightly younger. 17 17 This manuscript follows the STROBE reporting guidelines for observational studies. We analyzed patients aged 75 years or older who visited the primary care clinics regularly, defined as at least one visit every 3 months during the study period. This restriction reflected 2 considerations. First, since STOPP-J defines PIMs based on long-term prescriptions, capturing PIM prescribing patterns accurately requires focusing on patients whose prescriptions reflect ongoing rather than sporadic care; physicians would be unlikely to prescribe long-term medications to patients who visited sporadically. Second, prescription lengths in Japan are capped at 90 days by law, meaning that even clinically stable patients typically need to visit at least once every 3 months to have their prescriptions renewed. To focus on clinics engaged in primary care of older adults, we included patients who visited clinics with more than 100 total patients and with more than 20 patients aged 75 years or older during the study period. This process led to the exclusion of 0.004% of patients. To accurately attribute medical practice to individual physicians, we further restricted our analysis to solo-practice clinics, excluding patients who visited group-practice clinics. The database contains clinic identifiers and information about the clinics where physicians practice. While it enables identification of individual physicians in solo-practice clinics—which account for approximately 50% of all medical institutions in Japan 9 —it does not allow us to determine which physician provided specific healthcare services in group-practice clinics. This process led to the exclusion of 47.1% of the remaining patients. Finally, we excluded patients who visited primary care clinics whose owner physicians' age or the number of working physicians was missing. This process led to the exclusion of 1.9% of the remaining patients. 17 The deprescribing conceptual framework suggests that prescribing behaviors are shaped by both rational factors (prescribers' knowledge, beliefs, and skills) and non-rational factors (heuristics and biases). Guided by this framework and previous findings, 19 we selected physician characteristics reflecting these mechanisms: sex, age, board certification, volume of older patients, and practice regions. 11 , 20 Age was categorized as <45, 45-59, and ≥60 years. Board certification was categorized as internal medicine, non-internal medicine, and non-board-certified ( Method 1 ). It should be noted that geriatricians were categorized under internal medicine due to their extremely small number in Japan. Furthermore, in Japan, many primary care physicians completed specialist training in hospitals before transitioning to primary care, and physicians can establish primary care clinics regardless of their specialty and even if they do not have any board certification. Volume of older patients was categorized as “low,” “medium,” and “high” according to the physician-level tertiles of annual number of patients aged 75 years or older seen by each physician. Regions were categorized as western, central, and eastern Japan. 21 The primary outcome was whether the patient was prescribed PIMs for 28 days or more during the study period. PIMs were defined using the STOPP-J criteria, a Japanese adaptation of the STOPP criteria 12 developed by the Japan Geriatrics Society in 2015. STOPP-J identifies medication as potentially inappropriate when prescribed continuously for one month or longer, reflecting its focus on chronic, long-term prescribing. In accordance with a previous study, 14 we applied these criteria at the drug level and did not incorporate patient diagnoses, concomitant medications, or drug–drug interactions since the purpose of STOPP-J is to screen medications that are potentially rather than definitively inappropriate. Our data did not include information on prescription fills; thus, our analysis focused primarily on physicians' intention to treat as determined by prescriptions ordered, regardless of whether they were filled. PIMs were defined based on oral medications listed in STOPP-J. Previous research has shown that the use of PIMs defined by the STOPP-J criteria is associated with increased risks of hospitalizations and mortality among older adults, 8 , 22 supporting the clinical relevance of PIM prescription as an indicator of prescribing quality. These PIMs consisted of 187 individual oral drugs. The drugs were organized in a hierarchical structure: first classified into 29 drug classes, and then further grouped into 17 broader drug categories ( 23 Table S2 ). The drug classes were determined according to chemical or pharmacological subgroup, corresponding to the third and fourth levels of the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system (eg, benzodiazepines or nonbenzodiazepines). The drug categories were primarily determined according to therapeutic subgroups, corresponding to the second level of the ATC classification system (eg, hypnotics, antithrombotic agents, or laxatives). We adjusted for the characteristics of patients, including age (75-80, 80-84, 85-89, and ≥ 90 years old), sex, and indicators of comorbidities potentially associated with PIM prescription (determined using the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems 10 recorded at least once during the study period). Comorbidities that are potentially associated with PIM prescription were selected according to previous literature (see details in th Revision Method 2 ). 22 , 24 First, we described the characteristics of physicians and patients using means and standard deviations for continuous variables and numbers, and using percentages for categorical variables. Second, the number and proportion of patients who were prescribed PIMs was described for each PIM drug category examined.
