title: Effects of Dental Follow-up on Oral Health, Antibiotic Prescriptions, and Hospitalizations in Pediatric Home Care Patients: A Single-Group Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: A BSTRACT Objective: To evaluate oral health, antibiotic prescriptions, and hospitalizations before and after dental follow-up among children assisted by the Home Care Service (HCS). Methods: This single-group quasi-experimental, nonrandomized study was conducted at the HCS of the Clinical Hospital, at a Federal University in Brazil. This study involved 29 children undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation and gastrostomy. Oral healthcare data were collected at two time points: T1 (December 2021) and T2 (December 2022). Dental interventions and oral health education activities were conducted between January and December 2022. Monthly data on hospitalizations and antibiotic prescriptions were collected for 2021 and 2022. Oral health assessment was based on the simplified oral hygiene index, gingival bleeding, and gingival hyperplasia. Statistical analysis was performed using the Wilcoxon paired test, with a 5% significance level. Results: There was a reduction in gingival bleeding (47.4%, P = 0.044) and the presence of dental plaque (50.0%, P = 0.011) and calculus (50.0%, P = 0.024). The number of antibiotic prescriptions decreased by 51.5% ( P = 0.043). No significant difference was observed in the hospitalization rates ( P > 0.050). Conclusion: Over the course of the dental follow-up, homebound pediatric patients showed a reduction in dental plaque, calculus, gingival bleeding, and antibiotic use. This is particularly relevant given that children with disabilities who are homebound often lack access to dental care. Regular dental checkups can reduce plaque accumulation, gingival bleeding, calculus formation, and the need for antibiotic prescriptions. Therefore, integrating dentists into home care teams may strengthen the relationship between improved oral health, reduced antibiotic use, and lower hospitalization rates in vulnerable pediatric populations.
body: A person with a disability is defined as an individual with long-term physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory impairments that, in interaction with various barriers, may hinder full participation in the society.[ 1 ] Oral healthcare has become increasingly important for the restoration of the general health and quality of life of individuals with disabilities. This is particularly true for hospitalized or bedridden patients with acute or chronic respiratory insufficiency who often undergo systemic treatments and are dependent on respiratory support.[ 2 , 3 ] Although hospital and outpatient settings are traditionally recognized as the primary contexts for healthcare delivery, it is emphasized that the home and community constitute the environments in which most children receive their daily medical care. This model of care assumes particular relevance for the promotion of health and well-being among children with disabilities.[ 4 , 5 ] Consequently, a progressive increase in this population has been observed, resulting in an increasing number of children being discharged from hospital to the home with specialized medical equipment and/or requiring structured home healthcare services.[ 4 ] Oral health is characterized by intraoral homeostasis, which facilitates essential functions, such as chewing, speaking, swallowing, and breathing, and is, therefore, fundamental to well-being. Poor oral health is associated with various systemic conditions including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, respiratory diseases, and obesity.[ 6 , 7 ] In this context, oral healthcare, especially for individuals with disabilities, plays a crucial role in preventing multiple systemic disorders.[ 8 ] Homebound and bedridden patients with disabilities and exacerbated chronic conditions often require oral healthcare but are unable to access conventional dental services. Therefore, adapted dental care approaches, incorporating strategies that prioritize comprehensive, continuous, and humanized care, are necessary. Home Care Services (HCSs) are organized by a multidisciplinary team to support prolonged healthcare delivery.[ 9 , 10 ] In Brazil, the classification of HC complexity level in public services prioritizes cases that require the most healthcare resources, considering the frequency of visits, intensity of required care, and need for equipment. These levels are categorized as home care (HC) 1, HC2, and HC3. HC1 patients require less frequent visits and minimal intervention from multiple professionals and are often managed through primary care units or rehabilitation centers. In contrast, HC2 and HC3 patients are referred to the HCS because of their need for more intensive care, multidisciplinary teams, and complex procedures. HCS teams in public service healthcare in Brazil are classified as type 1 or 2 depending on the population size of the municipality, with type 1 for populations ≥40,000 and type 2 for smaller municipalities.[ 11 ] Currently, the multidisciplinary team responsible for high-complexity pediatric HC in Brazil includes physicians, nurses, physical therapists, and nursing assistants or technicians but does not include a dentist. Homebound patients are at a high risk of developing serious infections and may present with systemic complications either due to their condition or therapeutic interventions.[ 12 ] Although the literature emphasizes the importance of oral care for medically compromised individuals and the need for daily professional attention, limited data exist on pediatric patients receiving home care support.[ 13 ] The integration of dentists into home visits remains limited, underscoring the need to strengthen the connection between healthcare teams and the communities they serve. Home visits play a fundamental role in promoting equity by addressing the needs of populations excluded from traditional dental care services and recognizing their specific vulnerabilities.[ 14 ] Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the oral health conditions of patients assisted by the HCS of the Clinical Hospital of a Federal University, as well as their frequency of hospitalizations and antibiotic prescriptions before and after regular dental follow-up. We hypothesized that dental follow-ups would be associated with changes in oral health, antibiotic prescriptions, and hospitalizations in this population. This was a single-group quasi-experimental, nonrandomized internal comparison study, conducted at the HCS of the Clinical Hospital of the Federal University of Uberlandia, located in Brazil. Since 1996, the HCS has supported hospital discharge of patients requiring HC. For the past 10 years, the service has been integrated into Brazil’s national “Better at home” program from the Ministry of Health and currently cares for more than 100 home-based patients. The HCS provides home healthcare for patients requiring rehabilitation, palliative care, or who are bedridden and comprises a multidisciplinary team (EMAD) and a support team (EMAP). The latter is only activated when required to complement the clinical actions of EMAD. There is no mandatory inclusion of dental care professionals in the EMAD; dentists are involved only through the EMAP. As of 2021, children under HCS’s care had not undergone routine dental evaluations and did not benefit from preventive or therapeutic dental care. All children aged up to 12 years and enrolled in HCS between January 2021 and December 2022 were included in this study. The exclusion criteria were as follows: patients who did not complete the minimum follow-up period; those with insufficient clinical information in their medical records; patients outside the defined age range (<4 years or >12 years); and cases in which the caregiver declined participation in the study. A total of 29 patients, encompassing the entire available sample, were monitored between 2021 and 2022. The absence of a control group was due to the difficulty in recruiting patients with the same comorbidities who were not receiving HC as hospitalized patients do not remain admitted long enough for follow-up. Additionally, selecting patients with different comorbidities or without comorbidities would have introduced control bias. Oral health outcomes were evaluated at two time points: T1 (December 2021) and T2 (December 2022). Weekly or monthly dental visits for preventive care, education, treatment, and follow-up were conducted from January to December 2022, totaling 12 months of dental intervention. The legal guardians of all participating children received information about the study protocol and consented for their participation through signed informed consent forms. Ethical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee of the University (CAAE 63903416.0.0000.5152). For T1 and T2 assessments, the research team accompanied the EMAD during home visits. The dentists attended weekly follow-up visits independently. Clinical evaluations were performed using no. 5 mouth mirrors (Golgran, São Caetano do Sul, SP, Brazil), World Health Organization probes (Golgran), and headlamps. The instruments were sterilized at the University School of Dentistry sterilization center. Two dentists assisted by two recorders conducted the oral examinations. All underwent theoretical training on diagnosing enamel defects, caries, dental plaque, and calculus, followed by clinical calibration with 10 pediatric patients not included in the study sample. Calibration was repeated after 1 week. One pediatric dentistry specialist was considered the gold standard. Interexaminer Kappa values exceeded 0.87, and intraexaminer Kappa values exceeded 0.92. Oral hygiene was assessed using the Simplified Oral Hygiene Index,[ 15 ] with scores ranging from 0 to 3 for the presence of plaque and calculus. The evaluated surfaces included the buccal surfaces of teeth 11/51, 31/71, 16/55, and 26/65 and lingual surfaces of teeth 36/75 and 46/85. Following the clinical examination, patients received oral hygiene care using a soft-bristle toothbrush (Oral-B Indicator Plus) and 1100-ppm fluoride toothpaste (Colgate) in age-appropriate quantities. Caries indices (Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth [DMFT] for permanent teeth and DMFT for primary teeth) were recorded.[ 14 ] Gingival hyperplasia and bleeding were also assessed (presence/absence). The frequency of dental visits was determined by the patient’s clinical needs at baseline. A preventive protocol, consisting of monthly visits, was applied to patients requiring only oral health education and monitoring. For patients presenting curative demands (e.g., periodontal scaling or tooth extractions), a treatment protocol was implemented with weekly appointments until the clinical condition was resolved, after which they transitioned to monthly maintenance visits. Regardless of the frequency, all visits followed a standardized approach: caregivers received verbal instructions and practical demonstrations on oral hygiene (brushing technique, flossing, and positioning). To facilitate access to the oral cavity, mouth openers made of wooden spatulas and gauze were utilized. All clinical findings and treatment transitions were recorded in standardized dental charts to ensure protocol adherence. To assess antibiotic prescriptions and hospitalizations, clinical records were reviewed for infectious events. Monthly records from January 2021 to December 2022 provided data on antibiotic use and hospital admissions (categorized as yes or no). These records were updated by EMAD healthcare professionals, including physicians, nurses, physical therapists, and nursing technicians. Dentists were not part of this routine reporting. Data on oral health and infection episodes were analyzed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) for Windows (version 22.0; SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Data distribution was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, which indicated non-normality for all variables. The Wilcoxon paired test was applied. A significance level of 5% and a 95% confidence interval were adopted. The sample consisted of 29 patients who were followed-up from 2021 to 2022, with no losses. The average age was 6 (standard deviation ± 5) years; 19 children (65.5%) were male and 10 (34.5%) were female. None of the evaluated children presented with carious lesions; therefore, this condition was excluded from the analysis. Figure 1 presents the data on gingival hyperplasia, gingival bleeding, visible plaques, and calculus collected at T1 (without dental care) and T2 (after dental care). Although a 44.4% reduction in the presence of gingival hyperplasia was observed between T1 and T2, the Wilcoxon paired test showed no significant difference ( P = 0.450). A significant difference was observed in the presence of gingival bleeding between the time points ( P = 0.044, Wilcoxon paired test), with a 47.4% reduction in the number of patients presenting with bleeding. Evaluation of visible dental plaque showed a significant difference between T1 and T2 ( P = 0.011, Wilcoxon paired test), with 50.0% reduction. The presence of calculus also showed 50.0% reduction at T2, which was a significant difference ( P = 0.024, Wilcoxon paired test). Stacked bar graph representing the prevalence of oral health conditions—gingival hyperplasia, gingival bleeding, visible plaques, and calculus collected at T1 (without dental care) and T2 (after dental care). *Statistical difference between groups ( P < 0 .05, Wilcoxon paired test) The results from a survey of antibiotic use over the months are shown in Figure 2 . The boxplot represents the comparison between 2021 (T1) and 2022 (T2) regarding the number of months in which antibiotics were prescribed, considering urinary infections (a) and respiratory infections (b). The number of months in which antibiotics were prescribed was higher in T1, for respiratory infection, compared to T2 (T1 = 4.5 [0.0–8.5]; T2 = 0 [0.0–4.0]; P = 0.043, Wilcoxon paired test). For urinary infection, the Wilcoxon paired test showed no statistical difference between T1 and T2 ( P > 0.05). Regarding the total number of hospitalization records, there were 23 recorded cases (14 patients) in 2021 and 27 (10 patients) in 2022, with no significant difference between the years ( P = 0.450, Wilcoxon paired test). Boxplot graphs representing the comparison between 2021 (T1) and 2022 (T2) regarding the number of months in which antibiotics were prescribed, considering urinary infections (a) and respiratory infections (b). Different letters indicate statistical significance difference between groups (T1 and T2, p < 0.05, Wilcoxon paired test) Oral health is essential for physical and psychosocial quality of life and overall health.[ 16 , 17 ] Therefore, oral care for homebound, medically complex patients is vital to ensure their well-being. Children with disabilities have a high risk of developing severe infections due to therapeutic procedures or underlying conditions.[ 12 ] A balanced oral microbiota can act as a barrier against pathogenic microorganisms, modulate the immune system, produce beneficial substances, and degrade toxins.[ 18 ] Oral bacteria can enter the bloodstream via the oral mucosa, making oral infections a potential cause of bacteremia and systemic infections.[ 19 ] Consequently, dental care and oral health promotion are effective in preventing or managing systemic conditions, potentially reducing respiratory infections, antibiotic use, and mortality in hospitalized patients.[ 20 ] The results of this study demonstrated a reduction in the number of antibiotics administered for respiratory infections during the year in which home-based dental care was provided to children with disabilities. Recent studies have emphasized the importance of plaque removal and basic periodontal care in the prevention and management of gingivitis and periodontal disease, both of which are associated with gingival bleeding.[ 21 , 22 ] This reaffirms the importance of multidisciplinary work, including the dentist in both hospital and home settings, to prevent the onset and progression of fungal diseases and periodontal disease. Although the data cited are not specifically related to oral health evaluations in homebound children, these findings are consistent with those observed in the present study. When analyzing infectious conditions, it was noted that the data found in previous research[ 23 ] reported that the presence of a dentist in intensive care units reduces the incidence of respiratory infections, reducing the need for antibiotics and the length of hospital stay. In addition, other study[ 24 ] validates a significant reduction in the incidence of pneumonia, the use of nonprophylactic antibiotics, and a decrease in mortality rates in the group receiving dental care. Furthermore, an association observed only with respiratory infections was expected in this study as the oral cavity has been considered a potential reservoir for respiratory pathogens.[ 25 ] In the present study, no dental caries was found in any of the participating patients. This is due to the fact that the patients had gastrostomies. Caries develops through acid attacks resulting from the decomposition of metabolized sugar by bacteria. Since food is not consumed orally, the risk of caries is reduced. Previous studies reinforce that patients with gastrostomies have a lower rate of cariogenic bacteria when compared to patients without gastrostomies.[ 26 ] Conversely, a higher presence of calculus was observed in this population. This is explained by an imbalance in the oral bacterial flora, which may be due to lack of chewing and oral inactivity, also interfering with the pH of the oral cavity and creating a favorable environment for calculus formation. Furthermore, the presence of calculus may be related to the caregiver’s failure to prioritize oral hygiene since these patients do not use their mouths to eat, and caregivers may disregard the importance of oral hygiene.[ 26 , 27 ] It is noted that there was no significant difference in gingival hyperplasia as it is a side effect of anticonvulsant medications in which the gingival tissue is not the intended target.[ 28 ] Throughout the 1-year follow-up, all visits included systematic oral hygiene guidance provided to patients’ caregivers at the end of each consultation. The implementation of these services, which had not previously been available, led to observable clinical changes from the onset of home-based dental care. Thus, it was possible to provide continuous intervention in oral care through the provision of technical support and individualized assistance tailored to each patient’s specific needs. However, despite the interventions performed, it was not possible to fully control the natural disease progression. During this study, we identified limited data regarding oral assessment and infectious conditions associated with hospitalization rates and antibiotic use in the highly complex pediatric population receiving HC before and after the dental follow-up. Recent studies have examined the association between home dental care and reduced hospital admissions, demonstrating its benefits. However, hospitalizations may occur for a variety of reasons. Nevertheless, access to home dental care can help prevent serious oral health complications in vulnerable populations with physical or cognitive disabilities.[ 29 ] Therefore, the amount of existing research on this topic is scarce, and this study corroborates the need for further studies in this line of research. The differences found appear to indicate the importance of dental treatment. This is one of the few studies evaluating pediatric patients with disabilities receiving HC, thus encouraging reflection and modification of the structure of the public service responsible for serving this extremely vulnerable population. The study presented important limitations. First, it was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which made it difficult to control the external research environment; however, none of the participating patients were diagnosed with COVID-19 during the study period. In addition, the small sample size limited the statistical power of the study, despite the inclusion of the entire population of patients registered in the HCS within the study setting. The absence of a control group also represents an important limitation of the present study. The main challenge was the difficulty in recruiting patients with comparable comorbidities who were not receiving HC as hospitalized patients typically do not remain admitted long enough to allow adequate follow-up. Furthermore, including patients with different comorbidity profiles or without comorbidities would have introduced significant control bias. Despite the positive outcomes observed following dental intervention, the absence of a control group constitutes a significant limitation to establishing a direct causal relationship. As a longitudinal study, the findings may have been influenced by external confounding factors and temporal trends. Notably, the study period overlapped with the COVID-19 pandemic and seasonal respiratory cycles, both of which significantly impacted hospitalization patterns. Furthermore, in homebound populations, the natural progression of underlying chronic conditions and frequent pharmacological adjustments (polypharmacy) represent dynamic variables that may interfere with clinical outcomes. Consequently, while the association between oral healthcare and antibiotic prescriptions is clinically suggestive, these results should be interpreted with caution, highlighting the need for future randomized controlled trials to validate these findings. 4 It can be concluded that the prevalence of plaque, calculus, gingival bleeding, and the use of antibiotics for respiratory infections among pediatric patients receiving HC decreased during the year in which regular dental care was provided. Poor oral health is associated with various systemic conditions including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, respiratory diseases, and obesity.[ 6 , 7 ] In this context, oral healthcare, especially for individuals with disabilities, plays a crucial role in preventing multiple systemic disorders.[ 8 ] Homebound and bedridden patients with disabilities and exacerbated chronic conditions often require oral healthcare but are unable to access conventional dental services. Therefore, adapted dental care approaches, incorporating strategies that prioritize comprehensive, continuous, and humanized care, are necessary. Home Care Services (HCSs) are organized by a multidisciplinary team to support prolonged healthcare delivery.[ 9 , 10 ] In Brazil, the classification of HC complexity level in public services prioritizes cases that require the most healthcare resources, considering the frequency of visits, intensity of required care, and need for equipment. These levels are categorized as home care (HC) 1, HC2, and HC3. HC1 patients require less frequent visits and minimal intervention from multiple professionals and are often managed through primary care units or rehabilitation centers. In contrast, HC2 and HC3 patients are referred to the HCS because of their need for more intensive care, multidisciplinary teams, and complex procedures. HCS teams in public service healthcare in Brazil are classified as type 1 or 2 depending on the population size of the municipality, with type 1 for populations ≥40,000 and type 2 for smaller municipalities.[ 11 ] Currently, the multidisciplinary team responsible for high-complexity pediatric HC in Brazil includes physicians, nurses, physical therapists, and nursing assistants or technicians but does not include a dentist. Homebound patients are at a high risk of developing serious infections and may present with systemic complications either due to their condition or therapeutic interventions.[ 12 ] Although the literature emphasizes the importance of oral care for medically compromised individuals and the need for daily professional attention, limited data exist on pediatric patients receiving home care support.[ 13 ] The integration of dentists into home visits remains limited, underscoring the need to strengthen the connection between healthcare teams and the communities they serve. Home visits play a fundamental role in promoting equity by addressing the needs of populations excluded from traditional dental care services and recognizing their specific vulnerabilities.[ 14 ] Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the oral health conditions of patients assisted by the HCS of the Clinical Hospital of a Federal University, as well as their frequency of hospitalizations and antibiotic prescriptions before and after regular dental follow-up. We hypothesized that dental follow-ups would be associated with changes in oral health, antibiotic prescriptions, and hospitalizations in this population. This was a single-group quasi-experimental, nonrandomized internal comparison study, conducted at the HCS of the Clinical Hospital of the Federal University of Uberlandia, located in Brazil. Since 1996, the HCS has supported hospital discharge of patients requiring HC. For the past 10 years, the service has been integrated into Brazil’s national “Better at home” program from the Ministry of Health and currently cares for more than 100 home-based patients. The HCS provides home healthcare for patients requiring rehabilitation, palliative care, or who are bedridden and comprises a multidisciplinary team (EMAD) and a support team (EMAP). The latter is only activated when required to complement the clinical actions of EMAD. There is no mandatory inclusion of dental care professionals in the EMAD; dentists are involved only through the EMAP. As of 2021, children under HCS’s care had not undergone routine dental evaluations and did not benefit from preventive or therapeutic dental care. All children aged up to 12 years and enrolled in HCS between January 2021 and December 2022 were included in this study. The exclusion criteria were as follows: patients who did not complete the minimum follow-up period; those with insufficient clinical information in their medical records; patients outside the defined age range (<4 years or >12 years); and cases in which the caregiver declined participation in the study. A total of 29 patients, encompassing the entire available sample, were monitored between 2021 and 2022. The absence of a control group was due to the difficulty in recruiting patients with the same comorbidities who were not receiving HC as hospitalized patients do not remain admitted long enough for follow-up. Additionally, selecting patients with different comorbidities or without comorbidities would have introduced control bias. Oral health outcomes were evaluated at two time points: T1 (December 2021) and T2 (December 2022). Weekly or monthly dental visits for preventive care, education, treatment, and follow-up were conducted from January to December 2022, totaling 12 months of dental intervention. The legal guardians of all participating children received information about the study protocol and consented for their participation through signed informed consent forms. Ethical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee of the University (CAAE 63903416.0.0000.5152). For T1 and T2 assessments, the research team accompanied the EMAD during home visits. The dentists attended weekly follow-up visits independently. Clinical evaluations were performed using no. 5 mouth mirrors (Golgran, São Caetano do Sul, SP, Brazil), World Health Organization probes (Golgran), and headlamps. The instruments were sterilized at the University School of Dentistry sterilization center. Two dentists assisted by two recorders conducted the oral examinations. All underwent theoretical training on diagnosing enamel defects, caries, dental plaque, and calculus, followed by clinical calibration with 10 pediatric patients not included in the study sample. Calibration was repeated after 1 week. One pediatric dentistry specialist was considered the gold standard. Interexaminer Kappa values exceeded 0.87, and intraexaminer Kappa values exceeded 0.92. Oral hygiene was assessed using the Simplified Oral Hygiene Index,[ 15 ] with scores ranging from 0 to 3 for the presence of plaque and calculus. The evaluated surfaces included the buccal surfaces of teeth 11/51, 31/71, 16/55, and 26/65 and lingual surfaces of teeth 36/75 and 46/85. Following the clinical examination, patients received oral hygiene care using a soft-bristle toothbrush (Oral-B Indicator Plus) and 1100-ppm fluoride toothpaste (Colgate) in age-appropriate quantities. Caries indices (Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth [DMFT] for permanent teeth and DMFT for primary teeth) were recorded.[ 14 ] Gingival hyperplasia and bleeding were also assessed (presence/absence). The frequency of dental visits was determined by the patient’s clinical needs at baseline. A preventive protocol, consisting of monthly visits, was applied to patients requiring only oral health education and monitoring. For patients presenting curative demands (e.g., periodontal scaling or tooth extractions), a treatment protocol was implemented with weekly appointments until the clinical condition was resolved, after which they transitioned to monthly maintenance visits. Regardless of the frequency, all visits followed a standardized approach: caregivers received verbal instructions and practical demonstrations on oral hygiene (brushing technique, flossing, and positioning). To facilitate access to the oral cavity, mouth openers made of wooden spatulas and gauze were utilized. All clinical findings and treatment transitions were recorded in standardized dental charts to ensure protocol adherence. To assess antibiotic prescriptions and hospitalizations, clinical records were reviewed for infectious events. Monthly records from January 2021 to December 2022 provided data on antibiotic use and hospital admissions (categorized as yes or no). These records were updated by EMAD healthcare professionals, including physicians, nurses, physical therapists, and nursing technicians. Dentists were not part of this routine reporting. Data on oral health and infection episodes were analyzed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) for Windows (version 22.0; SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Data distribution was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, which indicated non-normality for all variables. The Wilcoxon paired test was applied. A significance level of 5% and a 95% confidence interval were adopted. The sample consisted of 29 patients who were followed-up from 2021 to 2022, with no losses. The average age was 6 (standard deviation ± 5) years; 19 children (65.5%) were male and 10 (34.5%) were female. None of the evaluated children presented with carious lesions; therefore, this condition was excluded from the analysis. Figure 1 presents the data on gingival hyperplasia, gingival bleeding, visible plaques, and calculus collected at T1 (without dental care) and T2 (after dental care). Although a 44.4% reduction in the presence of gingival hyperplasia was observed between T1 and T2, the Wilcoxon paired test showed no significant difference ( P = 0.450). A significant difference was observed in the presence of gingival bleeding between the time points ( P = 0.044, Wilcoxon paired test), with a 47.4% reduction in the number of patients presenting with bleeding. Evaluation of visible dental plaque showed a significant difference between T1 and T2 ( P = 0.011, Wilcoxon paired test), with 50.0% reduction. The presence of calculus also showed 50.0% reduction at T2, which was a significant difference ( P = 0.024, Wilcoxon paired test). Stacked bar graph representing the prevalence of oral health conditions—gingival hyperplasia, gingival bleeding, visible plaques, and calculus collected at T1 (without dental care) and T2 (after dental care). *Statistical difference between groups ( P < 0 .05, Wilcoxon paired test) The results from a survey of antibiotic use over the months are shown in Figure 2 . The boxplot represents the comparison between 2021 (T1) and 2022 (T2) regarding the number of months in which antibiotics were prescribed, considering urinary infections (a) and respiratory infections (b). The number of months in which antibiotics were prescribed was higher in T1, for respiratory infection, compared to T2 (T1 = 4.5 [0.0–8.5]; T2 = 0 [0.0–4.0]; P = 0.043, Wilcoxon paired test). For urinary infection, the Wilcoxon paired test showed no statistical difference between T1 and T2 ( P > 0.05). Regarding the total number of hospitalization records, there were 23 recorded cases (14 patients) in 2021 and 27 (10 patients) in 2022, with no significant difference between the years ( P = 0.450, Wilcoxon paired test). Boxplot graphs representing the comparison between 2021 (T1) and 2022 (T2) regarding the number of months in which antibiotics were prescribed, considering urinary infections (a) and respiratory infections (b). Different letters indicate statistical significance difference between groups (T1 and T2, p < 0.05, Wilcoxon paired test) Oral health is essential for physical and psychosocial quality of life and overall health.[ 16 , 17 ] Therefore, oral care for homebound, medically complex patients is vital to ensure their well-being. Children with disabilities have a high risk of developing severe infections due to therapeutic procedures or underlying conditions.[ 12 ] A balanced oral microbiota can act as a barrier against pathogenic microorganisms, modulate the immune system, produce beneficial substances, and degrade toxins.[ 18 ] Oral bacteria can enter the bloodstream via the oral mucosa, making oral infections a potential cause of bacteremia and systemic infections.[ 19 ] Consequently, dental care and oral health promotion are effective in preventing or managing systemic conditions, potentially reducing respiratory infections, antibiotic use, and mortality in hospitalized patients.[ 20 ] The results of this study demonstrated a reduction in the number of antibiotics administered for respiratory infections during the year in which home-based dental care was provided to children with disabilities. Recent studies have emphasized the importance of plaque removal and basic periodontal care in the prevention and management of gingivitis and periodontal disease, both of which are associated with gingival bleeding.[ 21 , 22 ] This reaffirms the importance of multidisciplinary work, including the dentist in both hospital and home settings, to prevent the onset and progression of fungal diseases and periodontal disease. Although the data cited are not specifically related to oral health evaluations in homebound children, these findings are consistent with those observed in the present study. When analyzing infectious conditions, it was noted that the data found in previous research[ 23 ] reported that the presence of a dentist in intensive care units reduces the incidence of respiratory infections, reducing the need for antibiotics and the length of hospital stay. In addition, other study[ 24 ] validates a significant reduction in the incidence of pneumonia, the use of nonprophylactic antibiotics, and a decrease in mortality rates in the group receiving dental care. Furthermore, an association observed only with respiratory infections was expected in this study as the oral cavity has been considered a potential reservoir for respiratory pathogens.[ 25 ] In the present study, no dental caries was found in any of the participating patients. This is due to the fact that the patients had gastrostomies. Caries develops through acid attacks resulting from the decomposition of metabolized sugar by bacteria. Since food is not consumed orally, the risk of caries is reduced. Previous studies reinforce that patients with gastrostomies have a lower rate of cariogenic bacteria when compared to patients without gastrostomies.[ 26 ] Conversely, a higher presence of calculus was observed in this population. This is explained by an imbalance in the oral bacterial flora, which may be due to lack of chewing and oral inactivity, also interfering with the pH of the oral cavity and creating a favorable environment for calculus formation. Furthermore, the presence of calculus may be related to the caregiver’s failure to prioritize oral hygiene since these patients do not use their mouths to eat, and caregivers may disregard the importance of oral hygiene.[ 26 , 27 ] It is noted that there was no significant difference in gingival hyperplasia as it is a side effect of anticonvulsant medications in which the gingival tissue is not the intended target.[ 28 ] Throughout the 1-year follow-up, all visits included systematic oral hygiene guidance provided to patients’ caregivers at the end of each consultation. The implementation of these services, which had not previously been available, led to observable clinical changes from the onset of home-based dental care. Thus, it was possible to provide continuous intervention in oral care through the provision of technical support and individualized assistance tailored to each patient’s specific needs. However, despite the interventions performed, it was not possible to fully control the natural disease progression. During this study, we identified limited data regarding oral assessment and infectious conditions associated with hospitalization rates and antibiotic use in the highly complex pediatric population receiving HC before and after the dental follow-up. Recent studies have examined the association between home dental care and reduced hospital admissions, demonstrating its benefits. However, hospitalizations may occur for a variety of reasons. Nevertheless, access to home dental care can help prevent serious oral health complications in vulnerable populations with physical or cognitive disabilities.[ 29 ] Therefore, the amount of existing research on this topic is scarce, and this study corroborates the need for further studies in this line of research. The differences found appear to indicate the importance of dental treatment. This is one of the few studies evaluating pediatric patients with disabilities receiving HC, thus encouraging reflection and modification of the structure of the public service responsible for serving this extremely vulnerable population. The study presented important limitations. First, it was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which made it difficult to control the external research environment; however, none of the participating patients were diagnosed with COVID-19 during the study period. In addition, the small sample size limited the statistical power of the study, despite the inclusion of the entire population of patients registered in the HCS within the study setting. The absence of a control group also represents an important limitation of the present study. The main challenge was the difficulty in recruiting patients with comparable comorbidities who were not receiving HC as hospitalized patients typically do not remain admitted long enough to allow adequate follow-up. Furthermore, including patients with different comorbidity profiles or without comorbidities would have introduced significant control bias. Despite the positive outcomes observed following dental intervention, the absence of a control group constitutes a significant limitation to establishing a direct causal relationship. As a longitudinal study, the findings may have been influenced by external confounding factors and temporal trends. Notably, the study period overlapped with the COVID-19 pandemic and seasonal respiratory cycles, both of which significantly impacted hospitalization patterns. Furthermore, in homebound populations, the natural progression of underlying chronic conditions and frequent pharmacological adjustments (polypharmacy) represent dynamic variables that may interfere with clinical outcomes. Consequently, while the association between oral healthcare and antibiotic prescriptions is clinically suggestive, these results should be interpreted with caution, highlighting the need for future randomized controlled trials to validate these findings. 4 It can be concluded that the prevalence of plaque, calculus, gingival bleeding, and the use of antibiotics for respiratory infections among pediatric patients receiving HC decreased during the year in which regular dental care was provided. title: Oral Adverse Effects of Semaglutide Therapy: A Narrative Review
abstract: A BSTRACT Objective: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1-receptor agonist, is widely used for the management of type-2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. Despite its increasing clinical use, the drug’s oral adverse effect profile remains inadequately characterized. This narrative review aimed to analyze the current evidence on semaglutide-associated oral adverse effects, with emphasis on mechanistic pathways, integration of pharmacovigilance and clinical data, and emerging implications for oral health and dental practice. Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Keywords related to semaglutide and oral adverse effects were used. Eligible studies included clinical trials, pharmacovigilance analyses, observational studies, case reports, and preclinical research reporting oral adverse effects or relevant mechanistic insights. Studies lacking oral health correlates were excluded. Findings were narratively reviewed in accordance with Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles guidelines. Results: Xerostomia or hyposalivation is the most consistently reported oral adverse effect, although its prevalence varies across studies. However, xerostomia often occurs secondarily to gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea, reduced oral intake, and delayed gastric emptying. Additional manifestations included dysgeusia, dry throat, oral paresthesia or hypoesthesia, halitosis, frothy saliva, and increased dental caries. Pharmacovigilance data show significant signals for dry mouth and altered taste. Case-series confirm semaglutide-associated hyposalivation. Limited evidence suggests increased susceptibility to oral candidiasis. Early experimental and observational data indicate potential modulatory effects on inflammation, tissue repair, and bone metabolism. Conclusion: Semaglutide therapy is associated with oral adverse effects, mainly xerostomia and sensory disturbances, which may compromise oral health. Awareness of these outcomes highlights the need for interdisciplinary oral health monitoring.
body: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1-receptor agonist (GLP-1-RA), has revolutionized the management of type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity due to its potent glycemic control and weight-loss effects.[ 1 ] As a long-acting analog of human GLP-1, semaglutide enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon release, and delays gastric emptying, thereby addressing multiple pathophysiological mechanisms underlying metabolic disorders.[ 2 ] Its subcutaneous and oral formulations have demonstrated superior efficacy compared to earlier GLP-1-RAs, such as exenatide, liraglutide, and dulaglutide, leading to widespread clinical adoption.[ 3 ] However, the expanding use of semaglutide has also brought attention to its adverse effects, particularly those manifesting in the oral cavity, which remain poorly characterized despite their potential impact on patient quality of life and treatment adherence.[ 4 ] The oral cavity serves as a mirror of systemic health, often reflecting drug-induced physiological changes before they become apparent elsewhere.[ 5 , 6 ] GLP-1 receptors are expressed in the salivary glands and oral mucosa, suggesting that semaglutide may directly or indirectly influence oral homeostasis.[ 7 ] Emerging clinical observations report xerostomia, dysgeusia, and an increased incidence of dental caries among semaglutide users, likely secondary to reduced salivary flow and altered composition.[ 7 ] These adverse effects may stem from the drug’s gastrointestinal (GI) influence, including delayed gastric emptying and nausea, which can indirectly reduce oral hydration and alter microbial flora.[ 8 ] Furthermore, preclinical studies suggest that GLP-1 signaling modulates inflammatory pathways and tissue repair, raising questions about the role of semaglutide in periodontal disease and oral wound healing.[ 9 , 10 ] Despite these findings, no systematic analysis of evidence exists to guide clinicians in monitoring or mitigating oral complications. A critical gap in the literature is the lack of mechanistic studies linking semaglutide’s pharmacological actions to specific oral adverse effects. While its systemic effects are well documented, the localized impact on oral tissues remains speculative, with most data derived from anecdotal reports or secondary analyses of diabetes trials.[ 4 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] Additionally, the potential therapeutic applications of semaglutide in dentistry, including its antiinflammatory properties in periodontitis, effects on oral wound healing, and impact on dental implant osseointegration, have not been fully explored.[ 15 ] This review aimed to analyze the existing literature, with a focus on oral adverse effects associated with semaglutide, an area that has not been comprehensively addressed in prior reviews, which have primarily emphasized systemic safety outcomes. Furthermore, comparing evidences from clinical trials, pharmacovigilance databases, and case reports will provide a clinically relevant overview of oral adverse effects. In addition, the mechanistic pathways linking semaglutide’s GI effects to oral complications, particularly through salivary dysfunction, and the potential implications of semaglutide for bridging endocrinology and dental practice will be explored.[ 4 , 5 , 7 , 16 ] Furthermore, this work shall help identify novel research directions, such as the role of semaglutide in modulating oral microbiome dysbiosis or its potential as an adjunct in the treatment of oral inflammatory conditions.[ 17 ] Accordingly, this narrative review aims to elucidate the characteristics, prevalence, pathophysiology, and clinical implications of oral adverse effects in patients using semaglutide. The resultant findings will provide risk–benefit assessments for prescribers and dental practitioners, facilitating personalized patient care. The methodology for this narrative literature review followed the principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to ensure clarity, transparency, and methodological rigor.[ 18 ] The literature search was conducted on November 15, 2025. A focused research question, “What are the oral adverse effects of semaglutide?” guided a structured literature search across relevant databases, including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, to ensure broad coverage of clinical, pharmacological, and oral health-related evidence, published between 2015 and 2025. For structured synthesis of findings, PubMed was selected as the primary database due to its extensive coverage of clinical and preclinical studies in medicine. Scopus provided complementary interdisciplinary indexing, while Science Direct and Springer Link offered access to full-text articles from major journals. Web of Science was included for its citation tracking capabilities. Google Scholar served to identify supplementary resources not indexed in the primary databases. Boolean operators and field-specific search terms were tailored to each database. Search terms included the following: “semaglutide,” “oral adverse effects,” “GLP-1 receptor agonists,” “xerostomia,” “dysgeusia,” “oral wound healing,” “dental caries,” and relevant brand names “Ozempic” and “Wegovy.” For reproducibility, the full PubMed search strategy was as follows: ((Oral adverse effects [TIAB]) AND (semaglutide [TIAB] OR Wegovy [TIAB] OR Ozempic [TIAB])) OR Survey [Publication Type] OR Meta-analysis [Publication Type]) . Similar adaptations were made for other databases to maintain consistency across platforms. Study selection followed a structured screening process: title/abstract review followed by full-text assessment based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The review adhered to SANRA domains, including appropriate literature selection, transparent analysis, balanced interpretation, and accurate referencing. The focused research question was structured around three principal queries intended to clarify the scope and significance of semaglutide’s oral adverse effects. (1) Evaluate the safety profile of semaglutide in T2DM, obesity treatment, and their potential indirect effects on oral health; (2) characterize oral cavity-specific adverse events by assessing their prevalence, severity, and underlying mechanisms; and (3) analyze the available data on the prospective applications of semaglutide beyond metabolic disease, particularly its influence on oral tissues. A structured study selection process was followed and is illustrated in a flow diagram adapted from preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines [ Figure 1 ]. Although this review is narrative in nature, efforts were made to enhance transparency by reporting the number of records identified, screened, and included. Study selection criteria were defined to capture clinically relevant and mechanistically informative evidence appropriate for a narrative review. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed clinical or experimental research reporting primary or secondary oral healthcare outcomes associated with semaglutide. Clinical trials, observational studies, case reports, pharmacovigilance analyses, and review articles providing mechanistic insights were included. Articles published in English were considered without time restrictions. Editorials or commentaries lacking empirical data, studies addressing only systemic outcomes without oral relevance, and non-English publications were excluded. Study selection flow diagram based on preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines. The diagram illustrates the process of identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of studies in this narrative review Titles and abstracts were manually screened for relevance to oral healthcare outcomes or mechanisms potentially affecting oral tissues, including salivary function and mucosal immunity. Full-text articles meeting the inclusion criteria were reviewed in detail. Extracted data included study objectives, key findings, and reported oral adverse effects or mechanistic observations related to semaglutide exposure. The initial search yielded 312 records. After removal of duplicates, 256 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 214 records were excluded based on relevance criteria. The remaining 42 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, of which 13 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis. Consistent with SANRA principles, formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied. However, qualitative appraisal and scientific reasoning were employed throughout the review. Primary evidence was distinguished from secondary or hypothesis-generating sources. Consistency of reported oral adverse effects across independent data sources was evaluated, and methodological limitations were documented. This approach enabled balanced integration of heterogeneous evidence while acknowledging inherent constraints. The literature search yielded 366 records across databases and registers. After removal of duplicates and screening based on relevance, a subset of 40 studies underwent full-text review, of which 13 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis [ Figure 1 and Table 1 ]. Evidence-based literature revealed that earlier studies (2015–2022) primarily examined semaglutide’s efficacy and safety in metabolic disorders, with oral adverse effects being reported incidentally as secondary outcomes. However, recent literature (2023–2025) demonstrates a deliberate shift toward investigating adverse oral events. Methodologically, the progression from efficacy trials to adverse event analyses indicates maturation in understanding semaglutide’s oral effects. Initial efficacy studies established baseline safety profiles, while later works delve into pathophysiology, often employing biochemical assays or imaging to link drug mechanisms to clinical observations. This literature search identifies a spectrum of studies ranging from randomized clinical trials to pharmacovigilance reports and case series, revealing emerging but fragmented evidence on semaglutide’s oral adverse effects. The qualitative analysis findings relating to oral adverse effects of semaglutide, based on the current review of selected studies, are tabulated [ Table 1 ]. The pharmacological actions of semaglutide, while beneficial for metabolic control, may inadvertently affect oral homeostasis through both direct[ 7 , 25 ] and indirect mechanisms,[ 10 , 20 , 23 , 26 ] particularly in patients receiving long-term therapy.[ 17 ] Qualitative synthesis of findings from the reviewed studies reporting about oral adverse effects of semaglutide and other systemic adverse effects with indirect oral complications ICER = Institute for Clinical and Economic Review, PIONEER = Peptide innovation for early diabetes treatment, HbA1c = glycated hemoglobin A1c, GLP-1-RA = glucagon-like peptide-1-receptor agonist, AE = adverse effects, FDA = Food and Drug Administration, FAERS = FDA adverse event reporting system, T1DM = type 1 diabetes mellitus, T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus, GERD = gastroesophageal reflux disease, GI = gastrointestinal, STEP = semaglutide treatment effect in people with obesity. Gastrointestinal adverse effects (e.g., nausea, vomiting, eructation, and GERD) are included as indirect contributors to oral complications as they lead to dental caries, xerostomia, and hyposalivation through mechanisms such as enamel hypomineralization, reduced oral intake, dehydration, and salivary gland hypofunction Direct clinical evidence, primarily from observational studies and case series, suggests an association between semaglutide use and xerostomia, along with related alterations in salivary function.[ 7 ] However, a substantial proportion of the available data are derived from indirect sources, including pharmacovigilance databases and studies primarily focused on systemic or GI outcomes rather than oral-specific endpoints.[ 15 , 20 , 21 , 23 , 25 ] Currently, there is no definitive evidence supporting that oral adverse effects are directly attributable to the pharmacological action of semaglutide. Reported oral manifestations appear to be secondary, indirect, or mechanistically uncertain.[ 15 , 21 , 22 , 24 ] Based on the available evidence, these findings can be organized into two broad domains: Oral manifestations: Xerostomia (dry mouth) and hyposalivation are the most consistently reported oral adverse effects associated with semaglutide therapy.[ 5 , 26 , 27 ] While the reported prevalence varies substantially across studies—with clinical trials often reporting rates below 5% and observational studies suggesting higher frequencies—xerostomia remains a clinically relevant outcome.[ 7 , 11 , 13 , 24 ] Clinical observations and case series have confirmed semaglutide-associated hyposalivation and related symptoms such as frothy saliva and oral discomfort.[ 4 , 7 , 13 , 24 ] Furthermore, there is an increased susceptibility to secondary oral complications, including dental caries .[ and oral candidiasis.[ 15 , 17 , 22 ] 16 ] These manifestations are likely multifactorial, stemming from reduced salivary antimicrobial defense and alterations in the oral microbial ecology.[ 11 , 20 , 23 ] Furthermore, these findings are supported by indirect evidence suggesting salivary gland functional alteration and broader mucosal involvement, although causal mechanisms remain insufficiently defined.[ 7 ] In patients with poorly controlled diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia may further compound this risk.[ 28 ] Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms: The underlying pathological mechanisms may further be classified based on GI mechanisms and other multifactorial mechanisms.[ 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] Accordingly, (a) GI mechanisms are a significant pathway for oral complications through GI adverse events. These occur in approximately 20%–30% of patients, with presenting symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea leading to reduced oral intake and dehydration, thereby collectively diminishing salivary secretion.[ 11 , 12 , 19 , 20 , 22 ] Additionally, delayed gastric emptying and gastroesophageal reflux contribute to an altered oral environment, potentially resulting in enamel erosion and further reducing salivary flow.[ 16 , 25 ] These GI-driven mechanisms are considered primary indirect contributors to xerostomia, hyposalivation, and an increased risk of dental caries.[ 13 , 15 , 22 , 24 ] Secondarily, (b) certain semaglutide-related oral manifestations cannot be fully explained by GI pathways and may involve multifactorial or as-yet undefined mechanisms. These include the following: Dysgeusia: Altered taste is a statistically significant signal identified in pharmacovigilance analyses (e.g., food and drug administration adverse event reporting system).[ 21 ] Sensory disturbances: Reports of oral paresthesia and hypoesthesia suggest broader mucosal or sensory involvement.[ 13 , 21 ] Dry throat: Frequently reported alongside oropharyngeal discomfort.[ 22 ] Dysphonia: Voice changes have been noted in broader sensory and mucosal reports.[ 13 ] The above findings suggest that semaglutide’s effects may extend to the sensory and mucosal tissues of the upper aerodigestive tract, though whether this reflects direct GLP-1-receptor activity or indirect systemic effects remains unclear. Although adverse oral events are widely reported across the current literature, emerging evidence suggests semaglutide’s possible modulatory effects on inflammation, bone metabolism, and tissue repair.[ 33 , 34 , 35 ] However, insufficient evidence is available to determine the prevalence of therapeutic oral effects. Interestingly, semaglutide has been found to influence inflammatory pathways and bone metabolism relevant to periodontal disease and tissue repair.[ 35 , 36 ] Potential applications include periodontal disease modulation, dental implant stability, improved wound healing, and effects on osseointegration; however, these findings remain preliminary and largely indirect.[ 35 , 37 , 38 ] Despite the growing recognition of these adverse effects, the current evidence base remains limited. Most data are derived from secondary analyses of metabolic trials or from isolated case reports, rather than from studies specifically designed to evaluate oral adverse effects.[ 11 , 15 , 21 , 22 , 24 ] Future research should prioritize prospective studies with standardized oral healthcare assessments to quantify incidence, establish dose–response relationships, and elucidate molecular mechanisms linking semaglutide’s systemic actions to oral tissue responses. The evaluation of evidences across the published literature reveals a complex interplay between semaglutide’s systemic pharmacological actions and its oral manifestations, encompassing both adverse effects and preliminary signals of therapeutic relevance.[ 39 , 40 ] While semaglutide demonstrates robust efficacy in glycemic control and weight management, its mechanisms of action—particularly delayed gastric emptying and GI intolerance—indirectly disrupt oral homeostasis.[ 25 , 40 , 41 ] The predominance of oral adverse effects as secondary findings in metabolic trials suggests that these manifestations have historically been under-recognized rather than uncommon.[ 15 , 21 , 22 , 24 ] Accordingly, GI adverse effects are considered indirect contributors to primary oral manifestations.[ 7 , 11 , 13 ] The evidence base for semaglutide-associated oral adverse effects comprises both direct and indirect sources. Direct evidence from clinical observations and case series supports the occurrence of xerostomia and related salivary dysfunction as clinically relevant outcomes.[ 7 , 11 , 13 , 24 ] However, a considerable proportion of the available data are derived from indirect sources, including pharmacovigilance databases and studies primarily focused on systemic or GI effects.[ 16 , 19 , 20 , 23 ] These indirect findings provide mechanistic plausibility but do not establish causal relationships. Furthermore, these findings indicate the need for targeted clinical studies to elucidate potential mechanisms and establish causality.[ 42 ] While the current evidence base provides mechanistic plausibility for both direct and indirect effects, the reliance on secondary analyses and spontaneous reporting necessitates prospective research with standardized oral healthcare assessments to confirm these associations.[ 27 ] The apparent discrepancy in reported xerostomia frequency across studies likely reflects methodological differences, including reliance on spontaneous adverse event reporting in clinical trials versus targeted oral health assessments in observational studies.[ 7 , 11 ] Evidence from clinical trials, pharmacovigilance analyses, and case series indicates that xerostomia arises secondary to GI adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced oral intake, which collectively diminish salivary secretion.[ 22 , 23 ] This observation aligns with pharmacological data suggesting that GLP-1-receptor activation may influence exocrine gland function, although the precise mechanisms affecting salivary glands remain insufficiently proved.[ 28 , 43 ] Clinically, reduced salivary flow has important downstream consequences.[ 24 ] Saliva is essential for oral lubrication, buffering capacity, antimicrobial defense, and enamel remineralization; its reduction may, therefore, predispose patients to the risk of dental caries, mucosal irritation, halitosis, and impaired oral clearance.[ 7 , 11 , 15 , 23 ] The increased incidence of dental caries reported in some trials likely reflects a multifactorial process involving hyposalivation, gastroesophageal reflux, and alterations in the oral microbiome.[ 15 , 22 ] Persistent xerostomia and oral discomfort may also negatively influence medication adherence, particularly when GI…
