A BSTRACT Objective: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1-receptor agonist, is widely used for the management of type-2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. Despite its increasing clinical use, the drug’s oral adverse effect profile remains inadequately characterized. This narrative review aimed to analyze the current evidence on semaglutide-associated oral adverse effects, with emphasis on mechanistic pathways, integration of pharmacovigilance and clinical data, and emerging implications for oral health and dental practice. Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Keywords related to semaglutide and oral adverse effects were used. Eligible studies included clinical trials, pharmacovigilance analyses, observational studies, case reports, and preclinical research reporting oral adverse effects or relevant mechanistic insights. Studies lacking oral health correlates were excluded. Findings were narratively reviewed in accordance with Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles guidelines. Results: Xerostomia or hyposalivation is the most consistently reported oral adverse effect, although its prevalence varies across studies. However, xerostomia often occurs secondarily to gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea, reduced oral intake, and delayed gastric emptying. Additional manifestations included dysgeusia, dry throat, oral paresthesia or hypoesthesia, halitosis, frothy saliva, and increased dental caries. Pharmacovigilance data show significant signals for dry mouth and altered taste. Case-series confirm semaglutide-associated hyposalivation. Limited evidence suggests increased susceptibility to oral candidiasis. Early experimental and observational data indicate potential modulatory effects on inflammation, tissue repair, and bone metabolism. Conclusion: Semaglutide therapy is associated with oral adverse effects, mainly xerostomia and sensory disturbances, which may compromise oral health. Awareness of these outcomes highlights the need for interdisciplinary oral health monitoring.

Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1-receptor agonist (GLP-1-RA), has revolutionized the management of type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity due to its potent glycemic control and weight-loss effects.[ 1 ] As a long-acting analog of human GLP-1, semaglutide enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon release, and delays gastric emptying, thereby addressing multiple pathophysiological mechanisms underlying metabolic disorders.[ 2 ] Its subcutaneous and oral formulations have demonstrated superior efficacy compared to earlier GLP-1-RAs, such as exenatide, liraglutide, and dulaglutide, leading to widespread clinical adoption.[ 3 ] However, the expanding use of semaglutide has also brought attention to its adverse effects, particularly those manifesting in the oral cavity, which remain poorly characterized despite their potential impact on patient quality of life and treatment adherence.[ 4 ] The oral cavity serves as a mirror of systemic health, often reflecting drug-induced physiological changes before they become apparent elsewhere.[ 5 , 6 ] GLP-1 receptors are expressed in the salivary glands and oral mucosa, suggesting that semaglutide may directly or indirectly influence oral homeostasis.[ 7 ] Emerging clinical observations report xerostomia, dysgeusia, and an increased incidence of dental caries among semaglutide users, likely secondary to reduced salivary flow and altered composition.[ 7 ] These adverse effects may stem from the drug’s gastrointestinal (GI) influence, including delayed gastric emptying and nausea, which can indirectly reduce oral hydration and alter microbial flora.[ 8 ] Furthermore, preclinical studies suggest that GLP-1 signaling modulates inflammatory pathways and tissue repair, raising questions about the role of semaglutide in periodontal disease and oral wound healing.[ 9 , 10 ] Despite these findings, no systematic analysis of evidence exists to guide clinicians in monitoring or mitigating oral complications. A critical gap in the literature is the lack of mechanistic studies linking semaglutide’s pharmacological actions to specific oral adverse effects. While its systemic effects are well documented, the localized impact on oral tissues remains speculative, with most data derived from anecdotal reports or secondary analyses of diabetes trials.[ 4 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] Additionally, the potential therapeutic applications of semaglutide in dentistry, including its antiinflammatory properties in periodontitis, effects on oral wound healing, and impact on dental implant osseointegration, have not been fully explored.[ 15 ] This review aimed to analyze the existing literature, with a focus on oral adverse effects associated with semaglutide, an area that has not been comprehensively addressed in prior reviews, which have primarily emphasized systemic safety outcomes. Furthermore, comparing evidences from clinical trials, pharmacovigilance databases, and case reports will provide a clinically relevant overview of oral adverse effects. In addition, the mechanistic pathways linking semaglutide’s GI effects to oral complications, particularly through salivary dysfunction, and the potential implications of semaglutide for bridging endocrinology and dental practice will be explored.[ 4 , 5 , 7 , 16 ] Furthermore, this work shall help identify novel research directions, such as the role of semaglutide in modulating oral microbiome dysbiosis or its potential as an adjunct in the treatment of oral inflammatory conditions.[ 17 ] Accordingly, this narrative review aims to elucidate the characteristics, prevalence, pathophysiology, and clinical implications of oral adverse effects in patients using semaglutide. The resultant findings will provide risk–benefit assessments for prescribers and dental practitioners, facilitating personalized patient care. The methodology for this narrative literature review followed the principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to ensure clarity, transparency, and methodological rigor.[ 18 ] The literature search was conducted on November 15, 2025. A focused research question, “What are the oral adverse effects of semaglutide?” guided a structured literature search across relevant databases, including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, to ensure broad coverage of clinical, pharmacological, and oral health-related evidence, published between 2015 and 2025. For structured synthesis of findings, PubMed was selected as the primary database due to its extensive coverage of clinical and preclinical studies in medicine. Scopus provided complementary interdisciplinary indexing, while Science Direct and Springer Link offered access to full-text articles from major journals. Web of Science was included for its citation tracking capabilities. Google Scholar served to identify supplementary resources not indexed in the primary databases. Boolean operators and field-specific search terms were tailored to each database. Search terms included the following: “semaglutide,” “oral adverse effects,” “GLP-1 receptor agonists,” “xerostomia,” “dysgeusia,” “oral wound healing,” “dental caries,” and relevant brand names “Ozempic” and “Wegovy.” For reproducibility, the full PubMed search strategy was as follows: ((Oral adverse effects [TIAB]) AND (semaglutide [TIAB] OR Wegovy [TIAB] OR Ozempic [TIAB])) OR Survey [Publication Type] OR Meta-analysis [Publication Type]) . Similar adaptations were made for other databases to maintain consistency across platforms. Study selection followed a structured screening process: title/abstract review followed by full-text assessment based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The review adhered to SANRA domains, including appropriate literature selection, transparent analysis, balanced interpretation, and accurate referencing. The focused research question was structured around three principal queries intended to clarify the scope and significance of semaglutide’s oral adverse effects. (1) Evaluate the safety profile of semaglutide in T2DM, obesity treatment, and their potential indirect effects on oral health; (2) characterize oral cavity-specific adverse events by assessing their prevalence, severity, and underlying mechanisms; and (3) analyze the available data on the prospective applications of semaglutide beyond metabolic disease, particularly its influence on oral tissues. A structured study selection process was followed and is illustrated in a flow diagram adapted from preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines [ Figure 1 ]. Although this review is narrative in nature, efforts were made to enhance transparency by reporting the number of records identified, screened, and included. Study selection criteria were defined to capture clinically relevant and mechanistically informative evidence appropriate for a narrative review. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed clinical or experimental research reporting primary or secondary oral healthcare outcomes associated with semaglutide. Clinical trials, observational studies, case reports, pharmacovigilance analyses, and review articles providing mechanistic insights were included. Articles published in English were considered without time restrictions. Editorials or commentaries lacking empirical data, studies addressing only systemic outcomes without oral relevance, and non-English publications were excluded. Study selection flow diagram based on preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines. The diagram illustrates the process of identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of studies in this narrative review Titles and abstracts were manually screened for relevance to oral healthcare outcomes or mechanisms potentially affecting oral tissues, including salivary function and mucosal immunity. Full-text articles meeting the inclusion criteria were reviewed in detail. Extracted data included study objectives, key findings, and reported oral adverse effects or mechanistic observations related to semaglutide exposure. The initial search yielded 312 records. After removal of duplicates, 256 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 214 records were excluded based on relevance criteria. The remaining 42 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, of which 13 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis. Consistent with SANRA principles, formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied. However, qualitative appraisal and scientific reasoning were employed throughout the review. Primary evidence was distinguished from secondary or hypothesis-generating sources. Consistency of reported oral adverse effects across independent data sources was evaluated, and methodological limitations were documented. This approach enabled balanced integration of heterogeneous evidence while acknowledging inherent constraints. The literature search yielded 366 records across databases and registers. After removal of duplicates and screening based on relevance, a subset of 40 studies underwent full-text review, of which 13 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis [ Figure 1 and Table 1 ]. Evidence-based literature revealed that earlier studies (2015–2022) primarily examined semaglutide’s efficacy and safety in metabolic disorders, with oral adverse effects being reported incidentally as secondary outcomes. However, recent literature (2023–2025) demonstrates a deliberate shift toward investigating adverse oral events. Methodologically, the progression from efficacy trials to adverse event analyses indicates maturation in understanding semaglutide’s oral effects. Initial efficacy studies established baseline safety profiles, while later works delve into pathophysiology, often employing biochemical assays or imaging to link drug mechanisms to clinical observations. This literature search identifies a spectrum of studies ranging from randomized clinical trials to pharmacovigilance reports and case series, revealing emerging but fragmented evidence on semaglutide’s oral adverse effects. The qualitative analysis findings relating to oral adverse effects of semaglutide, based on the current review of selected studies, are tabulated [ Table 1 ]. The pharmacological actions of semaglutide, while beneficial for metabolic control, may inadvertently affect oral homeostasis through both direct[ 7 , 25 ] and indirect mechanisms,[ 10 , 20 , 23 , 26 ] particularly in patients receiving long-term therapy.[ 17 ] Qualitative synthesis of findings from the reviewed studies reporting about oral adverse effects of semaglutide and other systemic adverse effects with indirect oral complications ICER = Institute for Clinical and Economic Review, PIONEER = Peptide innovation for early diabetes treatment, HbA1c = glycated hemoglobin A1c, GLP-1-RA = glucagon-like peptide-1-receptor agonist, AE = adverse effects, FDA = Food and Drug Administration, FAERS = FDA adverse event reporting system, T1DM = type 1 diabetes mellitus, T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus, GERD = gastroesophageal reflux disease, GI = gastrointestinal, STEP = semaglutide treatment effect in people with obesity. Gastrointestinal adverse effects (e.g., nausea, vomiting, eructation, and GERD) are included as indirect contributors to oral complications as they lead to dental caries, xerostomia, and hyposalivation through mechanisms such as enamel hypomineralization, reduced oral intake, dehydration, and salivary gland hypofunction Direct clinical evidence, primarily from observational studies and case series, suggests an association between semaglutide use and xerostomia, along with related alterations in salivary function.[ 7 ] However, a substantial proportion of the available data are derived from indirect sources, including pharmacovigilance databases and studies primarily focused on systemic or GI outcomes rather than oral-specific endpoints.[ 15 , 20 , 21 , 23 , 25 ] Currently, there is no definitive evidence supporting that oral adverse effects are directly attributable to the pharmacological action of semaglutide. Reported oral manifestations appear to be secondary, indirect, or mechanistically uncertain.[ 15 , 21 , 22 , 24 ] Based on the available evidence, these findings can be organized into two broad domains: Oral manifestations: Xerostomia (dry mouth) and hyposalivation are the most consistently reported oral adverse effects associated with semaglutide therapy.[ 5 , 26 , 27 ] While the reported prevalence varies substantially across studies—with clinical trials often reporting rates below 5% and observational studies suggesting higher frequencies—xerostomia remains a clinically relevant outcome.[ 7 , 11 , 13 , 24 ] Clinical observations and case series have confirmed semaglutide-associated hyposalivation and related symptoms such as frothy saliva and oral discomfort.[ 4 , 7 , 13 , 24 ] Furthermore, there is an increased susceptibility to secondary oral complications, including dental caries .[ and oral candidiasis.[ 15 , 17 , 22 ] 16 ] These manifestations are likely multifactorial, stemming from reduced salivary antimicrobial defense and alterations in the oral microbial ecology.[ 11 , 20 , 23 ] Furthermore, these findings are supported by indirect evidence suggesting salivary gland functional alteration and broader mucosal involvement, although causal mechanisms remain insufficiently defined.[ 7 ] In patients with poorly controlled diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia may further compound this risk.[ 28 ] Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms: The underlying pathological mechanisms may further be classified based on GI mechanisms and other multifactorial mechanisms.[ 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] Accordingly, (a) GI mechanisms are a significant pathway for oral complications through GI adverse events. These occur in approximately 20%–30% of patients, with presenting symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea leading to reduced oral intake and dehydration, thereby collectively diminishing salivary secretion.[ 11 , 12 , 19 , 20 , 22 ] Additionally, delayed gastric emptying and gastroesophageal reflux contribute to an altered oral environment, potentially resulting in enamel erosion and further reducing salivary flow.[ 16 , 25 ] These GI-driven mechanisms are considered primary indirect contributors to xerostomia, hyposalivation, and an increased risk of dental caries.[ 13 , 15 , 22 , 24 ] Secondarily, (b) certain semaglutide-related oral manifestations cannot be fully explained by GI pathways and may involve multifactorial or as-yet undefined mechanisms. These include the following: Dysgeusia: Altered taste is a statistically significant signal identified in pharmacovigilance analyses (e.g., food and drug administration adverse event reporting system).[ 21 ] Sensory disturbances: Reports of oral paresthesia and hypoesthesia suggest broader mucosal or sensory involvement.[ 13 , 21 ] Dry throat: Frequently reported alongside oropharyngeal discomfort.[ 22 ] Dysphonia: Voice changes have been noted in broader sensory and mucosal reports.[ 13 ] The above findings suggest that semaglutide’s effects may extend to the sensory and mucosal tissues of the upper aerodigestive tract, though whether this reflects direct GLP-1-receptor activity or indirect systemic effects remains unclear. Although adverse oral events are widely reported across the current literature, emerging evidence suggests semaglutide’s possible modulatory effects on inflammation, bone metabolism, and tissue repair.[ 33 , 34 , 35 ] However, insufficient evidence is available to determine the prevalence of therapeutic oral effects. Interestingly, semaglutide has been found to influence inflammatory pathways and bone metabolism relevant to periodontal disease and tissue repair.[ 35 , 36 ] Potential applications include periodontal disease modulation, dental implant stability, improved wound healing, and effects on osseointegration; however, these findings remain preliminary and largely indirect.[ 35 , 37 , 38 ] Despite the growing recognition of these adverse effects, the current evidence base remains limited. Most data are derived from secondary analyses of metabolic trials or from isolated case reports, rather than from studies specifically designed to evaluate oral adverse effects.[ 11 , 15 , 21 , 22 , 24 ] Future research should prioritize prospective studies with standardized oral healthcare assessments to quantify incidence, establish dose–response relationships, and elucidate molecular mechanisms linking semaglutide’s systemic actions to oral tissue responses. The evaluation of evidences across the published literature reveals a complex interplay between semaglutide’s systemic pharmacological actions and its oral manifestations, encompassing both adverse effects and preliminary signals of therapeutic relevance.[ 39 , 40 ] While semaglutide demonstrates robust efficacy in glycemic control and weight management, its mechanisms of action—particularly delayed gastric emptying and GI intolerance—indirectly disrupt oral homeostasis.[ 25 , 40 , 41 ] The predominance of oral adverse effects as secondary findings in metabolic trials suggests that these manifestations have historically been under-recognized rather than uncommon.[ 15 , 21 , 22 , 24 ] Accordingly, GI adverse effects are considered indirect contributors to primary oral manifestations.[ 7 , 11 , 13 ] The evidence base for semaglutide-associated oral adverse effects comprises both direct and indirect sources. Direct evidence from clinical observations and case series supports the occurrence of xerostomia and related salivary dysfunction as clinically relevant outcomes.[ 7 , 11 , 13 , 24 ] However, a considerable proportion of the available data are derived from indirect sources, including pharmacovigilance databases and studies primarily focused on systemic or GI effects.[ 16 , 19 , 20 , 23 ] These indirect findings provide mechanistic plausibility but do not establish causal relationships. Furthermore, these findings indicate the need for targeted clinical studies to elucidate potential mechanisms and establish causality.[ 42 ] While the current evidence base provides mechanistic plausibility for both direct and indirect effects, the reliance on secondary analyses and spontaneous reporting necessitates prospective research with standardized oral healthcare assessments to confirm these associations.[ 27 ] The apparent discrepancy in reported xerostomia frequency across studies likely reflects methodological differences, including reliance on spontaneous adverse event reporting in clinical trials versus targeted oral health assessments in observational studies.[ 7 , 11 ] Evidence from clinical trials, pharmacovigilance analyses, and case series indicates that xerostomia arises secondary to GI adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced oral intake, which collectively diminish salivary secretion.[ 22 , 23 ] This observation aligns with pharmacological data suggesting that GLP-1-receptor activation may influence exocrine gland function, although the precise mechanisms affecting salivary glands remain insufficiently proved.[ 28 , 43 ] Clinically, reduced salivary flow has important downstream consequences.[ 24 ] Saliva is essential for oral lubrication, buffering capacity, antimicrobial defense, and enamel remineralization; its reduction may, therefore, predispose patients to the risk of dental caries, mucosal irritation, halitosis, and impaired oral clearance.[ 7 , 11 , 15 , 23 ] The increased incidence of dental caries reported in some trials likely reflects a multifactorial process involving hyposalivation, gastroesophageal reflux, and alterations in the oral microbiome.[ 15 , 22 ] Persistent xerostomia and oral discomfort may also negatively influence medication adherence, particularly when GI…

title: Prevalence and Systemic Factors Associated with Periodontitis among Kidney Transplant Recipients: A Cross-sectional Study in Vietnam
abstract: A BSTRACT Objective: Kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) are particularly vulnerable to periodontal disease due to long-term immunosuppression, metabolic disturbances, and chronic inflammation. However, data in Southeast Asia remain scarce. The aim of the study was to determine the prevalence, stage distribution of periodontitis, and to examine systemic and behavioral factors associated with the disease among Vietnamese KTRs; as a secondary exploratory aim, we evaluated selected systemic biomarkers (C-reactive protein [CRP], serum urea, and platelet count [PLT]) and descriptively summarized their cross-sectional discrimination with respect to the periodontitis status using prespecified receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. A cross-sectional analytical study among 300 KTRs at 103 Military Hospital, Vietnam Military University, Hanoi, Vietnam. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 300 KTRs at a teaching hospital in Hanoi, Vietnam, from June 2025 to October 2025. Periodontitis was defined and staged according to the 2017 World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions (American Academy of Periodontology/European Federation of Periodontology). Descriptive statistics, chi-square/Fisher’s exact test, and logistic regression were used to examine associations. Crude and adjusted odds ratios (ORs and aORs) were calculated. An exploratory ROC analysis was performed to assess the discriminatory ability of selected clinical and biochemical variables. Chi-square, t test, analysis of variance, multivariate logistic regression, and ROC analysis using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 27.0 were used for statistical analyses. Results: Periodontitis was present in 77.7% of participants. Stage I disease was most prevalent (33.0%), followed by Stage II (27.0%) and Stage III (16.3%); only 1.3% of patients had Stage IV disease. In multivariable analysis, poor oral hygiene (OHI-S; aOR = 3.47), lower PLTs (aOR = 0.986), higher CRP levels (CRP; aOR = 1.32), and elevated serum urea (aOR = 2.09) were independently associated with periodontitis. Conclusion: Periodontitis is highly prevalent in Vietnamese KTRs, predominantly in moderate stages, underscoring the need for preventive strategies. Systemic inflammation, renal biomarkers, and poor oral hygiene were strongly associated with disease. Integrating periodontal assessment into routine post-transplant care may support preventive oral health strategies in this population.
body: Periodontal disease (PD), encompassing gingivitis and periodontitis, is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the supporting structures of the teeth (gingiva, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone). Periodontitis, the advanced form of PD, is characterized by infection-driven inflammation, leading to progressive tissue destruction and eventual tooth loss. Beyond its local effects, periodontitis has been linked to a wide range of systemic conditions, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease (CKD), through mechanisms involving bacteremia, systemic dissemination of proinflammatory mediators, and immune dysregulation.[ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] Kidney transplantation improves many outcomes of end-stage renal disease, but kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) remain at risk for developing or worsening PD. Lifelong immunosuppressive therapy increases infection susceptibility and can adversely affect oral tissues; for example, cyclosporine can induce gingival overgrowth that hinders oral hygiene and promotes plaque accumulation, aggravating periodontal inflammation.[ 5 ] Additionally, the immunosuppressed state may blunt host responses to periodontal bacteria.[ 6 ] KTRs often have comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes and hypertension) and residual CKD that further heighten their periodontal risk.[ 7 ] Given these systemic influences, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, and platelet count (PLT) are clinically accessible biomarkers with biological relevance to PD: CRP reflects systemic inflammatory burden, urea captures the uremic/renal milieu associated with impaired immune function and tissue repair, and PLT integrates inflammation–hemostasis interactions.[ 8 , 9 , 10 ] Together, these markers provide plausible systemic correlates of periodontal status in KTRs. Despite this, periodontal care is frequently underutilized in transplant follow-up; for instance, only approximately 6% of KTRs in one cohort had ever been evaluated by a periodontist.[ 11 ] Several studies from Europe and South America have reported very high prevalences of periodontitis among KTRs, often exceeding 80%–90%, with a substantial proportion of patients exhibiting severe disease.[ 4 , 6 , 12 ] Identified risk factors include poor oral hygiene, older age, and systemic markers of inflammation or metabolic imbalance.[ 4 , 13 , 14 ] Nevertheless, evidence from Asian populations, particularly Vietnam, remains scarce. Vietnam has an increasing number of individuals living with kidney transplants; however, data on periodontal burden and associated factors in Vietnam are limited, restricting the generalizability of existing evidence to this setting.[ 15 , 16 ] Importantly, Asian populations, including Vietnamese KTRs, may differ considerably from Western cohorts with respect to oral hygiene practices, access to periodontal care, dietary and nutritional patterns, immunosuppressive regimens, and systemic inflammatory burden.[ 2 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] These population-specific differences underscore a critical knowledge gap regarding the periodontal health profile of Vietnamese KTRs and the extent to which systemic biomarkers such as CRP, urea, or PLTs may influence their PD risk. Closing this gap is essential not only for understanding the true burden of disease but also for developing tailored preventive strategies and integrating periodontal assessment into long-term transplant management in Vietnam. Therefore, this study aimed primarily to determine the prevalence and severity of periodontitis among Vietnamese KTRs and to evaluate demographic, behavioral, and clinical factors associated with its occurrence; as a secondary exploratory aim, we evaluated selected systemic biomarkers (CRP, serum urea, and PLT) and descriptively summarized their cross-sectional discrimination with respect to periodontitis status using prespecified receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. The minimum sample size was calculated using the single proportion formula: where we assume a periodontitis prevalence of 80% in KTRs based on previous international studies,[ 20 ] a 95% confidence level ( Z = 1.96), and ( d ) is allowable error ( d = 0.05). The required minimum sample was 246, and 300 participants were ultimately enrolled to increase statistical power. This cross-sectional study was conducted at the Department of Odonto-Stomatology, Military Hospital 103 (Vietnam Military Medical University), Hanoi, Vietnam, from June 2025 to October 2025. The study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the 108 Institute of Clinical Medical and Pharmaceutical Sciences (approval no. 4285/GCN-BV). We employed a consecutive sampling approach, enrolling all eligible KTRs who attended the transplant outpatient clinic during the study period. “Written informed consent (signed patient consent form) was obtained from all participants before enrollment and before any study-related procedures.” Inclusion criteria: A functioning kidney transplant for ≥6 months. Ability to provide informed consent and undergo periodontal examination. Exclusion criteria: Periodontal therapy or systemic antibiotics within the previous 3 months. Uncontrolled systemic conditions or bleeding disorders contraindicate periodontal probing. Pregnancy or inability to cooperate with clinical examination. Information on demographics, medical history, and transplant characteristics was retrieved from structured interviews and medical records. Periodontal examinations were conducted during the scheduled transplant outpatient follow-up visit; CRP, serum urea, and PLT were abstracted from routine blood investigations performed at the same visit, and when same-day testing was not available, the closest routine laboratory results within ±7 days of the periodontal examination were used. All eligible KTRs attending the outpatient transplant clinic during the study period were systematically screened against the predefined eligibility criteria and invited to participate, ensuring complete coverage of the accessible population and minimizing selection bias by avoiding preferential recruitment. Periodontal examinations were performed by five calibrated examiners using the University of North Carolina (UNC)-15 Probe, Hu-Friedy, Chicago, IL, USA. The examiners were blinded to participants’ medical and transplant-related information (including laboratory values and transplant follow-up records) during periodontal charting, and only eligibility/safety-related information was available to them. Periodontal probing depth (PPD) and clinical attachment level (CAL) were measured at six sites per tooth. Bleeding on probing (BOP), plaque index (PI), gingival index (GI), and simplified oral hygiene index (OHI-S) were assessed following standard protocols. The overall oral hygiene status was evaluated with the OHI-S. Radiographic assessment was performed using periapical radiographs, and alveolar bone loss was evaluated by estimating the distance from the cemento-enamel junction (CEJ) to the alveolar crest relative to root length, following standard periodontal radiographic criteria. Interexaminer agreement was assessed using Cohen’s Kappa coefficient for categorical measures (BOP, PI, and GI) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for continuous variables (PPD and CAL). Both Kappa (>0.80) and ICC (>0.85) values indicated excellent reliability. Calibration was conducted on 20 volunteer patients before data collection. The reported interexaminer reliability statistics were calculated after the initial calibration exercise on the 20 volunteer patients and before participant enrollment/data collection. A mid-study recalibration session was performed after examining 150 participants to maintain consistency [ Figure 1 ]. Flowchart illustrating the selection of participants included in the final analysis Periodontitis was defined and classified according to the 2017 World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions. A participant was diagnosed with periodontitis if (i) interdental CAL was detectable at ≥2 nonadjacent teeth or (ii) buccal/oral CAL ≥3 mm with PDD >3 mm was detectable at ≥2 teeth, and the observed attachment loss could not be attributed to nonperiodontitis causes (e.g., traumatic recession, cervical caries/restorations extending to the CEJ, endodontic lesions draining through the marginal periodontium, or tooth fractures). Radiographic bone loss was recorded as the percentage of root length affected (CEJ-to-crest distance/root length) and used to support staging according to the 2017 American Academy of Periodontology [AAP]/European Federation of Periodontology [EFP] criteria. Disease severity was staged (stages I–IV) based on the level of interdental CAL, radiographic bone loss, and tooth loss due to periodontitis, following the 2017 AAP/EFP criteria. Disease extent was classified as localized (<30% of teeth involved) or generalized (≥30%). Because longitudinal data on progression and baseline radiographs were not available for grading, analyses focused on the staging framework. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (IQR). Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Group differences were examined via t test, Mann–Whitney U , χ 2 , or Fisher’s exact tests as appropriate. Bivariable analyses were conducted solely to describe distributional differences between groups, whereas logistic regression analyses were used to estimate the association magnitude. For regression analyses, periodontal clinical parameters used to define or closely overlap with the diagnosis of periodontitis (PPD, CAL, BOP, GI, and PI) were excluded a priori to avoid circularity. Candidate covariates were selected based on clinical plausibility and prior literature, including demographic, behavioral, transplant-related, comorbid, oral hygiene, and systemic laboratory variables. A complete accounting of all variables considered during model building, including coding, inclusion/exclusion status, and the reason for exclusion or nonretention, is provided in Supplementary Table S1 . Univariate logistic regression was performed as an exploratory analysis only and was not used as the sole criterion for variable selection. Variables considered clinically relevant and/or showing suggestive univariable associations were entered into the multivariable logistic regression model. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Model fit was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test as a supplementary calibration check. To complement the association analyses, and not to develop, test, or validate a clinical prediction or diagnostic model, a prespecified exploratory descriptive ROC analysis was performed for a limited set of clinically plausible and routinely available variables in kidney transplant follow-up (OHI-S, CRP, serum urea, and PLT). Discrimination was summarized using the area under the ROC curve (AUC) with 95% CIs and P value testing AUC against the no-discrimination value of 0.50. For each variable, a provisional optimal cutoff was identified by maximizing the Youden index (J = sensitivity + specificity − 1), and the corresponding sensitivity and specificity were reported. For variables with AUC < 0.50, discrimination was interpreted in the opposite direction (i.e., lower values indicating a higher likelihood of periodontitis), and cutoffs were reported accordingly. Because no prediction model development, internal validation, or external validation was performed, these ROC findings and derived cutoffs should be interpreted strictly as exploratory, descriptive, and hypothesis-generating only, with no direct diagnostic or predictive implication. All analyses were performed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The cohort comprised 219 males (73.0%) and 81 females (27.0%), with a mean age of 43.5 ± 11.1 years. Most were middle-aged (39.7% aged 35–44, 21.0% aged 45–54, and 4.3% ≥65). The median post-transplant duration was 60 months (IQR 48). Diabetes prevalence was 13.0%, that of hypertension was 36.7%, and 20.7% were current smokers [ Table 1 ]. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of kidney transplant recipients ( n = 300) SD = standard deviation, IQR = interquartile range Oral hygiene habits among the KTRs were generally suboptimal. A total of 76.3% of participants reported brushing their teeth twice daily, while 23.7% brushed less than twice a day. Only 34.7% used interdental cleaning aids such as dental floss or similar tools, whereas 65.3% did not use any interdental aids. Regular dental visits were infrequent: merely 20.0% of participants received at least one dental examination per year, while 80.0% had fewer than one checkup annually. Among all participants, 233 (77.7%) had clinical periodontitis. By the 2017 AAP/EFP classification, Stage I was most frequent (99 patients, 33.0%), followed by Stage II (81, 27.0%) and Stage III (49, 16.3%); only four patients (1.3%) had Stage IV. Disease extent was usually localized: among periodontitis cases, 225/233 (96.6%) had <30% of teeth affected [ Figure 2 ]. Distribution of periodontitis severity (2017 American Academy of Periodontology/European Federation of Periodontology classification) in the total sample ( n = 300) and disease extent among periodontitis cases ( n = 233) The bivariable analysis [ Table 2 ] descriptively summarizes distributional differences in selected demographic and behavioral characteristics according to the periodontitis status. Periodontitis prevalence was higher among rural than urban residents (82.5% vs 71.3%, P = 0.02). Periodontitis prevalence was 79.0% in current smokers and 77.3% in nonsmokers. A strong relationship was observed for both personal (93.5% vs 6.5%, P < 0.001) and family history of periodontitis (92.1% vs 7.9%, P < 0.001). In contrast, sex, age group, education, and post-transplant duration did not show statistically significant differences between groups. Bivariate comparisons for factors related to periodontitis ( n = 300) PD: periodontal disease. Chi-square test; Fisher’s exact test; Table 2 presents bivariable descriptive comparisons only and is intended to summarize group distributions; estimates of association magnitude are provided in the logistic regression analyses [ Tables 3 and 4 ] In the univariate analysis [ Table 3 ], several nondiagnostic behavioral and biochemical factors showed significant crude associations with periodontitis. Age (per 10-year increase) and rural residence were associated with higher crude odds of periodontitis (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.05–1.80; and OR = 1.90, 95% CI: 1.10–3.30, respectively. Personal history of periodontitis (OR = 2.24; 95% CI: 1.3–3.9) and family history of periodontitis (OR = 4.16; 95% CI: 2.2–7.9) were associated with higher odds of disease. Higher OHI-S (OR = 9.05; 95% CI: 5.06–16.2), CRP (OR = 1.37; 95% CI: 1.16–1.49), urea (OR = 2.4; 95% CI: 1.9–3.04), creatinine (OR = 1.03; 95% CI: 1.02–1.04), and lower PLT (OR = 0.99; 95% CI: 0.99–1) were also significantly associated with periodontitis. In contrast, demographic variables, education, post-transplant duration, smoking, diabetes, and hypertension did not show statistically meaningful crude associations. Prevalence and Systemic Factors Associated with Periodontitis among Kidney Transplant Recipients: A Cross-sectional Study in Vietnam

A BSTRACT Objective: Kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) are particularly vulnerable to periodontal disease due to long-term immunosuppression, metabolic disturbances, and chronic inflammation. However, data in Southeast Asia remain scarce. The aim of the study was to determine the prevalence, stage distribution of periodontitis, and to examine systemic and behavioral factors associated with the disease among Vietnamese KTRs; as a secondary exploratory aim, we evaluated selected systemic biomarkers (C-reactive protein [CRP], serum urea, and platelet count [PLT]) and descriptively summarized their cross-sectional discrimination with respect to the periodontitis status using prespecified receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. A cross-sectional analytical study among 300 KTRs at 103 Military Hospital, Vietnam Military University, Hanoi, Vietnam. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 300 KTRs at a teaching hospital in Hanoi, Vietnam, from June 2025 to October 2025. Periodontitis was defined and staged according to the 2017 World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions (American Academy of Periodontology/European Federation of Periodontology). Descriptive statistics, chi-square/Fisher’s exact test, and logistic regression were used to examine associations. Crude and adjusted odds ratios (ORs and aORs) were calculated. An exploratory ROC analysis was performed to assess the discriminatory ability of selected clinical and biochemical variables. Chi-square, t test, analysis of variance, multivariate logistic regression, and ROC analysis using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 27.0 were used for statistical analyses. Results: Periodontitis was present in 77.7% of participants. Stage I disease was most prevalent (33.0%), followed by Stage II (27.0%) and Stage III (16.3%); only 1.3% of patients had Stage IV disease. In multivariable analysis, poor oral hygiene (OHI-S; aOR = 3.47), lower PLTs (aOR = 0.986), higher CRP levels (CRP; aOR = 1.32), and elevated serum urea (aOR = 2.09) were independently associated with periodontitis. Conclusion: Periodontitis is highly prevalent in Vietnamese KTRs, predominantly in moderate stages, underscoring the need for preventive strategies. Systemic inflammation, renal biomarkers, and poor oral hygiene were strongly associated with disease. Integrating periodontal assessment into routine post-transplant care may support preventive oral health strategies in this population.

Periodontal disease (PD), encompassing gingivitis and periodontitis, is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the supporting structures of the teeth (gingiva, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone). Periodontitis, the advanced form of PD, is characterized by infection-driven inflammation, leading to progressive tissue destruction and eventual tooth loss. Beyond its local effects, periodontitis has been linked to a wide range of systemic conditions, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease (CKD), through mechanisms involving bacteremia, systemic dissemination of proinflammatory mediators, and immune dysregulation.[ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] Kidney transplantation improves many outcomes of end-stage renal disease, but kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) remain at risk for developing or worsening PD. Lifelong immunosuppressive therapy increases infection susceptibility and can adversely affect oral tissues; for example, cyclosporine can induce gingival overgrowth that hinders oral hygiene and promotes plaque accumulation, aggravating periodontal inflammation.[ 5 ] Additionally, the immunosuppressed state may blunt host responses to periodontal bacteria.[ 6 ] KTRs often have comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes and hypertension) and residual CKD that further heighten their periodontal risk.[ 7 ] Given these systemic influences, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, and platelet count (PLT) are clinically accessible biomarkers with biological relevance to PD: CRP reflects systemic inflammatory burden, urea captures the uremic/renal milieu associated with impaired immune function and tissue repair, and PLT integrates inflammation–hemostasis interactions.[ 8 , 9 , 10 ] Together, these markers provide plausible systemic correlates of periodontal status in KTRs. Despite this, periodontal care is frequently underutilized in transplant follow-up; for instance, only approximately 6% of KTRs in one cohort had ever been evaluated by a periodontist.[ 11 ] Several studies from Europe and South America have reported very high prevalences of periodontitis among KTRs, often exceeding 80%–90%, with a substantial proportion of patients exhibiting severe disease.[ 4 , 6 , 12 ] Identified risk factors include poor oral hygiene, older age, and systemic markers of inflammation or metabolic imbalance.[ 4 , 13 , 14 ] Nevertheless, evidence from Asian populations, particularly Vietnam, remains scarce. Vietnam has an increasing number of individuals living with kidney transplants; however, data on periodontal burden and associated factors in Vietnam are limited, restricting the generalizability of existing evidence to this setting.[ 15 , 16 ] Importantly, Asian populations, including Vietnamese KTRs, may differ considerably from Western cohorts with respect to oral hygiene practices, access to periodontal care, dietary and nutritional patterns, immunosuppressive regimens, and systemic inflammatory burden.[ 2 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] These population-specific differences underscore a critical knowledge gap regarding the periodontal health profile of Vietnamese KTRs and the extent to which systemic biomarkers such as CRP, urea, or PLTs may influence their PD risk. Closing this gap is essential not only for understanding the true burden of disease but also for developing tailored preventive strategies and integrating periodontal assessment into long-term transplant management in Vietnam. Therefore, this study aimed primarily to determine the prevalence and severity of periodontitis among Vietnamese KTRs and to evaluate demographic, behavioral, and clinical factors associated with its occurrence; as a secondary exploratory aim, we evaluated selected systemic biomarkers (CRP, serum urea, and PLT) and descriptively summarized their cross-sectional discrimination with respect to periodontitis status using prespecified receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. The minimum sample size was calculated using the single proportion formula: where we assume a periodontitis prevalence of 80% in KTRs based on previous international studies,[ 20 ] a 95% confidence level ( Z = 1.96), and ( d ) is allowable error ( d = 0.05). The required minimum sample was 246, and 300 participants were ultimately enrolled to increase statistical power. This cross-sectional study was conducted at the Department of Odonto-Stomatology, Military Hospital 103 (Vietnam Military Medical University), Hanoi, Vietnam, from June 2025 to October 2025. The study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the 108 Institute of Clinical Medical and Pharmaceutical Sciences (approval no. 4285/GCN-BV). We employed a consecutive sampling approach, enrolling all eligible KTRs who attended the transplant outpatient clinic during the study period. “Written informed consent (signed patient consent form) was obtained from all participants before enrollment and before any study-related procedures.” Inclusion criteria: A functioning kidney transplant for ≥6 months. Ability to provide informed consent and undergo periodontal examination. Exclusion criteria: Periodontal therapy or systemic antibiotics within the previous 3 months. Uncontrolled systemic conditions or bleeding disorders contraindicate periodontal probing. Pregnancy or inability to cooperate with clinical examination. Information on demographics, medical history, and transplant characteristics was retrieved from structured interviews and medical records. Periodontal examinations were conducted during the scheduled transplant outpatient follow-up visit; CRP, serum urea, and PLT were abstracted from routine blood investigations performed at the same visit, and when same-day testing was not available, the closest routine laboratory results within ±7 days of the periodontal examination were used. All eligible KTRs attending the outpatient transplant clinic during the study period were systematically screened against the predefined eligibility criteria and invited to participate, ensuring complete coverage of the accessible population and minimizing selection bias by avoiding preferential recruitment. Periodontal examinations were performed by five calibrated examiners using the University of North Carolina (UNC)-15 Probe, Hu-Friedy, Chicago, IL, USA. The examiners were blinded to participants’ medical and transplant-related information (including laboratory values and transplant follow-up records) during periodontal charting, and only eligibility/safety-related information was available to them. Periodontal probing depth (PPD) and clinical attachment level (CAL) were measured at six sites per tooth. Bleeding on probing (BOP), plaque index (PI), gingival index (GI), and simplified oral hygiene index (OHI-S) were assessed following standard protocols. The overall oral hygiene status was evaluated with the OHI-S. Radiographic assessment was performed using periapical radiographs, and alveolar bone loss was evaluated by estimating the distance from the cemento-enamel junction (CEJ) to the alveolar crest relative to root length, following standard periodontal radiographic criteria. Interexaminer agreement was assessed using Cohen’s Kappa coefficient for categorical measures (BOP, PI, and GI) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for continuous variables (PPD and CAL). Both Kappa (>0.80) and ICC (>0.85) values indicated excellent reliability. Calibration was conducted on 20 volunteer patients before data collection. The reported interexaminer reliability statistics were calculated after the initial calibration exercise on the 20 volunteer patients and before participant enrollment/data collection. A mid-study recalibration session was performed after examining 150 participants to maintain consistency [ Figure 1 ]. A participant was diagnosed with periodontitis if (i) interdental CAL was detectable at ≥2 nonadjacent teeth or (ii) buccal/oral CAL ≥3 mm with PDD >3 mm was detectable at ≥2 teeth, and the observed attachment loss could not be attributed to nonperiodontitis causes (e.g., traumatic recession, cervical caries/restorations extending to the CEJ, endodontic lesions draining through the marginal periodontium, or tooth fractures). Radiographic bone loss was recorded as the percentage of root length affected (CEJ-to-crest distance/root length) and used to support staging according to the 2017 American Academy of Periodontology [AAP]/European Federation of Periodontology [EFP] criteria. Disease severity was staged (stages I–IV) based on the level of interdental CAL, radiographic bone loss, and tooth loss due to periodontitis, following the 2017 AAP/EFP criteria. Disease extent was classified as localized (<30% of teeth involved) or generalized (≥30%). Because longitudinal data on progression and baseline radiographs were not available for grading, analyses focused on the staging framework. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (IQR). Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Group differences were examined via t test, Mann–Whitney U , χ 2 , or Fisher’s exact tests as appropriate. Bivariable analyses were conducted solely to describe distributional differences between groups, whereas logistic regression analyses were used to estimate the association magnitude. For regression analyses, periodontal clinical parameters used to define or closely overlap with the diagnosis of periodontitis (PPD, CAL, BOP, GI, and PI) were excluded a priori to avoid circularity. Candidate covariates were selected based on clinical plausibility and prior literature, including demographic, behavioral, transplant-related, comorbid, oral hygiene, and systemic laboratory variables. A complete accounting of all variables considered during model building, including coding, inclusion/exclusion status, and the reason for exclusion or nonretention, is provided in Supplementary Table S1 . Univariate logistic regression was performed as an exploratory analysis only and was not used as the sole criterion for variable selection. Variables considered clinically relevant and/or showing suggestive univariable associations were entered into the multivariable logistic regression model. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Model fit was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test as a supplementary calibration check. Discrimination was summarized using the area under the ROC curve (AUC) with 95% CIs and P value testing AUC against the no-discrimination value of 0.50. For each variable, a provisional optimal cutoff was identified by maximizing the Youden index (J = sensitivity + specificity − 1), and the corresponding sensitivity and specificity were reported. For variables with AUC < 0.50, discrimination was interpreted in the opposite direction (i.e., lower values indicating a higher likelihood of periodontitis), and cutoffs were reported accordingly. Because no prediction model development, internal validation, or external validation was performed, these ROC findings and derived cutoffs should be interpreted strictly as exploratory, descriptive, and hypothesis-generating only, with no direct diagnostic or predictive implication. All analyses were performed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The cohort comprised 219 males (73.0%) and 81 females (27.0%), with a mean age of 43.5 ± 11.1 years. Most were middle-aged (39.7% aged 35–44, 21.0% aged 45–54, and 4.3% ≥65). The median post-transplant duration was 60 months (IQR 48). Diabetes prevalence was 13.0%, that of hypertension was 36.7%, and 20.7% were current smokers [ Table 1 ]. Only 34.7% used interdental cleaning aids such as dental floss or similar tools, whereas 65.3% did not use any interdental aids. title: A Case Report of Interdisciplinary Prosthodontic Rehabilitation and Voice Restoration in a Diabetic Professional Singer with Complex Dental Failure
abstract: A BSTRACT Dental pathology in professional singers can compromise the oral resonance chamber, jeopardizing their vocal performance and career longevity. Complex cases involving systemic diseases, psychological distress, and advanced oral deterioration require integrated multidisciplinary management. This report describes the interdisciplinary rehabilitation of a professional singer with severe oral structural compromise and significant systemic and psychological challenges. The management plan combined psychological counseling, medical optimization, surgical reconstruction, prosthetic rehabilitation, and targeted voice retraining. An 8-month program of structured psychological counseling reduced dental anxiety and restored treatment confidence in the patient. Medical optimization through coordinated endocrinology care achieved glycemic stability before the surgical intervention. Guided bone regeneration and staged implant placement ensured stable osseointegration, despite the presence of systemic risk factors. Prosthetic rehabilitation with a screw-retained metal–ceramic prosthesis restored gingival function and white and pink esthetics, while specialized vocal rehabilitation facilitated the recovery of resonance and projection. The integrated approach yielded complete restoration of oral function, resolution of psychological distress, stable implant integration, optimal prosthetic performance, and full return to professional vocal activity. This case demonstrates that with meticulous planning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and comprehensive psychological support, even high-risk patients with diabetes can achieve successful fixed prosthodontic rehabilitation, restoring both function and professional identity.
body: Tooth loss represents more than just a physical gap in dentition; it creates profound functional, esthetic, and psychological challenges that significantly impact the quality of life. Professional vocalists develop an intimate relationship with their oral anatomy over decades of training. The loss of teeth disrupts mastication and esthetics and alters the acoustic properties essential for professional-level vocal performance, similar to a violinist losing fingers, rendering the instrument unplayable. Diabetes mellitus compounds these challenges by impairing wound healing, increasing susceptibility to infection, and accelerating periodontal destruction.[ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] Research shows that uncontrolled diabetes significantly increases implant failure rates; however, with appropriate systemic control, predictable outcomes are possible.[ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] The psychological consequences of tooth loss, particularly in professional performers, extend beyond functional deficits to affect self-esteem, identity, and social participation.[ 1 ] This case is descriptive, which demonstrates how an integrated interdisciplinary approach addressing systemic health, oral function, and psychological resilience can restore both performance capacity and quality of life. This case report describes the successful rehabilitation of a professional singer, showing how a comprehensive approach that addressed physical, systemic, and psychological factors restored oral function and helped the patient return to her professional life. The management strategy involved coordinated dental rehabilitation with implant-supported prosthetic reconstruction, medical management, psychological counseling, and voice rehabilitation to address the patient’s functional, communicative, and psychosocial challenges. The outcomes assessed included restoration of oral function, implant success and prosthetic performance, improvement in psychological well-being, and recovery of voice function during the follow-up period. Through this comprehensive approach, the report highlights the potential benefits of integrated rehabilitation in enhancing patient-centered outcomes and quality of life. A 52-year-old female, professionally active as a singer, visited the prosthodontic department with concerns regarding multiple missing teeth and difficulties in chewing and vocalizing. She also expressed deep psychological distress stemming from repeated refusals of fixed dental treatment at other clinics, largely due to her poorly controlled diabetes and insufficient bone in the upper jaw. This emotional toll caused anxiety, loss of confidence, and mistrust of dental care. She also reported social isolation and suspension of her career for the past 18 months, accompanied by a complete loss of her professional confidence. She had type 2 diabetes mellitus, diagnosed 8 years ago, with a history of suboptimal glycemic control, as indicated by a recent glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level of 8.2% (reference range for nondiabetic individuals: <5.7%; controlled diabetes target: <7.0%). Intraoral examination revealed a failed 10-unit maxillary fixed partial denture (FPD) with extensive mobility and generalized horizontal bone loss, accompanied by severe vertical defects in the abutment region. The soft tissues appeared inflamed and edematous, with multiple carious lesions evident under the crown margins. In the mandibular arch, the natural dentition was largely intact, with some posterior restorations but no significant mobility or acute pathology. She received a FPD at a private practice 7 years ago. The prosthesis functioned adequately for 4 years before progressive failure occurred. As her dental condition worsened, her voice became weaker and less clear, eventually forcing her to stop working. This further intensified her psychological distress and reinforced her belief that her singing career had come to a permanent end. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) examination revealed generalized horizontal bone loss ranging from 4 to 6 mm, along with pronounced vertical bone defects surrounding the previously used abutment teeth [ Figure 1 ]. Residual vertical bone height ranged from 10.2 mm (sites 11 and 21) to 12.5 mm (posterior), sufficient for planned implant lengths without sinus augmentation. Bone density was classified as D2 (850–1050 Hounsfield units [HU]) in the anterior maxilla and D3 (350–650 HU) in the posterior region according to Misch’s classification, reflecting diabetic-related trabecular porosity. Despite bone loss, adequate vertical height was present in the maxillary region, eliminating the need for sinus lift procedures. Pre-/post-orthopantomogram showing generalized bone loss and a failed maxillary fixed partial denture before implant (A) and after 6 months of implant placement (B) Psychological counseling was provided by a clinical psychologist as part of the multidisciplinary rehabilitation program. Psychological status was assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and scores were recorded during follow-up evaluations. No formal psychiatric diagnosis was made using standardized diagnostic criteria. The pretreatment HADS-anxiety (HADS-A) and HADS-depression (HADS-D) scores were 19 and 18, respectively, indicating clinically significant anxiety and depression symptoms. Following rehabilitation, the scores decreased to 7 for anxiety and 6 for depression, reflecting improvement in psychological well-being. These findings are presented in Table 1 . HADS scores assessed at preconsultation (baseline), post-Phase II (presurgery), and 3 months postprosthesis HADS-A = Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-anxiety, HADS-D = Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-depression To address the patient’s severe dental anxiety and professional identity distress, a clinical psychologist was integrated into the interdisciplinary team. Over 8 months, 12 structured counseling sessions were conducted in parallel with the dental treatment. The initial sessions focused on psychological assessment using standardized tools, evaluation of dental trauma, and establishment of therapeutic objectives. Cognitive-behavioral therapy was employed to identify catastrophic thoughts, challenge hopelessness, and develop coping strategies using relaxation techniques and guided imagery. Mid-phase sessions addressed professional identity reconstruction, helping the patient redefine her self-worth beyond singing and set realistic, achievable treatment goals. Ongoing support focused on maintaining psychological progress, preparing for her return to professional activities, and preventing relapse. Key interventions included systematic desensitization through virtual and in vivo exposure, cognitive restructuring, mindfulness-based stress reduction, professional identity exploration, and strengthening her social support network. A comprehensive glycemic control protocol was initiated in collaboration with the patient’s endocrinologist to optimize diabetes management. This included intensive glucose monitoring, appropriate adjustment of medications (metformin 1000 mg twice daily and insulin glargine 20 units at bedtime), nutritional counseling, and lifestyle modifications, with the target of achieving an HbA1c level below 6.7% before surgical intervention. Dental preparation involved careful sectioning and removal of the failed FPD under local anesthesia, followed by thorough debridement and curettage. Antibiotic prophylaxis with amoxicillin (500 mg three times daily for 7 days) was prescribed, and chlorhexidine rinses were recommended for tissue conditioning. A conventional maxillary complete denture was fabricated as a transitional prosthesis to facilitate tissue healing and reconditioning. The denture also served to restore function and esthetics during the healing phase. Follow-up over 3 months showed significant improvements in soft tissue health and comfort. Following CBCT-guided planning and glycemic stability, implant surgery employed a full-thickness buccal envelope flap (crestal incision at 5 mm from the cementoenamel junction, vertical releases at premolars) for visibility and bone augmentation access. A flapless approach was not used due to vertical defects, which required Geistlich Bio-Oss (Geistlich Pharma AG, Wolhusen, Switzerland) (0.5 g per site) and autologous platelet-rich fibrin mixture. Neodent Grand Morse tapered implants (JJGC Indústria e Comércio de Materiais Dentários S.A., Curitiba, Paraná, Brazil) (surface: TiUnite-equivalent nanostructured sandblasted, large-grit, acid-etched) were placed under prophylactic amoxicillin (2 g, single dose), followed by 500 mg three times daily for 7 days postoperatively. Maxillary implant placement involved six implants at sites 11 and 21 (3.5 × 13 mm, 35 N · cm insertion torque) and at sites 13, 15, 23, and 26 (3.75 mm × 11.5 mm, 32–38 N · cm). [ 11 ] on an oboist highlights that, similar to singers, wind instrument players are highly sensitive to changes in oral anatomy. title: The 100 Most-Cited Articles on Periodontal Disease and Atherosclerosis: A Bibliometric Study (1989–2025)
abstract: A BSTRACT Objective: The association between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis has gained significant attention, yet the intellectual structure and most influential works in this interdisciplinary field have not been systematically mapped. This study aimed to identify and analyze the characteristics, collaborative networks, and evolving research trends of the 100 most-cited articles concerning the relationship between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis. Methods: A comprehensive search was performed in the Web of Science Core Collection on January 24, 2025. Bibliometric analysis and visualization were conducted using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the “bibliometrix” R package. Metrics included total citations, h-index, and keyword burst detection. Results: The 100 articles garnered a total of 13,968 citations (average: 195.6 citations per article). The United States was the leading contributor ( n = 40), with the University of North Carolina identified as the most productive institution. The Journal of Periodontology and Circulation were the primary publication venues. Keyword clustering identified six research hotspots: risk factors, inflammatory responses, infection, confounding variables, Porphyromonas gingivalis , and related cardiovascular conditions. Burst analysis revealed a paradigm shift in research focus from mechanistic “infection” (2004–2005) to clinical “therapy” (2013–2020). Conclusion: This study delineates the foundational literature and thematic evolution of the periodontal–atherosclerosis link. The observed shift in the literature from mechanistic to interventional studies may correlate with an increase in publications on periodontal treatment for cardiovascular prevention. These findings provide a data-driven roadmap for future longitudinal trials and clinical guidelines.
body: Periodontal disease is characterized as a chronic inflammatory disorder that results in the degradation of periodontal tissues. It manifests through various symptoms, including gingival erythema, hemorrhage, the development of periodontal pockets, and the deterioration of the supporting structures associated with the teeth.[ 1 ] Epidemiological research indicates a growing global prevalence of periodontal disease, with incidence rates demonstrating an upward trend as age increases.[ 2 ] The etiology of periodontal disease is complex and multifaceted, encompassing a range of contributing factors, including bacterial infections, inadequate oral hygiene practices, tobacco use, and genetic susceptibility.[ 3 ] Bacterial infections, especially those caused by pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis ( P. gingivalis ), Tannerella forsythia , and Fusobacterium nucleatum , are regarded as significant contributors to the development of periodontal disease.[ 4 ] Atherosclerosis, which is predominantly influenced by persistent low-grade inflammation, is defined by the accumulation of lipids, the proliferation of smooth muscle cells, and the development of a fibrous cap within the walls of arteries.[ 5 ] Periodontal disease is thought to play a role in the development of atherosclerosis via multiple mechanisms. Pathogens originating from the oral cavity may infiltrate the bloodstream, thereby initiating systemic immune responses that result in a persistent state of inflammation.[ 6 ] The systemic inflammation associated with periodontal disease not only heightens oxidative stress, thereby worsening atherosclerosis, but also entails interactions between oral microbiota and the host immune system, which may play a crucial role in the advancement of atherosclerosis.[ 7 ] Consequently, an in-depth examination of the research pertaining to the interplay between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis is crucial for a thorough comprehension of their intricate interactions. Bibliometrics applies quantitative and statistical methods to analyze scholarly literature. This methodology examines dimensions such as publication volume, citation frequency, research hotspots, and trends to reveal the characteristics, influence, and development of a research field.[ 8 ] While bibliometric analyses have recently explored links between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis,[ 9 ] the top 100 most-cited articles in this area remain unexamined. Given varying study quality, early-career researchers may struggle to identify credible work. Citation analysis—central to bibliometrics—assesses an article’s impact based on citation counts, with higher numbers generally indicating greater scholarly significance.[ 10 ] This study analyzes the 100 most-cited articles on periodontal disease and atherosclerosis, investigating their features, research trends, and leading contributors across countries, institutions, journals, and authors, as well as collaboration patterns. The findings aim to provide a reference for guiding future research directions. The literature review for this study was performed utilizing the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC). The WoSCC was chosen as the primary data source due to its status as one of the most reputable and extensively utilized databases for bibliometric research. It offers high-quality, peer-reviewed literature accompanied by detailed citation metrics, facilitating a thorough assessment of research impact. Additionally, the WoSCC provides advanced search capabilities and data export functionalities that are compatible with bibliometric analysis tools, thereby ensuring precision and consistency in the processes of data collection and visualization.[ 11 ] The search was performed on January 24, 2025. The search formula was as follows: (TS=(Periodontal diseases OR Periodont* OR Gingiv* OR Tooth loss OR Tooth migration OR Tooth mobility)) AND TS=(Atherosclerosis OR Atheroscleroses OR Atherogenesis OR Atherogeneses). The scope of the search was limited to publications authored in the English language. Additionally, all document types other than articles were excluded. Extracted data included publications and citations, titles, author affiliations, institutional associations, geographical regions, keywords, and journal names. Three advanced bibliometric tools were employed for the visualization and in-depth analysis of academic data: VOSviewer (version 1.6.20; Centre for Science and Technology Studies, Leiden University, Leiden, the Netherlands), CiteSpace (version 6.3.R1; Chaomei Chen, Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA, USA), and the R package “bibliometrix” (version 3.2.1; Massimo Aria and Corrado Cuccurullo, Naples, Italy). VOSviewer, acknowledged for its versatility, was used for the visualization and analysis of institutional and author collaborations, co-authorship dynamics, citation patterns, keyword co-occurrence networks, and co-citation networks.[ 12 ] This tool facilitated the visualization and examination of complex collaborative networks within the academic sphere, yielding significant insights into the relationships among authors, institutions, and publications. To improve the understanding of emerging trends and research focal points, CiteSpace was employed to detect instances of keyword bursts.[ 13 ] The parameters were defined in the following manner: time slicing was defined from 2004 to November 2020, with keywords designated as the selected node type. This study aimed to identify and analyze the characteristics, collaborative networks, and evolving research trends of the 100 most-cited articles concerning the relationship between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis. Methods: A comprehensive search was performed in the Web of Science Core Collection on January 24, 2025. Bibliometric analysis and visualization were conducted using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the “bibliometrix” R package. Metrics included total citations, h-index, and keyword burst detection. Conclusion: This study delineates the foundational literature and thematic evolution of the periodontal–atherosclerosis link. The observed shift in the literature from mechanistic to interventional studies may correlate with an increase in publications on periodontal treatment for cardiovascular prevention. These findings provide a data-driven roadmap for future longitudinal trials and clinical guidelines.

title: Polyvascular Atherosclerotic Disease: A Narrative Review of the Role of Systematic Bedside Vascular Examination
abstract: Polyvascular atherosclerotic disease refers to clinically significant atherosclerosis involving two or more arterial territories and is associated with a greater risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events than disease confined to a single vascular bed. Because atherosclerosis is a systemic process, the identification of disease in one territory should prompt clinicians to consider involvement elsewhere. Despite increasing reliance on advanced imaging, a systematic bedside vascular examination remains an accessible and inexpensive first step for identifying findings that may justify targeted investigation. This narrative review examines the role of clinical history and physical examination in evaluating patients with established or suspected atherosclerotic disease across multiple vascular territories. Particular attention is given to carotid auscultation, bilateral upper-extremity blood pressure and pulse assessment, cardiac evaluation, abdominal vascular examination, and examination of the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries, together with inspection for limb ischemic changes. The review also discusses the diagnostic limitations of individual physical findings and emphasizes that bedside examination should not be considered a substitute for objective testing. Rather, abnormal or suspicious findings can guide the selective use of ankle-brachial index (ABI) measurement, duplex ultrasonography, computed tomography angiography (CTA), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), and appropriate cardiac investigations. A structured approach that begins with systematic clinical assessment and progresses to targeted testing may help identify clinically important multiterritory disease while avoiding indiscriminate imaging of asymptomatic vascular beds. Incorporating comprehensive vascular examination into routine assessment may therefore strengthen cardiovascular risk recognition and support more individualized investigation and management of patients with systemic atherosclerosis.
body: Atherosclerosis is a systemic arterial disorder that can affect multiple vascular territories simultaneously or sequentially. Although patients frequently come to medical attention because of manifestations within a single organ system, such as coronary artery disease (CAD), ischemic cerebrovascular disease, or lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD), clinically relevant atherosclerosis may coexist in other vascular beds. Polyvascular disease, also termed multisite arterial disease in parts of the vascular literature, generally refers to clinically established atherosclerotic disease involving two or more major arterial territories [ 1 - 4 ]. The evidence base informing this narrative review includes contemporary clinical outcome studies, registries, and foundational approaches to the recognition of polyvascular disease [ 5 - 12 ]; diagnostic, screening, and clinical-examination studies evaluating carotid findings, inter-arm blood-pressure differences, subclavian disease, and lower-extremity vascular examination [ 13 - 20 ]; and disease-specific evidence addressing coronary assessment, aortic examination, renovascular disease, mesenteric ischemia, ankle-brachial index (ABI) assessment, and cardiovascular risk management [ 21 - 26 ]. Contemporary reviews estimate that polyvascular involvement may be present in approximately 30%-70% of selected populations with established atherosclerotic disease, although prevalence varies substantially according to the index vascular territory, disease severity, population characteristics, and methods used to identify additional disease [ 3 , 4 ]. Recognition of multiterritory disease is clinically important because cardiovascular risk increases as additional vascular beds become involved. In the European cohort of the REACH (Reduction of Atherothrombosis for Continued Health Registry), 22.8% of 19,117 symptomatic patients had polyvascular rather than single-territory disease, and patients with multiterritory involvement had a greater cardiovascular risk-factor burden and higher subsequent event rates [ 8 ].
