title: lncRNA Gm10451 mediates β-cell functional impairment in type 1 diabetes through the miR-24-3p/G6PD axis
abstract: Background Pancreatic β-cell dysfunction underlies type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) progression. Previous study showed that lncRNA Gm10451 is upregulated by high glucose and contributes to β-cell impairment, but its mechanism remains unclear. Methods Interactions among Gm10451, miR-24-3p, and G6PD were validated by dual-luciferase assay and Ago2-RNA immunoprecipitation (Ago2-RIP). Expression was measured by RT-qPCR and Western blot. β-cell functions were evaluated by glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS), CCK-8, TUNEL, ELISA, and hyperglycemic clamp in 30 mM glucose-treated MIN6 cell and STZ-treated C57BL/6 mice (Control injected with citrate buffer). Results Gm10451 was upregulated in diabetic models. Gm10451 acted as ceRNA to spomge miR-24-3p, which directly targeted G6PD. Overexpression of Gm10451 suppressed G6PD, aggravated oxidative/ER stress and inflammation, inhibited insulin secretion and promoted β-cell apoptosis. miR-24-3p mimic reversed these impairments. Conclusion Gm10451 promotes β-cell dysfunction via the miR-24-3p/G6PD axis, representing a poteniall therapeutic target for diabetes-related β-cell dysfunction. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12020-026-04736-y .
body: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is one of the common endocrine and metabolic diseases in children and adolescents, and T1DM is also known as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus [ 1 ]. T1DM pathology is characterized by T-cell mediated β-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency, and high blood glucose levels [ 2 ]. Disease progression can cause complications in the retina, kidneys, limbs, and other organs, severely hindering the development and growth of children and adolescents [ 3 , 4 ]. According to statistics, T1DM accounts for about 5% of all diabetes cases in children, but its incidence is increasing worldwide [ 5 – 7 ]. The pathogenesis of T1DM is complex, and there is currently no specific curative treatment available.Therefore, understanding the pathological process of T1DM and revealing its underlying molecular mechanisms is a critical step in the treatment of the disease. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are non-coding transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides that play a regulatory role in various physiological processes in organisms, such as gene silencing, histone modification, and DNA methylation [ 8 , 9 ]. Study shows that lncRNA affects islet function and T1DM development [ 10 – 12 ]. For example, pancreatic islet-specific lncRNA βlinc1 was crucial for maintaining the normal function of β-cell. To Knockdown the βlinc1 in Endo C-βH6 cell down-regulates the expression of pancreatic transcription factors Nkx2.2, Pax6, and Mafb [ 13 ]. In vivo inhibition of lncRNA Meg3 expression in mice directly leads to impaired β-cell insulin synthesis and secretion [ 14 , 15 ]. Additionally, down-regulation of lncRNA TUG1 in high blood glucose mouse β-cells leads to β-cell dysfunction and apoptosis [ 16 ]. In our previous work, we identified lncRNA Gm10451 as a hyperglycemia-induced transcript in pancreatic β-cell, and we observed that its overexpression correlated with β-cell function [ 17 ]. However, the downstream molecular mechanisms remained unknown. In this study, we test the hypothesis that Gm10451 acts as a ceRNA for miR-24-3p to regulate G6PD and oxidative stress in β-cell. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are non-coding RNAs that function mainly through complete or incomplete binding to their target genes [ 18 , 19 ]. They play important and complex roles in the progression of diseases, including cell differentiation, proliferation, metabolism, and apoptosis [ 20 ]. Increasing evidence indicates the involvement of miRNAs in the pathogenesis of T1DM.For example, miR-21 [ 21 ], miR-29 [ 22 ], and miR-124 [ 23 ] have been shown to regulate β-cell function and affect insulin production and secretion. In the past decade, previous researchers have clarified the function and role of miR-24-3p as a tumor suppressor in a variety of cancers, including lung cancer, colorectal cancer, bladder cancer and prostate cancer [ 24 – 27 ]. Interestingly, recent reports showed that miR-24-3p is dysregulated in T1DM and may serve as a biomarker for T1DM [ 28 ]. Therefore, we hypothesized that miR-24-3p may directly involved in T1DM pathogenesis, but its role in regulating β-cell function in T1DM is still unclear. Oxidative stress is closely related to β-cell dysfunction in diabetes [ 29 , 30 ]. Studies have shown that increased glycolytic flux in pancreatic β-cell promotes insulin secretion to counteract high blood glucose levels in diabetes mellitus [ 31 ]. However, sustained and excessive glycolytic flux also activates oxidative stress, leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid peroxidation levels rising, resulting in β-cell damage and apoptosis [ 32 ]. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes NADPH production in an NADP-dependent manner, further eliminating ROS and maintaining the reduced state of glutathione to counteract oxidative stress [ 33 ]. Prevalence of G6PD deficiency is higher in diabetic patients than in the general population [ 34 ]. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the imbalance of G6PD in T1DM may mediate oxidative stress reactions in β-cell and cause β-cell dysfunction. LncRNAs typically act as sponges to regulate the expression of downstream target genes of miRNAs [ 35 ]. Based on our previous observation that Gm10451 is upregulated under hyperglycemic conditions, we speculated that Gm10451 may regulate β-cell oxidative stress and cause β-cell dysfunction through the miR-24-3p/G6PD pathway. However, we acknowledge that the role of Gm10451 remains largely uncharacterized, and the current study is a hypothesis-driven investigation to explore its potential mechanism. Sixty male neonatal (2-day-old) C57BL/6 mice (college of veterinary medicine Yangzhou University) were randomly divided into two groups: Control group ( n = 10, intraperitoneally injected with euqal-volume citrate buffer, 10 mM, pH = 4.5) and Experimental group ( n = 50, intraperitoneally injected with 160 mg/kg STZ dissolved in citrate buffer). The animals were kept under controlled temperature and a 12 h dark-light cycle, with balanced food and free access to water. After 7 weeks, diabetes status was confirmed by measuring urinary glucose levels, and animals with glucose levels above 250 mg/dL were included in the study. Diabetic mice were randomly divided into four groups ( n = 10): Model group, oe-NC group (injected with oe-NC lentivirus via tail vein), oe-Gm10451 group (injected with oe-Gm10451 lentivirus via tail vein ), sh-NC group (injected with sh-NC lentivirus via tail vein), and sh-Gm10451 group (injected with sh-Gm10451 lentivirus via tail vein). Lentiviral injections were administered at 7 weeks after diabetes confirmation as a therapeutic intervention. Neonatal mice were used because they exhibit enhanced β-cell proliferation and regeneration capacity, allowing for the assessment of long-term metabolic effects following STZ-induced β-cell damage, which better mimics the progressive β-cell loss observed in human T1DM. After successfully constructing diabetic mice for 60 days, the experimental mice were fasted for 6 h and injected intraperitoneally with sodium pentobarbital at 80 mg/kg body weight for anesthesia. They were then fixed on the experimental table. Prior to the start of the experiment, tail blood was collected for testing fasting serum insulin (FINS) and fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels. Standard hyperglycemic clamp assay was performed with target blood glucose maintained at 15 mM by variable glucose infusion. Tail blood samples were collected at 1 min, 5 min, 10 min, and 15 min to measure the first-phase insulin levels. The average value of glucose infusion rate (GIR) was calculated at steady state (60–180 min). GIR [mg/(kg·min)] = glucose infusion rate (ml/min) × 100 (mg/ml) ÷ body weight (kg). The pancreatic tissue of young mice was cut into small pieces and fixed with neutral buffered formalin solution. Then, the tissue was decalcified in a 30% formic acid solution for 14 days, then dehydrated with ethanol in a routine gradient. The tissue was embedded in paraffin and cut into thin sections at 5 μm. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining, pancreatic tissue was stained with hematoxylin (Shanghai Beyotime, C0105M) for 5 min after dewaxing and hydration. After washing in 0.5% hydrochloric acid alcohol for 10 s, the sections were stained with eosin for 3 min. The stained sections were dehydrated twice for 2 min each, cleared in xylene twice for 5 min each, mounted with neutral balsam. The pancreatic tissue structure of each group of mice was observed under an optical microscope (Olympus, BX51, Japan) and photographed. MIN6 cells and 293T cells were obtained from ATCC. They were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% penicillin and streptomycin (American Hyclone Company). The culture was maintained at 37℃ with 5% CO 2 . MIN6 cells were incubated with 30 mM glucose for 24 h to establish an in vitro glucotoxicity model (HG group). miR-24-3p mimic and miR-NC were purchased from RiboBio (Guangzhou, China). Amplification of miR-24-3p cDNA sequence and its introduction into pcDNA vector (PEI; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) to construct the plasmid complementary DNA Gm10451. The full length of overexpressed Gm10451 was synthesized by GeneART (Life Technologies, UK) and cloned into the plasmid using KpnI and XhoI sites. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions, MIN6 cells in logarithmic growth phase were digested, counted, and transferred to a 96-well plate. Each group was designed with 5 wells. After adding the relevant factors, 10% CCK-8 solution (Shanghai Beyotime, C0037) was added to each well. Then, cells were incubated at room temperature in CO 2 incubator with 37 °C and 5% CO 2 for 4 h. Then, 150 µL DMSO was added to each well, and the absorbance values (OD values) of each well were measured using a microplate reader (ThermoFisher, Multiskan 51119000, USA). The results were then calculated. The mouse pancreatic tissue was collected and homogenized, washing twice with PBS. The cell nuclear RNA and cytoplasmic RNA were isolated using the Ambion PARIS Kit (Thermo Fisher, AM1921) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Subsequently, reverse transcription and RT-qPCR were performed, and the relative expression levels of Gm10451 in the cell nucleus and cytoplasm were calculated separately. U6 was used as the endogenous control for the cell nucleus, and GAPDH was used as the endogenous control for the cytoplasm. First, washing the cells with PBS and fixing in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min. Then, the cells were washed with PBS. Add PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 to the wells and incubate with the cells for 5 min at room temperature. PBS second wash of cells. Add 50 µL of TUNEL reaction mixture to the cells and incubate at 37 °C for 60 min away from light. The cells were washed with PBS for the third time. lncRNA Gm10451 mediates β-cell functional impairment in type 1 diabetes through the miR-24-3p/G6PD axis

Background Pancreatic β-cell dysfunction underlies type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) progression. Previous study showed that lncRNA Gm10451 is upregulated by high glucose and contributes to β-cell impairment, but its mechanism remains unclear. Methods Interactions among Gm10451, miR-24-3p, and G6PD were validated by dual-luciferase assay and Ago2-RNA immunoprecipitation (Ago2-RIP). Expression was measured by RT-qPCR and Western blot. β-cell functions were evaluated by glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS), CCK-8, TUNEL, ELISA, and hyperglycemic clamp in 30 mM glucose-treated MIN6 cell and STZ-treated C57BL/6 mice (Control injected with citrate buffer). Results Gm10451 was upregulated in diabetic models. Gm10451 acted as ceRNA to spomge miR-24-3p, which directly targeted G6PD. Overexpression of Gm10451 suppressed G6PD, aggravated oxidative/ER stress and inflammation, inhibited insulin secretion and promoted β-cell apoptosis. miR-24-3p mimic reversed these impairments. Conclusion Gm10451 promotes β-cell dysfunction via the miR-24-3p/G6PD axis, representing a poteniall therapeutic target for diabetes-related β-cell dysfunction. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is one of the common endocrine and metabolic diseases in children and adolescents, and T1DM is also known as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus [ 1 ]. T1DM pathology is characterized by T-cell mediated β-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency, and high blood glucose levels [ 2 ]. Disease progression can cause complications in the retina, kidneys, limbs, and other organs, severely hindering the development and growth of children and adolescents [ 3 , 4 ]. According to statistics, T1DM accounts for about 5% of all diabetes cases in children, but its incidence is increasing worldwide [ 5 – 7 ]. The pathogenesis of T1DM is complex, and there is currently no specific curative treatment available.Therefore, understanding the pathological process of T1DM and revealing its underlying molecular mechanisms is a critical step in the treatment of the disease. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are non-coding transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides that play a regulatory role in various physiological processes in organisms, such as gene silencing, histone modification, and DNA methylation [ 8 , 9 ]. Study shows that lncRNA affects islet function and T1DM development [ 10 – 12 ]. For example, pancreatic islet-specific lncRNA βlinc1 was crucial for maintaining the normal function of β-cell. To Knockdown the βlinc1 in Endo C-βH6 cell down-regulates the expression of pancreatic transcription factors Nkx2.2, Pax6, and Mafb [ 13 ]. In vivo inhibition of lncRNA Meg3 expression in mice directly leads to impaired β-cell insulin synthesis and secretion [ 14 , 15 ]. Additionally, down-regulation of lncRNA TUG1 in high blood glucose mouse β-cells leads to β-cell dysfunction and apoptosis [ 16 ]. In our previous work, we identified lncRNA Gm10451 as a hyperglycemia-induced transcript in pancreatic β-cell, and we observed that its overexpression correlated with β-cell function [ 17 ]. However, the downstream molecular mechanisms remained unknown. In this study, we test the hypothesis that Gm10451 acts as a ceRNA for miR-24-3p to regulate G6PD and oxidative stress in β-cell. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are non-coding RNAs that function mainly through complete or incomplete binding to their target genes [ 18 , 19 ]. They play important and complex roles in the progression of diseases, including cell differentiation, proliferation, metabolism, and apoptosis [ 20 ]. Increasing evidence indicates the involvement of miRNAs in the pathogenesis of T1DM.For example, miR-21 [ 21 ], miR-29 [ 22 ], and miR-124 [ 23 ] have been shown to regulate β-cell function and affect insulin production and secretion. In the past decade, previous researchers have clarified the function and role of miR-24-3p as a tumor suppressor in a variety of cancers, including lung cancer, colorectal cancer, bladder cancer and prostate cancer [ 24 – 27 ]. Interestingly, recent reports showed that miR-24-3p is dysregulated in T1DM and may serve as a biomarker for T1DM [ 28 ]. Therefore, we hypothesized that miR-24-3p may directly involved in T1DM pathogenesis, but its role in regulating β-cell function in T1DM is still unclear. Oxidative stress is closely related to β-cell dysfunction in diabetes [ 29 , 30 ]. Studies have shown that increased glycolytic flux in pancreatic β-cell promotes insulin secretion to counteract high blood glucose levels in diabetes mellitus [ 31 ]. However, sustained and excessive glycolytic flux also activates oxidative stress, leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lipid peroxidation levels rising, resulting in β-cell damage and apoptosis [ 32 ]. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes NADPH production in an NADP-dependent manner, further eliminating ROS and maintaining the reduced state of glutathione to counteract oxidative stress [ 33 ]. Prevalence of G6PD deficiency is higher in diabetic patients than in the general population [ 34 ]. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the imbalance of G6PD in T1DM may mediate oxidative stress reactions in β-cell and cause β-cell dysfunction. LncRNAs typically act as sponges to regulate the expression of downstream target genes of miRNAs [ 35 ]. Based on our previous observation that Gm10451 is upregulated under hyperglycemic conditions, we speculated that Gm10451 may regulate β-cell oxidative stress and cause β-cell dysfunction through the miR-24-3p/G6PD pathway. However, we acknowledge that the role of Gm10451 remains largely uncharacterized, and the current study is a hypothesis-driven investigation to explore its potential mechanism. title: Development and reliability testing of BRANT-MERQS-2A: A quality assessment tool for medication review type 2a reports
abstract: Introduction Medication reviews (MRs) are increasingly implemented to optimize medication use and address drug-related problems in patients with complex pharmacotherapy, with medication review type 2a (MR2a) representing an intermediate format involving a pharmacist-led structured assessment with patient interview, based on clinical and medication data, without direct prescriber interaction. Despite their widespread implementation, systematic and operational approaches to evaluate the quality of MRs remain limited. In Belgium, Medication Review type 2a (MR2a) has been implemented in routine practice of community pharmacies since 2023, yet no validated instruments exist to evaluate the quality of written MR2a reports. Aim This study aimed to adapt the existing BRANT-MERQS framework for the quality evaluation of MR2a reports and to assess the usability, reproducibility and reliability of the resulting tool (BRANT-MERQS-2A). Method Relevant criteria were selected from the original BRANT-MERQS and expanded with criterion-specific instructions to form the BRANT-MERQS-2A. Initial testing involved two student assessors independently evaluating 98 MR2a reports, with interrater agreement (IRA) assessed using weighted Cohen’s Kappa. In a subsequent extended testing phase, the same reports were assessed by 61 final-year pharmacy students, with three randomly selected students evaluating each MR2A report. Interrater reliability was evaluated using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and Gwet’s AC1. Assessment duration was recorded to evaluate feasibility. Results Initial testing demonstrated strong IRA between the two student assessors. In the extended student cohort, agreement at the criterion level ranged from poor to moderate, with an overall ICC of 0.62, indicating moderate reliability. Criteria differed in discriminatory capacity, with some showing high absolute agreement but limited variability. Assessment time decreased over successive rounds, reflecting a learning effect and improved efficiency. Conclusion The BRANT-MERQS-2A provides a feasible and structured approach for assessing the quality of MR2a reports. While variability at criterion level reflects the inherent complexity of MR2a, the tool demonstrates potential for self-and peer-assessment and offers a valuable foundation for further refinement and integration into routine quality monitoring. Improving the quality of medication reviews may enhance the identification and management of drug-related problems, contributing to safer and more effective medication use for patients. Over the past decades, pharmacists have evolved from primarily dispensing and compounding medications toward providing clinical advice, patient education and comprehensive pharmaceutical care [ 1 , 2 ]. According to the Pharmaceutical Care Network Europe (PCNE), pharmaceutical care is defined as the pharmacist’s contribution to the care of individuals, in order to optimize medicines use and improve health outcomes [ 3 ]. This shift is particularly relevant in the context of an aging population, where increasing life expectancy is accompanied by a higher prevalence of chronic diseases and, consequently, more complex medication regimens and polypharmacy [ 4 – 8 ]. To address the challenges with these complex regimens, medication review (MR) has become an increasingly adopted strategy [ 9 – 11 ]. The PCNE defines MR as a structured evaluation of a patient’s medications to optimize medication use and improve outcomes by identifying and addressing drug-related problems (DRPs) [ 12 , 13 ]. The PCNE further classifies MR into a simple form (Type 1), and intermediate form (Type 2) and a comprehensive form (Type 3) [ 12 , 14 ]. In multiple countries, different types of MR have been integrated into routine practice, although the extent of their adoption varies considerably [ 15 – 18 ]. Multiple studies demonstrate that MR interventions are effective in identifying, preventing and resolving DRPs, highlighting their potential value in improving medication management [ 18 – 20 ]. However, evidence supporting their impact on patient outcomes remains inconsistent, meaning that the overall clinical benefit and effectiveness of this service cannot yet be fully determined [ 9 , 18 , 19 , 21 , 22 ]. In addition, uncertainty persists regarding the quality of MR delivery, primarily due to limited reporting on essential intervention components and fidelity, hindering interpretation of their effectiveness [ 18 ]. Medication Review Type 2a (MR2a) has been implemented and reimbursed in Belgium since April 1, 2023 [ 23 ]. To support transparency and standardized documentation of this service, FarmaFlux developed an online electronic documentation form (e-form), integrated into community pharmacy software [ 24 , 25 ]. FarmaFlux is a non-profit umbrella organization responsible for secure and uniform exchange of data between pharmacies and supervising the quality and privacy of the information stored in the Shared Pharmaceutical Record (SPR) [ 25 , 26 ]. The e-form guides pharmacists through the MR2a process while systematically capturing key elements of the intervention [ 24 ]. It automatically loads predefined patient and medication data, allowing pharmacists to complete additional fields and to specify which medications are considered during the MR2a [ 24 ]. Despite the availability of this tool, MR2a uptake has remained relatively stable and occasional concerns regarding service quality persist [ 27 ]. Assessing the quality of MR is challenging due to the multifaceted nature of the intervention and the absence of a universally accepted definition of quality [ 28 – 30 ]. Systematic monitoring of care processes is essential for sustainability, as quality measurement and standardized indicators enhance transparency, identify variation in practice, and support targeted quality improvement [ 31 ]. Quality controls are therefore particularly relevant for MR implementation, as they contribute to patient safety, build trust among stakeholders and support long-term service sustainability [ 32 – 39 ]. Although international organizations have proposed conceptual quality frameworks for community pharmacy, their practical applicability remains limited due to their theoretical nature and the lack of operational tools to monitor clinical services, such as MR [ 40 , 41 ]. Despite extensive research demonstrating the potential clinical and economic value of MR, insight into professional standardization and real-time quality assurance remains limited [ 27 , 42 , 43 ]. Recent studies highlight significant variability in MR delivery, underscoring the lack of structured frameworks to monitor process quality [ 27 , 42 ]. While PCNE indicators provide a useful benchmark for process and structural aspect of services, such as MR, they do not capture clinical quality at the individual patient level and cannot determine whether the most relevant pharmacotherapeutic problems are identified or resolved, meaning high process scores do not guarantee optimal clinical outcomes [ 40 , 44 ]. In a previous study, a quality assessment tool was developed specifically for MR3, the BRussels ANTwerp Medication Review Quality Score (BRANT-MERQS), which evaluates MR quality based on a set of predefined criteria [ 45 , 46 ]. Although MR involves additional elements beyond the written report, this study focuses solely on this key part of the procedure [ 45 ]. Variability between assessors observed in the original study highlighted the need for a detailed scoring manual with clear guidance [ 45 ]. However, MR3 has not yet been systematically implemented in Belgium, in contrast to MR2a. To date, there are no comparable tools available for this type of MR. Given the growing emphasis on quality in healthcare, the development of robust quality measures for MR services is essential to ensure consistent, high-level delivery and to support the sustainable implementation and reimbursement of these services [ 33 , 35 – 39 ]. This study aims to adapt the existing BRANT-MERQS approach for MR2a quality evaluation and assess its usability, reproducibility and reliability. The Brussels-Antwerp Medication Review Quality Score for MR2a (BRANT-MERQS-2A) was modified from the original BRANT-MERQS [ 45 ]. Criteria potentially applicable to MR2a were independently screened for relevance by four researchers (ET, YQ, NB and AP), resulting in a preliminary list. Following consensus meetings including a fifth researcher (HDL), eleven criteria were selected based on their applicability to the Belgian MR2a context and their compatibility to the current e-form. Selection was conducted through iterative discussions, whereby discrepancies were resolved through deliberation until full consensus was reached for each criterion. To minimize inter-rater variability, a scoring manual with explicit, criterion-specific instructions for each level of the 0–3 scale (0: absence; 3 high quality) was developed. Consensus on wording and scoring structure was reached among ET, HDL, AP and NB, resulting in the initial BRANT-MERQS-2A version. The MR2a reports analyzed were anonymized PDF outputs automatically generated from the e-form, used to document MR2a performed by pharmacy students during their final internship. Final-year students are required to conduct at least four MR2a with their internship mentor. These reports were submitted as part of a mandatory internship assignment, and students could consent to their use for research. The MR2a’s were not restricted to a specific patient population, disease group, or demographic characteristics, but were conducted in accordance with the Belgian reimbursement criteria for MR2a, including, among others the use of at least five chronically reimbursed medications [ 23 ]. As such, the sample reflects routine practice rather than a predefined clinical subgroup. This data collection was routinely conducted as part of students’ final internship assignments. The initial testing phase took place between March 2025 and June 2025. Following the decision to pursue publication, an ethics committee application was initiated in October 2025 as a precautionary measure for the final testing phase, in which students assessed MR2a reports authored by peers. Due to the illness of ET, final approval from the ethics committee was obtained in January 2026. The final testing phase and subsequent analysis of the data were conducted between January and March 2026. A pilot phase was conducted to evaluate the clarity and preliminary usability of the BRANT-MERQS-2A scoring instrument prior to full application. An initial sample of 20 MR2a reports was independently assessed by two student assessors (NB and AP) using the preliminary version of BRANT-MERQS-2A. Following independent scoring, discrepancies between assessors were reviewed and discussed until consensus was achieved. The consensus ratings and interpretation of scoring criteria were subsequently reviewed and validated by ET and HDL. Based on observations from this pilot exercise, minor refinements were made to the wording and instructions of several scoring items to improve clarity and consistency of interpretation before commencing the main assessment phase. Subsequently, in the initial testing phase, 98 MR2a reports were independently evaluated by two student assessors (NB and AP). Inter-rater agreement (IRA) per criterion was assessed using weighted Cohen’s kappa in IBM SPSS [ 47 – 49 ]. Agreement patterns were additionally visualized using a Microsoft Excel-generated color-coded matrix (heatmap) [ 50 ]. Furthermore, assessment duration was tracked to estimate the practical feasibility of BRANT-MERQS-2A. In the final testing phase, 61 final-year master’s students in Pharmaceutical Sciences independently applied BRANT-MERQS-2A to the same 98 MR2a reports from the initial testing phase, all authored by other individuals. Participation was voluntary but encouraged. Participation was open to all final year master’s students without additional eligibility criteria. Students were randomly assigned to unique MR2a identification numbers. An allocation key ensured that assessors remained blinded to co-assessors, minimizing potential bias. Scores were submitted via an online Qualtrics survey [ 51 ], which also included limited background questions such as prior internship experience (weeks). IRR was interpreted using predefined agreement thresholds based on existing literature [ 52 , 56 ]. ICC values between 0.50 and 0.75 were considered indicative of moderate agreement according to Koo and Li [ 52 ], while Gwet’s AC1 values between 0.41 and 0.60 and between 0.61 and 0.80 were interpreted as moderate and substantial agreement, respectively, based on the benchmarks proposed by Landis and Koch [ 56 ]. AC1 evaluates absolute agreement, whereas the ICC assesses the consistency of relative ratings across items [ 57 ]. title: Association between High-Risk Pregnancy History and High-Efficacy Postpartum Contraception Use in North Carolina
abstract: Objective To evaluate factors associated with postpartum use of high-efficacy contraception among postpartum individuals in North Carolina and to assess whether a history of high-risk pregnancy was associated with increased use of WHO Tier 1 contraceptive methods. Study Design North Carolina Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) data from 2012 to 2020 were analyzed. The analytic sample included 6,993 postpartum respondents. A composite high-risk pregnancy history index was created using self-reported and birth certificate variables including preterm birth, low birth weight, obesity, hypertension, diabetes, depression, and inadequate prenatal care. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with postpartum use of WHO Tier 1 contraception. Results A cumulative sample of 13,866 postpartum persons were selected and invited to complete the survey; 6,993 responded and were considered participants. History of high-risk pregnancy was associated with slightly increased odds of postpartum Tier 1 contraception use (aOR 1.18, 95% CI 1.00–1.39, p < 0.05), although the association was modest. Other significant factors associated with high-efficacy contraception use included multiparity (aOR = 2.00, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.36), planned conception (aOR = 0.72, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.85), living infant (aOR = 2.85, 95%CI 1.42 to 5.72), postpartum contraception counseling (aOR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.45), postpartum depression screening (aOR = 1.40, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.89), Black and Asian races (aOR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.95 and aOR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.59, respectively), a bachelor’s or master’s degree (aOR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.82 and aOR = 0.66, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.89, respectively), and age groups 30–34 and 35–39 year-olds (aOR = 1.31, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.59 and aOR = 1.50, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.89, respectively). Conclusion In this North Carolina population, high-risk pregnancy history was only modestly associated with postpartum use of high-efficacy contraception. Other findings of this study suggest that high efficacy postpartum contraception use is influenced by demographic, reproductive, and healthcare interaction factors beyond pregnancy risk status alone. Interventions focused on equitable, patient-centered counseling and access to postpartum contraception may improve reproductive planning among patients with high-risk pregnancies who desire pregnancy spacing or prevention.
body: High-risk pregnancy is broadly defined as a pregnancy complicated by maternal medical, obstetric, behavioral, or social conditions associated with increased risk of adverse maternal, fetal, or neonatal outcomes. Common contributors include chronic hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obesity, previous preterm birth, low birth weight delivery, inadequate prenatal care, and mental health conditions, all of which are associated with increased risks of maternal morbidity, mortality, and recurrent pregnancy complications (Miller et al., 2022 ; Mvunta et al., 2019 ; Soltsman et al., 2021 ). Individuals with these conditions may benefit from pregnancy spacing and preconception optimization of chronic health conditions prior to subsequent pregnancies, particularly when future pregnancy is desired (Miller et al., 2022 ). Postpartum contraception is an important component of reproductive healthcare because it allows individuals to achieve their reproductive goals, including pregnancy prevention, pregnancy spacing, or planning future pregnancies after optimization of health conditions. Short interpregnancy intervals have been associated with adverse outcomes including preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age infants (Vricella et al., 2019 ). For patients with medical or obstetric conditions that increase pregnancy-related risks, access to effective contraception may provide additional opportunities to improve health prior to a subsequent pregnancy (Miller et al., 2022 ). The World Health Organization (WHO) tiered-effectiveness framework categorizes contraceptive methods according to typical-use effectiveness. Tier 1 methods, the most effective reversible and permanent contraceptive options, include intrauterine devices (IUDs), contraceptive implants, tubal sterilization, and partner vasectomy (Stanback et al., 2015 ). Previous studies examining postpartum contraceptive use among patients with high-risk pregnancies have produced mixed findings. A study from Thailand reported higher utilization of Tier 1 contraception among patients with high-risk pregnancies, particularly permanent contraception (Jaruamornjit et al., 2022 ). In contrast, a United States-based cohort study found that although patients with high-risk pregnancies expressed greater interest in highly effective contraception, actual uptake did not differ significantly from those without high-risk pregnancies (French et al., 2016 ). These conflicting findings suggest that factors beyond pregnancy risk status may influence postpartum contraceptive decision-making. North Carolina provides an important setting in which to examine postpartum contraceptive utilization. The state continues to experience substantial maternal health challenges, including high rates of chronic disease, pregnancy-related morbidity, and persistent racial disparities in maternal outcomes. Hypertensive disorders, cardiovascular disease, mental health conditions, and substance use disorders remain major contributors to pregnancy-related mortality, while Black women experience disproportionately higher rates of severe maternal morbidity and mortality compared with White women (North Carolina Maternal Mortality Review Committee, 2024 ). Additionally, North Carolina has implemented several policies intended to improve access to postpartum contraception, including Medicaid reimbursement for immediate postpartum long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) placement prior to hospital discharge. At the same time, federally mandated Medicaid sterilization consent requirements may create barriers to desired permanent contraception for some patients. Understanding how these healthcare and policy factors intersect with pregnancy risk status may help inform reproductive healthcare delivery within the state. Discussions of postpartum contraception must also acknowledge the historical and contemporary context of reproductive autonomy. North Carolina’s history of forced sterilization through the state Eugenics Board disproportionately affected Black women, individuals living in poverty, and other marginalized populations. These experiences continue to shape concerns regarding reproductive coercion, healthcare mistrust, and inequities in contraceptive counseling (Dehlendorf et al. 2011a , b ). Consequently, efforts to improve postpartum contraceptive care should be grounded in principles of reproductive justice, emphasizing informed consent, shared decision-making, and support for individual reproductive goals rather than increasing uptake of any specific contraceptive method. Although previous studies have examined postpartum contraception among patients with high-risk pregnancies, many have been limited to single institutions, specific patient populations, or clinical settings. The North Carolina Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) provides a population-based dataset that captures self-reported reproductive, behavioral, and healthcare experiences among postpartum individuals across the state, allowing evaluation of postpartum contraceptive use in a large and geographically diverse population. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate whether a history of high-risk pregnancy was associated with postpartum use of WHO Tier 1 contraception among North Carolina PRAMS respondents. Secondary exploratory analyses examined demographic, reproductive, and healthcare-related factors associated with postpartum Tier 1 contraceptive use. We hypothesized that respondents with a history of high-risk pregnancy would have greater odds of using WHO Tier 1 contraception postpartum compared with respondents without such a history. We further explored associations between postpartum contraceptive use and maternal age, race, educational attainment, parity, pregnancy intention, insurance status, healthcare interactions, and experiences of interpersonal violence during pregnancy. This study was a cross-sectional secondary analysis of data from the North Carolina Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) collected between 2012 and 2020, excluding 2013 due to unavailable statewide data. PRAMS is a population-based surveillance system developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in collaboration with participating state health departments to monitor maternal experiences and health behaviors before, during, and after pregnancy in the United States (Shulman et al., 2018 ). North Carolina participates in PRAMS and surveys approximately 1,700 postpartum individuals annually using a stratified random sampling design derived from state birth certificate records. Disproportionate numbers of women with low-birth-weight infants are selected to participate in PRAMS to adequately weight the samples to account for the underrepresentation of this population. Exclusion criteria utilized by North Carolina PRAMS included out-of-state births to North Carolina residents, in-state births to non-residents, records missing the mother’s surname, higher-order multiple gestations involving four or more infants, and births to mothers aged 12 years or younger. Survey administration included mailed questionnaires with repeated follow-up mailings for nonresponse, followed by telephone interviews when necessary. PRAMS survey responses are self-reported and linked with de-identified birth certificate data. The present analysis included only respondents who completed at least part of the PRAMS survey. Individuals sampled by PRAMS but lacking survey responses were excluded from analysis. The final analytic sample therefore consisted of postpartum respondents with both birth certificate data and survey data available. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate factors associated with postpartum use of high-efficacy contraception among postpartum individuals in North Carolina. A secondary objective was to assess whether a history of high-risk pregnancy characteristics was associated with postpartum uptake of World Health Organization (WHO) Tier 1 contraceptive methods. Importantly, the analytic sample was not limited exclusively to respondents with a history of high-risk pregnancy. Rather, all eligible PRAMS respondents were included, and high-risk pregnancy history was evaluated as an exposure variable within the larger cohort. A composite “high-risk pregnancy history” index was created a priori using maternal health characteristics and adverse obstetric outcomes identified in prior literature as associated with increased maternal or neonatal morbidity (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists [ACOG], 2021 ; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2022 ). Respondents were classified as having a history of high-risk pregnancy if they reported one or more of the following conditions or outcomes: Preterm delivery of the index pregnancy (< 37 weeks gestation). Previous preterm birth. Low birth weight delivery in the index pregnancy (< 2500 g). Previous low birth weight delivery. Pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes. Hypertensive disorders before or during pregnancy. Pre-pregnancy obesity (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m²). No prenatal care during the index pregnancy. Depression before or during pregnancy. Preterm delivery of the index pregnancy (< 37 weeks gestation). Previous preterm birth. Low birth weight delivery in the index pregnancy (< 2500 g). Previous low birth weight delivery. Pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes. Hypertensive disorders before or during pregnancy. Pre-pregnancy obesity (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m²). No prenatal care during the index pregnancy. Depression before or during pregnancy. Variables were identified using linked birth certificate data and PRAMS survey responses. All components of the index were weighted equally. Because this study pooled seven distinct PRAMS cohorts with year-specific sampling weights and stratification procedures, a weighted composite index was not constructed to avoid introducing disproportionate influence from any single survey year. The authors acknowledge that inclusion of depression within the composite index may differ from traditional clinical definitions of “high-risk pregnancy”; however, depression was retained due to its established association with adverse perinatal outcomes, impaired healthcare utilization, maternal morbidity, substance use disorders, and maternal mortality in pregnancy and the postpartum period (ACOG, 2023 ; Gavin et al., 2005 ; Jarde et al., 2016 ). The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recognizes perinatal mental health conditions as significant contributors to maternal morbidity and mortality and recommends routine screening and treatment during pregnancy and postpartum care (ACOG, 2023 ). This consideration is particularly relevant in North Carolina, where suicide and drug overdose are among the leading causes of pregnancy-associated maternal death according to the North Carolina Maternal Mortality Review Committee (North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, 2022 ). Given these public health concerns, depression was included as part of the broader high-risk pregnancy history construct. Nevertheless, this broader operational definition likely contributed to a higher observed prevalence of “high-risk pregnancy history” within the analytic sample compared with national estimates and should be interpreted accordingly. The primary outcome was postpartum use of a high-efficacy contraceptive method. A dichotomous variable was created to identify respondents reporting use of WHO Tier 1 contraceptive methods postpartum, including intrauterine devices (IUDs), contraceptive implants, tubal ligation, or partner vasectomy (World Health Organization, 2018 ). Covariates were selected based on prior literature examining postpartum contraceptive utilization, maternal healthcare access, and reproductive decision-making. Variables included maternal age, race and ethnicity, marital status, educational attainment, parity, pregnancy intention, infant mortality, and postpartum insurance status categorized as public insurance (Medicaid or Children’s Health Insurance Program [CHIP]), private/other insurance, or uninsured. Additional healthcare-related and psychosocial variables included interpersonal violence during pregnancy by a current or former partner, attendance at a postpartum healthcare visit, prenatal counseling regarding postpartum contraception, and postpartum counseling related to contraception, birth spacing, depression, and contraceptive prescription receipt. Insurance status was included given known structural barriers affecting access to immediate postpartum long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) and sterilization, particularly among Medicaid beneficiaries. During portions of the study period, reimbursement policies and federal sterilization consent requirements may have limited access to immediate postpartum Tier 1 contraceptive methods for publicly insured patients in North Carolina (Moniz et al., 2017 ; Borrero et al., 2014 ). Descriptive statistics and frequencies were calculated for all study variables among the full analytic cohort and among respondents reporting postpartum Tier 1 contraceptive use. Missing data were retained and reported descriptively. Missingness resulted from respondents leaving survey items unanswered or selecting “prefer not to answer” where applicable. Nonrespondents to the PRAMS survey were excluded entirely prior to analysis. Complete-case analysis was used for regression modeling; respondents with missing data for variables included in a given model were excluded from that analysis only. The proportion of missing data varied by variable and is reported in the study tables. Multivariable binary logistic regression was performed to examine factors associated with postpartum use of Tier 1 contraception. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and p-values were calculated. Variables were entered simultaneously into the regression model based on theoretical and literature-supported relevance rather than stepwise selection procedures. To improve interpretability, all regression findings were reported as increased or decreased odds of Tier 1 contraceptive use. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 28 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Between 2012 and 2020 (excluding 2013 due to unavailable statewide data), 13,866 postpartum individuals were selected to participate in the North Carolina PRAMS survey. Of these, 6,993 respondents completed at least part of the survey and were included in the analytic sample, corresponding to an overall response proportion of 50.4%. Among all respondents, 68.7% ( n = 4,802) met criteria for the composite high-risk pregnancy history index. Overall, 29.7% ( n = 2,078) of respondents reported postpartum use of a World Health Organization (WHO) Tier 1 contraceptive method, including intrauterine devices, contraceptive implants, tubal ligation, or partner vasectomy. Among respondents reporting Tier 1 contraceptive use, 71.6% ( n = 1,487) had a history of high-risk pregnancy. Participant demographic, obstetric, and healthcare-related characteristics are summarized in Tables 1 and 2 . Missing data varied across variables because some respondents did not answer specific survey questions or selected “prefer not to answer.” Only survey respondents were included in analyses; sampled nonrespondents were excluded prior to analysis. Exclusion criteria utilized by North Carolina PRAMS included out-of-state births to North Carolina residents, in-state births to non-residents, records missing the mother’s surname, higher-order multiple gestations involving four or more infants, and births to mothers aged 12 years or younger. Survey administration included mailed questionnaires with repeated follow-up mailings for nonresponse, followed by telephone interviews when necessary. PRAMS survey responses are self-reported and linked with de-identified birth certificate data. The present analysis included only respondents who completed at least part of the PRAMS survey. Individuals sampled by PRAMS but lacking survey responses were excluded from analysis. The final analytic sample therefore consisted of postpartum respondents with both birth certificate data and survey data available. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate factors associated with postpartum use of high-efficacy contraception among postpartum individuals in North Carolina. A secondary objective was to assess whether a history of high-risk pregnancy characteristics was associated with postpartum uptake of World Health Organization (WHO) Tier 1 contraceptive methods. Importantly, the analytic sample was not limited exclusively to respondents with a history of high-risk pregnancy. Rather, all eligible PRAMS respondents were included, and high-risk pregnancy history was evaluated as an exposure variable within the larger cohort. A composite “high-risk pregnancy history” index was created a priori using maternal health characteristics and adverse obstetric outcomes identified in prior literature as associated with increased maternal or neonatal morbidity (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists [ACOG], 2021 ; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2022 ). Respondents were classified as having a history of high-risk pregnancy if they reported one or more of the following conditions or outcomes: Preterm delivery of the index pregnancy (< 37 weeks gestation). Previous preterm birth. Low birth weight delivery in the index pregnancy (< 2500 g). Previous low birth weight delivery. Pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes. Hypertensive disorders before or during pregnancy. Pre-pregnancy obesity (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m²). No prenatal care during the index pregnancy. Depression before or during pregnancy. Preterm delivery of the index pregnancy (< 37 weeks gestation). Previous preterm birth. Low birth weight delivery in the index pregnancy (< 2500 g). Previous low birth weight delivery. Pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes. Hypertensive disorders before or during pregnancy. Pre-pregnancy obesity (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m²). No prenatal care during the index pregnancy. Depression before or during pregnancy. Variables were identified using linked birth certificate data and PRAMS survey responses. All components of the index were weighted equally. Because this study pooled seven distinct PRAMS cohorts with year-specific sampling weights and stratification procedures, a weighted composite index was not constructed to avoid introducing disproportionate influence from any single survey year. The authors acknowledge that inclusion of depression within the composite index may differ from traditional clinical definitions of “high-risk pregnancy”; however, depression was retained due to its established association with adverse perinatal outcomes, impaired healthcare utilization, maternal morbidity, substance use disorders, and maternal mortality in pregnancy and the postpartum period (ACOG, 2023 ; Gavin et al., 2005 ; Jarde et al., 2016 ). The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recognizes perinatal mental health conditions as significant contributors to maternal morbidity and mortality and recommends routine screening and treatment during pregnancy and postpartum care (ACOG, 2023 ). This consideration is particularly relevant in North Carolina, where suicide and drug overdose are among the leading causes of pregnancy-associated maternal death according to the North Carolina Maternal Mortality Review Committee (North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, 2022 ). Given these public health concerns, depression was included as part of the broader high-risk pregnancy history construct. Nevertheless, this broader operational definition likely contributed to a higher observed prevalence of “high-risk pregnancy history” within the analytic sample compared with national estimates and should be interpreted accordingly. The primary outcome was postpartum use of a high-efficacy contraceptive method. A dichotomous variable was created to identify respondents reporting use of WHO Tier 1 contraceptive methods postpartum, including intrauterine devices (IUDs), contraceptive implants, tubal ligation, or partner vasectomy (World Health Organization, 2018 ). Covariates were selected based on prior literature examining postpartum contraceptive utilization, maternal healthcare access, and reproductive decision-making. Variables included maternal age, race and ethnicity, marital status, educational attainment, parity, pregnancy intention, infant mortality, and postpartum insurance status categorized as public insurance (Medicaid or Children’s Health Insurance Program [CHIP]), private/other insurance, or uninsured. Additional healthcare-related and psychosocial variables included interpersonal violence during pregnancy by a current or former partner, attendance at a postpartum healthcare visit, prenatal counseling regarding postpartum contraception, and postpartum counseling related to contraception, birth spacing, depression, and contraceptive prescription receipt. Insurance status was included given known structural barriers affecting access to immediate postpartum long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) and sterilization, particularly among Medicaid beneficiaries. During portions of the study period, reimbursement policies and federal sterilization consent requirements may have limited access to immediate postpartum Tier 1 contraceptive methods for publicly insured patients in North Carolina (Moniz et al., 2017 ; Borrero et al., 2014 ). Descriptive statistics and frequencies were calculated for all study variables among the full analytic cohort and among respondents reporting postpartum Tier 1 contraceptive use. Missing data were retained and reported descriptively. Missingness resulted from respondents leaving survey items unanswered or selecting “prefer not to answer” where applicable. Nonrespondents to the PRAMS survey were excluded entirely prior to analysis. Complete-case analysis was used for regression modeling; respondents with missing data for variables included in a given model were excluded from that analysis only. The proportion of missing data varied by variable and is reported in the study tables. Multivariable binary logistic regression was performed to examine factors associated with postpartum use of Tier 1 contraception. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and p-values were calculated. Variables were entered simultaneously into the regression model based on theoretical and literature-supported relevance rather than stepwise selection procedures. To improve interpretability, all regression findings were reported as increased or decreased odds of Tier 1 contraceptive use. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 28 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Between 2012 and 2020 (excluding 2013 due to unavailable statewide data), 13,866 postpartum individuals were selected to participate in the North Carolina PRAMS survey. Of these, 6,993 respondents completed at least part of the survey and were included in the analytic sample, corresponding to an overall response proportion of 50.4%. Among all respondents, 68.7% ( n = 4,802) met criteria for the composite high-risk pregnancy history index. Overall, 29.7% ( n = 2,078) of respondents reported postpartum use of a World Health Organization (WHO) Tier 1 contraceptive method, including intrauterine devices, contraceptive implants, tubal ligation, or partner vasectomy. Among respondents reporting Tier 1 contraceptive use, 71.6% ( n = 1,487) had a history of high-risk pregnancy. Participant demographic, obstetric, and healthcare-related characteristics are summarized in Tables 1 and 2 . Missing data varied across variables because some respondents did not answer specific survey questions or selected “prefer not to answer.” Only survey respondents were included in analyses; sampled nonrespondents were excluded prior to analysis. title: Impact of preoperative dual antiplatelet therapy vs. aspirin monotherapy on perioperative outcomes in carotid endarterectomy patients: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Introduction The preoperative use of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) in patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is controversial. Aim This study aimed to compare perioperative major bleeding and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) between patients receiving aspirin alone and those receiving DAPT (clopidogrel plus aspirin). Method This retrospective cohort study included patients with carotid artery stenosis who underwent CEA between January 2020 and December 2024. Patients were grouped according to preoperative antiplatelet therapy (DAPT vs. aspirin), and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to adjust for baseline imbalances. The primary outcome was 30-day post-CEA major bleeding (neck hemorrhage requiring reoperation or intracranial hemorrhage). The secondary outcome was 30-day post-CEA MACEs (ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, or death). Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify the predictors of major bleeding. Results A total of 741 patients were included (aspirin, n = 504; DAPT, n = 237). Patients in the DAPT group had a higher prevalence of symptom, prior stroke, coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and prior revascularization. After IPTW adjustment, DAPT was associated with a higher risk of major bleeding than Aspirin (OR 4.21, 95% CI 1.81–9.78), with no significant difference in MACEs (OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.57–3.85). Multivariate analysis confirmed DAPT as an independent predictor of major bleeding (OR 3.40, 95% CI 1.42–8.19, p = 0.006), whereas preoperative statin use was independently associated with a reduced risk (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03–0.51, p = 0.003). Conclusion Compared with aspirin monotherapy, preoperative DAPT was associated with an increased risk of perioperative major bleeding without a reduction in perioperative MACEs in patients undergoing CEA. Larger multicenter prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11096-026-02160-w .
body: Preoperative DAPT is associated with a significantly increased risk of 30-day major bleeding following carotid endarterectomy compared with aspirin monotherapy. Preoperative DAPT is associated with a comparable risk of 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events compared with that of aspirin monotherapy. Caution is warranted when DAPT is administered within 5 days prior to carotid endarterectomy. Preoperative DAPT is associated with a significantly increased risk of 30-day major bleeding following carotid endarterectomy compared with aspirin monotherapy. Preoperative DAPT is associated with a comparable risk of 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events compared with that of aspirin monotherapy. Caution is warranted when DAPT is administered within 5 days prior to carotid endarterectomy. Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) remains a cornerstone intervention for stroke prevention in patients with significant symptomatic or asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis [ 1 ]. Antiplatelet therapy is fundamental to the perioperative management of CEA and serves to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is increasingly used in patients undergoing CEA due to concurrent cardiac or cerebrovascular conditions such as coronary artery disease or ischemic stroke [ 2 ]. Recent data indicate that approximately 35% of these patients receive preoperative DAPT [ 3 ]. This trend places surgeons in a clinical dilemma [ 4 ]: whether DAPT should be continued before CEA. Substantial evidence suggests that continued DAPT may provide benefits, such as reduced restenosis and perioperative stroke [ 5 , 6 ]; however, other studies have reported increased risks of bleeding [ 7 , 8 ], prolonged length of stay [ 9 ], and even higher mortality [ 10 ]. These conflicting findings highlight the critical trade-off between thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications. Despite its widespread clinical use, no definitive consensus exists regarding the optimal preoperative antithrombotic management strategy for patients undergoing CEA [ 11 – 13 ]. The Society for Vascular Surgery recommends individualizing perioperative DAPT decisions [ 14 ]. Reflecting this uncertainty, a survey of European vascular surgeons showed that although nearly all surgeons would continue aspirin prior to CEA, 43% and 55% would discontinue clopidogrel before CEA in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients, respectively [ 15 ]. Against this backdrop of clinical uncertainty and practice variability, targeted research on preoperative antiplatelet strategies in patients undergoing CEA has become increasingly important. However, most studies have been conducted in Western populations. There are well-documented racial disparities in antithrombotic treatment responses, particularly the higher susceptibility to bleeding complications observed in Asian populations [ 16 – 18 ], which limits the generalizability of the existing evidence. Consequently, the risk–benefit balance of continued DAPT versus aspirin monotherapy in Asian patients undergoing CEA remains unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing CEA to evaluate the perioperative outcomes associated with preoperative DAPT compared with aspirin monotherapy in this population. This study aimed to compare perioperative major bleeding and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) between patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy receiving aspirin monotherapy and those receiving dual antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel plus aspirin). This retrospective cohort study included inpatients who underwent CEA for carotid artery stenosis between January 2020 and December 2024 at a Chinese tertiary-care hospital. The study protocol adhered to the STROCSS guidelines [ 19 ]. Clinical data were obtained from the electronic medical records database. Patients who underwent CEA for asymptomatic stenosis ≥ 70% or symptomatic stenosis ≥ 50% and who received antiplatelet therapy within 2 weeks prior to CEA were included. Patients meeting any of the following criteria were excluded: (1) those who underwent concomitant procedures with CEA; (2) those receiving clopidogrel monotherapy or ticagrelor therapy before CEA; and (3) those lost to follow-up within 30 days after CEA. The decision to continue or discontinue clopidogrel before surgery and the duration of discontinuation were at the surgeon’s discretion. Patients were categorized into two groups based on antiplatelet therapy status 5 days prior to the CEA procedure: (1) aspirin group—patients receiving aspirin alone and (2) DAPT group—patients receiving aspirin plus clopidogrel. The 5-day cutoff was selected based on the pharmacodynamic profile of clopidogrel, whose antiplatelet effects persisted for the lifespan of platelets. Discontinuation for ≥ 5 days prior to surgery is widely considered sufficient to allow recovery of platelet function, according to clinical guidelines [ 20 , 21 ]. A chart review was conducted for each patient included in this study. Demographic characteristics (sex, age, weight, and height) and baseline laboratory values (hemoglobin, platelet count, and serum creatinine) were recorded for each patient. The clinical data included symptomatic status (ipsilateral amaurosis fugax, transient ischemic attack, or stroke within 6 months) [ 5 ], degree of carotid stenosis, smoking history and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure (CHF), coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and renal insufficiency (defined as creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min using the Cockcroft–Gault equation). Preoperative medications, including β-blockers, oral anticoagulants, proton pump inhibitors, statins, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), were documented, along with prior revascularization procedures (coronary artery bypass grafting [CABG], percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI], prior CEA, or carotid artery stenting [CAS]). Operative variables, including American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class, surgery type (conventional or eversion), patch use, and protamine administration, were also collected. The degree of carotid stenosis was categorized according to the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial criteria and classified as > 70% or 50–70% [ 22 ]. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight (kg) divided by height squared (m 2 ) and categorized as low (< 24 kg/m 2 ) or high (≥ 24 kg/m 2 ). All patients were operated underwent general anesthesia. Systemic intra-operative heparinization was given routinely as 50 IU sodium heparin per kilogram body weight, up to a maximum of 5000 IU. Protamine use was as per surgeon preference. Activated clotting time was not measured routinely. Drain was placed in every case. All patients were monitored in the intensive care unit for a minimum 12 h before transfer to the surgical ward. The primary outcome was the occurrence of major bleeding events within 30 days following CEA, defined as neck hemorrhage requiring reoperation or intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). The secondary outcome was the occurrence of MACEs within 30 days following CEA, defined as a composite of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction (MI), and all-cause death. Detailed definitions of the study outcomes are provided in Supplementary Table 1. All events were identified from subsequent outpatient and inpatient electronic medical record reviews. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables are presented as numbers (percentages). Covariate imbalance between the two groups was addressed using stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Propensity scores were estimated using logistic regression, including the following baseline variables: sex, age, BMI, symptomatic status, degree of carotid stenosis, comorbidities, smoking history, preoperative medications, prior cardiovascular procedures, hemoglobin, platelet count, ASA class, and operative factors. Individual weights were calculated and stabilized by multiplying by the marginal probability of treatment. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were used to assess the balance of baseline characteristics, with an SMD of < 0.1 indicating a negligible imbalance. Univariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between preoperative antiplatelet therapy (DAPT vs. aspirin alone) and clinical outcomes, with odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reported before and after IPTW. Subgroup analyses for major bleeding were performed stratified by age (< 75 and ≥ 75 years), symptomatic status, degree of carotid stenosis (50–70% and > 70%), prior CEA/CAS, and statin use. For subgroup analyses, multivariable logistic regression and propensity score–based methods (IPTW) were applied. A P -value for interaction < 0.1 was used to assess potential interactions between the treatment groups and subgroups. To identify the predictors of major bleeding, multivariable analysis was conducted using stepwise logistic regression. The covariates included in the univariable analysis were sex, age, BMI, symptomatic status, degree of carotid stenosis, comorbidities, preoperative medications, prior cardiovascular procedures, and operative factors. Variables with a significance level ≤ 0.20 in the univariate analysis were entered into the final multivariable model. All statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.3). Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was granted by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine on 20 Dec 2024 (NO. 2024-1490). As shown in Fig. 1 , between January 2020 and December 2024, 905 inpatients underwent CEA. Patients who were not receiving antiplatelet therapy before CEA (n = 60), underwent concomitant procedures (n = 10), received clopidogrel monotherapy (n = 60) or ticagrelor therapy (n = 26), or were lost to follow-up (n = 8) were excluded from the study. Ultimately, 741 patients were included in this analysis. Fig. 1 Study population and flow chart. Abbreviations: CEA, carotid endarterectomy Study population and flow chart. Abbreviations: CEA, carotid endarterectomy The mean age of the study population was 68.32 ± 7.79 years, and 616 patients (83.1%) were men. Ipsilateral stenosis > 70% was present in 80.3% of the patients, and 24.7% were symptomatic. Proton pump inhibitors were used in 89.1% of patients (pantoprazole, 80.2%; lansoprazole, 5.4%; rabeprazole, 3.5%), and 97.3% received statins. The detailed distribution of statin medications is presented in Supplementary Table 2. Compared with the aspirin group, patients in the DAPT group were more likely to be symptomatic (30.4% vs. 22.0%) and had higher rates of prior stroke (53.6% vs. 39.5%), coronary artery disease (40.9% vs. 17.7%), hyperlipidemia (19.8% vs. 13.9%), prior PCI or CABG (32.5% vs. 9.7%), and prior CEA/CAS (14.8% vs. 6.9%). No significant differences were observed between the groups in other comorbidities, including hypertension, diabetes, renal insufficiency, CHF, and COPD. Preoperative β-blocker use was more common in the DAPT than in the aspirin group (36.3% vs. 25.4%). Patients in the DAPT group were also more likely to undergo eversion CEA (44.7% vs. 25.2%) and receive protamine (42.2% vs. 22.6%). After IPTW adjustment, the baseline characteristics of the two groups were well balanced (Table 1 ; Supplementary Fig. 1). Compared with the aspirin group, the DAPT group had a significantly higher risk of major bleeding (5.5% vs. 1.8%; OR 3.19, 95% CI 1.34–7.58), primarily driven by an increased incidence of neck hemorrhage (4.2% vs. 1.6%; OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.06–7.01). Using a cutoff of 75 years, DAPT was associated with an increased bleeding risk in both age groups (OR 3.06, 95% CI 1.07–8.76 vs. OR 13.17, 95% CI 1.35–128.41; p for interaction = 0.254). Similarly, an increased bleeding risk was observed regardless of stenosis severity (OR 9.67, 95% CI 0.98–95.87 vs. OR 3.54, 95% CI 1.24–10.08; p for interaction = 0.434). Among asymptomatic patients, DAPT was associated with a higher risk of major bleeding (OR 5.51, 95% CI 1.98–15.35), whereas this association was not observed in symptomatic patients (OR 1.35, 95% CI 0.16–11.64). A similar pattern was observed in patients without prior CEA/CAS (OR 4.65 [95% CI 1.75–12.32]). In addition, statin users receiving DAPT had a higher risk of major bleeding than those receiving ASAA (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.46–10.73). No significant differences in major bleeding were observed between high- and moderate-intensity statins ( p = 0.546) or between hydrophilic and lipophilic statins ( p = 0.655) (Supplementary Table 4). Impact of preoperative dual antiplatelet therapy vs. aspirin monotherapy on perioperative outcomes in carotid endarterectomy patients: a retrospective cohort study

Introduction The preoperative use of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) in patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is controversial. Aim This study aimed to compare perioperative major bleeding and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) between patients receiving aspirin alone and those receiving DAPT (clopidogrel plus aspirin). Method This retrospective cohort study included patients with carotid artery stenosis who underwent CEA between January 2020 and December 2024. Patients were grouped according to preoperative antiplatelet therapy (DAPT vs. aspirin), and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to adjust for baseline imbalances. The primary outcome was 30-day post-CEA major bleeding (neck hemorrhage requiring reoperation or intracranial hemorrhage). The secondary outcome was 30-day post-CEA MACEs (ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, or death). Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify the predictors of major bleeding. Results A total of 741 patients were included (aspirin, n = 504; DAPT, n = 237). Patients in the DAPT group had a higher prevalence of symptom, prior stroke, coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and prior revascularization. After IPTW adjustment, DAPT was associated with a higher risk of major bleeding than Aspirin (OR 4.21, 95% CI 1.81–9.78), with no significant difference in MACEs (OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.57–3.85). Multivariate analysis confirmed DAPT as an independent predictor of major bleeding (OR 3.40, 95% CI 1.42–8.19, p = 0.006), whereas preoperative statin use was independently associated with a reduced risk (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03–0.51, p = 0.003). Conclusion Compared with aspirin monotherapy, preoperative DAPT was associated with an increased risk of perioperative major bleeding without a reduction in perioperative MACEs in patients undergoing CEA. Larger multicenter prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.
