Preoperative DAPT is associated with a significantly increased risk of 30-day major bleeding following carotid endarterectomy compared with aspirin monotherapy. Preoperative DAPT is associated with a comparable risk of 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events compared with that of aspirin monotherapy. Caution is warranted when DAPT is administered within 5 days prior to carotid endarterectomy. Preoperative DAPT is associated with a significantly increased risk of 30-day major bleeding following carotid endarterectomy compared with aspirin monotherapy. Preoperative DAPT is associated with a comparable risk of 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events compared with that of aspirin monotherapy. Caution is warranted when DAPT is administered within 5 days prior to carotid endarterectomy. Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) remains a cornerstone intervention for stroke prevention in patients with significant symptomatic or asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis [ 1 ]. Antiplatelet therapy is fundamental to the perioperative management of CEA and serves to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is increasingly used in patients undergoing CEA due to concurrent cardiac or cerebrovascular conditions such as coronary artery disease or ischemic stroke [ 2 ]. Recent data indicate that approximately 35% of these patients receive preoperative DAPT [ 3 ]. This trend places surgeons in a clinical dilemma [ 4 ]: whether DAPT should be continued before CEA. Substantial evidence suggests that continued DAPT may provide benefits, such as reduced restenosis and perioperative stroke [ 5 , 6 ]; however, other studies have reported increased risks of bleeding [ 7 , 8 ], prolonged length of stay [ 9 ], and even higher mortality [ 10 ]. These conflicting findings highlight the critical trade-off between thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications. Despite its widespread clinical use, no definitive consensus exists regarding the optimal preoperative antithrombotic management strategy for patients undergoing CEA [ 11 – 13 ]. The Society for Vascular Surgery recommends individualizing perioperative DAPT decisions [ 14 ]. Reflecting this uncertainty, a survey of European vascular surgeons showed that although nearly all surgeons would continue aspirin prior to CEA, 43% and 55% would discontinue clopidogrel before CEA in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients, respectively [ 15 ]. Against this backdrop of clinical uncertainty and practice variability, targeted research on preoperative antiplatelet strategies in patients undergoing CEA has become increasingly important. However, most studies have been conducted in Western populations. There are well-documented racial disparities in antithrombotic treatment responses, particularly the higher susceptibility to bleeding complications observed in Asian populations [ 16 – 18 ], which limits the generalizability of the existing evidence. Consequently, the risk–benefit balance of continued DAPT versus aspirin monotherapy in Asian patients undergoing CEA remains unclear. To address this gap, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing CEA to evaluate the perioperative outcomes associated with preoperative DAPT compared with aspirin monotherapy in this population. This study aimed to compare perioperative major bleeding and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) between patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy receiving aspirin monotherapy and those receiving dual antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel plus aspirin). This retrospective cohort study included inpatients who underwent CEA for carotid artery stenosis between January 2020 and December 2024 at a Chinese tertiary-care hospital. The study protocol adhered to the STROCSS guidelines [ 19 ]. Clinical data were obtained from the electronic medical records database. Patients who underwent CEA for asymptomatic stenosis ≥ 70% or symptomatic stenosis ≥ 50% and who received antiplatelet therapy within 2 weeks prior to CEA were included. Patients meeting any of the following criteria were excluded: (1) those who underwent concomitant procedures with CEA; (2) those receiving clopidogrel monotherapy or ticagrelor therapy before CEA; and (3) those lost to follow-up within 30 days after CEA. The decision to continue or discontinue clopidogrel before surgery and the duration of discontinuation were at the surgeon’s discretion. Patients were categorized into two groups based on antiplatelet therapy status 5 days prior to the CEA procedure: (1) aspirin group—patients receiving aspirin alone and (2) DAPT group—patients receiving aspirin plus clopidogrel. The 5-day cutoff was selected based on the pharmacodynamic profile of clopidogrel, whose antiplatelet effects persisted for the lifespan of platelets. Discontinuation for ≥ 5 days prior to surgery is widely considered sufficient to allow recovery of platelet function, according to clinical guidelines [ 20 , 21 ]. A chart review was conducted for each patient included in this study. Demographic characteristics (sex, age, weight, and height) and baseline laboratory values (hemoglobin, platelet count, and serum creatinine) were recorded for each patient. The clinical data included symptomatic status (ipsilateral amaurosis fugax, transient ischemic attack, or stroke within 6 months) [ 5 ], degree of carotid stenosis, smoking history and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure (CHF), coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and renal insufficiency (defined as creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min using the Cockcroft–Gault equation). Preoperative medications, including β-blockers, oral anticoagulants, proton pump inhibitors, statins, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), were documented, along with prior revascularization procedures (coronary artery bypass grafting [CABG], percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI], prior CEA, or carotid artery stenting [CAS]). Operative variables, including American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class, surgery type (conventional or eversion), patch use, and protamine administration, were also collected. The degree of carotid stenosis was categorized according to the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial criteria and classified as > 70% or 50–70% [ 22 ]. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight (kg) divided by height squared (m 2 ) and categorized as low (< 24 kg/m 2 ) or high (≥ 24 kg/m 2 ). All patients were operated underwent general anesthesia. Systemic intra-operative heparinization was given routinely as 50 IU sodium heparin per kilogram body weight, up to a maximum of 5000 IU. Protamine use was as per surgeon preference. Activated clotting time was not measured routinely. Drain was placed in every case. All patients were monitored in the intensive care unit for a minimum 12 h before transfer to the surgical ward. The primary outcome was the occurrence of major bleeding events within 30 days following CEA, defined as neck hemorrhage requiring reoperation or intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). The secondary outcome was the occurrence of MACEs within 30 days following CEA, defined as a composite of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction (MI), and all-cause death. Detailed definitions of the study outcomes are provided in Supplementary Table 1. All events were identified from subsequent outpatient and inpatient electronic medical record reviews. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables are presented as numbers (percentages). Covariate imbalance between the two groups was addressed using stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Propensity scores were estimated using logistic regression, including the following baseline variables: sex, age, BMI, symptomatic status, degree of carotid stenosis, comorbidities, smoking history, preoperative medications, prior cardiovascular procedures, hemoglobin, platelet count, ASA class, and operative factors. Individual weights were calculated and stabilized by multiplying by the marginal probability of treatment. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were used to assess the balance of baseline characteristics, with an SMD of < 0.1 indicating a negligible imbalance. Univariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between preoperative antiplatelet therapy (DAPT vs. aspirin alone) and clinical outcomes, with odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reported before and after IPTW. Subgroup analyses for major bleeding were performed stratified by age (< 75 and ≥ 75 years), symptomatic status, degree of carotid stenosis (50–70% and > 70%), prior CEA/CAS, and statin use. For subgroup analyses, multivariable logistic regression and propensity score–based methods (IPTW) were applied. A P -value for interaction < 0.1 was used to assess potential interactions between the treatment groups and subgroups. To identify the predictors of major bleeding, multivariable analysis was conducted using stepwise logistic regression. The covariates included in the univariable analysis were sex, age, BMI, symptomatic status, degree of carotid stenosis, comorbidities, preoperative medications, prior cardiovascular procedures, and operative factors. Variables with a significance level ≤ 0.20 in the univariate analysis were entered into the final multivariable model. All statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.3). Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was granted by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine on 20 Dec 2024 (NO. 2024-1490). As shown in Fig. 1 , between January 2020 and December 2024, 905 inpatients underwent CEA. Patients who were not receiving antiplatelet therapy before CEA (n = 60), underwent concomitant procedures (n = 10), received clopidogrel monotherapy (n = 60) or ticagrelor therapy (n = 26), or were lost to follow-up (n = 8) were excluded from the study. Ultimately, 741 patients were included in this analysis. Fig. 1 Study population and flow chart. Abbreviations: CEA, carotid endarterectomy Study population and flow chart. Abbreviations: CEA, carotid endarterectomy The mean age of the study population was 68.32 ± 7.79 years, and 616 patients (83.1%) were men. Ipsilateral stenosis > 70% was present in 80.3% of the patients, and 24.7% were symptomatic. Proton pump inhibitors were used in 89.1% of patients (pantoprazole, 80.2%; lansoprazole, 5.4%; rabeprazole, 3.5%), and 97.3% received statins. The detailed distribution of statin medications is presented in Supplementary Table 2. Compared with the aspirin group, patients in the DAPT group were more likely to be symptomatic (30.4% vs. 22.0%) and had higher rates of prior stroke (53.6% vs. 39.5%), coronary artery disease (40.9% vs. 17.7%), hyperlipidemia (19.8% vs. 13.9%), prior PCI or CABG (32.5% vs. 9.7%), and prior CEA/CAS (14.8% vs. 6.9%). No significant differences were observed between the groups in other comorbidities, including hypertension, diabetes, renal insufficiency, CHF, and COPD. Preoperative β-blocker use was more common in the DAPT than in the aspirin group (36.3% vs. 25.4%). Patients in the DAPT group were also more likely to undergo eversion CEA (44.7% vs. 25.2%) and receive protamine (42.2% vs. 22.6%). After IPTW adjustment, the baseline characteristics of the two groups were well balanced (Table 1 ; Supplementary Fig. 1). title: Potential Role for the Ubiquitin Ligase SIAH2 in Modulating Bone Morphology and Adiposity
abstract: Marrow adipose expansion, with obesity or ageing, increases fracture risk. Skeletal stem cells can commit to osteoblast or adipocyte endpoints, an inverse relationship influenced by peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ). Seven in absentia homologue 2 (SIAH2) is a ubiquitin ligase that acts in peripheral adipose tissue stromal progenitors, promoting PPARγ activity and adipogenesis. The pivotal role of PPARγ in bone marrow adipose tissue accumulation prompted us to evaluate SIAH2’s role in the balance between osteogenesis and adipogenesis. Using adherent skeletal stem and/or progenitor cells (SSPCs) isolated from the marrow of wild-type (WT) and Siah2 mice, we assessed in vitro osteogenic and adipogenic capacity. Bone morphology and adiposity were assessed, in vivo, using WT and −/− Siah2 −/− mice in the context of dietary, high-fat diet, and pharmacological, rosiglitazone, PPARγ stimulation. We hypothesized increased osteogenesis in Siah2 SSPCs and expected −/− Siah2 −/− mice would be resistant to the effects of PPARγ activation on trabecular morphology and marrow fat expansion. Our results show that Siah2 −/− SSPCs display increased capacity for both osteogenesis and adipogenesis in vitro. Further, exploratory experiments in vivo indicate Siah2 −/− mice have fewer, yet thicker, trabeculae on a low fat diet, while Siah2 −/ mice on a high-fat diet paired with rosiglitazone trend toward more marrow adipose, decreased bone mass and increased trabecular spacing compared to WT. Our results suggest SIAH2 moderates both osteogenic and adipogenic commitment as the absence of SIAH2 results in progenitor cells that will more readily commit to either outcome. These observations underscore SIAH2’s context-specific modulatory effects on PPARγ activities determined by tissue, nutrients and pharmacological cues. − Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00223-026-01596-6 .
body: Bones undergo remodeling throughout the lifespan to maintain their strength and physiological function. Remodeling is largely determined via the interaction of bone forming osteoblasts and bone resorbing osteoclasts, but the aggregate of contributing factors is complex. Bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) is a substantial modulatory factor in bone remodeling, and at the tissue level, increased BMAT is generally associated with reduced bone mass and increased fracture risk [ 1 ], a negative relationship that is best characterized in anorexia nervosa but also described in diseases such as type II diabetes mellitus and obesity [ 2 ]. At the cellular level, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and marrow adipocytes are derived from non-differentiated cells within the marrow space. While osteoclasts are derived from myeloid progenitors [ 3 ], common stromal progenitors of mesenchymal lineage (skeletal stem cells, SSCs) exist for bone marrow adipocytes and osteoblasts [ 4 – 6 ]. Differentiation of SSCs toward adipogenic, in lieu of osteogenic, endpoints is thought to play some role in the negative relationship between BMAT and bone mass. The determinants of SSC differentiation toward adipogenesis or osteogenesis are numerous and have been reviewed previously [ 7 , 8 ]. Of the contributing factors, master transcriptional regulators Peroxisome Proliferator-activated Receptor Gamma 2 (PPARg2) and Runt-related Transcription Factor 2 (RUNX2) are generally accepted as the “tipping” point for adipogenic or osteogenic commitment, respectively. Reciprocal control of PPARγ2 and RUNX2 is modulated by the canonical Wnt signaling pathway [ 9 ]. Wnt signaling stabilizes β-catenin to up-regulate RUNX2 transcription and subsequently down-regulate PPARγ2, resulting in osteoblastogenesis. Alternatively, up-regulation of PPARγ2 results in PPARγ2-mediated de-stabilization of β-catenin, inhibiting osteogenesis and promoting adipogenesis. Other examples of factors that inversely modulate PPARγ2 and RUNX2 include TAZ (transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), and Protein Phosphatase 5 [ 10 – 12 ]. Continued identification of PPARγ2 and RUNX2 modulators may provide new vectors for improved understanding and/or treatment of increased marrow adiposity and fracture risk. Seven-in absentia homolog 2 (SIAH2) is a ubiquitin ligase commonly studied for its role in cancer and hypoxia [ 13 , 14 ], but our lab previously showed SIAH2 also influences adipogenesis in peripheral fat depots. SIAH2 promotes adipogenesis by forming a complex with the pro-adipogenic early B-cell factor 1 (EBF1) and pro-bone forming zinc-finger protein 521 (ZFP521) [ 15 ] to destabilize ZFP521 and stabilize EBF-1, leading to activation of PPARγ transcriptional activity and adipogenesis [ 16 ]. Considering the role of ZFP521 in bone formation and the pivotal role of PPARγ in the balance between adipogenesis and osteogenesis, SIAH2 may contribute to the balance between bone and bone marrow adiposity. Frew et al. reported SIAH2’s potential role in bone remodeling in their initial characterization of globally deleted Siah2 in mice on a C57BL/6J background ( Siah2 ) [ −/− 17 ]. Characterization of the Siah2 mice, using mononuclear cells isolated from whole bone marrow, described increased osteoclastogenesis, suggesting SIAH2 modulates bone resorption. Based on in vitro data alone, increased osteoclastogenesis would result in more bone resorption; however, bone histology on 10-week-old wild-type and −/− Siah2 mice found no significant difference in the surface of bone occupied by bone resorbing osteoclasts with no difference in overall bone structure [ −/− 17 ]. In contrast, we found that impaired adipogenesis in Siah2 adipose tissue stromal vascular fraction cells was associated with increased expression of β-catenin, Wnt10a, Wnt10b and Wnt6 [ −/− 18 ], factors that promote osteogenesis. Upregulation of the genes encoding β-catenin and Wnt signaling proteins in the stromal cell population suggests SIAH2 may inhibit bone formation while promoting adipocyte development. Potential Role for the Ubiquitin Ligase SIAH2 in Modulating Bone Morphology and Adiposity

Marrow adipose expansion, with obesity or ageing, increases fracture risk. Skeletal stem cells can commit to osteoblast or adipocyte endpoints, an inverse relationship influenced by peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ). Seven in absentia homologue 2 (SIAH2) is a ubiquitin ligase that acts in peripheral adipose tissue stromal progenitors, promoting PPARγ activity and adipogenesis. The pivotal role of PPARγ in bone marrow adipose tissue accumulation prompted us to evaluate SIAH2’s role in the balance between osteogenesis and adipogenesis. Using adherent skeletal stem and/or progenitor cells (SSPCs) isolated from the marrow of wild-type (WT) and Siah2 mice, we assessed in vitro osteogenic and adipogenic capacity. Bone morphology and adiposity were assessed, in vivo, using WT and −/− Siah2 −/− mice in the context of dietary, high-fat diet, and pharmacological, rosiglitazone, PPARγ stimulation. We hypothesized increased osteogenesis in Siah2 SSPCs and expected −/− Siah2 −/− mice would be resistant to the effects of PPARγ activation on trabecular morphology and marrow fat expansion. Our results show that Siah2 −/− SSPCs display increased capacity for both osteogenesis and adipogenesis in vitro. Further, exploratory experiments in vivo indicate Siah2 −/− mice have fewer, yet thicker, trabeculae on a low fat diet, while Siah2 −/ mice on a high-fat diet paired with rosiglitazone trend toward more marrow adipose, decreased bone mass and increased trabecular spacing compared to WT. Our results suggest SIAH2 moderates both osteogenic and adipogenic commitment as the absence of SIAH2 results in progenitor cells that will more readily commit to either outcome. These observations underscore SIAH2’s context-specific modulatory effects on PPARγ activities determined by tissue, nutrients and pharmacological cues. − Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00223-026-01596-6 .

title: Differential associations of arousals and respiratory events on oxygen desaturation and resaturation parameters in sleep
abstract: Background The severity of nocturnal blood oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) is associated with age, sex, and cardiorespiratory comorbidities. Frequency and timing of nocturnal arousals and respiratory events also display age, sex, and comorbidity-based differences. Hence, it is plausible that resaturation parameters may present an alternative avenue for the assessment of nocturnal arousals. Methods First visit data from the Sleep Heart Health Study was utilised to derive SpO 2 parameters from 5804 participants. Participants missing SpO 2 parameters, or with no desaturation events were excluded from final analysis. Manually scored arousals were linked to automatically scored SpO 2 events and defined temporally as pre-event (arousal terminated ≤ 10 s prior to desaturation onset) or within-event (arousal began within the desaturation event or ≤ 5 s after desaturation offset). Results 5,484 participants (49% female, median age 63 years) were included with 235,996 saturation events. 1.2% of events had pre-event arousals ( n = 2,850), while 47.6% had within-event arousals ( n = 112,271). Pre-event arousals were associated with faster desaturation rates (standardized effect: 0.54–0.58) and shorter desaturation durations (by 25–36%). Within-event arousals were associated with lower nadirs, longer desaturation durations, and larger desaturation areas (standardized effects: 0.24–0.51). Both arousal types increased resaturation rates, but through different mechanisms: pre-event arousals shortened resaturation durations while within-event arousals increased resaturation height. These effects were amplified with respiratory events, with the strongest associations observed during apnoeas. Conclusions Arousals significantly influence SpO 2 event architecture, with differential changes seen between desaturation and resaturation parameters. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11325-026-03797-7 .
body: Nocturnal blood oxygen desaturation metrics have shown significant associations with adverse outcomes stemming from obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) [ 1 – 8 ]. These metrics range from simple counts of occurrence of desaturation events to more complex temporal models, which are assumed to better display the downstream hypoxemic effects associated with apnoeas and hypopnoeas [ 9 ]. Desaturation metrics have typically focussed upon the desaturation event as a whole, or only the desaturated ‘half’ of a desaturation event [ 9 ]. However, the recovery ‘half’ of a desaturation event (i.e. the “Resaturation”) also displays significant associations with acute outcomes [ 10 ] (such as daytime sleepiness assessed via multiple sleep latency test), presence of comorbidities [ 11 ] (such as arterial hypertension, heart disease, and stroke) and sleep stages [ 12 ], independent of the desaturation side’s parameters. Furthermore, there are significant differences in resaturation parameters and how they change over time based on sex, age, and body mass index (BMI) [ 10 , 13 ]. Taken together, this suggests that resaturation parameters should be considered as vital metrics for the personalisation of sleep medicine [ 14 ]. Although desaturation and resaturation parameters show significant associations with OSA sequelae and comorbidities, they are by no means the only sleep-based parameters associated with sleep disorders [ 15 ]. Sleep arousals – defined as abrupt shifts in electroencephalogram (EEG) frequency – are also significantly associated with both short and long-term OSA-related outcomes [ 16 ]. Among patients with OSA and particularly severe OSA, the arousal burden is higher compared to non-OSA patients, resulting in significantly more fragmented, discontinuous sleep [ 17 ]. Arousals may be preceded by a variety of stimuli, including disruptive respiratory events such as apnoeas or hypopnoeas, abrupt limb movements, external and/or environmental stimuli, or particular chemical thresholds being exceeded [ 16 , 18 , 19 ]. There is, thus, a significant interplay between arousals and desaturation parameters [ 20 ]. In addition, airflow increases resulting from ventilatory responses to arousal contribute to restoring blood oxygen levels and reducing excess carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in the blood [ 16 ]. On the other hand, chemoreceptor activations due to hypoxia and hypercapnia can contribute to elicit arousal [ 19 ], and the association of lower blood oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) nadirs with arousal occurrence has been demonstrated previously [ 21 ]. However, no studies have examined the effect of arousals on resaturation parameters or vice versa. Given that both resaturation parameters and the threshold for arousal differ between sexes, and are modulated by age and BMI, it is plausible that resaturation parameters represent another avenue to evaluate the presence of arousals [ 22 ]. The use of limited channel sleep studies and home oximeter studies for the assessment of OSA is increasing, and fills a vital healthcare gap for populations with poor access to healthcare [ 23 ]. Research has demonstrated that autonomic arousal detection and cardiorespiratory sleep staging can significantly improve the accuracy of home sleep apnoea tests [ 24 ]. Furthermore, automated approaches for detecting subtle non-apnoeic/non-hypopnoeic arousal events from polysomnography recordings have shown promising results [ 25 ]. These advancements highlight the potential clinical value of identifying novel biomarkers of arousal from limited channel parameters. Understanding the relationship between arousals and oxygen resaturation patterns could therefore provide an additional avenue for improving diagnostic accuracy in simplified sleep testing environments where traditional EEG-based arousal detection is unavailable. We hypothesised that the presence and timing of arousals significantly influences oxygen resaturation parameters, with differential effects depending on whether arousals occur before or during desaturation events. Furthermore, we anticipated that these effects would be modulated by the presence and type of respiratory events (apnoeas vs. hypopnoeas). Therefore, in this study, we aimed to characterise the effect of nocturnal arousal presence and timing stratified by respiratory event type on oxygen resaturation parameters. For this retrospective analysis of oxygen saturation event-wise data, first-visit data from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) was utilised. Further details regarding the setting, implementation, and outcomes of the SHHS are available elsewhere [ 26 , 27 ]. In brief, 5,804 participants from existing prospective cohort studies aged > 40 years completed a baseline examination between 1995 and 1998. Participants provided information on demographic and clinical factors, including medications and comorbidities. For the purposes of this study, we included age, sex, smoking history, height, weight, BMI, comorbidities, and medications as detailed in our previous report [ 11 ]. SpO 2 was captured via an oximeter (Nonin, Minneapolis, MN) recorded at a sampling rate of 1 Hz. Due to the known data corruption issues in SHHS data [ 28 ] and scoring rules, existing manual labels for desaturation events within polysomnography’s were not used. Instead, European data format files for patients were downloaded and SpO 2 data analysed utilising the ABOSA (i.e. Automated blood oxygen saturation analysis) software (version 1.1), a freely available automated blood SpO 2 analysis tool with validated accuracy for detecting and characterizing desaturation events [ 29 , 30 ]. However, it must be noted that there are currently no formal standards for the assessment of oxygen desaturation events [ 31 ]. Therefore, for the ABOSA analyses, the following settings were used: minimum desaturation event duration of five seconds, minimum transient drop 4%, automated artefact removal, and total analysed time defined from sleep onset to offset. From the ABOSA outputs, the following parameters were extracted for analysis: SpO 2 value at start of desaturation, SpO 2 value at end of resaturation, duration of desaturations and resaturations (seconds), desaturation depth (percentile point change from event baseline to nadir), and resaturation height (percentile point change from nadir to new baseline), desaturation and resaturation rate (depth (height)/duration) and the desaturation and resaturation area (Fig. 1 ). Hypnograms were downloaded from the SHHS Profusion files and sleep stages were defined as Wake, N1, N2, N3, and rapid eye movement (REM). The sleep stage during which the event occurred was defined to be the sleep stage in which a desaturation event started, regardless of whether the sleep stage changed during the event. Participants were excluded if they had corrupted or missing nocturnal oximetry data ( n = 22, 0.4%), or if they recorded no desaturation or resaturation events ( n = 61, 1.1%). Events that occurred during epochs scored as ‘wake’ were excluded from the analysis ( n = 58,405, 19.6%), which also resulted in 230 more participants being excluded from the analysis. Manually annotated arousals did not specify the type of arousal (e.g. respiratory, limb-related, or spontaneous); therefore, no breakdown of arousal type was attempted. To study the association between presence and timing of arousals upon saturation event parameters, in addition to “no arousals”, arousals were divided into two temporal categories: (i) Pre-event Arousal – arousals which ended within 10 s prior to the ABOSA calculated start of desaturation event, and (ii) Within-event Arousals – arousals which started between the ABOSA defined start of the desaturation event up until 5 s after the ABOSA defined end of resaturation, or 5 s after the defined end of desaturation in the case of events which did not have a resaturation recorded (Fig. 1 ). As the Pre- and Within-event arousal scoring criteria were non exclusionary (i.e. an arousal could be scored 2 s before desaturation beginning and 2 s before resaturation ending), events for which multiple arousals were scored were excluded from the analysis ( n = 2,444, 1%), which also resulted in seven participants being excluded from analysis. Both sleep staging and arousal definitions were scored according to SHHS rules (found via references [ 32 , 33 ]). SpO : Oxygen saturation 2 Depiction of the classification method for association with respiratory event, and association with pre-event or within-event arousal. The inset depicts the parameters extracted from ABOSA. SpO : Oxygen saturation 2 Saturation events were additionally categorised by their connection to respiratory events as (i) related to hypopnoea - if the ABOSA defined start of the desaturation fell between the start of a hypopnoea until 60 s after the start of a hypopnoea, (ii) related to apnoea - if the ABOSA defined start of the desaturation fell between the start of an apnoea until 60 s after the start of an apnoea, or (iii) having no related respiratory event (Fig. 2 ). The 10-second search window prior to desaturation onset and 5-second post-event window for linking arousals align with recent polysomnographic studies of arousal-respiratory event temporal relationships. Leppänen et al. [ 34 ] demonstrated that 95% of respiratory event-associated arousals occur within 10 s of event termination. Furthermore, Zitting et al. [ 35 ] found that 90% of apnoea-associated cortical arousals initiate within four seconds pre- to nine seconds post-event termination, while hypopnoea-associated arousals occur within six seconds pre- to 14 s post-event. Our selected windows capture this critical period while avoiding overlap with subsequent events in clustered respiratory sequences. Rules for the scoring of respiratory events within the SHHS were: Apnoeas – amplitude of airflow signal decreased by ≥ 75% of baseline (defined as period of stable breathing with stable SpO 2 ) for ≥ 10 s; Hypopnoeas - amplitude of airflow signal decreased by ≥ 30% of baseline for ≥ 10 s and for ≥ 2 breaths [ 36 ]. Fig. 2 Breakdown of saturation event categories of interaction between respiratory event and arousal timing Breakdown of saturation event categories of interaction between respiratory event and arousal timing Initial permissions for the data collection are presented elsewhere [ 26 , 27 ]. For the present study, National Sleep Research Resource granted the permission to use the data. Significant differences in event-wise SpO 2 parameters between males and females were tested via univariate quantile regression for participant-level summary statistics which exhibited skewed distributions. In contrast, mixed effects regression was employed for event-wise analyses to appropriately account for repeated measures within individuals and variability across events. Univariate logistic regression models were utilised to assess differences between males and females in the likelihood of having an SpO 2 event associated with no respiratory event, hypopnoea or apnoea and no arousal, pre-event arousal or within-event arousal. Associations between presence and timing of arousal (pre-event and within-event against reference of no-arousal, and comparison of pre-event against within-event arousal) were initially assessed via univariate mixed effects regression stratified by no associated respiratory event, hypopnoea and apnoea. Following this, retaining the respiratory event stratification, the association between presence and timing of arousal upon SpO 2 parameters was assessed in multivariate mixed effects models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, forced expiratory volume in one second (percentage of predicted value utilising ethnic neutral norms via the updated global lung initiative 2023 equations [ 37 ]), sleep stage of event, smoking history and presence of arterial hypertension, lung disease, myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus, stroke, heart failure, use of hormone therapy or mental health medications (covariates chosen on the basis of our previous research [ 11 , 12 ]). Event nadir and desaturation duration, depth, rate and area were additionally adjusted for pre-event SpO 2 value, while post-event SpO 2 value and resaturation duration, height, rate and area were additionally adjusted for pre-event SpO 2 value and event nadir. All statistical tests were adjusted for via Bonferroni correction, and all analyses conducted in STATA 18 (College station, Texas). A total of 5,484 participants (49% female) were included for analysis. Participants were a median 63 years of age (interquartile range (IQR) 55, 72), with the majority being overweight (42.1%) or obese (31.3%) (Supplement 1 ). Around half (53.5%) of the participants had a history of smoking and the majority of participants had at least one comorbidity (85.7%), of which arterial hypertension was the most common (49.5%). One-third of female participants recorded use of hormone therapy (30%). Overall, 235,996 desaturation events were recorded (participant median 19 (IQR 6, 50)), though 16,881 (7.1%) desaturation events did not have a corresponding resaturation recorded. Males recorded a significantly higher number of desaturations and resaturations than females (median difference 14 & 13 respectively) and numerous significant differences were seen in SpO 2 architecture parameters (Table 1 ). Pre- and post-SpO 2 values were a median 0.2% lower among females, desaturation and resaturation durations 1.8 & 0.3 s shorter, and the desaturation and resaturation areas 13.1 & 3.4%s smaller than males. Sleep arousals – defined as abrupt shifts in electroencephalogram (EEG) frequency – are also significantly associated with both short and long-term OSA-related outcomes [ 16 ]. Among patients with OSA and particularly severe OSA, the arousal burden is higher compared to non-OSA patients, resulting in significantly more fragmented, discontinuous sleep [ 17 ]. Arousals may be preceded by a variety of stimuli, including disruptive respiratory events such as apnoeas or hypopnoeas, abrupt limb movements, external and/or environmental stimuli, or particular chemical thresholds being exceeded [ 16 , 18 , 19 ]. There is, thus, a significant interplay between arousals and desaturation parameters [ 20 ]. In addition, airflow increases resulting from ventilatory responses to arousal contribute to restoring blood oxygen levels and reducing excess carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in the blood [ 16 ]. On the other hand, chemoreceptor activations due to hypoxia and hypercapnia can contribute to elicit arousal [ 19 ], and the association of lower blood oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) nadirs with arousal occurrence has been demonstrated previously [ 21 ]. However, no studies have examined the effect of arousals on resaturation parameters or vice versa. Given that both resaturation parameters and the threshold for arousal differ between sexes, and are modulated by age and BMI, it is plausible that resaturation parameters represent another avenue to evaluate the presence of arousals [ 22 ]. The use of limited channel sleep studies and home oximeter studies for the assessment of OSA is increasing, and fills a vital healthcare gap for populations with poor access to healthcare [ 23 ]. Research has demonstrated that autonomic arousal detection and cardiorespiratory sleep staging can significantly improve the accuracy of home sleep apnoea tests [ 24 ]. Furthermore, automated approaches for detecting subtle non-apnoeic/non-hypopnoeic arousal events from polysomnography recordings have shown promising results [ 25 ]. These advancements highlight the potential clinical value of identifying novel biomarkers of arousal from limited channel parameters. Understanding the relationship between arousals and oxygen resaturation patterns could therefore provide an additional avenue for improving diagnostic accuracy in simplified sleep testing environments where traditional EEG-based arousal detection is unavailable. We hypothesised that the presence and timing of arousals significantly influences oxygen resaturation parameters, with differential effects depending on whether arousals occur before or during desaturation events. Furthermore, we anticipated that these effects would be modulated by the presence and type of respiratory events (apnoeas vs. hypopnoeas). Therefore, in this study, we aimed to characterise the effect of nocturnal arousal presence and timing stratified by respiratory event type on oxygen resaturation parameters. For this retrospective analysis of oxygen saturation event-wise data, first-visit data from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) was utilised. Further details regarding the setting, implementation, and outcomes of the SHHS are available elsewhere [ 26 , 27 ]. In brief, 5,804 participants from existing prospective cohort studies aged > 40 years completed a baseline examination between 1995 and 1998. Participants provided information on demographic and clinical factors, including medications and comorbidities. For the purposes of this study, we included age, sex, smoking history, height, weight, BMI, comorbidities, and medications as detailed in our previous report [ 11 ]. SpO 2 was captured via an oximeter (Nonin, Minneapolis, MN) recorded at a sampling rate of 1 Hz. Due to the known data corruption issues in SHHS data [ 28 ] and scoring rules, existing manual labels for desaturation events within polysomnography’s were not used. Instead, European data format files for patients were downloaded and SpO 2 data analysed utilising the ABOSA (i.e. Automated blood oxygen saturation analysis) software (version 1.1), a freely available automated blood SpO 2 analysis tool with validated accuracy for detecting and characterizing desaturation events [ 29 , 30 ]. However, it must be noted that there are currently no formal standards for the assessment of oxygen desaturation events [ 31 ]. Therefore, for the ABOSA analyses, the following settings were used: minimum desaturation event duration of five seconds, minimum transient drop 4%, automated artefact removal, and total analysed time defined from sleep onset to offset. From the ABOSA outputs, the following parameters were extracted for analysis: SpO 2 value at start of desaturation, SpO 2 value at end of resaturation, duration of desaturations and resaturations (seconds), desaturation depth (percentile point change from event baseline to nadir), and resaturation height (percentile point change from nadir to new baseline), desaturation and resaturation rate (depth (height)/duration) and the desaturation and resaturation area (Fig. 1 ). Hypnograms were downloaded from the SHHS Profusion files and sleep stages were defined as Wake, N1, N2, N3, and rapid eye movement (REM). The sleep stage during which the event occurred was defined to be the sleep stage in which a desaturation event started, regardless of whether the sleep stage changed during the event. Participants were excluded if they had corrupted or missing nocturnal oximetry data ( n = 22, 0.4%), or if they recorded no desaturation or resaturation events ( n = 61, 1.1%). Events that occurred during epochs scored as ‘wake’ were excluded from the analysis ( n = 58,405, 19.6%), which also resulted in 230 more participants being excluded from the analysis. Manually annotated arousals did not specify the type of arousal (e.g. respiratory, limb-related, or spontaneous); therefore, no breakdown of arousal type was attempted. To study the association between presence and timing of arousals upon saturation event parameters, in addition to “no arousals”, arousals were divided into two temporal categories: (i) Pre-event Arousal – arousals which ended within 10 s prior to the ABOSA calculated start of desaturation event, and (ii) Within-event Arousals – arousals which started between the ABOSA defined start of the desaturation event up until 5 s after the ABOSA defined end of resaturation, or 5 s after the defined end of desaturation in the case of events which did not have a resaturation recorded (Fig. 1 ). As the Pre- and Within-event arousal scoring criteria were non exclusionary (i.e. an arousal could be scored 2 s before desaturation beginning and 2 s before resaturation ending), events for which multiple arousals were scored were excluded from the analysis ( n = 2,444, 1%), which also resulted in seven participants being excluded from analysis. Both sleep staging and arousal definitions were scored according to SHHS rules (found via references [ 32 , 33 ]). The 10-second search window prior to desaturation onset and 5-second post-event window for linking arousals align with recent polysomnographic studies of arousal-respiratory event temporal relationships. Leppänen et al. [ 34 ] demonstrated that 95% of respiratory event-associated arousals occur within 10 s of event termination. Furthermore, Zitting et al. [ 35 ] found that 90% of apnoea-associated cortical arousals initiate within four seconds pre- to nine seconds post-event termination, while hypopnoea-associated arousals occur within six seconds pre- to 14 s post-event. Our selected windows capture this critical period while avoiding overlap with subsequent events in clustered respiratory sequences. Rules for the scoring of respiratory events within the SHHS were: Apnoeas – amplitude of airflow signal decreased by ≥ 75% of baseline (defined as period of stable breathing with stable SpO 2 ) for ≥ 10 s; Hypopnoeas - amplitude of airflow signal decreased by ≥ 30% of baseline for ≥ 10 s and for ≥ 2 breaths [ 36 ]. For the present study, National Sleep Research Resource granted the permission to use the data. Significant differences in event-wise SpO 2 parameters between males and females were tested via univariate quantile regression for participant-level summary statistics which exhibited skewed distributions. In contrast, mixed effects regression was employed for event-wise analyses to appropriately account for repeated measures within individuals and variability across events. Univariate logistic regression models were utilised to assess differences between males and females in the likelihood of having an SpO 2 event associated with no respiratory event, hypopnoea or apnoea and no arousal, pre-event arousal or within-event arousal. Associations between presence and timing of arousal (pre-event and within-event against reference of no-arousal, and comparison of pre-event against within-event arousal) were initially assessed via univariate mixed effects regression stratified by no associated respiratory event, hypopnoea and apnoea. Following this, retaining the respiratory event stratification, the association between presence and timing of arousal upon SpO 2 parameters was assessed in multivariate mixed effects models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, forced expiratory volume in one second (percentage of predicted value utilising ethnic neutral norms via the updated global lung initiative 2023 equations [ 37 ]), sleep stage of event, smoking history and presence of arterial hypertension, lung disease, myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus, stroke, heart failure, use of hormone therapy or mental health medications (covariates chosen on the basis of our previous research [ 11 , 12 ]). Event nadir and desaturation duration, depth, rate and area were additionally adjusted for pre-event SpO 2 value, while post-event SpO 2 value and resaturation duration, height, rate and area were additionally adjusted for pre-event SpO 2 value and event nadir. All statistical tests were adjusted for via Bonferroni correction, and all analyses conducted in STATA 18 (College station, Texas). A total of 5,484 participants (49% female) were included for analysis. Participants were a median 63 years of age (interquartile range (IQR) 55, 72), with the majority being overweight (42.1%) or obese (31.3%) (Supplement 1 ). Around half (53.5%) of the participants had a history of smoking and the majority of participants had at least one comorbidity (85.7%), of which arterial hypertension was the most common (49.5%). One-third of female participants recorded use of hormone therapy (30%). Overall, 235,996 desaturation events were recorded (participant median 19 (IQR 6, 50)), though 16,881 (7.1%) desaturation events did not have a corresponding resaturation recorded. Males recorded a significantly higher number of desaturations and resaturations than females (median difference 14 & 13 respectively) and numerous significant differences were seen in SpO 2 architecture parameters (Table 1 ). Pre- and post-SpO 2 values were a median 0.2% lower among females, desaturation and resaturation durations 1.8 & 0.3 s shorter, and the desaturation and resaturation areas 13.1 & 3.4%s smaller than males. title: Development and validation of a PD-L1 and tumor mutational burden-based predictive model for pathological complete response after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable lung cancer
abstract: Introduction Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has demonstrated promising efficacy in resectable lung cancer; however, substantial interindividual variability in the treatment response remains. Although programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are established biomarkers of immunotherapy response, the performance of predictive models that integrate these biomarkers remains unclear. Aim To develop and validate predictive models integrating PD-L1 expression and TMB for estimating pathological complete response (pCR) following neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with resectable lung cancer and to compare the performance of a nomogram and a random forest model. Method This retrospective cohort study included 232 patients who underwent surgical resection following neoadjuvant immunotherapy as the model development cohort and were randomly assigned to the training and internal validation sets (7:3). A temporally independent validation cohort of 115 consecutive patients treated at the same institution during a later study period was used to assess the generalizability of the model. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of pCR. A nomogram and random forest model were developed and evaluated in terms of discrimination, calibration, and classification performance. Results Clinical stage II (odds ratio [OR] 0.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31–0.94), absence of lymph node metastasis (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16–0.77), receipt of immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy (OR 4.00, 95% CI 1.54–10.39), higher PD-L1 expression (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.03–2.54), and higher TMB (OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.42–6.65) were independently associated with pCR (all P < 0.05). In the random forest (RF) model, PD-L1 expression and TMB were the most influential predictors. The RF model demonstrated superior discrimination compared with the nomogram in both the training cohort (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.866 vs. 0.782; P < 0.001) and the internal validation cohort (AUC 0.769 vs. 0.669; P < 0.001), with better overall classification performance. In the temporally independent validation cohort, the RF model achieved an AUC of 0.757 (95% CI 0.682–0.902), a sensitivity of 82.6%, and a specificity of 76.2%, although the calibration was suboptimal. Conclusion PD-L1 expression and TMB were independently associated with pathological response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with resectable lung cancer. The predictive model incorporating these biomarkers demonstrated acceptable performance, with the RF model outperforming the nomogram. However, the model should be considered exploratory and requires prospective multicenter external validation before routine clinical application. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11096-026-02191-3 .
body: A prediction model integrating PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and clinical characteristics may help identify patients who are more likely to achieve pathological complete response following neoadjuvant immunotherapy. The random forest model demonstrated better discrimination and classification performance than the nomogram, suggesting its potential to support biomarker-informed risk stratification and treatment planning in clinical practice. Following further prospective external validation, such predictive tools may help optimize neoadjuvant treatment strategies and support individualized multidisciplinary care while reducing unnecessary exposure to ineffective, potentially harmful immunotherapy. A prediction model integrating PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and clinical characteristics may help identify patients who are more likely to achieve pathological complete response following neoadjuvant immunotherapy. The random forest model demonstrated better discrimination and classification performance than the nomogram, suggesting its potential to support biomarker-informed risk stratification and treatment planning in clinical practice. Following further prospective external validation, such predictive tools may help optimize neoadjuvant treatment strategies and support individualized multidisciplinary care while reducing unnecessary exposure to ineffective, potentially harmful immunotherapy. Lung cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for > 80% of all cases. A considerable proportion of patients present with locally advanced disease, for whom surgical resection alone is associated with a high risk of recurrence and a 5-year survival rate of less than 50% [ 1 ]. Therefore, optimizing perioperative treatment strategies is critical for improving long-term outcomes. Neoadjuvant therapy is administered before surgery to reduce tumor burden and eradicate micrometastatic disease. Previous studies have demonstrated that neoadjuvant chemotherapy, either alone or in combination, can improve pathological complete response (pCR) rates in patients with locally advanced resectable NSCLC [ 2 – 4 ]. Recently, immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the programmed death-1 (PD-1)/ programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathway have been incorporated into neoadjuvant treatment regimens with promising efficacy. However, the treatment response remains highly heterogeneous. A substantial proportion of patients derive limited or no benefit while being exposed to immune-related adverse events, disease progression, or delays in definitive surgery [ 5 ]. Therefore, identifying patients who are most likely to benefit from neoadjuvant immunotherapy is essential for optimizing individualized treatment strategies and minimizing unnecessary treatment exposure. Predictive modeling has emerged as an important approach to support treatment decision-making in oncology. Nomograms based on multivariable regression models provide user-friendly tools for estimating the probability of clinical outcomes and are widely used because of their interpretability [ 6 ]. In contrast, machine learning approaches, such as random forest (RF) algorithms, can capture complex nonlinear relationships and interactions among variables, offering potential advantages for multifactorial predictions [ 7 ]. The integration of these complementary approaches may improve the accuracy and robustness of predictive models. PD-L1 expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are among the most extensively studied biomarkers of immunotherapy response in NSCLC. PD-L1 mediates immune evasion by binding to PD-1 receptors on T cells, whereas TMB reflects the number of somatic mutations within the tumor genome and is associated with increased neoantigen generation and tumor immunogenicity [ 8 , 9 ]. Higher PD-L1 expression and elevated TMB have been associated with improved responses to immunotherapy in lung cancer [ 10 , 11 ]. Nevertheless, the predictive value of either biomarker alone remains limited, and the integration of both biomarkers may better characterize the tumor immune microenvironment and improve predictive accuracy. Although several predictive models for immunotherapy response in lung cancer have been reported, most rely on a single biomarker or a limited number of clinical variables. Moreover, few studies have simultaneously incorporated PD-L1 expression and TMB while directly comparing traditional regression-based models with machine learning approaches in the neoadjuvant setting for treating resectable NSCLC. Therefore, there is a need for clinically applicable prediction models that integrate molecular biomarkers with clinical characteristics to support biomarker-informed treatment strategies. This study aimed to develop and validate predictive models integrating PD-L1 expression and TMB for estimating pCR following neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with resectable lung cancer and to compare the performance of a nomogram and RF model. This retrospective cohort study included patients with resectable lung cancer who underwent surgical resection following neoadjuvant immunotherapy at the Henan Provincial Chest Hospital. A total of 232 consecutive patients treated between January 2023, and December 2024 were enrolled in the model development cohort. The cohort was randomly assigned to training and internal validation sets in a 7:3 ratio using a random-number table. The training set was used for model development, and the internal validation set was used to evaluate the model performance. A temporally independent validation cohort consisting of 115 consecutive patients who met the same eligibility criteria and were treated between January and December 2025 was used to assess model generalizability. The sample collection process is shown in Supplemental Fig. 1 . The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) pathologically confirmed lung cancer; (2) clinically resectable disease (stage II–IIIB according to the 8th edition of the TNM staging system [ 12 ]); (3) receipt of neoadjuvant immunotherapy followed by surgical resection; (4) availability of tumor tissue for PD-L1 testing and next-generation sequencing (NGS); and (5) complete clinical and pathological data were available. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) concurrent malignancies; (2) incomplete clinical or follow-up data; (3) incomplete neoadjuvant therapy or treatment modification; (4) autoimmune disease or severe hepatic or renal dysfunction; and (5) prior exposure to immunotherapy or targeted therapies. Clinical data were extracted from the electronic medical records. Baseline variables included age, sex, smoking history (≥ 100 cigarettes/year), histological type (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, or other), clinical stage (II, IIIA, or IIIB), tumor size, lymph node metastasis status, tumor location, history of pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, neoadjuvant treatment regimen, number of treatment cycles, and type of chemotherapy agent. Performance status was assessed using the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status scale [ 13 ]. The laboratory parameters included PD-L1 expression, TMB, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA). Tumor samples were obtained before the initiation of neoadjuvant therapy. PD-L1 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry using the SP263 antibody kit (Roche Diagnostics). Two experienced pathologists independently evaluated the staining results in a blinded manner, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus agreement. PD-L1 expression was quantified using the tumor proportion score (TPS) and categorized as negative (TPS < 1%), low (TPS 1% to < 50%), or high (TPS ≥ 50%) [ 14 ]. TMB was measured using next-generation sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform with a targeted panel of 422 genes. After excluding germline and synonymous mutations, TMB was calculated as the number of somatic non-synonymous mutations per megabase (mut/Mb). Patients were categorized as having low (< 10 mut/Mb) or high (≥ 10 mut/Mb) TMB [ 15 ]. CEA levels were measured using a chemiluminescent immunoassay (UniCel DxI 800; Beckman Coulter), with an upper reference limit of 5.0 ng/mL. The primary outcome was pCR, assessed approximately 4 weeks after the completion of neoadjuvant immunotherapy. All surgical specimens were independently evaluated by two senior pathologists according to the criteria of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer [ 16 ], with discrepancies resolved by consensus agreement. pCR was defined as the complete absence of viable tumor cells in both the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes (0% residual tumor cellularity). Neoadjuvant treatment consisted of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy or PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor combined with platinum-based chemotherapy. Treatment regimens were selected by a multidisciplinary team according to the tumor histology, clinical stage, and patient condition. For immunotherapy monotherapy, patients received atezolizumab (1200 mg every 3 weeks), durvalumab (1500 mg every 4 weeks), nivolumab (240 mg every 2 weeks or 360 mg every 3 weeks), or pembrolizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks) administered intravenously for 2–4 cycles. For combination therapy, patients with adenocarcinoma received pemetrexed plus cisplatin or carboplatin, whereas those with squamous cell carcinoma received paclitaxel plus platinum-based chemotherapy. Immunotherapy was administered concurrently with chemotherapy for two to four cycles. Detailed information on treatment regimens and treatment cycle distribution is presented in Table 1 . Development and validation of a PD-L1 and tumor mutational burden-based predictive model for pathological complete response after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable lung cancer

Introduction Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has demonstrated promising efficacy in resectable lung cancer; however, substantial interindividual variability in the treatment response remains. Although programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are established biomarkers of immunotherapy response, the performance of predictive models that integrate these biomarkers remains unclear. Aim To develop and validate predictive models integrating PD-L1 expression and TMB for estimating pathological complete response (pCR) following neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with resectable lung cancer and to compare the performance of a nomogram and a random forest model. Method This retrospective cohort study included 232 patients who underwent surgical resection following neoadjuvant immunotherapy as the model development cohort and were randomly assigned to the training and internal validation sets (7:3). A temporally independent validation cohort of 115 consecutive patients treated at the same institution during a later study period was used to assess the generalizability of the model. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of pCR. A nomogram and random forest model were developed and evaluated in terms of discrimination, calibration, and classification performance. Results Clinical stage II (odds ratio [OR] 0.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31–0.94), absence of lymph node metastasis (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16–0.77), receipt of immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy (OR 4.00, 95% CI 1.54–10.39), higher PD-L1 expression (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.03–2.54), and higher TMB (OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.42–6.65) were independently associated with pCR (all P < 0.05). In the random forest (RF) model, PD-L1 expression and TMB were the most influential predictors. The RF model demonstrated superior discrimination compared with the nomogram in both the training cohort (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.866 vs. 0.782; P < 0.001) and the internal validation cohort (AUC 0.769 vs. 0.669; P < 0.001), with better overall classification performance. In the temporally independent validation cohort, the RF model achieved an AUC of 0.757 (95% CI 0.682–0.902), a sensitivity of 82.6%, and a specificity of 76.2%, although the calibration was suboptimal. Conclusion PD-L1 expression and TMB were independently associated with pathological response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with resectable lung cancer. The predictive model incorporating these biomarkers demonstrated acceptable performance, with the RF model outperforming the nomogram. However, the model should be considered exploratory and requires prospective multicenter external validation before routine clinical application. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11096-026-02191-3 .

A prediction model integrating PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and clinical characteristics may help identify patients who are more likely to achieve pathological complete response following neoadjuvant immunotherapy. The random forest model demonstrated better discrimination and classification performance than the nomogram, suggesting its potential to support biomarker-informed risk stratification and treatment planning in clinical practice. Following further prospective external validation, such predictive tools may help optimize neoadjuvant treatment strategies and support individualized multidisciplinary care while reducing unnecessary exposure to ineffective, potentially harmful immunotherapy. Lung cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for > 80% of all cases. A considerable proportion of patients present with locally advanced disease, for whom surgical resection alone is associated with a high risk of recurrence and a 5-year survival rate of less than 50% [ 1 ]. Therefore, optimizing perioperative treatment strategies is critical for improving long-term outcomes. Neoadjuvant therapy is administered before surgery to reduce tumor burden and eradicate micrometastatic disease. Previous studies have demonstrated that neoadjuvant chemotherapy, either alone or in combination, can improve pathological complete response (pCR) rates in patients with locally advanced resectable NSCLC [ 2 – 4 ]. Recently, immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the programmed death-1 (PD-1)/ programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathway have been incorporated into neoadjuvant treatment regimens with promising efficacy. However, the treatment response remains highly heterogeneous. A substantial proportion of patients derive limited or no benefit while being exposed to immune-related adverse events, disease progression, or delays in definitive surgery [ 5 ]. Therefore, identifying patients who are most likely to benefit from neoadjuvant immunotherapy is essential for optimizing individualized treatment strategies and minimizing unnecessary treatment exposure. Predictive modeling has emerged as an important approach to support treatment decision-making in oncology. Nomograms based on multivariable regression models provide user-friendly tools for estimating the probability of clinical outcomes and are widely used because of their interpretability [ 6 ]. In contrast, machine learning approaches, such as random forest (RF) algorithms, can capture complex nonlinear relationships and interactions among variables, offering potential advantages for multifactorial predictions [ 7 ]. The integration of these complementary approaches may improve the accuracy and robustness of predictive models. PD-L1 expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are among the most extensively studied biomarkers of immunotherapy response in NSCLC. PD-L1 mediates immune evasion by binding to PD-1 receptors on T cells, whereas TMB reflects the number of somatic mutations within the tumor genome and is associated with increased neoantigen generation and tumor immunogenicity [ 8 , 9 ]. Higher PD-L1 expression and elevated TMB have been associated with improved responses to immunotherapy in lung cancer [ 10 , 11 ]. Nevertheless, the predictive value of either biomarker alone remains limited, and the integration of both biomarkers may better characterize the tumor immune microenvironment and improve predictive accuracy. Although several predictive models for immunotherapy response in lung cancer have been reported, most rely on a single biomarker or a limited number of clinical variables. Moreover, few studies have simultaneously incorporated PD-L1 expression and TMB while directly comparing traditional regression-based models with machine learning approaches in the neoadjuvant setting for treating resectable NSCLC. Therefore, there is a need for clinically applicable prediction models that integrate molecular biomarkers with clinical characteristics to support biomarker-informed treatment strategies. This study aimed to develop and validate predictive models integrating PD-L1 expression and TMB for estimating pCR following neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with resectable lung cancer and to compare the performance of a nomogram and RF model. This retrospective cohort study included patients with resectable lung cancer who underwent surgical resection following neoadjuvant immunotherapy at the Henan Provincial Chest Hospital. A total of 232 consecutive patients treated between January 2023, and December 2024 were enrolled in the model development cohort. The cohort was randomly assigned to training and internal validation sets in a 7:3 ratio using a random-number table. The training set was used for model development, and the internal validation set was used to evaluate the model performance. A temporally independent validation cohort consisting of 115 consecutive patients who met the same eligibility criteria and were treated between January and December 2025 was used to assess model generalizability. The sample collection process is shown in Supplemental Fig. 1 . The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) pathologically confirmed lung cancer; (2) clinically resectable disease (stage II–IIIB according to the 8th edition of the TNM staging system [ 12 ]); (3) receipt of neoadjuvant immunotherapy followed by surgical resection; (4) availability of tumor tissue for PD-L1 testing and next-generation sequencing (NGS); and (5) complete clinical and pathological data were available. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) concurrent malignancies; (2) incomplete clinical or follow-up data; (3) incomplete neoadjuvant therapy or treatment modification; (4) autoimmune disease or severe hepatic or renal dysfunction; and (5) prior exposure to immunotherapy or targeted therapies. Clinical data were extracted from the electronic medical records. Baseline variables included age, sex, smoking history (≥ 100 cigarettes/year), histological type (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, or other), clinical stage (II, IIIA, or IIIB), tumor size, lymph node metastasis status, tumor location, history of pulmonary disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, neoadjuvant treatment regimen, number of treatment cycles, and type of chemotherapy agent. Performance status was assessed using the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status scale [ 13 ]. The laboratory parameters included PD-L1 expression, TMB, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA). Tumor samples were obtained before the initiation of neoadjuvant therapy. PD-L1 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry using the SP263 antibody kit (Roche Diagnostics). Two experienced pathologists independently evaluated the staining results in a blinded manner, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus agreement. PD-L1 expression was quantified using the tumor proportion score (TPS) and categorized as negative (TPS < 1%), low (TPS 1% to < 50%), or high (TPS ≥ 50%) [ 14 ]. TMB was measured using next-generation sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform with a targeted panel of 422 genes. After excluding germline and synonymous mutations, TMB was calculated as the number of somatic non-synonymous mutations per megabase (mut/Mb). Patients were categorized as having low (< 10 mut/Mb) or high (≥ 10 mut/Mb) TMB [ 15 ]. CEA levels were measured using a chemiluminescent immunoassay (UniCel DxI 800; Beckman Coulter), with an upper reference limit of 5.0 ng/mL. The primary outcome was pCR, assessed approximately 4 weeks after the completion of neoadjuvant immunotherapy. All surgical specimens were independently evaluated by two senior pathologists according to the criteria of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer [ 16 ], with discrepancies resolved by consensus agreement. pCR was defined as the complete absence of viable tumor cells in both the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes (0% residual tumor cellularity). Neoadjuvant treatment consisted of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy or PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor combined with platinum-based chemotherapy. Treatment regimens were selected by a multidisciplinary team according to the tumor histology, clinical stage, and patient condition. For immunotherapy monotherapy, patients received atezolizumab (1200 mg every 3 weeks), durvalumab (1500 mg every 4 weeks), nivolumab (240 mg every 2 weeks or 360 mg every 3 weeks), or pembrolizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks) administered intravenously for 2–4 cycles. For combination therapy, patients with adenocarcinoma received pemetrexed plus cisplatin or carboplatin, whereas those with squamous cell carcinoma received paclitaxel plus platinum-based chemotherapy. Immunotherapy was administered concurrently with chemotherapy for two to four cycles. Detailed information on treatment regimens and treatment cycle distribution is presented in Table 1 .
