title: Efficacy of Melatonin in Alleviating Radiotherapy-Induced Fatigue, Anxiety, and Depression in Breast Cancer Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background Breast cancer (BRCA) remains the most diagnosed malignancy among women globally and is predominantly managed through multimodal therapy. Radiotherapy, an essential component of BRCA management, often causes fatigue, anxiety, and depression that compromise the quality of life (QoL) of patients. Melatonin, an endogenous hormone with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and circadian rhythm–modulating properties, has shown potential for preventing radiotherapy-associated toxicities. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of melatonin in alleviating radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression among breast cancer patients. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251144916), a comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Google Scholar up to August 2025. RCTSs comparing melatonin with placebo in adult female patients with non-metastatic breast cancer undergoing adjuvant radiotherapy were included. The Cochrane RoB-2 tool was employed for quality assessment. Pooled standardized mean differences (SMDs) and mean differences (MDs) were calculated using a random-effects model in RevMan 5.4 software. Results Five RCTs encompassing 561 patients were analyzed. Melatonin significantly reduced fatigue severity (SMD = –0.43; 95% CI –0.65 to –0.20; p = 0.0002) and improved cognitive functioning (MD = 1.16; 95% CI 0.95 to 1.36; p < 0.00001) and global health status (MD = 2.47; 95% CI 2.07 to 2.87; p < 0.00001). No significant effects were observed for emotional, social, or physical functioning, nor for gastrointestinal, pain, or sleep-related domains. Conclusion Based on limited number of studies, melatonin supplementation appears to be a safe, well-tolerated, and low-cost adjunct to radiotherapy, capable of improving fatigue, cognitive performance, and overall QoL in breast cancer patients. However, small sample sizes and heterogeneous dosing regimens require further large-scale RCTs to establish optimal dosing and long-term efficacy.
body: Breast cancer (BRCA) is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy among women. In 2022, approximately 2.3 million new BRCA cases and around 670,000 deaths were reported worldwide, making it the leading cause of cancer-related disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). 1 One in eight women is likely to develop BRCA over the course of life. 2 Histopathologically, BRCA is heterogeneous, comprising more than 20 diagnostic subtypes, most of which originate from epithelial tissue. Prognosis is primarily determined by tumor size and lymph node involvement. 3 BRCA is characterized by uncontrolled cellular proliferation, with the potential of local invasion and distant metastases. 4 Advances in surgery, systemic therapy, and screening have substantially improved early detection and survival. 5 Currently, five standard therapeutic modalities are involved in BRCA management: surgery, chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, targeted therapy, and radiotherapy. 2 Radiotherapy, an essential component of treatment, is administered to more than 90 % of patients to reduce locoregional recurrence and improve overall survival. 6 However, the global incidence of BRCA continues to rise. 7 , 8 4 Radiotherapy effectively eradicates residual malignant cells to lower the risk of distant dissemination, but it is associated with both immediate and long-term toxic effects. Fatigue is one of the most prevalent adverse effects, reported in up to 79–81 % of patients undergoing treatment. It is a multidimensional symptom, encompassing physical, cognitive, and emotional domains, and significantly compromises social functioning and self-esteem. 7 Anxiety and depression are also common during radiotherapy, with prevalence rates ranging from 21–54 % for anxiety and 12–31 % for depression. 3 These conditions frequently coexist among cancer patients. 9 They are associated with treatment non-compliance, reduced quality of life (QoL), prolonged hospitalization, and increased cancer-related mortality. 3 In addition, persistent concerns about disease progression and treatment-related adverse effects further intensify psychological distress. 8 Standardized assessment tools are frequently used in clinical research to evaluate these symptoms. Fatigue severity is commonly measured with the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI), whereas anxiety and depression are assessed using the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). 9 The European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-30) is a 30-item cancer-specific questionnaire, widely used in international clinical trials to assess the QoL of cancer patients. 4 10 Management of radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression incorporates non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches. Non-pharmacologic interventions include physical and occupational therapy, exercise, yoga, and cognitive-behavioral strategies, whereas pharmacologic measures may involve psychostimulants such as methylphenidate and modafinil. Nevertheless, radiotherapy-induced fatigue remains underreported, underdiagnosed, and undertreated. Randomized studies investigating relaxation therapy, group psychotherapy, exercise, and sleep management have demonstrated promising outcomes; however, no single approach has been established as standard of care. 8 , 10 Given these limitations, melatonin has gained increasing attention owing to its potential anti-cancer effects. Evidence indicates that it may mitigate radiotherapy-associated adverse effects. 11 Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous hormone secreted by the pineal gland that protects cells from radiation-induced oxidative damage by neutralizing reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and enhancing antioxidant enzyme activity. In addition to its role in circadian rhythms, melatonin exhibits radioprotective and radiosensitizing properties, as well as anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects. 4 Several studies have also demonstrated that melatonin inhibits tumor growth. 12 , 13 Randomized clinical trials have reported that melatonin supplementation at bedtime significantly reduces fatigue severity, improves QoL, and sleep outcomes in patients with BRCA. 14 15 The current evidence on melatonin as an adjuvant in BRCA radiotherapy remains inconclusive, with small sample sizes, variable dosages, treatment durations, and outcome measures limiting the applicability of results. Most investigations have evaluated participants only during radiotherapy, leaving the efficacy and safety of melatonin in hypofractionated regimens and over longer follow-up periods still uncertain. The optimal dose and mode of administration remain undefined, underscoring the need for further clinical trials to establish its therapeutic value. 4 13 The current evidence on melatonin as an adjuvant in radiotherapy for BRCA is limited and varies across studies in terms of sample size, dosage, treatment duration, and outcome measures. In addition, most studies have focused primarily on outcomes during radiotherapy, with limited evidence available on longer-term effects and across different radiotherapy regimens. Therefore, this study was conducted as a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of melatonin in reducing radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression in BRCA patients. 4 This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. The registration in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) was accepted under the registration number (CRD420251144916). 16 We systematically conducted a comprehensive literature search across PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, Cochrane Library and Embase to identify all relevant records up to August 2025. Additionally, Clinicaltrials.gov was searched for published or unpublished clinical trials. The research question was structured using the PICO strategy design (Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes). The following search terms were used: (“breast neoplasms” OR “breast cancer”) AND (“radiotherapy” OR “adjuvant radiotherapy”) AND (“melatonin”) AND (“fatigue” OR “anxiety” OR “depression” OR “treatment-related symptoms” OR “quality of life”). Two authors conducted the search without any limitations or conflicts of interest. Supplementary Table 1 shows the Search strategy. The title and abstract of the articles were reviewed individually by three independent authors. Full texts of the articles deemed relevant were then read thoroughly to confirm whether they met the eligibility criteria. This was done to ensure that only articles meeting specified criteria were selected for the final analysis. Any discrepancy was resolved through discussion with another author. The eligibility criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing melatonin with placebo to evaluate its efficacy in alleviating radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression in BRCA patients, enrolling adult women (≥18 years) with histologically confirmed, non-metastatic BRCA scheduled for adjuvant radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. Exclusion criteria comprised pregnancy or lactation, previous breast or chest irradiation, and serious uncontrolled medical or psychiatric conditions. Single-arm studies and studies without relevant outcomes or original data were excluded. The research screening excluded non-English literature. Additionally, Studies were excluded if they lacked relevant efficacy outcomes or original data. Cross-sectional studies, letters, case reports, case series, reviews, and editorials were also excluded. Across the included studies, the primary outcomes comprised mean fatigue score, physical functioning, social functioning, emotional functioning, and global health status. The secondary outcomes included functional well-being (FWB) and additional QLQ-C30 domains such as role functioning, cognitive functioning, nausea/vomiting, pain, dyspnoea, insomnia, appetite loss, constipation, diarrhoea, and financial difficulties. Two independent reviewers extracted the data, and discrepancies were resolved through consensus after discussion. An online Microsoft Excel spreadsheet was created using data from the included studies for baseline characteristics and outcomes. Baseline parameters are as follows: total population, age, body mass index (BMI), breast volume, race, and number of patients. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB-2). Two independent reviewers evaluated the studies based on predefined criteria. The factors evaluated were measurement of the outcome, randomization process, selective reporting, missing data, and overall bias. Based on these factors, each trial was categorized as having either high risk, low risk, or some concerns. Any disagreements were initially addressed through discussion. In cases where consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer resolved the final decision. 17 Statistical analyses were conducted using RevMan (Review Manager, version 5.4, Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK. Relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was used to analyze dichotomous data. In contrast, for continuous outcomes, either the weighted mean difference (WMD) or the SMD with 95% CIs was applied. A two-sided p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I 2 values. The values between 50-75% were considered as moderate heterogeneity, while values > 75% were indicative of severe heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis was performed for studies exhibiting high heterogeneity to identify the impact of potential sources of variation. Forest plots were generated to display pooled effect sizes and CIs for each outcome, enabling comparison across studies. These plots also illustrated both heterogeneity and the overall summary estimate under the random-effects model. Meta-regression was performed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (version 4), and results were reported as regression coefficients (Coeff) and P-values. Initially, a total of 81 studies were identified through comprehensive searches on various databases. After removing 29 duplicate entries, 52 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 42 were excluded because they did not meet the eligibility criteria. Subsequently, a full text assessment was conducted on the remaining 10 articles, resulting in the exclusion of five reports because of an ineligible population, non-relevant outcomes and wrong study design. Consequently, five RCTs satisfied all inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the final qualitative synthesis. Publication dates ranged from 2022 to 2024. The detailed study selection process is presented in 18 - 22 Figure 1 . Figure 1. PRISMA 2020 flow diagram for new systematic reviews which included searches of databases and registers only PRISMA 2020 flow diagram for new systematic reviews which included searches of databases and registers only The five included RCTs included a total of 561 BRCA patients with sample sizes ranging from 48 to 203 patients in each study. The average age in the studies was mostly between 50 and 60, with most patients in their late 40s to early 60s. BMI was not reported consistently; however, in the two RCTs that did report it, the mean BMI in the intervention groups ranged from 26.4(8.1) to 29.5(6.5), and in the placebo groups from 26(5.3) to 44.0(14.2), indicating that participants were generally overweight. Some studies reported baseline comorbidities, including diabetes mellitus in 32.7% of participants in the intervention group and 26.4% in the control group, hypertension in 18.5% and 20.7%, and hypothyroidism in 8.54% and 7.86%, respectively. Most participants had received doxorubicin-based chemotherapy and conventional radiotherapy, while hypofractionated regimens were less common. Before starting adjuvant therapy, surgical options included both radical mastectomy and breast-conserving surgery, with no significant differences between the groups. Overall, baseline characteristics were well balanced between melatonin and placebo groups across the included trials, supporting the comparability of study populations. Efficacy of Melatonin in Alleviating Radiotherapy-Induced Fatigue, Anxiety, and Depression in Breast Cancer Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

Background Breast cancer (BRCA) remains the most diagnosed malignancy among women globally and is predominantly managed through multimodal therapy. Radiotherapy, an essential component of BRCA management, often causes fatigue, anxiety, and depression that compromise the quality of life (QoL) of patients. Melatonin, an endogenous hormone with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and circadian rhythm–modulating properties, has shown potential for preventing radiotherapy-associated toxicities. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of melatonin in alleviating radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression among breast cancer patients. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251144916), a comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Google Scholar up to August 2025. RCTSs comparing melatonin with placebo in adult female patients with non-metastatic breast cancer undergoing adjuvant radiotherapy were included. The Cochrane RoB-2 tool was employed for quality assessment. Pooled standardized mean differences (SMDs) and mean differences (MDs) were calculated using a random-effects model in RevMan 5.4 software. Results Five RCTs encompassing 561 patients were analyzed. Melatonin significantly reduced fatigue severity (SMD = –0.43; 95% CI –0.65 to –0.20; p = 0.0002) and improved cognitive functioning (MD = 1.16; 95% CI 0.95 to 1.36; p < 0.00001) and global health status (MD = 2.47; 95% CI 2.07 to 2.87; p < 0.00001). No significant effects were observed for emotional, social, or physical functioning, nor for gastrointestinal, pain, or sleep-related domains. Conclusion Based on limited number of studies, melatonin supplementation appears to be a safe, well-tolerated, and low-cost adjunct to radiotherapy, capable of improving fatigue, cognitive performance, and overall QoL in breast cancer patients. However, small sample sizes and heterogeneous dosing regimens require further large-scale RCTs to establish optimal dosing and long-term efficacy.

Breast cancer (BRCA) is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy among women. In 2022, approximately 2.3 million new BRCA cases and around 670,000 deaths were reported worldwide, making it the leading cause of cancer-related disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). 1 One in eight women is likely to develop BRCA over the course of life. 2 Histopathologically, BRCA is heterogeneous, comprising more than 20 diagnostic subtypes, most of which originate from epithelial tissue. Prognosis is primarily determined by tumor size and lymph node involvement. 3 BRCA is characterized by uncontrolled cellular proliferation, with the potential of local invasion and distant metastases. 4 Advances in surgery, systemic therapy, and screening have substantially improved early detection and survival. 5 Currently, five standard therapeutic modalities are involved in BRCA management: surgery, chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, targeted therapy, and radiotherapy. 2 Radiotherapy, an essential component of treatment, is administered to more than 90 % of patients to reduce locoregional recurrence and improve overall survival. 6 However, the global incidence of BRCA continues to rise. 7 , 8 4 Radiotherapy effectively eradicates residual malignant cells to lower the risk of distant dissemination, but it is associated with both immediate and long-term toxic effects. Fatigue is one of the most prevalent adverse effects, reported in up to 79–81 % of patients undergoing treatment. It is a multidimensional symptom, encompassing physical, cognitive, and emotional domains, and significantly compromises social functioning and self-esteem. 7 Anxiety and depression are also common during radiotherapy, with prevalence rates ranging from 21–54 % for anxiety and 12–31 % for depression. 3 These conditions frequently coexist among cancer patients. 9 They are associated with treatment non-compliance, reduced quality of life (QoL), prolonged hospitalization, and increased cancer-related mortality. 3 In addition, persistent concerns about disease progression and treatment-related adverse effects further intensify psychological distress. 8 Standardized assessment tools are frequently used in clinical research to evaluate these symptoms. Fatigue severity is commonly measured with the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI), whereas anxiety and depression are assessed using the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). 9 The European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-30) is a 30-item cancer-specific questionnaire, widely used in international clinical trials to assess the QoL of cancer patients. 4 10 Management of radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression incorporates non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches. Non-pharmacologic interventions include physical and occupational therapy, exercise, yoga, and cognitive-behavioral strategies, whereas pharmacologic measures may involve psychostimulants such as methylphenidate and modafinil. Nevertheless, radiotherapy-induced fatigue remains underreported, underdiagnosed, and undertreated. Randomized studies investigating relaxation therapy, group psychotherapy, exercise, and sleep management have demonstrated promising outcomes; however, no single approach has been established as standard of care. 8 , 10 Given these limitations, melatonin has gained increasing attention owing to its potential anti-cancer effects. Evidence indicates that it may mitigate radiotherapy-associated adverse effects. 11 Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous hormone secreted by the pineal gland that protects cells from radiation-induced oxidative damage by neutralizing reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and enhancing antioxidant enzyme activity. In addition to its role in circadian rhythms, melatonin exhibits radioprotective and radiosensitizing properties, as well as anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects. 4 Several studies have also demonstrated that melatonin inhibits tumor growth. 12 , 13 Randomized clinical trials have reported that melatonin supplementation at bedtime significantly reduces fatigue severity, improves QoL, and sleep outcomes in patients with BRCA. 14 15 The current evidence on melatonin as an adjuvant in BRCA radiotherapy remains inconclusive, with small sample sizes, variable dosages, treatment durations, and outcome measures limiting the applicability of results. Most investigations have evaluated participants only during radiotherapy, leaving the efficacy and safety of melatonin in hypofractionated regimens and over longer follow-up periods still uncertain. The optimal dose and mode of administration remain undefined, underscoring the need for further clinical trials to establish its therapeutic value. 4 13 The current evidence on melatonin as an adjuvant in radiotherapy for BRCA is limited and varies across studies in terms of sample size, dosage, treatment duration, and outcome measures. In addition, most studies have focused primarily on outcomes during radiotherapy, with limited evidence available on longer-term effects and across different radiotherapy regimens. Therefore, this study was conducted as a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of melatonin in reducing radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression in BRCA patients. 4 This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. The registration in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) was accepted under the registration number (CRD420251144916). 16 We systematically conducted a comprehensive literature search across PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, Cochrane Library and Embase to identify all relevant records up to August 2025. Additionally, Clinicaltrials.gov was searched for published or unpublished clinical trials. The research question was structured using the PICO strategy design (Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes). The following search terms were used: (“breast neoplasms” OR “breast cancer”) AND (“radiotherapy” OR “adjuvant radiotherapy”) AND (“melatonin”) AND (“fatigue” OR “anxiety” OR “depression” OR “treatment-related symptoms” OR “quality of life”). Two authors conducted the search without any limitations or conflicts of interest. Supplementary Table 1 shows the Search strategy. The title and abstract of the articles were reviewed individually by three independent authors. Full texts of the articles deemed relevant were then read thoroughly to confirm whether they met the eligibility criteria. This was done to ensure that only articles meeting specified criteria were selected for the final analysis. Any discrepancy was resolved through discussion with another author. The eligibility criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing melatonin with placebo to evaluate its efficacy in alleviating radiotherapy-induced fatigue, anxiety, and depression in BRCA patients, enrolling adult women (≥18 years) with histologically confirmed, non-metastatic BRCA scheduled for adjuvant radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. Exclusion criteria comprised pregnancy or lactation, previous breast or chest irradiation, and serious uncontrolled medical or psychiatric conditions. Single-arm studies and studies without relevant outcomes or original data were excluded. The research screening excluded non-English literature. Additionally, Studies were excluded if they lacked relevant efficacy outcomes or original data. Cross-sectional studies, letters, case reports, case series, reviews, and editorials were also excluded. Across the included studies, the primary outcomes comprised mean fatigue score, physical functioning, social functioning, emotional functioning, and global health status. The secondary outcomes included functional well-being (FWB) and additional QLQ-C30 domains such as role functioning, cognitive functioning, nausea/vomiting, pain, dyspnoea, insomnia, appetite loss, constipation, diarrhoea, and financial difficulties. Two independent reviewers extracted the data, and discrepancies were resolved through consensus after discussion. An online Microsoft Excel spreadsheet was created using data from the included studies for baseline characteristics and outcomes. Baseline parameters are as follows: total population, age, body mass index (BMI), breast volume, race, and number of patients. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB-2). Two independent reviewers evaluated the studies based on predefined criteria. The factors evaluated were measurement of the outcome, randomization process, selective reporting, missing data, and overall bias. Based on these factors, each trial was categorized as having either high risk, low risk, or some concerns. Any disagreements were initially addressed through discussion. In cases where consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer resolved the final decision. 17 Statistical analyses were conducted using RevMan (Review Manager, version 5.4, Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK. Relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was used to analyze dichotomous data. In contrast, for continuous outcomes, either the weighted mean difference (WMD) or the SMD with 95% CIs was applied. A two-sided p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I 2 values. The values between 50-75% were considered as moderate heterogeneity, while values > 75% were indicative of severe heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis was performed for studies exhibiting high heterogeneity to identify the impact of potential sources of variation. Forest plots were generated to display pooled effect sizes and CIs for each outcome, enabling comparison across studies. These plots also illustrated both heterogeneity and the overall summary estimate under the random-effects model. Meta-regression was performed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (version 4), and results were reported as regression coefficients (Coeff) and P-values. Initially, a total of 81 studies were identified through comprehensive searches on various databases. After removing 29 duplicate entries, 52 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 42 were excluded because they did not meet the eligibility criteria. Subsequently, a full text assessment was conducted on the remaining 10 articles, resulting in the exclusion of five reports because of an ineligible population, non-relevant outcomes and wrong study design. Consequently, five RCTs satisfied all inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the final qualitative synthesis. Publication dates ranged from 2022 to 2024. title: Durable Insulin-free Remission in A−β+ Ketosis-Prone Diabetes With SGLT2 Inhibition: A Case Report With Longitudinal C-Peptide and CGM Data
abstract: Ketosis-prone diabetes (KPD) is a heterogeneous diabetes phenotype in which some patients with preserved β-cell function can achieve insulin independence after diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The role of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in maintaining remission in A−β+ KPD remains uncertain because of concerns regarding ketoacidosis risk. We report the case of a 45-year-old man who presented with severe DKA and was classified as A−β+ KPD based on negative islet autoantibodies and preserved C-peptide secretion. Following acute management, structured insulin withdrawal was performed, and dapagliflozin was initiated at week 4 with intensive metabolic monitoring. Over 12 months, the patient achieved sustained insulin-free remission, with significant improvements in HbA1c (12.1% to 6.4%), robust recovery of stimulated C-peptide (peak 4.8 ng/mL), and a continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) time-in-range of 82%, without recurrence of ketosis. This case suggests that in carefully selected A−β+ KPD patients with preserved β-cell reserve, SGLT2 inhibition may be safely integrated into the remission phase under close surveillance. However, these findings are hypothesis-generating, and the contribution of dapagliflozin to remission cannot be determined from a single uncontrolled observation. Prospective studies are required before this strategy can be recommended for routine use.
body: Ketosis-prone diabetes (KPD) is a heterogeneous form of diabetes mellitus characterised by presentation with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in individuals who lack the classical phenotype of autoimmune type 1 diabetes. Unlike traditional diabetes classifications, KPD encompasses distinct clinical subgroups that differ substantially in their underlying pathophysiology, β-cell reserve, and long-term therapeutic requirements. The Aβ classification system, based on the presence or absence of islet autoantibodies (A+/A−) and preserved or absent β-cell functional reserve (β+/β−), has become the most widely accepted framework for stratifying patients and predicting clinical outcomes. Among these subgroups, patients with A−β+ KPD exhibit preserved endogenous insulin secretion despite severe metabolic decompensation and frequently demonstrate progressive recovery of β-cell function following resolution of glucotoxicity. Consequently, many achieve prolonged insulin independence after the acute episode, highlighting the reversible nature of β-cell dysfunction in this phenotype and underscoring the importance of accurate subclassification to guide long-term management rather than assuming lifelong insulin dependence. 1 - 5 The therapeutic management of A−β+ KPD following recovery from DKA remains an area of ongoing clinical interest. Although metformin is commonly employed after insulin withdrawal, the optimal strategy for maintaining durable remission and preserving β-cell function has not been established. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors provide effective glucose lowering while promoting weight reduction and conferring substantial cardiovascular and renal protection. However, their use in individuals with a history of ketosis presents a therapeutic dilemma because these agents have been associated with an increased risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, including euglycaemic DKA. Consequently, current evidence supporting their use in remission-prone KPD is extremely limited, and careful patient selection with close metabolic surveillance is considered essential. 6 - 8 Despite increasing recognition of KPD over the past two decades, reports describing long-term remission with comprehensive metabolic phenotyping remain uncommon, particularly those incorporating serial fasting and stimulated C-peptide measurements together with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Furthermore, published literature evaluating SGLT2 inhibitor therapy after successful insulin withdrawal in A−β+ KPD is scarce. We report a patient with newly diagnosed A−β+ ketosis-prone diabetes who presented with severe DKA and subsequently achieved durable insulin-free remission following structured insulin withdrawal, initiation of dapagliflozin at week 4, and intensive longitudinal follow-up. This case provides detailed clinical, biochemical, β-cell functional, and CGM data over 12 months, offering novel insight into the potential role of carefully monitored SGLT2 inhibition in maintaining remission in this unique diabetes phenotype. A 45-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of polyuria, polydipsia, significant unintentional weight loss of 10 pounds, nausea, and generalized weakness. He reported that his symptoms began insidiously but escalated rapidly over the past 48 hours, culminating in severe fatigue and confusion at work. He denied any recent infections, medication changes, or dietary indiscretions. His past medical history was notable for hypertension diagnosed 5 years ago, which was well-controlled on lisinopril 10 mg daily, hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin 20 mg daily, and obstructive sleep apnea for which he used CPAP intermittently. He had no prior history of diabetes or prediabetes, no history of gestational diabetes, and no history of pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery. Family history revealed that his father and two older brothers had type 2 diabetes diagnosed after age 50, while his mother was healthy. There was no history of autoimmune diseases, thyroid disease, or vitiligo. His social history was significant for rotating shift work with 12-hour shifts performed 3-4 days per week. He consumed a standard Western diet with high carbohydrate intake estimated at 300-400 grams per day and drank alcohol socially, consuming 2-3 beers per week amounting to approximately 15-20 grams of alcohol weekly. He was a non-smoker with no history of illicit drug use. He was married and lived with his spouse and two children. On physical examination, vital signs revealed blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg (supine) and 122/80 mmHg (sitting), heart rate 105 beats per minute (regular), respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, temperature 37.0°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Orthostatic hypotension was noted with a systolic drop >20 mmHg upon standing, associated with dizziness. The patient appeared acutely ill and dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. Kussmaul respirations were present. He was alert but lethargic, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14/15. Anthropometric measurements included height 175 cm, weight 92 kg, BMI 30.0 kg/m 2 , and waist circumference 104 cm. Examination revealed no acanthosis nigricans, no goiter, no lymphadenopathy, and normal cardiovascular, abdominal, extremity, and neurological findings. On presentation to the Emergency Department, point-of-care testing revealed a capillary glucose of 685 mg/dL, with urinalysis showing glucose greater than 1000 mg/dL and large ketones at 80 mg/dL. Venous blood gas analysis demonstrated a pH of 7.15 with a pCO2 of 28 mmHg, bicarbonate of 9 mmol/L, and an anion gap of 28 mEq/L. Serum chemistry revealed a sodium of 132 mEq/L (corrected for glucose: 148 mEq/L), potassium of 5.1 mEq/L, creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL, eGFR of 55 mL/min/1.73m 2 , BUN of 32 mg/dL, and an osmolality of 315 mOsm/kg. The diagnosis of severe diabetic ketoacidosis with acute kidney injury stage 1 was established, and the patient was admitted to the Medical Intensive Care Unit for management. For diabetes classification, a comprehensive laboratory panel was obtained on day 2-3 of admission after initial stabilization. Beta-cell function assessment revealed a fasting C-peptide of 1.2 ng/mL (within the preserved range and consistent with the β+ subtype). The autoantibody panel showed GAD-65 antibody <5 IU/mL, IA-2 antibody <0.8 IU/mL, and ZnT8 antibody <15 IU/mL, all of which were negative. Islet cell antibody (ICA) testing was not performed. The interpretation of negative autoantibodies with preserved beta-cell function established the diagnosis of A−β+ KPD subtype. Table 1 presents the baseline and follow-up laboratory data. Glycemic parameters showed steady improvement over the 12-month period, with HbA1c declining from 12.1% at baseline to 6.4% at month 12 ( Table 2 ). Beta-cell function demonstrated progressive recovery, with fasting C-peptide increasing from 1.2 to 2.8 ng/mL and stimulated C-peptide on mixed-meal tolerance testing (MMTT) reaching 4.8 ng/mL at month 12 ( Table 3 ). All autoantibodies remained negative throughout follow-up. Lipid and inflammatory markers showed substantial improvement, likely reflecting the multifactorial effects of weight loss, dietary changes, improved glycemic control, and statin therapy ( Table 1 ). Renal function normalized with eGFR improving from 55 to 92 mL/min/1.73m 2 (this improvement primarily reflects resolution of volume depletion and acute kidney injury). Table 1. Durable Insulin-free Remission in A−β+ Ketosis-Prone Diabetes With SGLT2 Inhibition: A Case Report With Longitudinal C-Peptide and CGM Data

Ketosis-prone diabetes (KPD) is a heterogeneous diabetes phenotype in which some patients with preserved β-cell function can achieve insulin independence after diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The role of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in maintaining remission in A−β+ KPD remains uncertain because of concerns regarding ketoacidosis risk. We report the case of a 45-year-old man who presented with severe DKA and was classified as A−β+ KPD based on negative islet autoantibodies and preserved C-peptide secretion. Following acute management, structured insulin withdrawal was performed, and dapagliflozin was initiated at week 4 with intensive metabolic monitoring. Over 12 months, the patient achieved sustained insulin-free remission, with significant improvements in HbA1c (12.1% to 6.4%), robust recovery of stimulated C-peptide (peak 4.8 ng/mL), and a continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) time-in-range of 82%, without recurrence of ketosis. This case suggests that in carefully selected A−β+ KPD patients with preserved β-cell reserve, SGLT2 inhibition may be safely integrated into the remission phase under close surveillance. However, these findings are hypothesis-generating, and the contribution of dapagliflozin to remission cannot be determined from a single uncontrolled observation. Prospective studies are required before this strategy can be recommended for routine use.

Ketosis-prone diabetes (KPD) is a heterogeneous form of diabetes mellitus characterised by presentation with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in individuals who lack the classical phenotype of autoimmune type 1 diabetes. Unlike traditional diabetes classifications, KPD encompasses distinct clinical subgroups that differ substantially in their underlying pathophysiology, β-cell reserve, and long-term therapeutic requirements. The Aβ classification system, based on the presence or absence of islet autoantibodies (A+/A−) and preserved or absent β-cell functional reserve (β+/β−), has become the most widely accepted framework for stratifying patients and predicting clinical outcomes. Among these subgroups, patients with A−β+ KPD exhibit preserved endogenous insulin secretion despite severe metabolic decompensation and frequently demonstrate progressive recovery of β-cell function following resolution of glucotoxicity. Consequently, many achieve prolonged insulin independence after the acute episode, highlighting the reversible nature of β-cell dysfunction in this phenotype and underscoring the importance of accurate subclassification to guide long-term management rather than assuming lifelong insulin dependence. 1 - 5 The therapeutic management of A−β+ KPD following recovery from DKA remains an area of ongoing clinical interest. Although metformin is commonly employed after insulin withdrawal, the optimal strategy for maintaining durable remission and preserving β-cell function has not been established. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors provide effective glucose lowering while promoting weight reduction and conferring substantial cardiovascular and renal protection. However, their use in individuals with a history of ketosis presents a therapeutic dilemma because these agents have been associated with an increased risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, including euglycaemic DKA. Consequently, current evidence supporting their use in remission-prone KPD is extremely limited, and careful patient selection with close metabolic surveillance is considered essential. 6 - 8 Despite increasing recognition of KPD over the past two decades, reports describing long-term remission with comprehensive metabolic phenotyping remain uncommon, particularly those incorporating serial fasting and stimulated C-peptide measurements together with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Furthermore, published literature evaluating SGLT2 inhibitor therapy after successful insulin withdrawal in A−β+ KPD is scarce. We report a patient with newly diagnosed A−β+ ketosis-prone diabetes who presented with severe DKA and subsequently achieved durable insulin-free remission following structured insulin withdrawal, initiation of dapagliflozin at week 4, and intensive longitudinal follow-up. This case provides detailed clinical, biochemical, β-cell functional, and CGM data over 12 months, offering novel insight into the potential role of carefully monitored SGLT2 inhibition in maintaining remission in this unique diabetes phenotype. A 45-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of polyuria, polydipsia, significant unintentional weight loss of 10 pounds, nausea, and generalized weakness. He reported that his symptoms began insidiously but escalated rapidly over the past 48 hours, culminating in severe fatigue and confusion at work. He denied any recent infections, medication changes, or dietary indiscretions. His past medical history was notable for hypertension diagnosed 5 years ago, which was well-controlled on lisinopril 10 mg daily, hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin 20 mg daily, and obstructive sleep apnea for which he used CPAP intermittently. He had no prior history of diabetes or prediabetes, no history of gestational diabetes, and no history of pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery. Family history revealed that his father and two older brothers had type 2 diabetes diagnosed after age 50, while his mother was healthy. There was no history of autoimmune diseases, thyroid disease, or vitiligo. His social history was significant for rotating shift work with 12-hour shifts performed 3-4 days per week. He consumed a standard Western diet with high carbohydrate intake estimated at 300-400 grams per day and drank alcohol socially, consuming 2-3 beers per week amounting to approximately 15-20 grams of alcohol weekly. He was a non-smoker with no history of illicit drug use. He was married and lived with his spouse and two children. On physical examination, vital signs revealed blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg (supine) and 122/80 mmHg (sitting), heart rate 105 beats per minute (regular), respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, temperature 37.0°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Orthostatic hypotension was noted with a systolic drop >20 mmHg upon standing, associated with dizziness. The patient appeared acutely ill and dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. Kussmaul respirations were present. He was alert but lethargic, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14/15. Anthropometric measurements included height 175 cm, weight 92 kg, BMI 30.0 kg/m 2 , and waist circumference 104 cm. Examination revealed no acanthosis nigricans, no goiter, no lymphadenopathy, and normal cardiovascular, abdominal, extremity, and neurological findings. On presentation to the Emergency Department, point-of-care testing revealed a capillary glucose of 685 mg/dL, with urinalysis showing glucose greater than 1000 mg/dL and large ketones at 80 mg/dL. Venous blood gas analysis demonstrated a pH of 7.15 with a pCO2 of 28 mmHg, bicarbonate of 9 mmol/L, and an anion gap of 28 mEq/L. Serum chemistry revealed a sodium of 132 mEq/L (corrected for glucose: 148 mEq/L), potassium of 5.1 mEq/L, creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL, eGFR of 55 mL/min/1.73m 2 , BUN of 32 mg/dL, and an osmolality of 315 mOsm/kg. The diagnosis of severe diabetic ketoacidosis with acute kidney injury stage 1 was established, and the patient was admitted to the Medical Intensive Care Unit for management. Lipid and inflammatory markers showed substantial improvement, likely reflecting the multifactorial effects of weight loss, dietary changes, improved glycemic control, and statin therapy ( Table 1 ). title: Sex-related differences in echocardiography parameters for predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with acute pulmonary embolism
abstract: Background Risk stratification of acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is primarily based on systolic arterial pressure, right ventricular (RV) function, and cardiac troponin levels. Objectives To investigate sex-related differences in simple RV echocardiographic parameters for predicting all-cause in-hospital mortality in acute PE. Design Multicenter, observational, retrospective, registry-based cohort study. Methods We analyzed data from the Regional Pulmonary Embolism Registry, including consecutive patients with acute PE confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography between January 2015 and January 2026. Of 2776 patients, 2408 had at least one RV echocardiographic parameter measured at admission (RV diastolic diameter, RV systolic pressure, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion [TAPSE], and ratio TAPSE/RV systolic pressure). Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex-specific differences, and shock at admission (systolic arterial pressure <90 mmHg), was used to identify predictors of all-cause in-hospital mortality. Sex-specific cutoffs of echocardiographic parameters with the strongest predictive value for all-cause mortality were determined using a decision tree. Results All-cause in-hospital mortality rates were similar between men (7.6%, 83/1125) and women (9.2%, 118/1283; p=0.107). TAPSE was the only echocardiographic parameter independently associated with all-cause in-hospital mortality in women (adjusted hazard ratio [95% confidence interval] 0.84 [0.77–0.90], p<0.001), but not in men (0.92 [0.85–1.01], p=0.075). Decision-tree analyses identified TAPSE cutoffs of >19 mm for women and >16 mm for men, enabling discrimination between low- and high-risk patients. Mortality was 10.2% versus 0.9% in women (≤19 vs. >19 mm, p<0.001) and 9.0% versus 2.5% in men (≤16 vs. >16 mm, p=0.001). In women, TAPSE >19 mm identified a subgroup with very low in-hospital mortality (1.4%) and an excellent negative predictive value (98.6%). Conclusion In patients with acute PE, TAPSE measured at admission in women, but not in men, was the only echocardiographic parameter independently associated with all-cause in-hospital mortality.
body: In the past decade, careful risk stratification of patients at high risk of mortality or deterioration has become a cornerstone of acute pulmonary embolism (PE) management. In patients with severe PE, treatment must balance effective thrombus prevention with the risk of therapy-related bleeding. Patient stratification should be guided by the estimated bleeding risk: high-risk patients without bleeding risk can be treated with systemic thrombolysis, whereas those with substantial bleeding risk can be treated with mechanical thrombectomy. However, many patients fall into an intermediate-risk category that requires additional factors to guide treatment decisions. 1 Risk assessment might be influenced by multiple factors, including sex as a prominent factor. The acute hemodynamic response to sudden pulmonary artery obstruction by a thrombus may differ between men and women, as right ventricular (RV) function, particularly under stress conditions, exhibits sex-related physiological differences reflected in several echocardiographic parameters. Transthoracic echocardiography is a readily available bedside tool for repeated assessment and is widely used for risk stratification in patients with acute PE. RV dysfunction, measured by echocardiography or computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA), is a well-recognized risk factor for mortality in acute PE. Although several echocardiographic parameters are recommended for risk assessment in acute PE, 2 many of these parameters are difficult to obtain in some echocardiographic devices, particularly in the hands of less experienced echocardiographers. Moreover, various echocardiographic parameters require validation for predicting mortality in large, real-world cohorts of consecutive patients with PE. 3 , 4 The role of sex in the prognosis of acute PE remains unclear, as even a large-scale Cochrane meta-analysis assessing its influence on mortality has yielded inconclusive results. In the included studies, women were generally older than men and had different comorbidities and characteristics that may influence outcomes. Thus, generalizations regarding the role of sex in predicting all-cause and PE-related mortality based on large datasets, as in the meta-analysis, 5 , 6 may oversimplify patient heterogeneity and limit clinical utility. 5 , 6 Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of easily obtainable echocardiographic parameters (RV diastolic diameter [RVDD], RV systolic pressure [RVSP], tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion [TAPSE], the TAPSE/RVSP ratio as a measure of RV–pulmonary artery coupling, and left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]) measured at hospital admission in a relatively large cohort of consecutive patients with acute PE from a regional PE registry. We aimed to determine the most reliable echocardiographic parameters and their cutoff values for predicting mortality in patients with acute PE with respect to sex differences. In this multicenter, retrospective, observational, registry-based study, we enrolled consecutive patients who were hospitalized in cardiology or pulmonology wards (intensive or standard care) for acute PE (symptom onset <14 days) confirmed by CTPA during admission between January 2015 and January 2026. Data were obtained from the Regional Pulmonary Embolism Registry (REPER) founded in 2015 which currently involves eight hospitals (seven university hospitals and one general hospital). This study adheres to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. The corresponding checklist is submitted as 5 Supplemental File 1 . Exclusion criteria were the diagnosis of PE in terminally ill patients and isolated 1–2 subsegmental pulmonary artery defects on CTPA. The main protocol details and the definitions of comorbidities in the REPER have been reported previously. 6 , 7 Transthoracic echocardiography was performed during hospital admission, either in the emergency care unit or at the bedside upon ward admission. Patients with at least one of the three basic RV echocardiographic parameters (RVDD, RVSP, TAPSE) measured at admission were included in the study. These parameters can be obtained at any participating hospital on a 24/7 basis by a cardiologist on duty. All patients were treated according to the 2014 and 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines on Acute PE. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed before or after CTPA. RVDD was measured in four-chamber view just below the tricuspid annulus. TAPSE was assessed in M mode at the RV free wall annulus. RVSP was determined as the peak velocity of tricuspid regurgitation using continuous Doppler sonography, and LVEF was calculated using parasternal long-axis view and M mode (Teicholz method) or using Simpson’s method from the apical four-chamber view. In some patients with expert echocardiography examination in the 6 months before the acute PE episode, LVEF was obtained from the recently performed echocardiography examination. 8 Risk stratification, according to slightly modified 2019 ESC guidelines, was performed throughout the hospitalization period. High-risk patients had a systolic blood pressure of <90 mmHg after fluid loading or under inotropic support, most probably due to massive PE, had cardiac arrest, or required mechanical ventilation. Intermediate-risk patients had RV dysfunction with or without elevated cardiac troponin, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), or N-terminal-proBNP (NT-proBNP) levels in the blood. Low-risk patients had no RV dysfunction determined by the lack of echocardiographic signs or an RV-to-LV ratio of <1.0 on initial CTPA. Low-risk patients did not undergo routine biomarker measurements. 1 The primary endpoint was all-cause in-hospital mortality. All continuous variables had non-normal distribution and are presented as medians and 25 th –75 th percentiles. Differences between variables regarding sex were estimated using Student’s t-test, the Mann–Whitney test, or the chi-squared test. Univariate Cox regression analysis was used to assess the association between time to all-cause in-hospital mortality and the independent variables, including echocardiographic parameters, variables that differed significantly between men and women, and systolic arterial pressure <90 mmHg, as this hemodynamic parameter was strongly associated with in-hospital mortality. Both univariate and multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed separately in men and women. In the final models, only variables that were significantly associated (p<0.1) with all-cause in-hospital mortality in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariable regression model with all-cause mortality as the primary outcome. Optimal cutoff values for the prediction of all-cause in-hospital mortality were determined using the decision tree Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detection (CHAID) method. At each step, CHAID chooses the cutoff values of the independent (echocardiographic parameters) variables that have the strongest interaction with the all-cause mortality. These cutoff values were then tested with univariate and multivariable Cox regression using the same covariates to determine adjusted hazard ratios for the separate prediction of all-cause mortality in men and women. 9 To estimate the predictive value of the three echocardiographic parameters for all-cause in-hospital mortality, we analyzed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with De Long’s test for comparing areas under the curves (AUCs) separately in men and women. We also compared the positive and negative predictive values (PNV and NPV, respectively) of TAPSE (cutoff values 14–19 mm) for all-cause in-hospital mortality according to sex. 10 Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM Statistics SPSS version 26. Of the 2776 patients with acute PE included in the REPER, 368 were excluded because none of the RV echocardiographic parameters measured at admission were available. Among the remaining 2408 patients, the all-cause in-hospital mortality rate was 7.6% (83 of 1125) in men and 9.2% (118 of 1283) in women, which was not significantly different (p=0.107). The basic characteristics of the included patients are presented in Table 1 . Women were significantly older than men, had a significantly higher number of patients older than 75 years, and had a significantly lower number of patients younger than 60 years. The presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, coronary disease, and stroke did not differ significantly between sexes. Arterial hypertension, diabetes, renal failure, and anemia were more prevalent in women. Women also more frequently had active malignant disease and recent surgery than men. Table 1. Intermediate-risk patients had RV dysfunction with or without elevated cardiac troponin, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), or N-terminal-proBNP (NT-proBNP) levels in the blood. Low-risk patients had no RV dysfunction determined by the lack of echocardiographic signs or an RV-to-LV ratio of <1.0 on initial CTPA. Low-risk patients did not undergo routine biomarker measurements. 1 The primary endpoint was all-cause in-hospital mortality. All continuous variables had non-normal distribution and are presented as medians and 25 th –75 th percentiles. Differences between variables regarding sex were estimated using Student’s t-test, the Mann–Whitney test, or the chi-squared test. Univariate Cox regression analysis was used to assess the association between time to all-cause in-hospital mortality and the independent variables, including echocardiographic parameters, variables that differed significantly between men and women, and systolic arterial pressure <90 mmHg, as this hemodynamic parameter was strongly associated with in-hospital mortality. Both univariate and multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed separately in men and women. In the final models, only variables that were significantly associated (p<0.1) with all-cause in-hospital mortality in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariable regression model with all-cause mortality as the primary outcome. Optimal cutoff values for the prediction of all-cause in-hospital mortality were determined using the decision tree Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detection (CHAID) method. At each step, CHAID chooses the cutoff values of the independent (echocardiographic parameters) variables that have the strongest interaction with the all-cause mortality. These cutoff values were then tested with univariate and multivariable Cox regression using the same covariates to determine adjusted hazard ratios for the separate prediction of all-cause mortality in men and women. 9 To estimate the predictive value of the three echocardiographic parameters for all-cause in-hospital mortality, we analyzed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with De Long’s test for comparing areas under the curves (AUCs) separately in men and women. We also compared the positive and negative predictive values (PNV and NPV, respectively) of TAPSE (cutoff values 14–19 mm) for all-cause in-hospital mortality according to sex. 10 Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM Statistics SPSS version 26. Of the 2776 patients with acute PE included in the REPER, 368 were excluded because none of the RV echocardiographic parameters measured at admission were available. Among the remaining 2408 patients, the all-cause in-hospital mortality rate was 7.6% (83 of 1125) in men and 9.2% (118 of 1283) in women, which was not significantly different (p=0.107). Women were significantly older than men, had a significantly higher number of patients older than 75 years, and had a significantly lower number of patients younger than 60 years. The presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, coronary disease, and stroke did not differ significantly between sexes. Arterial hypertension, diabetes, renal failure, and anemia were more prevalent in women. Women also more frequently had active malignant disease and recent surgery than men. Table 1. title: Bridging with a single glucocorticoid injection in psoriatic arthritis: Real-world evidence of short-term effectiveness, safety, and enhanced response in high-inflammatory burden patients
abstract: Background The use of adjunctive systemic glucocorticoids (GC) as bridging therapy in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) remains controversial due to limited disease-specific evidence and safety concerns. Although clinical experience suggests potential benefits in selected patients, clear criteria for appropriate use are lacking. The unique pharmacokinetic profile of intramuscular compound betamethasone offers a bridging strategy but has been insufficiently studied. Objectives To investigate the real-world effectiveness and safety of single intramuscular GC injection as a bridging therapy for active PsA, and identify clinical characteristics associated with greater therapeutic response. Design A retrospective observational comparative study using longitudinal clinical data. Methods Data were derived from the PKUPsA cohort. Patients receiving a single intramuscular compound betamethasone injection alongside background disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) were compared with controls not receiving GC. Changes in disease activity, patient-reported outcomes, and adverse events were assessed at 1 month and over 6 months. Negative binomial regression and interaction analysis were used to assess treatment effects and explore differential responses. Results Of 183 enrolled patients (81 GC, 102 control), the GC group showed higher baseline tender joint count (TJC), Disease Activity in Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA), ESR and CRP, but lower Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI). At month 1, the GC group demonstrated greater SJC improvements (ΔSJC: 1 [0 to 2] vs. 0 [0 to 1], P =0.02). Adjusted negative binomial regression confirmed a conditional effect of GC on SJC at month 1, with Johnson–Neyman analysis indicating significance at baseline SJC > 6.6. Treatment benefits were consistent across subgroups and sustained over 6 months. Reported adverse events, including transient PASI increases, were not attributed to GC. Conclusion A single-dose intramuscular injection of compound betamethasone may provide articular improvements with a favorable short-term safety profile. Greater benefits in patients with high-inflammatory burden support its role as a bridging therapy.
body: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disorder with a broad spectrum of articular and extra-articular manifestations. Despite the expanding therapeutic arsenal, including biologics and Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKis), systemic glucocorticoids (GC) remain a frequently employed adjunct to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for their rapid suppression of inflammation and symptoms. Nevertheless, the role in PsA management is fraught with controversy. While GC can provide swift symptoms control and serve as an effective bridging during the latency period of DMARDs, its use is complicated by significant risks, for instance, increased infections susceptibility, potential exacerbation of metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidities, a longstanding concern regarding psoriasis flares or rebound upon GC withdrawal. 1 2 Although a 2022 systematic review concluded the risk of GC-induced psoriatic flares may be lower than previously thought, robust evidence to resolve these clinical controversies remains lacking. This uncertainty is mirrored in international guidelines. The 2019 EULAR recommendations assigned only a weak (grade C) recommendation for cautious use, 3 and the 2023 update omitted a formal recommendation altogether, citing insufficient evidence, despite acknowledging potential benefits of intramuscular GC injection in selected patients. 4 Recent expert consensus (2024) further advises against routine oral GC use, though intramuscular or intra-articular routes may be considered with caution. 5 6 Intramuscular GC injection, while cautiously endorsed, is understudied in PsA. More importantly, so far there are no criteria to identify which patients are more likely to benefit from this intervention. Existing evidence includes a trial in axial PsA, where a single intramuscular triamcinolone injection sustained clinical improvements for at least 4 weeks, and a sub-analysis of the TICOPA trial, which suggested intramuscular GC as a useful therapeutic option. 7 Notably, despite its rapid onset (1-2 hours) and prolonged duration (up to 4 weeks), the efficacy and safety of intramuscular compound betamethasone have not been specifically evaluated in PsA, representing a significant gap given its potential pharmacokinetic and practical advantages over other formulations. 8 To address these evidence gaps, this real-world study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a single intramuscular compound betamethasone injection as a bridging therapy in active PsA, and to identify clinical characteristics associated with a greater likelihood of treatment response. Our findings seek to inform more precise and practical guidance on systemic GC use in this complex disease. We performed a retrospective, observational, non-randomized comparative analysis using longitudinal clinical data from the Peking University First Hospital PsA (PKUPsA) cohort, a prospective, protocol-driven, longitudinal cohort formally established in 2010. This cohort enrolls patients fulfilling the Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR). 9 Patients are generally scheduled for a follow-up visit at approximately 1 month to evaluate early treatment response, followed by visits at intervals of 1-3 months for those with moderate to high disease activity (HDA) and 3-6 months for those in remission or low disease activity (LDA). Additional visits are scheduled as clinically required. The present study included eligible patients from the PKUPsA cohort with available clinical data documented between January 2008 and July 2024. The PKUPsA cohort has been conducted under successive ethics approvals. All patients enrolled in the PKUPsA cohort provided written broad informed consent at the time of enrollment for the prospective collection of clinical data and biospecimens, and for future secondary research use. For this retrospective analysis, the requirement for specific informed consent was waived by the Ethics Committee of Peking University First Hospital (Approval No. 2026R0555). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The reporting of this study conforms to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. 10 11 At enrollment, comprehensive data are collected, including demographics, symptom duration, medical and family history, previous treatments, and socioeconomic status. Each follow-up visit documents clinical symptoms, physical signs, patient-reported outcomes (PROs), comorbidities, laboratory and imaging findings and treatment details. Standardized measures include tender and swollen joint counts (TJC, SJC), Disease Activity index for PsA (DAPSA), psoriasis area and severity index (PASI), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) and PROs such as the visual analogue scale (VAS) for pain, patient and evaluator global assessment (PtGA, EGA), and the Health Assessment Questionnaire -Disability Index (HAQ-DI). Detailed methodology has been elaborated previously. 12 A total of 406 patients with PsA who had available clinical data documented between January 2008 and July 2024 were screened for eligibility. The detailed patient selection process is shown in Supplemental Figure S1 . For this analysis, eligible participants were divided into two groups according to GC exposure during follow-up: - GC Group: This group included 81 of 112 patients with a history of GC use who received a single intramuscular injection of compound betamethasone specifically for active PsA. The compound betamethasone used was 1 mL of Diprospan®, containing 5 mg of betamethasone dipropionate and 2 mg of betamethasone sodium phosphate. Twenty-three patients who received GC via routes other than intramuscular injection were excluded, including those receiving intra-articular GC injections or other forms of local corticosteroid therapy. Patients who had taken oral GCs within 3 months before the index injection were excluded to reduce confounding from concurrent systemic GC exposure and to isolate the effect of the intramuscular depot formulation. - Control Group: This group included 102 of 294 GC-naïve patients who did not receive systemic or local GC therapy during follow-up at our center. - GC Group: This group included 81 of 112 patients with a history of GC use who received a single intramuscular injection of compound betamethasone specifically for active PsA. The compound betamethasone used was 1 mL of Diprospan®, containing 5 mg of betamethasone dipropionate and 2 mg of betamethasone sodium phosphate. Twenty-three patients who received GC via routes other than intramuscular injection were excluded, including those receiving intra-articular GC injections or other forms of local corticosteroid therapy. Patients who had taken oral GCs within 3 months before the index injection were excluded to reduce confounding from concurrent systemic GC exposure and to isolate the effect of the intramuscular depot formulation. - Control Group: This group included 102 of 294 GC-naïve patients who did not receive systemic or local GC therapy during follow-up at our center. Additional inclusion criteria for both groups were: (1) age ≥18 years; (2) at least one follow-up visit within 6 months after baseline. Exclusion criteria were: (1) absence of 1-month follow-up data; or (2) concomitant diseases that could confound disease activity assessment, including rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, gout, or systemic lupus erythematosus. For GC group, only data related to a patient’s first intramuscular compound betamethasone injection were analyzed to avoid confounding from repeated exposures. If a subsequent administration of GC by any route occurred within 6 months, follow-up data were censored after the visit at which the subsequent GC was administered. Clinical and laboratory data from that visit were included only if they had been collected before the subsequent GC administration. Patients receiving compound betamethasone for any other indications were excluded. Baseline was defined as the visit at which compound betamethasone was administered for the GC group, and the first cohort visit for the control group. Detailed treatment information was collected, including the class and timing of antirheumatic therapies such as conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs), biologics and JAKis, as well as GC, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and treatments of comorbidities. Primary efficacy outcomes were the between-groups differences in changes from baseline to month 1 in TJC (ΔTJC), SJC (ΔSJC) and DAPSA (ΔDAPSA). Given baseline imbalance between groups, regression-based analyses were additionally performed using TJC, SJC, and DAPSA at month 1 as dependent variables, with baseline values included as covariates. Secondary efficacy outcomes included the between-groups differences in: (1) changes in ΔTJC, ΔSJC, ΔDAPSA over 6 months; (2) changes from baseline to month 1 in ESR, CRP, pain VAS, PtGA, EGA and HAQ-DI. Changes in all indices were calculated as: Δindex = (Baseline value) – (Follow-up value). The primary safety outcome was the incidence of a psoriasis skin flare within the first month post-injection, defined as an increase in PASI ≥ 2 or a transformation of plaque psoriasis into pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis. 8 , 13 , 14 Secondary safety outcomes included infections, clinically significant fluctuations in blood pressure, glucose and lipid levels, and any other adverse events (AEs) deemed related to GC use within 6 months post-injection. All available medical records during this period were also reviewed for clinically documented psoriasis worsening or phenotype changes. Continuous variables were assessed for normality and are presented as mean (standard deviation, SD) or median (interquartile range, IQR), as appropriate. Between-group comparisons were performed using Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages and compared using the Chi-squared test. Given overdispersion, negative binomial regression models were applied for TJC and SJC, with TJC, SJC, or DAPSA at month 1 as dependent variables, treatment group (intramuscular GC vs control) and corresponding baseline value (TJC0, SJC0, or DAPSA0) included as covariates. DAPSA was analyzed using the same framework for consistency. Covariates were selected a priori based on their clinical relevance to baseline disease activity, the outcome, and potential treatment-selection differences between groups. A complete-case approach was used to handle missing covariate data in the negative binomial regression model. Patients with missing values for any of the covariates were excluded. No imputation was performed. Interaction terms between treatment group and baseline disease activity were tested; if significant, Johnson-Neyman analysis was used to identify the range of baseline values for which the conditional treatment effect was statistically significant. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. In the subgroup comparisons, P-values are denoted as P * for csDMARDs-only vs. GC + csDMARDs, and P ** for GC + csDMARDs vs. biologics/JAKi (with/without csDMARDs). All analyses were conducted using SPSS Statistics (version 23.0), R (version 4.5.2) and GraphPad Prism (version 10.1.2). Several sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the primary negative binomial regression findings. The GC treatment-by-baseline SJC interaction was re-estimated using alternative covariate specifications, including a reduced model, a full-sample component-adjusted model replacing DAPSA with baseline TJC, pain VAS, and PtGA, and models additionally adjusting for baseline CRP, PsA duration, or biologic/JAK inhibitor use. A Johnson–Neyman analysis was also performed for the full-sample component-adjusted model to assess the consistency of the baseline SJC threshold with that identified in the primary analysis. Robustness was evaluated by comparing the direction, magnitude, 95% confidence intervals, and statistical significance of the interaction estimates across models. The final study cohort comprised 183 patients (81 in GC group and 102 in control group) ( Figure S1 ). Baseline demographic characteristics and comorbidity burden were comparable between the two groups. However, the GC group exhibited significantly higher measures of articular disease activity and systemic inflammation, including: TJC (median [IQR]: 4 [2-9] vs. 3 [1-6], P <0.01), SJC (3 [2-7] vs. 2 [1-5], P =0.05), DAPSA (16.48 [10.17-28.35] vs. 14.46 [6.28-23.69], P =0.02), ESR (15 [9-30] vs. 10 [5-17], P =0.01) and CRP (7.7 [2.8-18.5] vs. 4.0 [1.9-9,8], P =0.03). In contrast, cutaneous involvement was less severe in the GC group, as indicated by a lower PASI (1.0 [0.0-3.9] vs. 3.0 [0.3-6.2], P=0.01). Notable differences in baseline treatment patterns were observed. Most patients in both groups were receiving csDMARDs (98.8% in GC group and 66.7% in control group). However, csDMARD-only therapy was more common in the GC group (91.4% vs. 37.3%, P <0.01), whereas biologics (7.4% vs. 49.0%, P <0.01) and JAKi (1.2% vs. 13.7%, P= 0.01) were predominantly used in control group.
