Bridging with a single glucocorticoid injection in psoriatic arthritis: Real-world evidence of short-term effectiveness, safety, and enhanced response in high-inflammatory burden patients

Background The use of adjunctive systemic glucocorticoids (GC) as bridging therapy in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) remains controversial due to limited disease-specific evidence and safety concerns. Although clinical experience suggests potential benefits in selected patients, clear criteria for appropriate use are lacking. The unique pharmacokinetic profile of intramuscular compound betamethasone offers a bridging strategy but has been insufficiently studied. Objectives To investigate the real-world effectiveness and safety of single intramuscular GC injection as a bridging therapy for active PsA, and identify clinical characteristics associated with greater therapeutic response. Design A retrospective observational comparative study using longitudinal clinical data. Methods Data were derived from the PKUPsA cohort. Patients receiving a single intramuscular compound betamethasone injection alongside background disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) were compared with controls not receiving GC. Changes in disease activity, patient-reported outcomes, and adverse events were assessed at 1 month and over 6 months. Negative binomial regression and interaction analysis were used to assess treatment effects and explore differential responses. Results Of 183 enrolled patients (81 GC, 102 control), the GC group showed higher baseline tender joint count (TJC), Disease Activity in Psoriatic Arthritis (DAPSA), ESR and CRP, but lower Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI). At month 1, the GC group demonstrated greater SJC improvements (ΔSJC: 1 [0 to 2] vs. 0 [0 to 1], P =0.02). Adjusted negative binomial regression confirmed a conditional effect of GC on SJC at month 1, with Johnson–Neyman analysis indicating significance at baseline SJC > 6.6. Treatment benefits were consistent across subgroups and sustained over 6 months. Reported adverse events, including transient PASI increases, were not attributed to GC. Conclusion A single-dose intramuscular injection of compound betamethasone may provide articular improvements with a favorable short-term safety profile. Greater benefits in patients with high-inflammatory burden support its role as a bridging therapy.

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disorder with a broad spectrum of articular and extra-articular manifestations. Despite the expanding therapeutic arsenal, including biologics and Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKis), systemic glucocorticoids (GC) remain a frequently employed adjunct to disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for their rapid suppression of inflammation and symptoms. Nevertheless, the role in PsA management is fraught with controversy. While GC can provide swift symptoms control and serve as an effective bridging during the latency period of DMARDs, its use is complicated by significant risks, for instance, increased infections susceptibility, potential exacerbation of metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidities, a longstanding concern regarding psoriasis flares or rebound upon GC withdrawal. 1 2 Although a 2022 systematic review concluded the risk of GC-induced psoriatic flares may be lower than previously thought, robust evidence to resolve these clinical controversies remains lacking. This uncertainty is mirrored in international guidelines. The 2019 EULAR recommendations assigned only a weak (grade C) recommendation for cautious use, 3 and the 2023 update omitted a formal recommendation altogether, citing insufficient evidence, despite acknowledging potential benefits of intramuscular GC injection in selected patients. 4 Recent expert consensus (2024) further advises against routine oral GC use, though intramuscular or intra-articular routes may be considered with caution. 5 6 Intramuscular GC injection, while cautiously endorsed, is understudied in PsA. More importantly, so far there are no criteria to identify which patients are more likely to benefit from this intervention. Existing evidence includes a trial in axial PsA, where a single intramuscular triamcinolone injection sustained clinical improvements for at least 4 weeks, and a sub-analysis of the TICOPA trial, which suggested intramuscular GC as a useful therapeutic option. 7 Notably, despite its rapid onset (1-2 hours) and prolonged duration (up to 4 weeks), the efficacy and safety of intramuscular compound betamethasone have not been specifically evaluated in PsA, representing a significant gap given its potential pharmacokinetic and practical advantages over other formulations. 8 To address these evidence gaps, this real-world study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a single intramuscular compound betamethasone injection as a bridging therapy in active PsA, and to identify clinical characteristics associated with a greater likelihood of treatment response. Our findings seek to inform more precise and practical guidance on systemic GC use in this complex disease. We performed a retrospective, observational, non-randomized comparative analysis using longitudinal clinical data from the Peking University First Hospital PsA (PKUPsA) cohort, a prospective, protocol-driven, longitudinal cohort formally established in 2010. This cohort enrolls patients fulfilling the Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis (CASPAR). 9 Patients are generally scheduled for a follow-up visit at approximately 1 month to evaluate early treatment response, followed by visits at intervals of 1-3 months for those with moderate to high disease activity (HDA) and 3-6 months for those in remission or low disease activity (LDA). Additional visits are scheduled as clinically required. The present study included eligible patients from the PKUPsA cohort with available clinical data documented between January 2008 and July 2024. The PKUPsA cohort has been conducted under successive ethics approvals. All patients enrolled in the PKUPsA cohort provided written broad informed consent at the time of enrollment for the prospective collection of clinical data and biospecimens, and for future secondary research use. For this retrospective analysis, the requirement for specific informed consent was waived by the Ethics Committee of Peking University First Hospital (Approval No. 2026R0555). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The reporting of this study conforms to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. 10 11 At enrollment, comprehensive data are collected, including demographics, symptom duration, medical and family history, previous treatments, and socioeconomic status. Each follow-up visit documents clinical symptoms, physical signs, patient-reported outcomes (PROs), comorbidities, laboratory and imaging findings and treatment details. Standardized measures include tender and swollen joint counts (TJC, SJC), Disease Activity index for PsA (DAPSA), psoriasis area and severity index (PASI), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) and PROs such as the visual analogue scale (VAS) for pain, patient and evaluator global assessment (PtGA, EGA), and the Health Assessment Questionnaire -Disability Index (HAQ-DI). Detailed methodology has been elaborated previously. 12 A total of 406 patients with PsA who had available clinical data documented between January 2008 and July 2024 were screened for eligibility. The detailed patient selection process is shown in Supplemental Figure S1 . For this analysis, eligible participants were divided into two groups according to GC exposure during follow-up: - GC Group: This group included 81 of 112 patients with a history of GC use who received a single intramuscular injection of compound betamethasone specifically for active PsA. The compound betamethasone used was 1 mL of Diprospan®, containing 5 mg of betamethasone dipropionate and 2 mg of betamethasone sodium phosphate. Twenty-three patients who received GC via routes other than intramuscular injection were excluded, including those receiving intra-articular GC injections or other forms of local corticosteroid therapy. Patients who had taken oral GCs within 3 months before the index injection were excluded to reduce confounding from concurrent systemic GC exposure and to isolate the effect of the intramuscular depot formulation. - Control Group: This group included 102 of 294 GC-naïve patients who did not receive systemic or local GC therapy during follow-up at our center. - GC Group: This group included 81 of 112 patients with a history of GC use who received a single intramuscular injection of compound betamethasone specifically for active PsA. The compound betamethasone used was 1 mL of Diprospan®, containing 5 mg of betamethasone dipropionate and 2 mg of betamethasone sodium phosphate. Twenty-three patients who received GC via routes other than intramuscular injection were excluded, including those receiving intra-articular GC injections or other forms of local corticosteroid therapy. Patients who had taken oral GCs within 3 months before the index injection were excluded to reduce confounding from concurrent systemic GC exposure and to isolate the effect of the intramuscular depot formulation. - Control Group: This group included 102 of 294 GC-naïve patients who did not receive systemic or local GC therapy during follow-up at our center. Additional inclusion criteria for both groups were: (1) age ≥18 years; (2) at least one follow-up visit within 6 months after baseline. Exclusion criteria were: (1) absence of 1-month follow-up data; or (2) concomitant diseases that could confound disease activity assessment, including rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, gout, or systemic lupus erythematosus. For GC group, only data related to a patient’s first intramuscular compound betamethasone injection were analyzed to avoid confounding from repeated exposures. If a subsequent administration of GC by any route occurred within 6 months, follow-up data were censored after the visit at which the subsequent GC was administered. Clinical and laboratory data from that visit were included only if they had been collected before the subsequent GC administration. Patients receiving compound betamethasone for any other indications were excluded. Baseline was defined as the visit at which compound betamethasone was administered for the GC group, and the first cohort visit for the control group. Detailed treatment information was collected, including the class and timing of antirheumatic therapies such as conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs), biologics and JAKis, as well as GC, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and treatments of comorbidities. Primary efficacy outcomes were the between-groups differences in changes from baseline to month 1 in TJC (ΔTJC), SJC (ΔSJC) and DAPSA (ΔDAPSA). Given baseline imbalance between groups, regression-based analyses were additionally performed using TJC, SJC, and DAPSA at month 1 as dependent variables, with baseline values included as covariates. Secondary efficacy outcomes included the between-groups differences in: (1) changes in ΔTJC, ΔSJC, ΔDAPSA over 6 months; (2) changes from baseline to month 1 in ESR, CRP, pain VAS, PtGA, EGA and HAQ-DI. Changes in all indices were calculated as: Δindex = (Baseline value) – (Follow-up value). The primary safety outcome was the incidence of a psoriasis skin flare within the first month post-injection, defined as an increase in PASI ≥ 2 or a transformation of plaque psoriasis into pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis. 8 , 13 , 14 Secondary safety outcomes included infections, clinically significant fluctuations in blood pressure, glucose and lipid levels, and any other adverse events (AEs) deemed related to GC use within 6 months post-injection. All available medical records during this period were also reviewed for clinically documented psoriasis worsening or phenotype changes. Continuous variables were assessed for normality and are presented as mean (standard deviation, SD) or median (interquartile range, IQR), as appropriate. Between-group comparisons were performed using Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages and compared using the Chi-squared test. Given overdispersion, negative binomial regression models were applied for TJC and SJC, with TJC, SJC, or DAPSA at month 1 as dependent variables, treatment group (intramuscular GC vs control) and corresponding baseline value (TJC0, SJC0, or DAPSA0) included as covariates. DAPSA was analyzed using the same framework for consistency. Covariates were selected a priori based on their clinical relevance to baseline disease activity, the outcome, and potential treatment-selection differences between groups. A complete-case approach was used to handle missing covariate data in the negative binomial regression model. Patients with missing values for any of the covariates were excluded. No imputation was performed. Interaction terms between treatment group and baseline disease activity were tested; if significant, Johnson-Neyman analysis was used to identify the range of baseline values for which the conditional treatment effect was statistically significant. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. In the subgroup comparisons, P-values are denoted as P * for csDMARDs-only vs. GC + csDMARDs, and P ** for GC + csDMARDs vs. biologics/JAKi (with/without csDMARDs). All analyses were conducted using SPSS Statistics (version 23.0), R (version 4.5.2) and GraphPad Prism (version 10.1.2). Several sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the primary negative binomial regression findings. The GC treatment-by-baseline SJC interaction was re-estimated using alternative covariate specifications, including a reduced model, a full-sample component-adjusted model replacing DAPSA with baseline TJC, pain VAS, and PtGA, and models additionally adjusting for baseline CRP, PsA duration, or biologic/JAK inhibitor use. A Johnson–Neyman analysis was also performed for the full-sample component-adjusted model to assess the consistency of the baseline SJC threshold with that identified in the primary analysis. Robustness was evaluated by comparing the direction, magnitude, 95% confidence intervals, and statistical significance of the interaction estimates across models. The final study cohort comprised 183 patients (81 in GC group and 102 in control group) ( Figure S1 ). Baseline demographic characteristics and comorbidity burden were comparable between the two groups. However, the GC group exhibited significantly higher measures of articular disease activity and systemic inflammation, including: TJC (median [IQR]: 4 [2-9] vs. 3 [1-6], P <0.01), SJC (3 [2-7] vs. 2 [1-5], P =0.05), DAPSA (16.48 [10.17-28.35] vs. 14.46 [6.28-23.69], P =0.02), ESR (15 [9-30] vs. 10 [5-17], P =0.01) and CRP (7.7 [2.8-18.5] vs. 4.0 [1.9-9,8], P =0.03). In contrast, cutaneous involvement was less severe in the GC group, as indicated by a lower PASI (1.0 [0.0-3.9] vs. 3.0 [0.3-6.2], P=0.01). Notable differences in baseline treatment patterns were observed. Most patients in both groups were receiving csDMARDs (98.8% in GC group and 66.7% in control group). However, csDMARD-only therapy was more common in the GC group (91.4% vs. 37.3%, P <0.01), whereas biologics (7.4% vs. 49.0%, P <0.01) and JAKi (1.2% vs. 13.7%, P= 0.01) were predominantly used in control group. Additionally, 29.4% patients in the control group were not receiving any csDMARDs at baseline ( Table 1 ). Table 1. title: Nationwide Burden and Hospital Costs of Surgical Site Complications in France: A Retrospective Analysis of the French National PMSI Administrative Database
abstract: Introduction Surgical site complications (SSCs) such as surgical site infections (SSIs) cause significant morbidity and mortality for patients and raise costs. Our goal was to estimate the frequency and cost of SSCs (including SSIs) in France for orthopedic, cardiac, digestive (gastrointestinal), and bariatric surgeries including costs of index admission and readmissions due to SSCs. Methods We used a national hospital database and included the prevalence of SSCs for patients admitted in 2018. Patients were categorized by type of SSC (infection related to surgery; infection associated to surgery; non-infectious complication; no complication related to the surgical incision). Cost, length of stay, and readmission data was analyzed using the French Diagnostic Related Groups (DRG), Groupements Homogènes de Séjours (GHS). Results Estimated SSIs rates ranged from 0.44% in orthopedic to 3.09% in digestive surgery. Cardiac surgery had the highest rate of overall complications (14.91%), of which 89.26% were non-infectious. Cardiac surgery SSCs had the highest rates of readmissions (from 3.6% at 30 days to 9.9% at 365 days) while orthopedic surgery SSCs had the lowest (1.5% and 4.1% respectively). The overall economic impact of SSIs in additional length of stay ranged from 11.1 to 28.1 days, and from 6,622 to 22,109 euros for costs. Considering the general population receiving surgery for these specialties in 2018, the added expense for payers due to readmissions related to SSCs reached approximately 840 M€. Conclusion The occurrence of an SSC generates a financial burden to the care organization. New indicators may support better control of SSCs.
body: What do We Already Know About This Topic? Surgical site complications (SSCs) are common (approximately 7% of cases) and result in significant increases in length of stay and health care costs. Surgical site infections (SSIs) are the most consequential surgical complications and are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as well as increased readmissions and health care costs. 1 Six strategies have been recommended to lower the rates of SSIs 2 because they are supported by randomized trials: avoiding razors for hair removal; decolonization with intranasal anti-staphylococcal agents and anti-staphylococcal skin antiseptics for high-risk procedures; use of chlorhexidine gluconate and alcohol-based skin preparation; maintaining normothermia with active warming such as warmed intravenous fluids, skin warming, and warm forced air to keep the body temperature warmer than 36 C; perioperative glycemic control; and use of negative pressure wound therapy. These are not systematically used in all settings. 3 How Does Your Research Contribute to the Field? There is published evidence suggesting that the true incidence of SSIs is under-reported, particularly for events occurring post discharge. Rehospitalizations due to SSIs are either not systematically accounted for in the calculation of the burden of SSIs in the literature, or they are pooled with all readmissions possibly due to other causes (unrelated to the initial surgery). Our study estimated the frequency and cost of SSCs (including SSIs) in France for orthopedic, cardiac, digestive (gastrointestinal), and bariatric surgeries including costs of index admission and readmissions due to SSCs based on reported ICD codes, using a nationwide administrative database. To our knowledge, this is the first study with such a precise selection and classification of post-discharge surgical infection events, because we selected codes from the Major Diagnostic Categories to ensure a specific connection between the complications leading to readmission and the initial surgery. What Are Your Research’s Implications Toward Theory, Practice, or Policy? The reduction of surgical site infections and other surgical major adverse events is an active research topic worldwide and in France in particular, given a national campaign against SSIs. Prevention programs and technology bundles should be used judiciously; our findings could potentially guide health care policy makers to use prevention methods on the highest risk patients and measure outcomes. The identification of accurate indicators incentivizes value-based healthcare. Surgical site infections (SSIs) are infections of the incision, organ, or space below the incision that occur after surgery. These infections can be superficial (involving only the skin and subcutaneous tissue), deep (involving deep soft tissues such as the fascial and muscle layers), or organ/space (involving any part of the body deeper than the fascial/muscle layers that is opened or manipulated during the surgical procedure). These infections are associated with increased morbidity and mortality. 4 According to a recent literature review, 2 SSIs affect approximately 0.5 to 3% of patients undergoing surgery and are associated with hospital stays 7 to 11 days longer than those of patients without SSIs. They are among the most prevalent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), leading to readmissions in 78% of cases and responsible for approximately $3.5 to $10 billion in healthcare costs annually in the US. Nepogodiev et al estimated that globally, at least 4.2 million people die within 30 days of surgery annually, representing 7.7% of all deaths and making surgery the third contributor to death, after ischaemic heart disease and stroke. 3 SSIs are considered avoidable. Besides these infections, various other surgical site complications (e.g., excessive blood loss, wound dehiscence, post-surgical edema, complications due to anesthesia) can contribute to poor outcomes. 5 Published evidence suggests that the true incidence of SSIs is under-reported, particularly for events occurring post discharge. Furthermore, SSIs are much more prevalent in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), where the majority of the costs fall on the patient/family, causing substantial financial implications. 6 Monahan et al 7 published a systematic review estimating the cost of SSIs in LMIC settings and comparing these estimates with a reference standard of studies who have explored these costs in high income European countries. The ranges of additional cost per infection were similar in both settings ($174-$29,610 for LMIC and $21-$34,000 for European countries) but a vast study design heterogeneity was encountered across the two settings, which affected the comparability. Nevertheless, the authors emphasized that SSIs represent a financial burden in both high income and LMIC settings and argued that their prevention will decrease the financial burden of both the patient and health system. Another study reporting on LMIC environments revealed an additional cost of SSIs ranging from $3865 (Brazil) to $29,610 (India). 8 A systematic review on SSI cost and health-related quality of life focused on six European countries also identified disparate reporting making cost comparisons difficult and concluded that SSIs are extremely costly. 9 These authors pointed out that costs are likely underestimated since most published studies do not consider costs associated with lost income and reduced work productivity, nor those associated with community healthcare visits. 2 In France, the RAISIN Network (Réseau d'Alerte, d'Investigation et de Surveillance des Infections Nosocomiales) has collected SSI surveillance data since 1999 and has been replaced by the SPICMI mission since 2020 (Surveillance et Prévention du risque Infectieux lié aux actes de Chirurgie et en Médecine Interventionnelle) to partially automate data collection using electronic data from hospital information systems. Data from the SSI Surveillance Network (INCISO, 1997-1999) indicated that 38% of deaths in SSI patients were attributable to infection. The French data from 2017 indicates that SSIs make up 15.92% of reported nosocomial infections. 10 The latest SPICMI report (2018 data) 11 states that SSIs are the second most frequent hospital-acquired infections in France and are associated with increased length of stay, revision surgery, cost and mortality. It also estimates the raw incidence of SSIs at 1.64% [1.55-1.72] and at 0.72% [0.56-0.91] for patients without risk factors. Of those diagnosed SSIs, 49.2% required additional surgery. The current recommendation from Santé Publique France is to follow all patients for 30 days post-surgery (or 90 days for orthopedic surgery) to identify SSIs occurring after hospital discharge. 12 This study aimed to estimate the frequency and cost of surgical site complications (SSCs), including SSIs, in France for orthopedic, cardiac, digestive (gastrointestinal), and bariatric surgeries through the costs of the initial (index) hospitalization and any readmissions due to SSCs based on reported ICD codes, using a nationwide administrative database. This retrospective observational cohort study was based on 2017-2019 data from the French National hospital discharge database for medicine, surgery, and obstetrics ( Programme de Médicalisation des Systèmes d’Information – PMSI ). We included patients who were admitted in 2018 and did not have prior hospitalization in 2017, and we monitored readmissions through 2019, therefore the database was reviewed for the entire period of 2017 to 2019. The PMSI is a nationwide database routinely implemented for care reimbursement and updated with data from all hospitals. Its primary goal is to ensure that hospitals get reimbursed by the government at the correct level for each procedure by documenting accurately the discharge information (analogous to the American Diagnosis Related Group, DRG). In France it is coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10 13 th revision (ICD-10), as described in more detail elsewhere. Since this study was retrospective, observational, based on anonymized data, and did not influence patient care, it was exempt from Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval according to the French Public Health Code (L1121-1, law number 2012-300, 5 March 2012). 14 , 15 Informed consent was therefore not necessary. Our study followed the French reference methodology MR 006 regulating the utilization of data from the PMSI database. The study was registered under the Health Datahub registration number F20230414144230 ( 16 https://www.health-data-hub.fr/projets/impact-des-infections-chirurgicales-sur-les-couts-hospitaliers ). We included patients 15 years or older (and excluded pediatric patients under 15 years of age) admitted for initial surgery in 2018 in private and public hospitals (and not hospitalized for 6 months prior to January 2018 for digestive, vascular or bariatric surgery or 12 months prior to January 2018 for orthopedic surgery) in one of the following groups: • Orthopedic surgery • Cardiac (vascular) surgery • Digestive (gastrointestinal) surgery (excluding bariatric) • Bariatric surgery ( gastroplasty for obesity/weight loss; other interventions for obesity; exploration and surveillance for endocrine and metabolic conditions) • Orthopedic surgery • Cardiac (vascular) surgery • Digestive (gastrointestinal) surgery (excluding bariatric) • Bariatric surgery ( gastroplasty for obesity/weight loss; other interventions for obesity; exploration and surveillance for endocrine and metabolic conditions) We selected this time period to exclude data from the COVID-19 pandemic period. All stays in the PMSI are routinely assigned to a DRG, which summarizes clinical data derived from patient and stay characteristics. For higher-level analysis, the DRGs can be assigned to one of 27 broad domains (e.g. digestive system, pulmonology) described in the Major Diagnostic Categories (MDC). 17 We retrieved data for all hospitalized patients having received one of the 4 surgery types listed above. We did not exclude specific activity groups for each type of surgery. 18 These activity groups are listed in Supplemental Methods. The number of patients identified in each activity group for each type of complications is presented in 19 Supplemental Tables 1-4 . Patients were then classified according to the type of surgical site complication : infection (of the incision) related to surgery (confirmed by coding); infection (of the incision) considered as associated to surgery (i.e., the causality is probable but not confirmed); non-infectious complication (of the incision site); no complication related to the surgical incision. The first two combined (both infectious complications) are considered surgical site infections (SSIs); the distinction between those was made using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). The current recommendation from Santé Publique France is to follow all patients for 30 days post-surgery (or 90 days for orthopedic surgery) to identify SSIs occurring after hospital discharge. 12 This study aimed to estimate the frequency and cost of surgical site complications (SSCs), including SSIs, in France for orthopedic, cardiac, digestive (gastrointestinal), and bariatric surgeries through the costs of the initial (index) hospitalization and any readmissions due to SSCs based on reported ICD codes, using a nationwide administrative database. This retrospective observational cohort study was based on 2017-2019 data from the French National hospital discharge database for medicine, surgery, and obstetrics ( Programme de Médicalisation des Systèmes d’Information – PMSI ). We included patients who were admitted in 2018 and did not have prior hospitalization in 2017, and we monitored readmissions through 2019, therefore the database was reviewed for the entire period of 2017 to 2019. The PMSI is a nationwide database routinely implemented for care reimbursement and updated with data from all hospitals. Its primary goal is to ensure that hospitals get reimbursed by the government at the correct level for each procedure by documenting accurately the discharge information (analogous to the American Diagnosis Related Group, DRG). In France it is coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10 13 th revision (ICD-10), as described in more detail elsewhere. Since this study was retrospective, observational, based on anonymized data, and did not influence patient care, it was exempt from Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval according to the French Public Health Code (L1121-1, law number 2012-300, 5 March 2012). 14 , 15 Informed consent was therefore not necessary. Our study followed the French reference methodology MR 006 regulating the utilization of data from the PMSI database. The study was registered under the Health Datahub registration number F20230414144230 ( 16 https://www.health-data-hub.fr/projets/impact-des-infections-chirurgicales-sur-les-couts-hospitaliers ). We included patients 15 years or older (and excluded pediatric patients under 15 years of age) admitted for initial surgery in 2018 in private and public hospitals (and not hospitalized for 6 months prior to January 2018 for digestive, vascular or bariatric surgery or 12 months prior to January 2018 for orthopedic surgery) in one of the following groups: • Orthopedic surgery • Cardiac (vascular) surgery • Digestive (gastrointestinal) surgery (excluding bariatric) • Bariatric surgery ( gastroplasty for obesity/weight loss; other interventions for obesity; exploration and surveillance for endocrine and metabolic conditions) • Orthopedic surgery • Cardiac (vascular) surgery • Digestive (gastrointestinal) surgery (excluding bariatric) • Bariatric surgery ( gastroplasty for obesity/weight loss; other interventions for obesity; exploration and surveillance for endocrine and metabolic conditions) We selected this time period to exclude data from the COVID-19 pandemic period. All stays in the PMSI are routinely assigned to a DRG, which summarizes clinical data derived from patient and stay characteristics. For higher-level analysis, the DRGs can be assigned to one of 27 broad domains (e.g. digestive system, pulmonology) described in the Major Diagnostic Categories (MDC). 17 We retrieved data for all hospitalized patients having received one of the 4 surgery types listed above. We did not exclude specific activity groups for each type of surgery. 18 These activity groups are listed in Supplemental Methods. The number of patients identified in each activity group for each type of complications is presented in 19 Supplemental Tables 1-4 . Patients were then classified according to the type of surgical site complication : infection (of the incision) related to surgery (confirmed by coding); infection (of the incision) considered as associated to surgery (i.e., the causality is probable but not confirmed); non-infectious complication (of the incision site); no complication related to the surgical incision. The first two combined (both infectious complications) are considered surgical site infections (SSIs); the distinction between those was made using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). title: Genetically Predicted Muscle Mass and Function in Relation to Deep Vein Thrombosis: A Two-step Mendelian Randomization Study Highlighting the Mediating Role of BMI
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is observationally linked to venous thromboembolism, but the causal architecture and underlying biological pathways remain largely unclear. This study investigated the causal effects of sarcopenia-related traits on lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and quantified potential mediating mechanisms. Methods We performed two-sample bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) and two-step mediation MR using large-scale GWAS data from UK Biobank, EMBL-EBI, and FinnGen. Exposures included appendicular lean mass (ALM), leg fat-free mass (LFM), hand grip strength, and walking pace. Eighteen candidate mediators were screened for indirect pathways. Results Genetically predicted higher ALM was significantly associated with increased DVT risk (FinnGen: OR = 1.288, 95% CI: 1.215–1.365, P < 0.001). Similar positive associations were observed for LFM (OR = 1.920–1.954, P < 0.001). By contrast, muscle functional traits - grip strength and walking pace - demonstrated no consistent causal effects. Reverse MR confirmed a unidirectional relationship. Body mass index (BMI) emerged as a pivotal mediator, accounting for 7.58% – 10.50% of the ALM–DVT effect and 52.74% – 62.73% of the LFM–DVT effect. Notably, the independent effect of ALM was largely attenuated after adjusting for metabolic confounders in multivariable MR. Conclusion Genetic predisposition to high muscle mass, rather than functional strength, increases DVT risk. This relationship appears to be significantly driven by metabolic adiposity, suggesting that the “muscle–vascular–coagulation” interaction is partly explained by body-size-related metabolic burden. Risk stratification should integrate muscle mass evaluation with comprehensive metabolic health assessments.
body: Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) remains a major driver of global morbidity and healthcare expenditure. DVT, together with its potentially fatal complication, pulmonary embolism, constitutes the spectrum of venous thromboembolism (VTE), which places a substantial burden on healthcare systems. In high-income countries, the annual incidence of DVT is estimated at 50 to 120 per 100,000 person-years. Critically, this risk is not evenly distributed across the lifespan; it increases exponentially with age, placing older adults at the center of this thrombotic crisis. 1 Clinically, the priority remains identifying and managing modifiable risk factors for DVT. 2 While traditional risk factors such as surgery, immobilization, and malignancy are well-documented, the role of skeletal muscle health - specifically, the relationship between muscle mass and the coagulation system - has only recently attracted research attention. Determining whether muscle mass acts as a modifiable protective or risk factor is critical for the development of novel primary prevention strategies focused on sarcopenia management. We note that these incidence estimates derive predominantly from European and North American populations, consistent with the European-ancestry GWAS analysed here. 3 A growing body of observational evidence points to a potential link between sarcopenia-related traits and VTE. For instance, sarcopenia has been reported as an independent predictor of VTE in bladder cancer patients following radical cystectomy. Similar associations have been found in patients undergoing surgical excision of head and neck cancer. 4 Furthermore, specific localized muscle metrics, such as lower thigh muscle volume, have been correlated with a higher prevalence of postoperative DVT after total knee arthroplasty. 5 However, these traditional observational designs are constrained by inherent methodological limitations. 6 They are highly susceptible to confounding from age-related comorbidities, baseline immobilization, and socioeconomic factors, and often cannot distinguish between true causality and reverse causation. It therefore remains unclear whether sarcopenia directly promotes a pro-thrombotic state or whether both conditions are parallel manifestations of shared pathophysiological processes, such as chronic systemic inflammation. 7 Thus, a more robust analytical framework is urgently needed to establish the directionality and causality of these relationships. 8 Mendelian randomization (MR) offers a solution to the pitfalls of observational research. By utilizing genetic variants as instrumental variables, MR mimics the design of a randomized controlled trial (RCT), as genetic alleles are randomly assigned at conception. Because these variants are generally independent of environmental influences and lifestyle factors, 9 , 10 MR offers a methodologically rigorous approach for causal inference that is less susceptible to confounding and reverse causation. 11 , 12 Recent MR studies have begun to explore the connection between sarcopenia-related traits, such as muscle mass and grip strength, and VTE risk. 9 , 13 While these studies have provided valuable insights, they have primarily focused on estimating the “total effect” of the exposure on the outcome. However, they have not dissected the potential mediating pathways that bridge muscle health and vascular coagulation. A critical knowledge gap remains: if skeletal muscle mass indeed influences DVT risk, what are the underlying biological “bridges” mediating this effect? 14 From a pathophysiological standpoint, the influence of skeletal muscle on thrombus formation may operate through three interrelated mechanisms, which together form what we define as the “muscle-vascular-coagulation” interaction network. First, the mechanical role of muscle mass cannot be overlooked. The lower limb muscle pump function, primarily driven by contraction of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, is vital for promoting venous return. Reduced muscle mass may lead to impaired pump efficiency, resulting in venous stasis and hemodynamic alterations. According to Virchow’s triad, venous stasis is a foundational prerequisite for thrombus formation, suggesting that muscle atrophy may provide the physical environment conducive to coagulation. Second, chronic low grade inflammation, often termed “inflammaging,” is a hallmark of the sarcopenic phenotype. 15 Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), are prevalent in individuals with sarcopenia. 16 These cytokines are known to promote a hypercoagulable state by damaging the vascular endothelium and activating the coagulation cascade. 17 Third, metabolic disturbances may serve as a crucial bridging mechanism. Reduced muscle mass is frequently associated with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome. 18 Notably, skeletal muscle is the primary organ for glucose disposal, and its loss can exacerbate adiposity and elevate Body Mass Index (BMI), which is a well-established and potent risk factor for venous thrombosis. 19 These interrelated pathways suggest that certain metabolic or inflammatory factors could mediate the causal relationship between sarcopenia and DVT. 20 Despite the theoretical plausibility of these mechanisms, no study has systematically integrated and quantified these potential mediating pathways in the sarcopenia-DVT relationship. Standard MR, while powerful, acts as a “black box” that estimates the overall impact but remains silent on the intermediate steps. To overcome this, we used Two-step MR, a sophisticated analytical strategy that combines MR estimates for exposure-to-mediator and mediator-to-outcome pathways to quantify mediation effects. Coupled with recent advances in proteomics and metabolomics, which allow for screening a wide range of candidate mediators - including cardiovascular risk factors and metabolic indicators - this study is uniquely positioned to move beyond simple “exposure-outcome” testing. 21 This study addresses three core research questions: Are specific sarcopenia-related traits, namely appendicular lean mass (ALM), leg fat-free mass (LFM), hand grip strength (HGS), and usual walking pace (UWP), genetically causal risk factors for lower extremity DVT? Do candidate metabolic or inflammatory factors mediate the association between muscle traits and DVT? What is the relative magnitude and proportion of these mediating effects? To answer these questions, we analyzed large-scale genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary data from the UK Biobank, EMBL-EBI, and FinnGen. We first performed two-sample bidirectional MR to establish the total causal effects. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive screen of 18 candidate mediators - including BMI, glycocholate, dodecanedioate, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, hypertension, myocardial infarction, VEGF receptors, glycine, and serum creatinine - to quantify their indirect effects via two-step MR. By elucidating these pathways, this study provides new genetic evidence for the “muscle-vascular-coagulation” interaction network. Clinically, these findings may facilitate the identification of high-risk populations, such as sarcopenic patients with elevated BMI, and offer a theoretical basis for targeted intervention strategies, including weight management and rehabilitation exercises to enhance muscle pump function. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to the development of primary prevention strategies for thrombosis based on holistic management of sarcopenia. This study employed a comprehensive Mendelian randomization (MR) framework consisting of two distinct analytical phases to investigate the “muscle-metabolic-vascular” axis. In accordance with the STROBE-MR (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology using Mendelian Randomization) guidelines, our design strictly adhered to the three fundamental instrumental variable (IV) assumptions: (1) Relevance—IVs must be robustly associated with the exposure; (2) Independence—IVs must not be associated with any confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship; and (3) Exclusion restriction—IVs affect the outcome exclusively through the exposure and not via alternative biological pathways. In the first phase, we performed a two-sample bidirectional MR analysis to estimate the total causal effects between sarcopenia-related traits (including appendicular lean mass [ALM], leg fat-free mass [LFM], hand grip strength, and usual walking pace) and lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Subsequently, multivariable MR (MVMR) was conducted to determine whether the causal effect of ALM on DVT risk remains independent after adjusting for potential metabolic confounders. The second phase used a two-step MR approach to identify candidate mediators and quantify their indirect effects. This mediation analysis was designed to determine the proportion of the total effect of ALM and LFM on DVT that is transmitted through body mass index (BMI) or other metabolic factors. The overall study schematic is illustrated in 22 , 23 Figure 1 . To minimize potential bias from sample overlap, we prioritized the use of GWAS summary statistics from independent consortia, such as UK Biobank and FinnGen, thereby ensuring the robustness of our causal estimates. Figure 1. Overview of the MR Study. The study consists of two analytical phases. In the first phase, univariable Mendelian randomization (UVMR) estimates the causal relationship between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT, suggesting that higher sarcopenia-related traits may causally increase the risk of DVT. In the second phase, two-step MR analysis was performed on 18 potential mediators, which may represent pathways between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT. The mediating effect and its proportion were also evaluated Overview of the MR Study. The study consists of two analytical phases. In the first phase, univariable Mendelian randomization (UVMR) estimates the causal relationship between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT, suggesting that higher sarcopenia-related traits may causally increase the risk of DVT. In the second phase, two-step MR analysis was performed on 18 potential mediators, which may represent pathways between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT. The mediating effect and its proportion were also evaluated Genetic instruments for each exposure and potential mediator were derived from high-quality, published genome-wide association studies (GWAS). To satisfy the relevance assumption, we prioritized single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) reaching the genome-wide significance threshold of P < 5 × 10 -8 . To ensure the independence of these instrumental variables (IVs) and minimize the impact of linkage disequilibrium, a rigorous clumping procedure was applied with an r 2 < 0.001 and a window size of 10,000 kb, using the European ancestry reference panel from the 1000 Genomes Project. To mitigate potential weak instrument bias, we evaluated the strength of the selected SNPs using the F-statistic; only IVs with an F > 10 were retained for the final analysis. For multivariable Mendelian randomization (MVMR), genetic variants were selected to estimate the independent causal effects of each exposure while adjusting for potential pleiotropic confounders. Furthermore, a systematic harmonization process was performed to ensure that the effect of the SNPs on the exposure and the outcome corresponded to the same effect allele. During this stage, palindromic SNPs with intermediate allele frequencies were excluded to avoid ambiguity in the directional estimates. Sarcopenia-related traits included appendicular lean mass (ALM), leg fat-free mass (LFM, left and right), hand grip strength (HGS, left and right) and usual walking pace (UWP). Genetic instruments for LFM (left, N = 454,805; right, N = 454,835), HGS (left, N = 461, 206; right, N = 461,089), and UWP (N = 459,915) were obtained from the UK Biobank. Instruments for ALM (N = 450,243) and serum creatinine (N = 344,104) were obtained from the EMBL-EBI GWAS catalog. DVT outcome data were obtained from three sources: (i) self-reported DVT in UK Biobank (cases = 9,241, controls = 453,692; GWAS ID: ukb-b-12040); (ii) hospital-diagnosed DVT of lower extremities in UK Biobank (cases = 2,116, controls = 359,078; ukb-d-I9_PHLETHROMBDVTLOW); and (iii) DVT of lower extremities in FinnGen (cases = 8,850, controls = 88,500; finngen_R9_I9_PHLETHROMBDVTLOW). All participants were of European ancestry. To address the inherent limitations of observational studies, we selected several physiological parameters as potential confounders. These included CCL19 levels (N = 982), PAI-1 levels (N = 1323), Adrenomedullin levels (N = 21758), MCP-2 plasma levels (N = 400), TIMP-1, MCP-1, HB-EGF. Based on biological plausibility and data availability, we initially screened 18 candidate mediators related to metabolism, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk. These included glycocholate, dodecanedioate, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, hypertension, myocardial infarction, VEGF receptors, Serum creatinine levels, glycine, and body mass index (BMI). Full details of the mediator GWAS sources, including sample sizes and consortia, are provided in Table 1 . The primary causal effect was estimated using the random-effects inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method, which provides the most robust estimates in the absence of horizontal pleiotropy. To evaluate the reliability of our findings across diverse modeling assumptions, four complementary sensitivity analyses were implemented: MR-Egger, weighted median, weighted mode, and simple mode. Heterogeneity among instrumental variables was quantified using Cochran’s Q test, with P < 0.05 indicating significant variability. Horizontal pleiotropy was assessed via the MR-Egger intercept; a significant intercept (P < 0.05) would suggest the presence of pleiotropic bias. Additionally, the Steiger directional test was applied to confirm the direction of causality and rule out reverse causation. For multivariable MR (MVMR), the multivariable inverse variance-weighted (MV-IVW) model served as the primary estimator, supplemented by the multivariable MR-Egger intercept to detect potential pleiotropy in a multivariable context. To mitigate the risk of Type I errors arising from multiple comparisons, a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold was established at P < 0.05/(N × N exposures ). outcomes Univariable MR (UVMR) was initially performed to estimate the total causal effects of appendicular lean mass (ALM), leg fat-free mass (LFM), hand grip strength (HGS), and usual walking pace (UWP) on DVT risk across three independent outcome datasets. To establish a unidirectional relationship, reverse bidirectional MR was conducted to evaluate whether DVT genetically influences these sarcopenia-related traits. Given the high biological correlation between musculature and metabolic health, we further utilized MVMR to adjust for established metabolic confounders. This approach allowed us to isolate the independent causal effect of muscle mass on DVT risk, ensuring that the observed associations were not merely driven by underlying metabolic disturbances. To elucidate the biological pathways linking sarcopenia-related traits to DVT, candidate mediators were evaluated through a rigorous two-step Mendelian randomization framework. Specifically, 18 potential mediators related to metabolic, inflammatory, and cardiovascular health were initially screened. A candidate was selected for formal mediation analysis only if it satisfied the following four criteria: 1). Exposure-to-Mediator Effect: The exposure (ALM or LFM) demonstrated a significant causal effect on the candidate mediator (P < 0.05 in UVMR). 2). Mediator-to-Outcome Effect: The candidate mediator showed a significant causal effect on DVT (P < 0.05 in UVMR). 3). Directional Integrity: There was no evidence of reverse causation between the mediator and the exposure, as verified by the Steiger directional test. 4). Consistency of Effect: The direction of the estimated indirect effect was consistent with the total causal effect of the exposure on DVT. In the two-step MR approach, we estimated the effect of the exposure on the mediator (β 1 ) and the effect of the mediator on DVT (β 2 ) using the IVW method as the primary estimator. The indirect (mediation) effect was calculated using the product of coefficients method (β = β indirect 1 × β 2 ). The proportion mediated was subsequently derived by dividing the indirect effect by the total effect (β ) of the exposure on DVT: Proportion = (β total 1 × β 2 )/β . Standard errors for the indirect effect and the mediated proportion were estimated via the Delta method. Similar positive associations were observed for LFM (OR = 1.920–1.954, P < 0.001). By contrast, muscle functional traits - grip strength and walking pace - demonstrated no consistent causal effects. Reverse MR confirmed a unidirectional relationship. Body mass index (BMI) emerged as a pivotal mediator, accounting for 7.58% – 10.50% of the ALM–DVT effect and 52.74% – 62.73% of the LFM–DVT effect. Notably, the independent effect of ALM was largely attenuated after adjusting for metabolic confounders in multivariable MR. Conclusion Genetic predisposition to high muscle mass, rather than functional strength, increases DVT risk. This relationship appears to be significantly driven by metabolic adiposity, suggesting that the “muscle–vascular–coagulation” interaction is partly explained by body-size-related metabolic burden. Risk stratification should integrate muscle mass evaluation with comprehensive metabolic health assessments.

Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) remains a major driver of global morbidity and healthcare expenditure. DVT, together with its potentially fatal complication, pulmonary embolism, constitutes the spectrum of venous thromboembolism (VTE), which places a substantial burden on healthcare systems. In high-income countries, the annual incidence of DVT is estimated at 50 to 120 per 100,000 person-years. Critically, this risk is not evenly distributed across the lifespan; it increases exponentially with age, placing older adults at the center of this thrombotic crisis. 1 Clinically, the priority remains identifying and managing modifiable risk factors for DVT. 2 While traditional risk factors such as surgery, immobilization, and malignancy are well-documented, the role of skeletal muscle health - specifically, the relationship between muscle mass and the coagulation system - has only recently attracted research attention. Determining whether muscle mass acts as a modifiable protective or risk factor is critical for the development of novel primary prevention strategies focused on sarcopenia management. We note that these incidence estimates derive predominantly from European and North American populations, consistent with the European-ancestry GWAS analysed here. 3 A growing body of observational evidence points to a potential link between sarcopenia-related traits and VTE. For instance, sarcopenia has been reported as an independent predictor of VTE in bladder cancer patients following radical cystectomy. Similar associations have been found in patients undergoing surgical excision of head and neck cancer. 4 Furthermore, specific localized muscle metrics, such as lower thigh muscle volume, have been correlated with a higher prevalence of postoperative DVT after total knee arthroplasty. 5 However, these traditional observational designs are constrained by inherent methodological limitations. 6 They are highly susceptible to confounding from age-related comorbidities, baseline immobilization, and socioeconomic factors, and often cannot distinguish between true causality and reverse causation. It therefore remains unclear whether sarcopenia directly promotes a pro-thrombotic state or whether both conditions are parallel manifestations of shared pathophysiological processes, such as chronic systemic inflammation. 7 Thus, a more robust analytical framework is urgently needed to establish the directionality and causality of these relationships. 8 Mendelian randomization (MR) offers a solution to the pitfalls of observational research. By utilizing genetic variants as instrumental variables, MR mimics the design of a randomized controlled trial (RCT), as genetic alleles are randomly assigned at conception. Because these variants are generally independent of environmental influences and lifestyle factors, 9 , 10 MR offers a methodologically rigorous approach for causal inference that is less susceptible to confounding and reverse causation. 11 , 12 Recent MR studies have begun to explore the connection between sarcopenia-related traits, such as muscle mass and grip strength, and VTE risk. 9 , 13 While these studies have provided valuable insights, they have primarily focused on estimating the “total effect” of the exposure on the outcome. However, they have not dissected the potential mediating pathways that bridge muscle health and vascular coagulation. A critical knowledge gap remains: if skeletal muscle mass indeed influences DVT risk, what are the underlying biological “bridges” mediating this effect? 14 From a pathophysiological standpoint, the influence of skeletal muscle on thrombus formation may operate through three interrelated mechanisms, which together form what we define as the “muscle-vascular-coagulation” interaction network. First, the mechanical role of muscle mass cannot be overlooked. The lower limb muscle pump function, primarily driven by contraction of the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, is vital for promoting venous return. Reduced muscle mass may lead to impaired pump efficiency, resulting in venous stasis and hemodynamic alterations. According to Virchow’s triad, venous stasis is a foundational prerequisite for thrombus formation, suggesting that muscle atrophy may provide the physical environment conducive to coagulation. Second, chronic low grade inflammation, often termed “inflammaging,” is a hallmark of the sarcopenic phenotype. 15 Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), are prevalent in individuals with sarcopenia. 16 These cytokines are known to promote a hypercoagulable state by damaging the vascular endothelium and activating the coagulation cascade. 17 Third, metabolic disturbances may serve as a crucial bridging mechanism. Reduced muscle mass is frequently associated with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome. 18 Notably, skeletal muscle is the primary organ for glucose disposal, and its loss can exacerbate adiposity and elevate Body Mass Index (BMI), which is a well-established and potent risk factor for venous thrombosis. 19 These interrelated pathways suggest that certain metabolic or inflammatory factors could mediate the causal relationship between sarcopenia and DVT. 20 Despite the theoretical plausibility of these mechanisms, no study has systematically integrated and quantified these potential mediating pathways in the sarcopenia-DVT relationship. Standard MR, while powerful, acts as a “black box” that estimates the overall impact but remains silent on the intermediate steps. To overcome this, we used Two-step MR, a sophisticated analytical strategy that combines MR estimates for exposure-to-mediator and mediator-to-outcome pathways to quantify mediation effects. Coupled with recent advances in proteomics and metabolomics, which allow for screening a wide range of candidate mediators - including cardiovascular risk factors and metabolic indicators - this study is uniquely positioned to move beyond simple “exposure-outcome” testing. 21 This study addresses three core research questions: Are specific sarcopenia-related traits, namely appendicular lean mass (ALM), leg fat-free mass (LFM), hand grip strength (HGS), and usual walking pace (UWP), genetically causal risk factors for lower extremity DVT? Do candidate metabolic or inflammatory factors mediate the association between muscle traits and DVT? What is the relative magnitude and proportion of these mediating effects? To answer these questions, we analyzed large-scale genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary data from the UK Biobank, EMBL-EBI, and FinnGen. We first performed two-sample bidirectional MR to establish the total causal effects. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive screen of 18 candidate mediators - including BMI, glycocholate, dodecanedioate, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, hypertension, myocardial infarction, VEGF receptors, glycine, and serum creatinine - to quantify their indirect effects via two-step MR. By elucidating these pathways, this study provides new genetic evidence for the “muscle-vascular-coagulation” interaction network. Clinically, these findings may facilitate the identification of high-risk populations, such as sarcopenic patients with elevated BMI, and offer a theoretical basis for targeted intervention strategies, including weight management and rehabilitation exercises to enhance muscle pump function. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to the development of primary prevention strategies for thrombosis based on holistic management of sarcopenia. This study employed a comprehensive Mendelian randomization (MR) framework consisting of two distinct analytical phases to investigate the “muscle-metabolic-vascular” axis. In accordance with the STROBE-MR (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology using Mendelian Randomization) guidelines, our design strictly adhered to the three fundamental instrumental variable (IV) assumptions: (1) Relevance—IVs must be robustly associated with the exposure; (2) Independence—IVs must not be associated with any confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship; and (3) Exclusion restriction—IVs affect the outcome exclusively through the exposure and not via alternative biological pathways. In the first phase, we performed a two-sample bidirectional MR analysis to estimate the total causal effects between sarcopenia-related traits (including appendicular lean mass [ALM], leg fat-free mass [LFM], hand grip strength, and usual walking pace) and lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Subsequently, multivariable MR (MVMR) was conducted to determine whether the causal effect of ALM on DVT risk remains independent after adjusting for potential metabolic confounders. The second phase used a two-step MR approach to identify candidate mediators and quantify their indirect effects. This mediation analysis was designed to determine the proportion of the total effect of ALM and LFM on DVT that is transmitted through body mass index (BMI) or other metabolic factors. The overall study schematic is illustrated in 22 , 23 Figure 1 . To minimize potential bias from sample overlap, we prioritized the use of GWAS summary statistics from independent consortia, such as UK Biobank and FinnGen, thereby ensuring the robustness of our causal estimates. Figure 1. Overview of the MR Study. The study consists of two analytical phases. In the first phase, univariable Mendelian randomization (UVMR) estimates the causal relationship between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT, suggesting that higher sarcopenia-related traits may causally increase the risk of DVT. In the second phase, two-step MR analysis was performed on 18 potential mediators, which may represent pathways between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT. In the first phase, univariable Mendelian randomization (UVMR) estimates the causal relationship between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT, suggesting that higher sarcopenia-related traits may causally increase the risk of DVT. In the second phase, two-step MR analysis was performed on 18 potential mediators, which may represent pathways between sarcopenia-related traits and DVT. The mediating effect and its proportion were also evaluated Genetic instruments for each exposure and potential mediator were derived from high-quality, published genome-wide association studies (GWAS). To satisfy the relevance assumption, we prioritized single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) reaching the genome-wide significance threshold of P < 5 × 10 -8 . To ensure the independence of these instrumental variables (IVs) and minimize the impact of linkage disequilibrium, a rigorous clumping procedure was applied with an r 2 < 0.001 and a window size of 10,000 kb, using the European ancestry reference panel from the 1000 Genomes Project. To mitigate potential weak instrument bias, we evaluated the strength of the selected SNPs using the F-statistic; only IVs with an F > 10 were retained for the final analysis. For multivariable Mendelian randomization (MVMR), genetic variants were selected to estimate the independent causal effects of each exposure while adjusting for potential pleiotropic confounders. Furthermore, a systematic harmonization process was performed to ensure that the effect of the SNPs on the exposure and the outcome corresponded to the same effect allele. During this stage, palindromic SNPs with intermediate allele frequencies were excluded to avoid ambiguity in the directional estimates. Instruments for ALM (N = 450,243) and serum creatinine (N = 344,104) were obtained from the EMBL-EBI GWAS catalog. DVT outcome data were obtained from three sources: (i) self-reported DVT in UK Biobank (cases = 9,241, controls = 453,692; GWAS ID: ukb-b-12040); (ii) hospital-diagnosed DVT of lower extremities in UK Biobank (cases = 2,116, controls = 359,078; ukb-d-I9_PHLETHROMBDVTLOW); and (iii) DVT of lower extremities in FinnGen (cases = 8,850, controls = 88,500; finngen_R9_I9_PHLETHROMBDVTLOW). These included CCL19 levels (N = 982), PAI-1 levels (N = 1323), Adrenomedullin levels (N = 21758), MCP-2 plasma levels (N = 400), TIMP-1, MCP-1, HB-EGF. Based on biological plausibility and data availability, we initially screened 18 candidate mediators related to metabolism, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk. These included glycocholate, dodecanedioate, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, hypertension, myocardial infarction, VEGF receptors, Serum creatinine levels, glycine, and body mass index (BMI). Full details of the mediator GWAS sources, including sample sizes and consortia, are provided in Table 1 . The primary causal effect was estimated using the random-effects inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method, which provides the most robust estimates in the absence of horizontal pleiotropy. To evaluate the reliability of our findings across diverse modeling assumptions, four complementary sensitivity analyses were implemented: MR-Egger, weighted median, weighted mode, and simple mode. Heterogeneity among instrumental variables was quantified using Cochran’s Q test, with P < 0.05 indicating significant variability. Horizontal pleiotropy was assessed via the MR-Egger intercept; a significant intercept (P < 0.05) would suggest the presence of pleiotropic bias. Additionally, the Steiger directional test was applied to confirm the direction of causality and rule out reverse causation. For multivariable MR (MVMR), the multivariable inverse variance-weighted (MV-IVW) model served as the primary estimator, supplemented by the multivariable MR-Egger intercept to detect potential pleiotropy in a multivariable context. To mitigate the risk of Type I errors arising from multiple comparisons, a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold was established at P < 0.05/(N × N exposures ). outcomes Univariable MR (UVMR) was initially performed to estimate the total causal effects of appendicular lean mass (ALM), leg fat-free mass (LFM), hand grip strength (HGS), and usual walking pace (UWP) on DVT risk across three independent outcome datasets. To establish a unidirectional relationship, reverse bidirectional MR was conducted to evaluate whether DVT genetically influences these sarcopenia-related traits. Given the high biological correlation between musculature and metabolic health, we further utilized MVMR to adjust for established metabolic confounders. This approach allowed us to isolate the independent causal effect of muscle mass on DVT risk, ensuring that the observed associations were not merely driven by underlying metabolic disturbances. To elucidate the biological pathways linking sarcopenia-related traits to DVT, candidate mediators were evaluated through a rigorous two-step Mendelian randomization framework. Specifically, 18 potential mediators related to metabolic, inflammatory, and cardiovascular health were initially screened. A candidate was selected for formal mediation analysis only if it satisfied the following four criteria: 1). Exposure-to-Mediator Effect: The exposure (ALM or LFM) demonstrated a significant causal effect on the candidate mediator (P < 0.05 in UVMR). 2). Mediator-to-Outcome Effect: The candidate mediator showed a significant causal effect on DVT (P < 0.05 in UVMR). 3). Directional Integrity: There was no evidence of reverse causation between the mediator and the exposure, as verified by the Steiger directional test. 4). Consistency of Effect: The direction of the estimated indirect effect was consistent with the total causal effect of the exposure on DVT. In the two-step MR approach, we estimated the effect of the exposure on the mediator (β 1 ) and the effect of the mediator on DVT (β 2 ) using the IVW method as the primary estimator. The indirect (mediation) effect was calculated using the product of coefficients method (β = β indirect 1 × β 2 ). The proportion mediated was subsequently derived by dividing the indirect effect by the total effect (β ) of the exposure on DVT: Proportion = (β total 1 × β 2 )/β . Standard errors for the indirect effect and the mediated proportion were estimated via the Delta method.
