title: Recovery Trajectory of Range of Motion and Its Association With Patient Factors During Early Postoperative Stiffness After Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair
abstract: Background: Postoperative shoulder stiffness may influence functional recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. However, predictors for progression to persistent shoulder stiffness have not been clearly established. Purpose: To identify factors associated with persistent stiffness and describe range of motion (ROM) recovery trajectory after arthroscopic repair of full-thickness rotator cuff tears. Study Design: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 352 patients who underwent arthroscopic complete repair. Stiffness was defined as forward flexion <120°, external rotation <30°, or internal rotation below L3. ROM, visual analog scale (VAS) score, American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score, Constant score, and tendon integrity were assessed, and patients reported the primary barrier to rehabilitation at 3 months. Predictors of persistent stiffness at 6 months were evaluated using multivariate logistic regression. Results: At 3 months, 165 patients (46.9%) met stiffness criteria. Compared with patients without stiffness, the stiffness group had poorer functional outcome ( P < .001), higher pain (VAS, 2.2 ± 1.1 vs 1.8 ± 1.2; P = .002), and a lower retear rate (6.7% vs 14.4%; P = .019). Among patients with early stiffness, 34 (20.6%) had persistent stiffness at 6 months. Fear or anxiety about tendon retear was the most common barrier (50.3%), followed by pain (32.7%); however, persistent stiffness was most prevalent when pain was the primary barrier (67.6%). Higher pain score at 3 months independently predicted persistent stiffness (odds ratio, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.01-2.05]; P = .044). Conclusion: Early stiffness after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair is heterogeneous. Pain-driven stiffness is associated with persistence, whereas stiffness related to fear or anxiety about tendon retear is common but largely reversible; tailored management may improve recovery.
body: Postoperative shoulder stiffness is one of the most common complications after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair, and it occurs in 11% to 35.4% of patients. It may lead to distressing and unsatisfactory situations for both patients and surgeons during the recovery period, despite successful rotator cuff repair. 5 However, stiffness during the early postoperative period is associated with improved tendon healing and a lower retear rate. 6 , 11 , 18 , 33 Patients with postoperative stiffness have functional deficits during the early recovery period; however, these typically improve over time, and their long-term outcomes are generally comparable to those of patients without stiffness. 12 , 13 , 23 , 27 , 33 3 , 17 , 25 , 27 Despite the favorable long-term outcomes of early postoperative stiffness, the recovery trajectory of the shoulder range of motion (ROM) varies among individuals. Approximately 20% of patients with early postoperative stiffness have persistent stiffness beyond 6 months, indicating interindividual variability in recovery patterns. Several studies have suggested greater postoperative pain in patients with persistent stiffness after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. 6 , 16 However, most have used a cross-sectional approach; they determined the relationship between pain and postoperative stiffness based on ROM measurements at a single time point and compared pain levels longitudinally. This approach limits the evaluation of pain progression relative to ROM recovery. Pain sensitization and kinesiophobia have recently been proposed as contributing mechanisms underlying the persistence of stiffness and poorer clinical outcomes. 11 , 25 , 34 The temporal pattern of postoperative pain may influence ROM recovery; however, its role in determining patients who will progress to persistent stiffness has not been clearly established. The factors that become predictive of persistent stiffness at specific time points also remain unknown. 14 This study aimed to identify the factors affecting the persistence of early postoperative stiffness and the trajectory of ROM recovery in patients with full-thickness rotator cuff tears after arthroscopic repair. We hypothesized that greater early postoperative pain would be associated with persistent stiffness and slower ROM recovery. The patients who underwent arthroscopic rotator cuff repair for symptomatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears at one institution between February 2019 and March 2023 were retrospectively analyzed. The inclusion criteria were as follows: having undergone arthroscopic rotator cuff repairs with full coverage of footprint for symptomatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears detected on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), completion of follow-up evaluations at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months, and confirmation of the integrity of the repaired tendon using MRI and ultrasonography performed at 6 months and 1 year postoperatively to confirm the repaired tendon integrity. The exclusion criteria were as follows: patients with preoperative shoulder stiffness, primary arthroscopic repair for partial-thickness rotator cuff tear or isolated subscapularis tear; additional augmentation procedures, such as patch augmentation or superior capsular reconstruction; revision surgeries; advanced glenohumeral osteoarthritis confirmed by imaging studies; neurologic or systemic disorders affecting the shoulder joint; history of acute trauma or infection; and incomplete medical records. Postoperative stiffness during the recovery period was defined based on the presence of any of the following criteria at the follow-up evaluation: forward flexion of <120°, external rotation of <30°, or internal rotation below the L3 level. The patients were categorized into those with (3-month stiff group) and without (3-month nonstiff group) stiffness based on their ROMs at 3 months postoperatively. The patients in the 3-month stiffness group were further categorized into those with stiffness (6-month stiff group) and those who had recovered from it (6-month nonstiff group) based on their status at 6 months postoperatively using the same criteria. This retrospective study was approved by the institutional review board of Ewha Womans University Seoul Hospital. 26 , 33 All patients completed the questionnaires before surgery. The questionnaires included questions about arm dominance, duration of shoulder symptoms, and the presence of diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and smoking. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated by dividing the body weight in kilograms by the square of the height in meters. The ROM in 3 directions, American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score, Constant score, and pain severity based on the visual analog scale (VAS) score were evaluated preoperatively, at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months postoperatively, and at the final follow-up in the outpatient clinic by a single experienced physician assistant. The shoulder ROM was determined based on the passive ROM in 3 planes: forward flexion, external rotation at the side, and internal rotation behind the back. The measurements were performed using a goniometer by a single experienced physician assistant. Forward flexion was defined as the angle formed between the arm and the thorax with the elbow extended. External rotation at the side was defined as the angle between the thorax and the forearm when the upper arm was adducted, and the elbow was flexed at 90°. Internal rotation behind the back was defined based on the vertebral level reached by the tip of the thumb. The vertebral levels were converted into a contiguous numerical scale (higher values indicate better internal rotation) for ease of statistical analysis: 6 T1 to T12, 19 to 8; L1 to L5, 7 to 3; sacrum, 2; buttock, 1; and thigh, 0. 26 The patients with shoulder stiffness at the 3-month postoperative follow-up were interviewed to determine the reasons for poor compliance with rehabilitation exercises. Their responses were as follows: (A) pain; (B) lack of time or motivation; and (C) fear or anxiety regarding tendon retear. The patients were stratified into the corresponding subgroups, and the proportions of those with persistent stiffness at 6 months postoperatively were determined. All patients underwent postoperative MRI at 6 months and ultrasound examination at 1 year to assess tendon integrity, regardless of symptoms. Tendon integrity was evaluated using the Sugaya classification, and retear was defined as type 4 or 5, indicating complete discontinuity of the repaired rotator cuff tendon. The pre- and postoperative MRI scans were interpreted by a musculoskeletal radiologist who was not involved in this study. 31 , 33 The tear size and pattern were determined intraoperatively after debridement of the degenerative tissue at the torn edge of the rotator cuff using a calibrated measuring device. The anteroposterior (AP) tear size was defined as the distance along the lateral edge of the exposed footprint. The mediolateral (ML) tear size was defined as the longest distance between the most medial margin of the retracted tendon and the footprint. The tear patterns were classified as crescent-shaped, U-shaped, anterior L-shaped, and posterior L-shaped. A crescent-shaped tear was defined as having an AP tear size larger than the ML tear size. A U-shaped tear was defined as having an ML tear size larger than the AP tear size. An anterior L-shaped tear was defined as a tear that propagated through the rotator interval and anterior rotator cable, resulting in exposure of the long head of the biceps tendon. A posterior L-shaped tear was defined as a tear that propagated along the interval between the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons. All patients were immobilized with an abduction brace for 1 month postoperatively, regardless of tear size or retraction. They were allowed to perform elbow, wrist, and finger exercises immediately after surgery. No shoulder-specific physical therapy was administered during the immobilization period. Passive ROM exercises were initiated at 1 month postoperatively, followed by gradual active-assisted motion based on pain tolerance. Muscle-strengthening exercises were initiated for the patients who had achieved >80% of the ROM of the contralateral shoulder at 3 months postoperatively. Rehabilitation was performed with home exercises, which were instructed by a single experienced physician assistant, and patients performed the exercises independently at home. The categorical variables (sex, operated side, tear type, history of diabetes or hyperlipidemia, smoking status, and retear) were compared using the chi-square test. The continuous variables (age, symptom duration, BMI, tear size, VAS score, and ASES score) were compared using Student t test. Forward flexion, external rotation, and internal rotation were measured at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively to assess the recovery trajectories of shoulder ROM in the stiff and nonstiff groups. Their recovery trajectories were compared using repeated-measures analysis of variance. Greenhouse-Geisser corrections were applied when the assumptions of sphericity were violated. The Mann-Whitney U test with Bonferroni correction was used for the intergroup comparisons at each time point because variance homogeneity was not met at several postoperative time points. Variables with P < 0.1 in the univariate analysis were entered into the multivariate logistic regression model. A post hoc power analysis was performed to assess the adequacy of the current sample size for the multivariable logistic regression model, based on the observed sample size, number of outcome events, and the effect size of the primary predictor of interest. Statistical significance was set at P < .05. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software, Version 29.0 (IBM Corp). Of the 643 patients, 291 were excluded because of preoperative stiffness (n = 153), isolated subscapularis tendon tears (n = 13), and revision surgeries (n = 19). The 106 irreparable cuff tears that required additional graft augmentation procedures were also excluded. A total of 352 patients were included in the study. Of these, 165 (46.9%) and 187 (53.1%) were classified into the 3-month stiff and nonstiff groups, respectively. The demographic variables of the 2 groups were comparable, except for a higher proportion of female patients in the stiff group ( Table 1 ). Comparison of the Demographic Data of the 3-Month Stiff and Nonstiff Groups a Data are presented as mean ± SD or n (%). AP, anteroposterior; BMI, body mass index; ML, mediolateral. The 3-month stiff group had significantly limited ROM in all 3 planes, lower ASES and Constant scores, and higher VAS scores than the nonstiff group ( P < .001) ( Table 2 ). The retear rate was significantly lower for the patients in the 3-month stiff group than for those in the 3-month nonstiff group ( P = .019). Of the 165 patients with early postoperative stiffness, 34 (20.6%) had persistent stiffness at 6 months, whereas 131 (79.4%) recovered full ROM. The 6-month stiff group had significantly more limited ROM and lower ASES (81.5 ± 8.6 vs 89.3 ± 7.3; P < .001) and Constant (71.5 ± 9.4 vs 83.8 ± 7.4; P < .001) scores at 6 months postoperatively and higher VAS scores at 3 months postoperatively (2.4 ± 1.3 vs 2 ± 1.1; P = .040) than the 6-month nonstiff group. However, their VAS scores did not differ significantly at 6 months (0.79 ± 0.88 vs 0.65 ± 0.83; P = .371). Both 3-month stiff and nonstiff groups showed significant improvements in ROM over time ( P < .001); however, their recovery trajectories differed significantly (forward flexion and external rotation: P < .001; internal rotation: P = .011) at 12 months. Consequently, no significant differences in ROM were observed between the groups at 24 months ( Figure 1 ). Comparison of the trajectories of ROM recovery for the 3-month stiff and nonstiff groups. (A) Forward flexion. (B) External rotation. (C) Internal rotation. An asterisk indicates a statistically significant difference between groups in ROM ( P < .05). ROM, range of motion. The interviews conducted at 3 months postoperatively revealed that fear or anxiety about tendon retear was the most frequently reported cause of poor adherence to rehabilitation exercises, followed by pain ( Table 3 ). However, the proportion of patients with persistent stiffness at 6 months postoperatively was highest for those who cited pain as the primary reason. In contrast, those who reported fear or anxiety had the lowest rate of persistent stiffness. Of the 54 patients who cited pain as the primary barrier at 3 months, 23 patients (42.6%) had persistent stiffness at 6 months. This proportion was substantially lower for those who reported a lack of motivation (17.9%) or fear or anxiety regarding tendon retear (7.2%). Eight patients who reported severe pain underwent injections of ropivacaine combined with corticosteroids into the intra-articular joint, subacromial space, or biceps tendon sheath. Distribution of Reported Barriers to Rehabilitation Among Patients With Shoulder Stiffness at 3 and 6 Months Postoperatively a Data are presented as n (%). Postop, postoperatively. The operated side ( P = .070) and the VAS score at 3 months postoperatively ( P = .040) were included in the multivariate logistic regression analysis to identify the factors associated with persistent stiffness at 6 months postoperatively. Recovery Trajectory of Range of Motion and Its Association With Patient Factors During Early Postoperative Stiffness After Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair

Background: Postoperative shoulder stiffness may influence functional recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. However, predictors for progression to persistent shoulder stiffness have not been clearly established. Purpose: To identify factors associated with persistent stiffness and describe range of motion (ROM) recovery trajectory after arthroscopic repair of full-thickness rotator cuff tears. Study Design: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 352 patients who underwent arthroscopic complete repair. Stiffness was defined as forward flexion <120°, external rotation <30°, or internal rotation below L3. ROM, visual analog scale (VAS) score, American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score, Constant score, and tendon integrity were assessed, and patients reported the primary barrier to rehabilitation at 3 months. Predictors of persistent stiffness at 6 months were evaluated using multivariate logistic regression. Results: At 3 months, 165 patients (46.9%) met stiffness criteria. Compared with patients without stiffness, the stiffness group had poorer functional outcome ( P < .001), higher pain (VAS, 2.2 ± 1.1 vs 1.8 ± 1.2; P = .002), and a lower retear rate (6.7% vs 14.4%; P = .019). Among patients with early stiffness, 34 (20.6%) had persistent stiffness at 6 months. Fear or anxiety about tendon retear was the most common barrier (50.3%), followed by pain (32.7%); however, persistent stiffness was most prevalent when pain was the primary barrier (67.6%). Higher pain score at 3 months independently predicted persistent stiffness (odds ratio, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.01-2.05]; P = .044). Conclusion: Early stiffness after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair is heterogeneous. Pain-driven stiffness is associated with persistence, whereas stiffness related to fear or anxiety about tendon retear is common but largely reversible; tailored management may improve recovery.

Postoperative shoulder stiffness is one of the most common complications after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair, and it occurs in 11% to 35.4% of patients. Approximately 20% of patients with early postoperative stiffness have persistent stiffness beyond 6 months, indicating interindividual variability in recovery patterns. Several studies have suggested greater postoperative pain in patients with persistent stiffness after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. 6 , 16 However, most have used a cross-sectional approach; they determined the relationship between pain and postoperative stiffness based on ROM measurements at a single time point and compared pain levels longitudinally. This approach limits the evaluation of pain progression relative to ROM recovery. Pain sensitization and kinesiophobia have recently been proposed as contributing mechanisms underlying the persistence of stiffness and poorer clinical outcomes. 11 , 25 , 34 The temporal pattern of postoperative pain may influence ROM recovery; however, its role in determining patients who will progress to persistent stiffness has not been clearly established. The factors that become predictive of persistent stiffness at specific time points also remain unknown. 14 This study aimed to identify the factors affecting the persistence of early postoperative stiffness and the trajectory of ROM recovery in patients with full-thickness rotator cuff tears after arthroscopic repair. We hypothesized that greater early postoperative pain would be associated with persistent stiffness and slower ROM recovery. The patients who underwent arthroscopic rotator cuff repair for symptomatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears at one institution between February 2019 and March 2023 were retrospectively analyzed. The inclusion criteria were as follows: having undergone arthroscopic rotator cuff repairs with full coverage of footprint for symptomatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears detected on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), completion of follow-up evaluations at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months, and confirmation of the integrity of the repaired tendon using MRI and ultrasonography performed at 6 months and 1 year postoperatively to confirm the repaired tendon integrity. The exclusion criteria were as follows: patients with preoperative shoulder stiffness, primary arthroscopic repair for partial-thickness rotator cuff tear or isolated subscapularis tear; additional augmentation procedures, such as patch augmentation or superior capsular reconstruction; revision surgeries; advanced glenohumeral osteoarthritis confirmed by imaging studies; neurologic or systemic disorders affecting the shoulder joint; history of acute trauma or infection; and incomplete medical records. Postoperative stiffness during the recovery period was defined based on the presence of any of the following criteria at the follow-up evaluation: forward flexion of <120°, external rotation of <30°, or internal rotation below the L3 level. title: Associations of sarcopenic obesity with chronic lung disease and peak expiratory flow in middle-aged and older adults: A cohort study based on CHARLS and ELSA
abstract: Background Evidence regarding the associations of sarcopenic obesity (SO) with chronic lung disease (CLD) and peak expiratory flow (PEF) remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the relationships between SO and CLD as well as PEF among middle-aged and older adults in China and the United Kingdom. Methods Data were derived from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020) and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA, waves 2–6). Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the associations of SO with incident CLD and PEF-related outcomes. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to balance baseline characteristics between participants with and without SO. Random forest–based analyses were conducted as supplementary analyses to support the main findings. Results A total of 3,572 participants from CHARLS and 2,436 from ELSA without CLD at baseline were included in the CLD analysis. During follow-up, SO was significantly associated with a higher risk of incident CLD. In the CHARLS cohort, SO was positively associated with CLD risk after full adjustment (Model 3: HR = 1.50, P = 0.003). Consistent results were observed in the ELSA cohort after adjustment for ethnicity (Model 1: HR = 2.19, P = 0.006). Associations between SO and PEF were not consistently observed across cohorts. Conclusions Sarcopenic obesity was associated with an increased risk of chronic lung disease among older adults, suggesting that SO may be a potential body composition–related marker of respiratory risk. Findings related to PEF were exploratory and warrant further investigation.
body: Chronic lung disease (CLD), including chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is a prevalent group of chronic respiratory disorders characterized by progressive airflow limitation and functional decline. Its burden increases with population ageing and is associated with reduced ventilatory capacity and impaired quality of life. 1 2 – 4 Peak expiratory flow (PEF) is a simple measure of expiratory airflow and respiratory muscle function, widely used to assess ventilatory status. Due to its sensitivity to age-related decline, it serves as a practical indicator in both clinical and epidemiological studies. 5 Sarcopenic obesity (SO), defined as the coexistence of excess adiposity and impaired muscle mass and function, is an emerging adverse body composition phenotype in older adults. Its prevalence is approximately 11% and increases with age. 6 SO is associated with cardiometabolic disease, functional decline, and mortality. 7 , 8 8 , 9 Evidence suggests that skeletal muscle dysfunction contributes to respiratory impairment. Sarcopenia has been linked to increased CLD risk and reduced PEF, while SO has been associated with lower FVC and FEV 10 – 12 1 . However, evidence on SO in relation to incident CLD and incident low PEF events remains limited. Clarifying this association may help identify older adults with respiratory vulnerability and improve risk stratification. 13 This study examined the associations of SO with incident CLD and incident low PEF events during follow-up. We used two population-based cohorts from China (CHARLS) and England (ELSA) to test consistency across different geographic, ethnic, and healthcare settings and enhance generalizability. This study used data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). CHARLS is a nationally representative cohort of Chinese adults aged ≥45 years, and ELSA is a population-based cohort of adults aged ≥50 years in England. 14 Participants were included from CHARLS (2011–2020) and ELSA (waves 2–6). Sarcopenic obesity (SO) was assessed at baseline (CHARLS 2011; ELSA wave 2). To minimize reverse causation, participants with baseline chronic lung disease (CLD) were excluded. Incident CLD was defined as the first self-reported physician diagnosis during follow-up (CHARLS 2013–2020; ELSA waves 3–5). Participants with missing exposure, outcome, or covariate data were excluded, yielding a complete-case analytic sample. 15 To ensure cross-cohort comparability, primary analyses included only variables available in both datasets. Details on cohort design and recruitment are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Sarcopenic obesity (SO) was defined as the co-existence of sarcopenia and obesity, using harmonized operational criteria consistent with the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism/European Association for the Study of Obesity consensus framework. Sarcopenia was defined according to the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia 2019 (AWGS 2019) criteria, 16 requiring low muscle mass plus low muscle strength and/or reduced physical performance. Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥25 kg/m 17 2 , and abdominal obesity as waist circumference ≥90 cm in men and ≥80 cm in women. 18 19 , 20 Muscle strength was assessed by handgrip strength, muscle mass by appendicular skeletal muscle mass index (ASMI = appendicular lean mass/height 2 ), and physical performance by the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), 6-m gait speed, or five-time chair-stand test. 21 Detailed testing procedures are provided in the Supplementary Methods. 22 For analytical purposes, sarcopenia was defined as low muscle mass combined with low muscle strength and/or impaired physical performance, with confirmed, and severe sarcopenia combined into a single category. The same SO definition and measurement procedures were applied consistently in both the CHARLS and ELSA cohorts. Chronic lung disease (CLD) was assessed via standardized interviewer-administered questionnaires. CLD was defined based on self-reported physician diagnosis of chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and/or self-reported use of respiratory medications, including bronchodilators and inhaled therapies commonly prescribed for chronic airway disease (e.g., inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators). This composite definition was applied to enhance case identification sensitivity in population-based cohorts, although potential misclassification due to self-reported diagnosis and non-specific medication use cannot be excluded. The same case definition was applied consistently in both the CHARLS and ELSA cohorts. For incident CLD, event time was defined as the first wave reporting CLD. 23 Peak expiratory flow (PEF) was measured with a handheld meter over three trials, retaining the highest value. PEF values were standardized to Z-scores for comparability. Exploratorily, a Z-score threshold of 0.75 indicated relatively low PEF, and its association with sarcopenic obesity (SO) was analyzed. The PEF endpoint was defined as time to first occurrence of Z-score <0.75 during follow-up. 5 Covariates included age, sex, education, marital status, smoking, alcohol use, depression, hypertension, and diabetes. These variables were selected a priori as potential confounders based on their established associations with both SO and respiratory outcomes, representing sociodemographic, lifestyle, and cardiometabolic factors. Diabetes was defined by fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, random glucose ≥200 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, physician diagnosis, or use of glucose-lowering drugs. Hypertension was defined as systolic BP ≥140 mmHg, diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg, physician diagnosis, or antihypertensive use. 24 Depressive symptoms were assessed via the 10-item CES-D, with scores ≥10 indicating depression. 25 26 Baseline characteristics were summarized by CLD status and PEF outcomes. Categorical variables were compared using χ 2 tests, continuous variables with Student’s t test or Mann–Whitney U test. To reduce baseline imbalance in assessing sarcopenic obesity (SO), inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on propensity scores (PS) was applied ( Supplementary Figure 1 and S4 ). PS were estimated via logistic regression with SO as the outcome and age, sex, education, marital status, smoking, alcohol, depression, hypertension, and diabetes as covariates. Stabilized weights were truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles; balance was assessed via standardized mean differences (SMD <0.10). Weighted Cox models estimated SO associations with incident CLD and PEF endpoints. Weighted Kaplan–Meier curves compared cumulative incidence. PEF time-to-event was defined as first low PEF occurrence, aligned with CLD modeling. Three models were used: Model 1 (unadjusted), Model 2 (demographics-adjusted), and Model 3 (further adjusted for lifestyle and comorbidities). Random survival forest (RSF) models assessed predictive performance. CHARLS was split 70/30 for training/testing, with external validation in ELSA . RSF included 500 trees, log-rank splitting, minimum node size 15; variable importance via Gini, discrimination via time-dependent ROC and AUC 27 . 28 Effect modification was assessed by including interaction terms between SO and selected covariates (sex, education, marital status, smoking, and alcohol consumption), followed by subgroup analyses. Detailed results of the interaction and subgroup analyses are presented in the Supplementary Results. All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2, and a two-sided P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sensitivity analyses used an alternative muscle mass index (ASM/weight ×100%) are presented in the Supplementary Materials. The screening process is shown in Figure 1 . For CLD analysis, 6,008 participants were eligible (CHARLS, n=3,572; ELSA, n=2,436), with a median follow-up of 8.0 years in both cohorts ( Table 1 ). Age distribution differed, with CHARLS having more participants aged <65 years, while ELSA had more aged ≥65 years (P<0.001). Baseline comorbidities varied: diabetes and depression were more common in CHARLS, and hypertension in ELSA (all P<0.001). Lifestyle factors also differed, with higher smoking prevalence in CHARLS and more alcohol use in ELSA (all P<0.001). Sarcopenic obesity prevalence varied across cohorts (P<0.001). CLD developed in 8.7% of participants, with a lower incidence in ELSA than CHARLS (P<0.001). Figure 1. Associations of sarcopenic obesity with chronic lung disease and peak expiratory flow in middle-aged and older adults: A cohort study based on CHARLS and ELSA

Background Evidence regarding the associations of sarcopenic obesity (SO) with chronic lung disease (CLD) and peak expiratory flow (PEF) remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the relationships between SO and CLD as well as PEF among middle-aged and older adults in China and the United Kingdom. Methods Data were derived from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020) and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA, waves 2–6). Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the associations of SO with incident CLD and PEF-related outcomes. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to balance baseline characteristics between participants with and without SO. Random forest–based analyses were conducted as supplementary analyses to support the main findings. Results A total of 3,572 participants from CHARLS and 2,436 from ELSA without CLD at baseline were included in the CLD analysis. During follow-up, SO was significantly associated with a higher risk of incident CLD. In the CHARLS cohort, SO was positively associated with CLD risk after full adjustment (Model 3: HR = 1.50, P = 0.003). Consistent results were observed in the ELSA cohort after adjustment for ethnicity (Model 1: HR = 2.19, P = 0.006). Associations between SO and PEF were not consistently observed across cohorts. Conclusions Sarcopenic obesity was associated with an increased risk of chronic lung disease among older adults, suggesting that SO may be a potential body composition–related marker of respiratory risk. Findings related to PEF were exploratory and warrant further investigation.

Chronic lung disease (CLD), including chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is a prevalent group of chronic respiratory disorders characterized by progressive airflow limitation and functional decline. Its burden increases with population ageing and is associated with reduced ventilatory capacity and impaired quality of life. 1 2 – 4 Peak expiratory flow (PEF) is a simple measure of expiratory airflow and respiratory muscle function, widely used to assess ventilatory status. Due to its sensitivity to age-related decline, it serves as a practical indicator in both clinical and epidemiological studies. 5 Sarcopenic obesity (SO), defined as the coexistence of excess adiposity and impaired muscle mass and function, is an emerging adverse body composition phenotype in older adults. Its prevalence is approximately 11% and increases with age. 6 SO is associated with cardiometabolic disease, functional decline, and mortality. 7 , 8 8 , 9 Evidence suggests that skeletal muscle dysfunction contributes to respiratory impairment. Sarcopenia has been linked to increased CLD risk and reduced PEF, while SO has been associated with lower FVC and FEV 10 – 12 1 . However, evidence on SO in relation to incident CLD and incident low PEF events remains limited. Clarifying this association may help identify older adults with respiratory vulnerability and improve risk stratification. 13 This study examined the associations of SO with incident CLD and incident low PEF events during follow-up. We used two population-based cohorts from China (CHARLS) and England (ELSA) to test consistency across different geographic, ethnic, and healthcare settings and enhance generalizability. This study used data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). CHARLS is a nationally representative cohort of Chinese adults aged ≥45 years, and ELSA is a population-based cohort of adults aged ≥50 years in England. 14 Participants were included from CHARLS (2011–2020) and ELSA (waves 2–6). Sarcopenic obesity (SO) was assessed at baseline (CHARLS 2011; ELSA wave 2). To minimize reverse causation, participants with baseline chronic lung disease (CLD) were excluded. Incident CLD was defined as the first self-reported physician diagnosis during follow-up (CHARLS 2013–2020; ELSA waves 3–5). Participants with missing exposure, outcome, or covariate data were excluded, yielding a complete-case analytic sample. 15 To ensure cross-cohort comparability, primary analyses included only variables available in both datasets. Details on cohort design and recruitment are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Sarcopenic obesity (SO) was defined as the co-existence of sarcopenia and obesity, using harmonized operational criteria consistent with the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism/European Association for the Study of Obesity consensus framework. Sarcopenia was defined according to the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia 2019 (AWGS 2019) criteria, 16 requiring low muscle mass plus low muscle strength and/or reduced physical performance. Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥25 kg/m 17 2 , and abdominal obesity as waist circumference ≥90 cm in men and ≥80 cm in women. 18 19 , 20 Muscle strength was assessed by handgrip strength, muscle mass by appendicular skeletal muscle mass index (ASMI = appendicular lean mass/height 2 ), and physical performance by the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), 6-m gait speed, or five-time chair-stand test. 21 Detailed testing procedures are provided in the Supplementary Methods. 22 For analytical purposes, sarcopenia was defined as low muscle mass combined with low muscle strength and/or impaired physical performance, with confirmed, and severe sarcopenia combined into a single category. The same SO definition and measurement procedures were applied consistently in both the CHARLS and ELSA cohorts. Chronic lung disease (CLD) was assessed via standardized interviewer-administered questionnaires. CLD was defined based on self-reported physician diagnosis of chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and/or self-reported use of respiratory medications, including bronchodilators and inhaled therapies commonly prescribed for chronic airway disease (e.g., inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators). This composite definition was applied to enhance case identification sensitivity in population-based cohorts, although potential misclassification due to self-reported diagnosis and non-specific medication use cannot be excluded. The same case definition was applied consistently in both the CHARLS and ELSA cohorts. For incident CLD, event time was defined as the first wave reporting CLD. 23 Peak expiratory flow (PEF) was measured with a handheld meter over three trials, retaining the highest value. PEF values were standardized to Z-scores for comparability. Exploratorily, a Z-score threshold of 0.75 indicated relatively low PEF, and its association with sarcopenic obesity (SO) was analyzed. The PEF endpoint was defined as time to first occurrence of Z-score <0.75 during follow-up. 5 Covariates included age, sex, education, marital status, smoking, alcohol use, depression, hypertension, and diabetes. These variables were selected a priori as potential confounders based on their established associations with both SO and respiratory outcomes, representing sociodemographic, lifestyle, and cardiometabolic factors. Diabetes was defined by fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, random glucose ≥200 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, physician diagnosis, or use of glucose-lowering drugs. Hypertension was defined as systolic BP ≥140 mmHg, diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg, physician diagnosis, or antihypertensive use. 24 Depressive symptoms were assessed via the 10-item CES-D, with scores ≥10 indicating depression. 25 26 Baseline characteristics were summarized by CLD status and PEF outcomes. Categorical variables were compared using χ 2 tests, continuous variables with Student’s t test or Mann–Whitney U test. To reduce baseline imbalance in assessing sarcopenic obesity (SO), inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on propensity scores (PS) was applied ( Supplementary Figure 1 and S4 ). PS were estimated via logistic regression with SO as the outcome and age, sex, education, marital status, smoking, alcohol, depression, hypertension, and diabetes as covariates. Stabilized weights were truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles; balance was assessed via standardized mean differences (SMD <0.10). Weighted Cox models estimated SO associations with incident CLD and PEF endpoints. Weighted Kaplan–Meier curves compared cumulative incidence. PEF time-to-event was defined as first low PEF occurrence, aligned with CLD modeling. Three models were used: Model 1 (unadjusted), Model 2 (demographics-adjusted), and Model 3 (further adjusted for lifestyle and comorbidities). Random survival forest (RSF) models assessed predictive performance. CHARLS was split 70/30 for training/testing, with external validation in ELSA . RSF included 500 trees, log-rank splitting, minimum node size 15; variable importance via Gini, discrimination via time-dependent ROC and AUC 27 . 28 Effect modification was assessed by including interaction terms between SO and selected covariates (sex, education, marital status, smoking, and alcohol consumption), followed by subgroup analyses. Detailed results of the interaction and subgroup analyses are presented in the Supplementary Results. All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.2, and a two-sided P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sensitivity analyses used an alternative muscle mass index (ASM/weight ×100%) are presented in the Supplementary Materials. The screening process is shown in Figure 1 . For CLD analysis, 6,008 participants were eligible (CHARLS, n=3,572; ELSA, n=2,436), with a median follow-up of 8.0 years in both cohorts ( Table 1 ). Age distribution differed, with CHARLS having more participants aged <65 years, while ELSA had more aged ≥65 years (P<0.001). Baseline comorbidities varied: diabetes and depression were more common in CHARLS, and hypertension in ELSA (all P<0.001). Lifestyle factors also differed, with higher smoking prevalence in CHARLS and more alcohol use in ELSA (all P<0.001). Sarcopenic obesity prevalence varied across cohorts (P<0.001). CLD developed in 8.7% of participants, with a lower incidence in ELSA than CHARLS (P<0.001). Figure 1. title: Donor Site Morbidity After Talar Mosaicplasty: Arthroscopic Medial Femoral Condyle vs Mini-Open Lateral Femoral Condyle Harvesting
abstract: Background: Osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs) are challenging injuries that may require osteochondral autograft transfer for large, cystic, or refractory defects. Although mosaicplasty can restore hyaline cartilage and subchondral bone, donor site morbidity remains a concern. This study compared knee donor site morbidity and ankle functional outcomes after 2 technique–donor site combinations used for talar mosaicplasty: arthroscopic medial femoral condyle harvesting and mini-open lateral femoral condyle harvesting. Methods: In this retrospective comparative cohort study, 40 patients with OLTs who underwent osteochondral autograft transfer were available for final analysis. Nineteen patients underwent arthroscopic harvesting from the medial femoral condyle, and 21 underwent mini-open harvesting from the lateral femoral condyle. The mean follow-up was 28.8 months. Baseline characteristics, lesion morphology, functional outcomes, pain scores, and postoperative complications were compared between groups. Donor site morbidity was assessed using the Lysholm score. Secondary outcomes included the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Foot and Ankle Outcome Score, Foot and Ankle Ability Measure, visual analog scale pain score, and complication rates. Results: Baseline demographics, follow-up duration, and measured lesion characteristics were broadly similar between groups; however, the small sample size limits interpretation of baseline comparability. With the available numbers, no significant between-group differences were detected in Lysholm, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Foot and Ankle Outcome Score, Foot and Ankle Ability Measure activities of daily living or sport subscales, or visual analog scale pain scores (all P > .05). Overall, complications occurred in 5 of 40 patients (12.5%): 2 of 19 patients in the arthroscopic medial femoral condyle group and 3 of 21 patients in the mini-open lateral femoral condyle group, with no statistically significant between-group difference in complication rates (Fisher exact test, P > .99). Conclusion: In this retrospective cohort, no statistically significant differences were detected between arthroscopic medial femoral condyle and mini-open lateral femoral condyle harvesting for talar mosaicplasty. However, because the surgical approach and donor condyle differed simultaneously, this study cannot isolate the independent effect of approach alone. The limited sample size and wide CIs preclude conclusions regarding equivalence, superiority, or noninferiority. Level of Evidence: Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.
body: Osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs) are injuries of the articular cartilage and subchondral bone, primarily affecting the talar dome. OLTs are frequently associated with acute ankle injuries or repeated microtrauma in adults. 1 These lesions provide a considerable therapeutic challenge owing to the limited intrinsic healing capacity of hyaline cartilage. 1 , 2 Because of the high congruency and contact stresses of the ankle joint, osteochondral defects significantly alter gait mechanics and weightbearing tolerance, often leading to persistent disability. 3 Consequently, if left untreated, symptomatic OLTs can lead to chronic pain, functional disability, and the progressive development of secondary osteoarthritis. 1 , 4 , 5 2 , 5 , 6 Management strategies are primarily guided by lesion size and cystic changes, with consideration of other factors such as lesion containment and location. Although marrow stimulation is effective for modest abnormalities, it produces fibrocartilage that frequently degrades with time. 7 - 9 Consequently, for large cystic lesions or unsuccessful first treatments, osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS) is the preferred therapeutic choice or a feasible salvage technique. 8 The transplantation of a viable osteochondral unit using OATS reinstates hyaline cartilage and structural integrity. 10 , 11 The treatment, originally executed through open techniques, has transitioned to all-arthroscopic methods aimed at reducing soft tissue morbidity and expediting recovery. 9 12 The ideal harvesting method remains debated. Arthroscopic OATS offers a minimally invasive option, but its limited visualization and smaller working surface make it technically challenging to achieve a perpendicular trajectory. Currently, direct clinical comparisons between arthroscopic and mini-open strategies are limited, and the trade-off between invasiveness and precision remains unclear in the literature. 13 , 14 The optimal harvest strategy for talar mosaicplasty remains uncertain. The relevant clinical question is not limited to the surgical exposure itself, but also includes the donor condyle, graft number, graft burden, ability to obtain perpendicular osteochondral plugs, lesion location, cystic morphology, and surgeon experience. In the present cohort, arthroscopic harvesting was performed from the medial femoral condyle, whereas mini-open harvesting was performed from the lateral femoral condyle. Therefore, this study compares 2 real-world technique–donor site combinations rather than isolating the independent effect of surgical approach alone. The primary aim was to compare final knee donor site morbidity, assessed using the Lysholm score, between arthroscopic medial femoral condyle harvesting and mini-open lateral femoral condyle harvesting for talar mosaicplasty. Secondary aims were to compare knee-related outcomes, ankle-related outcomes, pain, and postoperative complications. This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent osteochondral autograft transfer for osteochondral lesions of the talus between March 2018 and March 2024 at a tertiary orthopaedic referral center. Patients were identified through the hospital information system and orthopaedic registry and were screened according to predefined eligibility criteria. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Patients were retrospectively and consecutively screened through the hospital information system and orthopaedic registry. All patients who underwent osteochondral autograft transfer for osteochondral lesions of the talus during the study period were assessed against the predefined eligibility criteria. Patients who met all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria were included in the final analysis. Inclusion criteria were (1) age 16-50 years; (2) full-thickness osteochondral lesions of the talus (International Cartilage Repair Society [ICRS] grade III-IV) confirmed by computed tomographic (CT) scan; (3) failed nonoperative management and decision for autologous osteochondral transplantation (mosaicplasty); and (4) at least 12 months of follow-up. Exclusion criteria were (1) prior surgery on the same knee or ankle; (2) inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis; (3) severe ankle osteoarthritis (Kellgren-Lawrence grade ≥3); (4) uncorrected lower limb malalignment; and (5) neurogenic conditions such as poliomyelitis or cerebral palsy. Patients were included if they met all criteria and excluded if any criteria were met. No randomization was performed. Patients were categorized according to the technique and donor condyle used during the index procedure. Therefore, the comparison reflects 2 real-world technique–donor site combinations rather than a randomized comparison of surgical exposure alone. Preoperative lesion assessment was performed using standard ankle radiographs and preoperative CT. CT was available for all 40 included patients and was used as the principal modality for operative planning and lesion measurement, including lesion localization using the 9-zone grid, measurement of lesion length and width, assessment of subchondral cystic change, evaluation of lesion containment, and estimation of the number and orientation of the required osteochondral plugs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was available in 7 of 40 patients and had been obtained at outside centers before referral; therefore, MRI was used only as an adjunct to evaluate cartilage integrity and marrow signal changes and was not used for lesion size comparison. Because CT was available for all patients and MRI may overestimate lesion size, lesion measurements and between-group lesion size comparisons were based on CT rather than MRI. Routine diagnostic ankle arthroscopy was not performed before ankle exposure. Lesion surface area was approximated using the elliptical formula: length × width × 0.79. Preoperative CT images were reviewed independently by 2 fellowship-trained foot and ankle orthopaedic surgeons (A.S. and A.E.), and disagreements regarding lesion location, lesion size, cystic change, or containment were resolved by consensus. Patients were categorized into 2 technique–donor site groups according to the harvesting technique and donor condyle used during the index procedure: the arthroscopic medial femoral condyle (MFC) group and the mini-open lateral femoral condyle (LFC) group. The choice of technique was not randomized and reflected lesion location, required graft trajectory, expected graft burden, technical feasibility, and surgeon judgment. Procedures were performed under general or spinal anesthesia with the patient in the supine position and a pneumatic tourniquet. All procedures, including knee graft harvesting, ankle exposure, recipient-site preparation, and osteochondral plug implantation, were performed by a single fellowship-trained foot and ankle orthopaedic surgeon with experience in ankle reconstruction and knee arthroscopy. The lesion bed was prepared by drilling to expose healthy, bleeding subchondral bone. Representative intraoperative images of both knee harvesting techniques are shown in Figure 1 . Representative intraoperative images of knee osteochondral plug harvesting techniques. (A) Mini-open harvesting from the nonweightbearing lateral femoral condyle through a limited open approach. (B) Arthroscopic harvesting from the nonweightbearing medial femoral condyle using standard arthroscopic visualization. Routine primary ankle arthroscopy was not performed. Ankle exposure was selected according to the preoperative CT-based lesion location, lesion size, cystic morphology, and the need for perpendicular access for osteochondral plug implantation. For medial talar lesions requiring malleolar osteotomy, a medial curved incision was used. A guide pin was inserted from medial to lateral, exiting approximately 2 mm lateral to the axilla of the tibial plafond at an angle of approximately 30° to the long axis of the tibia. After protecting the posterior tibial tendon and neurovascular structures, medial malleolar osteotomy was performed using an oscillating saw and completed with an osteotome to avoid iatrogenic injury to the talar cartilage. The medial malleolus was then retracted distally to obtain wide access to the talar dome. For lateral talar lesions requiring lateral exposure, a lateral curved incision was used. After protecting the superficial branch of the peroneal nerve, the anterior distal tibiofibular ligaments were incised, and fibular osteotomy was performed approximately 3 cm proximal to the ankle joint line using an oscillating saw. The lateral malleolus was retracted externally to allow visualization of the lateral talar dome. The same osteochondral plug implantation principles were then applied for lateral lesions. The lesion was identified and probed after exposure. Stable native cartilage and fibrocartilaginous tissue were not routinely debrided before graft insertion. When a large loose osteochondral fragment was encountered, it was excised. The number of plugs was determined using preoperative CT planning and intraoperative sizing. Recipient tunnels were created using the OATS recipient instruments and were made approximately 2 mm deeper than the harvested osteochondral plugs. The harvested plugs were inserted sequentially and gently impacted with the standard OATS tamp until the cartilage surface was flush with the surrounding native talar cartilage. For larger defects, plugs were placed in a mosaic pattern to maximize coverage. Ankle range of motion was assessed intraoperatively to confirm graft congruity, graft stability, and absence of mechanical impingement ( Figure 2 ). Representative case of osteochondral autograft transfer (OAT) for an osteochondral lesion of the talus. (A) Preoperative radiograph depicting the osteochondral defect. (B) Intraoperative photograph of the recipient bed on the talar dome that was prepared after debridement. (C) Intraoperative photograph following the press-fit insertion of the osteochondral plugs, which illustrates a congruent and flush articular surface. (D) Postoperative radiograph confirming the restoration of the joint line. Medial malleolar osteotomies were fixed with two or three 4.0-mm cannulated screws placed perpendicular to the osteotomy line. Lateral malleolar/fibular osteotomies were fixed with plate fixation. The ankle was irrigated, hemostasis was achieved, and the wound was closed in layers. A sterile dressing and short-leg splint were applied. Procedure-related cost was considered descriptively based on the institutional cost of equipment and operating room setup required for each harvesting technique, rather than patient-level total hospitalization charges. Patient-level hospital bills were not compared because they were influenced by length of stay, medications, room type, and other non–procedure-related factors. No knee donor site backfilling was performed in either group. Postoperative admission followed the institutional protocol after talar mosaicplasty with malleolar or fibular osteotomy and was used for pain control, wound monitoring, early neurovascular assessment, and postoperative mobilization planning. A standardized postoperative protocol was used for all patients. Ankles were immobilized in a cast or splint for 2 weeks until suture removal. A controlled ankle motion (CAM) boot was then worn for 6 weeks to aid graft integration. Range of motion exercises started at week 4. Partial weightbearing was allowed from week 6, increasing to full weight at week 8, based on pain and evidence of healing. Impact activities and sports return were delayed until at least 6 months postsurgery. The ipsilateral knee was managed with a compressive dressing after graft harvest. No knee brace was routinely used. Knee range of motion exercises were allowed as tolerated from the early postoperative period, whereas weightbearing progression was primarily determined by the ankle reconstruction protocol. Data were collected from electronic medical records using standardized forms to document the study demographic characteristics, with data entry performed by an independent orthopaedic reviewer who was not involved in surgical procedures or postoperative management. At final follow-up, knee donor site morbidity was assessed using a combination of patient-reported knee outcome scores, donor knee clinical examination, and recorded donor knee complications. Knee-related patient-reported outcomes included the Lysholm score and the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Ankle-related patient-reported outcomes included the Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS), Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) activities of daily living (ADL) and sport subscales, and visual analog scale (VAS) pain score. The Lysholm score was used because it captures knee-specific symptoms relevant to donor site morbidity, including pain, swelling, instability, locking, stair climbing, and squatting. Donor-knee clinical assessment at routine follow-up included inspection for swelling or effusion, assessment of knee range of motion, donor site tenderness, anterior knee pain, crepitus, and extensor mechanism function. Donor-knee complications, including hemarthrosis, stiffness, persistent donor site pain, infection, and need for additional treatment, were recorded separately from ankle-site complications. Donor site morbidity was primarily assessed using the Lysholm score and by reviewing recorded donor knee symptoms and complications, including donor site pain, swelling, hemarthrosis, stiffness, infection, and need for additional treatment. Pain was assessed using the VAS. Postoperative complications, including infection, nonunion, ankle stiffness, hemarthrosis, and donor site pain, were recorded. Data were collected during routine clinical visits or, when information was incomplete or missing, by telephone to address gaps and request a clinic follow-up assessment; this approach was applied consistently across both groups. Among the 40 patients included in the final analysis, final follow-up data for the primary outcome were available in all patients. No patient was excluded or lost to follow-up after inclusion in the final cohort. Patients with incomplete outcome information before final assessment were not included in the final analytic cohort. Descriptive statistics were presented as mean ± SD or median (IQR) for quantitative variables, depending on the results of the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality, and as frequencies for qualitative variables. The independent t test (or nonparametric equivalent) was used to compare continuous variables, the χ test was used for categorical variables, and Fisher exact test was used when expected cell counts were small. A 2-sided 2 P value of less than .05 was considered statistically significant. Ninety-five percent CIs were reported for mean differences in continuous outcomes and for complication rate estimates. No adjustment for multiplicity was applied across secondary outcome comparisons; therefore, all secondary outcome comparisons were considered exploratory. Sex-stratified analyses were performed post hoc and are presented descriptively. No formal a priori sample size calculation was performed because the sample size was determined by the number of eligible patients treated during the study period. Established minimum clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds were considered when interpreting the clinical relevance of between-group differences. However, because preoperative patient-reported outcome scores were unavailable, individual patient-level achievement of MCID could not be calculated. Therefore, the Lysholm score was analyzed as a final follow-up between group outcome rather than as a change from baseline outcome. Of 48 consecutive patients screened during the study period, 8 were not included in the final analysis. In the arthroscopic MFC group, 5 patients were not included: 3 were excluded because of prior surgery or other eligibility-related problems, and 2 were lost to follow-up before final outcome assessment. In the mini-open LFC group, 3 patients were not included: 2 were excluded because of eligibility-related problems, and 1 was lost to follow-up before final outcome assessment. Therefore, 40 patients were included in the final analysis: 19 in the arthroscopic MFC group and 21 in the mini-open LFC group. No patient was excluded after inclusion in the final cohort, and final follow-up data for the primary outcome were available for all 40 included patients. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1 . The mean follow-up duration was 28.5 ± 4.2 months in the arthroscopic MFC group and 29.1 ± 3.8 months in the mini-open LFC group. Length of hospital stay was similar between groups and is reported in Table 1 . Baseline Characteristics and Demographics. Abbreviations: BMI, body mass index; LFC, lateral femoral condyle; MFC, medial femoral condyle. Lesion morphology and procedure-related characteristics are summarized in Table 2 . With the available numbers, no statistically significant between-group difference was detected in lesion area, ICRS grade distribution, CT-based 9-zone lesion location, subchondral cystic change, lesion containment, number of harvested osteochondral plugs, or osteotomy type (all P > .05; Table 2 ). The most frequent lesion locations were zone 4 and zone 7 in both groups. Medial malleolar osteotomy was performed in 14 of 19 patients (73.7%) in the arthroscopic MFC group and 16 of 21 patients (76.2%) in the mini-open LFC group, whereas lateral/fibular osteotomy was performed in 5 patients in each group. With the available numbers, no statistically significant between-group difference was detected in Lysholm score, KOOS total score, KOOS subscales, FAOS total score, FAOS subscales, FAAM ADL, FAAM sport, or VAS pain score (all P > .05; Table 3 ). The wide 95% CIs for several outcomes crossed clinically meaningful thresholds; therefore, the absence of statistically significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. Among female patients, mean knee-related scores were numerically higher in the mini-open LFC group than in the arthroscopic MFC group. Among male patients, mean outcome scores were broadly similar between groups. These subgroup findings were descriptive and were not used to infer differential treatment effects. In the present cohort, arthroscopic harvesting was performed from the medial femoral condyle, whereas mini-open harvesting was performed from the lateral femoral condyle. Therefore, this study compares 2 real-world technique–donor site combinations rather than isolating the independent effect of surgical approach alone. The primary aim was to compare final knee donor site morbidity, assessed using the Lysholm score, between arthroscopic medial femoral condyle harvesting and mini-open lateral femoral condyle harvesting for talar mosaicplasty. Secondary aims were to compare knee-related outcomes, ankle-related outcomes, pain, and postoperative complications. This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent osteochondral autograft transfer for osteochondral lesions of the talus between March 2018 and March 2024 at a tertiary orthopaedic referral center. Patients were identified through the hospital information system and orthopaedic registry and were screened according to predefined eligibility criteria. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Patients were retrospectively and consecutively screened through the hospital information system and orthopaedic registry. All patients who underwent osteochondral autograft transfer for osteochondral lesions of the talus during the study period were assessed against the predefined eligibility criteria. Patients who met all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria were included in the final analysis. Inclusion criteria were (1) age 16-50 years; (2) full-thickness osteochondral lesions of the talus (International Cartilage Repair Society [ICRS] grade III-IV) confirmed by computed tomographic (CT) scan; (3) failed nonoperative management and decision for autologous osteochondral transplantation (mosaicplasty); and (4) at least 12 months of follow-up. Exclusion criteria were (1) prior surgery on the same knee or ankle; (2) inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis; (3) severe ankle osteoarthritis (Kellgren-Lawrence grade ≥3); (4) uncorrected lower limb malalignment; and (5) neurogenic conditions such as poliomyelitis or cerebral palsy. Patients were included if they met all criteria and excluded if any criteria were met. No randomization was performed. Patients were categorized according to the technique and donor condyle used during the index procedure. Therefore, the comparison reflects 2 real-world technique–donor site combinations rather than a randomized comparison of surgical exposure alone. Preoperative lesion assessment was performed using standard ankle radiographs and preoperative CT. CT was available for all 40 included patients and was used as the principal modality for operative planning and lesion measurement, including lesion localization using the 9-zone grid, measurement of lesion length and width, assessment of subchondral cystic change, evaluation of lesion containment, and estimation of the number and orientation of the required osteochondral plugs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was available in 7 of 40 patients and had been obtained at outside centers before referral; therefore, MRI was used only as an adjunct to evaluate cartilage integrity and marrow signal changes and was not used for lesion size comparison. Because CT was available for all patients and MRI may overestimate lesion size, lesion measurements and between-group lesion size comparisons were based on CT rather than MRI. Routine diagnostic ankle arthroscopy was not performed before ankle exposure. Lesion surface area was approximated using the elliptical formula: length × width × 0.79. Preoperative CT images were reviewed independently by 2 fellowship-trained foot and ankle orthopaedic surgeons (A.S. and A.E.), and disagreements regarding lesion location, lesion size, cystic change, or containment were resolved by consensus. Patients were categorized into 2 technique–donor site groups according to the harvesting technique and donor condyle used during the index procedure: the arthroscopic medial femoral condyle (MFC) group and the mini-open lateral femoral condyle (LFC) group. The choice of technique was not randomized and reflected lesion location, required graft trajectory, expected graft burden, technical feasibility, and surgeon judgment. Procedures were performed under general or spinal anesthesia with the patient in the supine position and a pneumatic tourniquet. All procedures, including knee graft harvesting, ankle exposure, recipient-site preparation, and osteochondral plug implantation, were performed by a single fellowship-trained foot and ankle orthopaedic surgeon with experience in ankle reconstruction and knee arthroscopy. The lesion bed was prepared by drilling to expose healthy, bleeding subchondral bone. Representative intraoperative images of both knee harvesting techniques are shown in Figure 1 . Representative intraoperative images of knee osteochondral plug harvesting techniques. (A) Mini-open harvesting from the nonweightbearing lateral femoral condyle through a limited open approach. (B) Arthroscopic harvesting from the nonweightbearing medial femoral condyle using standard arthroscopic visualization. Routine primary ankle arthroscopy was not performed. Ankle exposure was selected according to the preoperative CT-based lesion location, lesion size, cystic morphology, and the need for perpendicular access for osteochondral plug implantation. For medial talar lesions requiring malleolar osteotomy, a medial curved incision was used. A guide pin was inserted from medial to lateral, exiting approximately 2 mm lateral to the axilla of the tibial plafond at an angle of approximately 30° to the long axis of the tibia. After protecting the posterior tibial tendon and neurovascular structures, medial malleolar osteotomy was performed using an oscillating saw and completed with an osteotome to avoid iatrogenic injury to the talar cartilage. The medial malleolus was then retracted distally to obtain wide access to the talar dome. For lateral talar lesions requiring lateral exposure, a lateral curved incision was used. After protecting the superficial branch of the peroneal nerve, the anterior distal tibiofibular ligaments were incised, and fibular osteotomy was performed approximately 3 cm proximal to the ankle joint line using an oscillating saw. The lateral malleolus was retracted externally to allow visualization of the lateral talar dome. The same osteochondral plug implantation principles were then applied for lateral lesions. The lesion was identified and probed after exposure. Stable native cartilage and fibrocartilaginous tissue were not routinely debrided before graft insertion. When a large loose osteochondral fragment was encountered, it was excised. The number of plugs was determined using preoperative CT planning and intraoperative sizing. Recipient tunnels were created using the OATS recipient instruments and were made approximately 2 mm deeper than the harvested osteochondral plugs. The harvested plugs were inserted sequentially and gently impacted with the standard OATS tamp until the cartilage surface was flush with the surrounding native talar cartilage. For larger defects, plugs were placed in a mosaic pattern to maximize coverage. Ankle range of motion was assessed intraoperatively to confirm graft congruity, graft stability, and absence of mechanical impingement ( Figure 2 ). Representative case of osteochondral autograft transfer (OAT) for an osteochondral lesion of the talus. (A) Preoperative radiograph depicting the osteochondral defect. (B) Intraoperative photograph of the recipient bed on the talar dome that was prepared after debridement. (C) Intraoperative photograph following the press-fit insertion of the osteochondral plugs, which illustrates a congruent and flush articular surface. (D) Postoperative radiograph confirming the restoration of the joint line. Medial malleolar osteotomies were fixed with two or three 4.0-mm cannulated screws placed perpendicular to the osteotomy line. Lateral malleolar/fibular osteotomies were fixed with plate fixation. The ankle was irrigated, hemostasis was achieved, and the wound was closed in layers. A sterile dressing and short-leg splint were applied. Procedure-related cost was considered descriptively based on the institutional cost of equipment and operating room setup required for each harvesting technique, rather than patient-level total hospitalization charges. Patient-level hospital bills were not compared because they were influenced by length of stay, medications, room type, and other non–procedure-related factors. No knee donor site backfilling was performed in either group. Postoperative admission followed the institutional protocol after talar mosaicplasty with malleolar or fibular osteotomy and was used for pain control, wound monitoring, early neurovascular assessment, and postoperative mobilization planning. A standardized postoperative protocol was used for all patients. Ankles were immobilized in a cast or splint for 2 weeks until suture removal. A controlled ankle motion (CAM) boot was then worn for 6 weeks to aid graft integration. Range of motion exercises started at week 4. Partial weightbearing was allowed from week 6, increasing to full weight at week 8, based on pain and evidence of healing. Impact activities and sports return were delayed until at least 6 months postsurgery. The ipsilateral knee was managed with a compressive dressing after graft harvest. No knee brace was routinely used. Knee range of motion exercises were allowed as tolerated from the early postoperative period, whereas weightbearing progression was primarily determined by the ankle reconstruction protocol. Data were collected from electronic medical records using standardized forms to document the study demographic characteristics, with data entry performed by an independent orthopaedic reviewer who was not involved in surgical procedures or postoperative management. At final follow-up, knee donor site morbidity was assessed using a combination of patient-reported knee outcome scores, donor knee clinical examination, and recorded donor knee complications. Knee-related patient-reported outcomes included the Lysholm score and the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Ankle-related patient-reported outcomes included the Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS), Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) activities of daily living (ADL) and sport subscales, and visual analog scale (VAS) pain score. The Lysholm score was used because it captures knee-specific symptoms relevant to donor site morbidity, including pain, swelling, instability, locking, stair climbing, and squatting. Donor-knee clinical assessment at routine follow-up included inspection for swelling or effusion, assessment of knee range of motion, donor site tenderness, anterior knee pain, crepitus, and extensor mechanism function. Donor-knee complications, including hemarthrosis, stiffness, persistent donor site pain, infection, and need for additional treatment, were recorded separately from ankle-site complications. Donor site morbidity was primarily assessed using the Lysholm score and by reviewing recorded donor knee symptoms and complications, including donor site pain, swelling, hemarthrosis, stiffness, infection, and need for additional treatment. Pain was assessed using the VAS. Postoperative complications, including infection, nonunion, ankle stiffness, hemarthrosis, and donor site pain, were recorded. Data were collected during routine clinical visits or, when information was incomplete or missing, by telephone to address gaps and request a clinic follow-up assessment; this approach was applied consistently across both groups. Among the 40 patients included in the final analysis, final follow-up data for the primary outcome were available in all patients. No patient was excluded or lost to follow-up after inclusion in the final cohort. Patients with incomplete outcome information before final assessment were not included in the final analytic cohort. Descriptive statistics were presented as mean ± SD or median (IQR) for quantitative variables, depending on the results of the Shapiro-Wilk test of normality, and as frequencies for qualitative variables. The independent t test (or nonparametric equivalent) was used to compare continuous variables, the χ test was used for categorical variables, and Fisher exact test was used when expected cell counts were small. A 2-sided 2 P value of less than .05 was considered statistically significant. Ninety-five percent CIs were reported for mean differences in continuous outcomes and for complication rate estimates. No adjustment for multiplicity was applied across secondary outcome comparisons; therefore, all secondary outcome comparisons were considered exploratory. Sex-stratified analyses were performed post hoc and are presented descriptively. No formal a priori sample size calculation was performed because the sample size was determined by the number of eligible patients treated during the study period. Established minimum clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds were considered when interpreting the clinical relevance of between-group differences. However, because preoperative patient-reported outcome scores were unavailable, individual patient-level achievement of MCID could not be calculated. Therefore, the Lysholm score was analyzed as a final follow-up between group outcome rather than as a change from baseline outcome. Of 48 consecutive patients screened during the study period, 8 were not included in the final analysis. In the arthroscopic MFC group, 5 patients were not included: 3 were excluded because of prior surgery or other eligibility-related problems, and 2 were lost to follow-up before final outcome assessment. In the mini-open LFC group, 3 patients were not included: 2 were excluded because of eligibility-related problems, and 1 was lost to follow-up before final outcome assessment. Therefore, 40 patients were included in the final analysis: 19 in the arthroscopic MFC group and 21 in the mini-open LFC group. No patient was excluded after inclusion in the final cohort, and final follow-up data for the primary outcome were available for all 40 included patients. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1 . The mean follow-up duration was 28.5 ± 4.2 months in the arthroscopic MFC group and 29.1 ± 3.8 months in the mini-open LFC group. Length of hospital stay was similar between groups and is reported in Table 1 . Baseline Characteristics and Demographics. With the available numbers, no statistically significant between-group difference was detected in lesion area, ICRS grade distribution, CT-based 9-zone lesion location, subchondral cystic change, lesion containment, number of harvested osteochondral plugs, or osteotomy type (all P > .05; Table 2 ). The most frequent lesion locations were zone 4 and zone 7 in both groups. Medial malleolar osteotomy was performed in 14 of 19 patients (73.7%) in the arthroscopic MFC group and 16 of 21 patients (76.2%) in the mini-open LFC group, whereas lateral/fibular osteotomy was performed in 5 patients in each group. Lesion area was calculated using the elliptical formula: length × width × 0.79. Lesion location, cystic change, and containment were assessed on preoperative CT. Functional outcomes at final follow-up are summarized in Table 3 . With the available numbers, no statistically significant between-group difference was detected in Lysholm score, KOOS total score, KOOS subscales, FAOS total score, FAOS subscales, FAAM ADL, FAAM sport, or VAS pain score (all P > .05; Table 3 ). The wide 95% CIs for several outcomes crossed clinically meaningful thresholds; therefore, the absence of statistically significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. Among female patients, mean knee-related scores were numerically higher in the mini-open LFC group than in the arthroscopic MFC group.
