title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity with liposomal bupivacaine: a case series and literature review
abstract: Background Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) is an uncommon complication, with manifestations ranging from mild, non-specific neurological symptoms to severe cardiac arrest. Toxicity specifically associated with liposomal bupivacaine is even more rarely documented in the literature. We report two cases of LAST following the administration of liposomal bupivacaine and provide a review of previously reported cases. Case presentation Case 1: A 55-year-old male received 266 mg of liposomal bupivacaine via intercostal nerve block during thoracoscopic lobectomy. During skin closure, he developed cardiac arrest and recurrent ventricular fibrillation. He was successfully extubated and weaned off all vasopressors two hours after lipid emulsion administration and subsequently recovered. Case 2: A 67-year-old male received 266 mg of liposomal bupivacaine via incision infiltration after lobectomy. Shortly after PACU arrival, he developed agitation, fixed gaze, and increased muscle tone. Lipid emulsion infusion led to neurological improvement within five minutes, and he was subsequently discharged successfully. Conclusions These two cases highlight the potential for catastrophic LAST associated with liposomal bupivacaine. To mitigate this risk, we recommend reducing the dose of local anesthetics when injecting into highly vascular areas and performing careful aspiration during injection to prevent intravascular injection. Furthermore, the early administration of intravenous lipid emulsion should be strongly considered upon any suspicion of LAST.
body: The use of local anesthetics during surgery is a crucial component of multimodal analgesia. It helps reduce perioperative opioid consumption, enhances patient satisfaction, decreases the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting, shortens hospital stays, and lowers the risk of chronic post-surgical pain. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication, most notably affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and cardiovascular system (CVS). Although local anesthetics are generally safe, LAST events still occur, with reported incidences ranging from 0.04 to 1.8 per 1,000 [ 1 – 4 ]. Liposomal bupivacaine is a novel extended-release formulation. Utilizing multivesicular liposome technology, it encapsulates bupivacaine within numerous non-concentric phospholipid bilayer vesicles. This structure allows slow degradation via internal fusion and fission after injection at the surgical site, enabling controlled and sustained release of bupivacaine over time, thereby providing prolonged local nerve signal blockade. This slow-release process has been shown to extend the duration of action to up to 96 h for local infiltration and 120 h for interscalene brachial plexus block [ 5 ]. Due to its relatively recent development, data regarding its adverse effects and toxicity profile remain limited. We report two cases of LAST following liposomal bupivacaine administration. A 55-year-old male (height: 170 cm, weight: 63 kg, BMI: 21.8 kg/m²) was admitted for a pulmonary nodule discovered during a health examination 20 + days ago. Past medical history included an ocular prosthesis implantation 30 years ago. Preoperative electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm. Echocardiography revealed mild tricuspid regurgitation with normal left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction, EF: 57%). Pulmonary function tests and laboratory tests were within normal range, except for mildly elevated serum triglycerides and cholesterol. He had no previous history of chronic diseases or drug allergies. Following standard anesthetic induction and double-lumen endobronchial intubation for one-lung ventilation, the patient underwent a planned video-assisted thoracoscopic left upper lobectomy and lymph node dissection. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane at 2% and remifentanil at 0.1–0.2 µg/kg/min. To maintain end-tidal carbon dioxide between 35 and 40 mmHg, volume-controlled ventilation was set with a tidal volume of 350 mL and a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min during one-lung ventilation, and 450 mL and 12 breaths/min during two-lung ventilation. Prior to chest closure, the surgeon performed an intercostal nerve block under direct thoracoscopic vision using 20 mL (266 mg) of liposomal bupivacaine. Twenty minutes later, while suturing the skin incision, the patient suddenly developed ventricular tachycardia and rapidly deteriorated into cardiac arrest. The patient was then immediately repositioned from the lateral decubitus to the supine position, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was initiated, including intravenous administration of 1 mg epinephrine every three minutes. Arterial cannulation was successfully established 15 min after cardiac arrest, with immediate arterial blood gas analysis revealing: pH 7.227, PaCO 2 63.3 mmHg, PaO 2 288.7 mmHg, Hb 156 g/L, Na + 146.6 mmol/L, K + 5.11 mmol/L, Ca 2+ 1.201 mmol/L, Glu 13 mmol/L, Lac 4.8 mmol/L, HCO3 − 25.7 mmol/L, and BE 3.32 mmol/L. The elevated PaCO 2 was attributed to inadequate ventilation during prolonged CPR, as pre-arrest ventilator settings and airway pressures were normal, coupled with stable oxygen saturation and end-tidal carbon dioxide. The diagnosis of pneumothorax, suggested by findings such as increased airway pressure, hypoxemia, and hypercapnia was ruled out by the absence of these signs prior to cardiac arrest and the lack of confirmatory sonographic evidence (e.g., absent lung sliding or a lung point). Similarly, pulmonary embolism, which would present with hypoxemia, a sudden drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide, and right heart strain on echocardiography, was excluded, given the patient’s stable vital signs before the event and a post-arrest echocardiogram showing no right heart enlargement or wall motion abnormalities. Hemoglobin level remained comparable to the preoperative value, effectively ruling out massive hemorrhage. The observed hyperglycemia was considered stress-related, given the patient’s normoglycemia and absence of diabetes mellitus preoperatively. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed globally reduced left ventricular contractility but no evidence of cardiac tamponade or regional wall motion abnormalities. The chest drain was checked and found to be in place and patent. The patient’s rhythm deteriorated from pulseless electrical activity (PEA) to ventricular fibrillation. After defibrillation, sinus rhythm was temporarily restored but was unstable, quickly reverting to ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. At this point, the anesthesiologist reviewed the anesthetic record and noted the administration of liposomal bupivacaine. Epinephrine was immediately discontinued, and lipid emulsion was given intravenously with a 100 mL bolus, followed by a continuous infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min. Subsequently, a 150 mg loading dose of amiodarone was administered, followed by a maintenance infusion at 30 mg/h to manage arrhythmias. Norepinephrine was infused at 0.1–0.2 ug/kg/min to maintain blood pressure. Following the lipid emulsion bolus, the patient’s rhythm converted to sinus tachycardia at approximately 120 beats per minute. However, blood pressure remained difficult to maintain, requiring a continuous norepinephrine infusion at 0.1 ug/kg/min. The patient was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). Two hours after lipid emulsion administration, the patient was fully awake, and his endotracheal tube was removed. His blood pressure stabilized, allowing discontinuation of norepinephrine and lipid emulsion. No further arrhythmias occurred, and amiodarone was discontinued. An echocardiogram on postoperative day 1 showed findings identical to the preoperative study, with no regional wall motion abnormalities, consistent with a non-cardiac cause. The patient was transferred out of the ICU on postoperative day 2. Serum bupivacaine concentration was not measured, as the result would not be available for 24 h and was deemed unlikely to alter clinical management. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 12. A telephone follow-up at 2 months post-operation was unremarkable. A 67-year-old male with a diagnosis of left upper lobe squamous cell carcinoma was admitted for planned left upper lobectomy and lymph node dissection. He was 176 cm tall and weighed 54 kg, with a body mass index of 17.4 kg/m². Prior to admission, he had undergone three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy. His preoperative vital signs on admission were as follows: body temperature 36.3 °C, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 20 bpm, and blood pressure 127/78 mmHg. Preoperative chest CT showed a small soft tissue shadow at the left pulmonary hilum with slightly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. ECG indicated sinus rhythm and incomplete right bundle branch block. Echocardiography revealed mild tricuspid regurgitation and normal left ventricular systolic function. Laboratory tests were unremarkable except for slightly elevated alkaline phosphatase (163 U/L, reference range 45–125 U/L). Past medical history was otherwise non-contributory. The patient underwent the planned left upper lobectomy, pulmonary arterioplasty, resection of a pulmonary conus mass, and lymph node dissection. The entire surgical and anesthetic course was uneventful. Upon surgical closure, the surgical incision site was infiltrated with 20 mL (266 mg) of liposomal bupivacaine. The patient was then transferred to the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU). Upon arrival in the PACU, the patient developed agitation accompanied by a fixed gaze, pinpoint pupils, bilateral fist clenching, and generalized hypertonia. He exhibited eye-opening responses to verbal stimuli but no command-following. An ABG was immediately performed, which showed no significant abnormalities. Suspecting LAST, 100 mL of 20% lipid emulsion was administered intravenously. Within five minutes, the patient became alert and responsive, with resolution of fist clenching, normalization of muscle tone, and restoration of normal eye movements. He was subsequently extubated. After a subsequent 2-hour observation period in the PACU, during which no further events occurred, he was transferred to the ward. The subsequent recovery course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 10. In Case 1, the patient developed pulseless electrical activity and refractory arrhythmias that were unresponsive to standard advanced cardiac life support. Following lipid emulsion administration, sinus rhythm was restored, and hemodynamic stability was gradually achieved. The patient regained full consciousness within two hours, allowing for tracheal extubation and discontinuation of vasopressors. This clinical course appears consistent with LAST [ 6 – 9 ]. Distinguishing the circulatory manifestations of LAST from those of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is critical. ACS is frequently associated with underlying coronary artery disease or cardiac insufficiency. Echocardiographically, ACS is characterized by regional wall motion abnormalities corresponding to the affected coronary territory, whereas LAST typically presents with global hypokinesis. The management of ACS necessitates prompt coronary reperfusion through anticoagulation, thrombolysis, or emergency percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). In contrast, the cardiovascular manifestations of LAST are generally reversible with intravenous lipid emulsion. In the present case (Case 1), the patient had no history of coronary artery disease or related risk factors, and preoperative electrocardiography and echocardiography were unremarkable. Post-resuscitation echocardiography revealed global hypokinesis, a finding inconsistent with the regional wall motion abnormalities typical of ACS. Following lipid emulsion therapy, repeat echocardiography on the following day demonstrated complete normalization of cardiac function, thereby effectively excluding ACS. In Case 2, the patient presented with non-specific neurological symptoms, including a fixed gaze and increased muscle tone. These symptoms resolved completely following lipid emulsion infusion, strongly suggestive of a treatment response and consistent with the recognized CNS manifestations of LAST [ 10 – 12 ]. Common etiologies of LAST include: (1) The administration of an excessive dose, either as a single bolus or cumulative dose, surpassing the threshold for systemic toxicity; (2) Unintended rapid systemic absorption from highly vascular injection sites; (3) Accidental intravascular injection, causing a precipitous rise in plasma drug concentration; and (4) Reduced patient tolerance due to factors such as frailty, hepatic or renal insufficiency, hypoalbuminemia, or advanced age, which impair drug metabolism. Both patients described in this report had no significant past medical history, with normal preoperative serum albumin and total protein levels, and no evidence of hepatic, renal, or cardiac impairment that would predispose them to altered drug metabolism. The recommended dosage of liposomal bupivacaine for an interscalene brachial plexus block is 10 mL (133 mg). Notably, in our first case, a dose of 266 mg was administered for an intercostal nerve block. The intercostal space is a region of rich vascularity, and the occurrence of LAST in this patient may be attributed to a confluence of factors: the relatively high dose, the potential for unintentional intravascular injection, and the rapid systemic absorption from the highly vascular site, collectively leading to a rapid and substantial rise in plasma concentration. Furthermore, bupivacaine is known for its inherent cardiotoxicity, which is greater than that of many other local anesthetics [ 12 ]. Particularly in scenarios of intravascular injection or overdose, it can precipitate severe ventricular arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation, or cardiac arrest, which are often refractory to standard resuscitation measures. The second patient also received 266 mg of liposomal bupivacaine for surgical incision site infiltration. Although this amount aligns with the maximum recommended adult dose for local infiltration, the highly vascularized nature of the thoracic wall, supplied by extensive intercostal vasculature, likely facilitated accelerated systemic absorption following peri-incisional administration, potentially elevating plasma concentrations beyond the toxic threshold, even without an absolute overdose. Consequently, when utilizing local anesthetics in highly vascular anatomical planes—such as the paravertebral, intrapleural, or intercostal regions—it is imperative to exercise heightened vigilance. Strategies should include considering dose reduction relative to the vascularity of the site and employing meticulous technique with frequent aspiration during injection to mitigate the risk of intravascular administration. Although the 266 mg dosage of liposomal bupivacaine used in our patients is within the manufacturer’s recommended dose for local infiltration, the highly vascular intercostal territory likely facilitates systemic uptake as the rate of systemic absorption of local anesthetics and the consequent rise in peak plasma concentrations are related to the vascularity of the injection site. A comprehensive review by Rosenberg et al. titled “Maximum Recommended Doses of Local Anesthetics: A Multifactorial Concept” highlights that the same dose of a local anesthetic can result in markedly different peak serum concentrations depending on the injection site, with intercostal blocks producing the highest concentrations, followed by epidural and brachial plexus blocks [ 13 ]. This pharmacokinetic ranking explains why a dose of 266 mg, which falls within the manufacturer’s recommended limit for low-vascularity local infiltration, may approach or exceed a safe threshold when administered in the highly vascular thoracic or intercostal region. Therefore, we argue that site-specific dosing guidelines are needed, and clinicians should exercise greater caution when using liposomal bupivacaine for thoracic/intercostal blocks. Crucially, accidental intravascular injection—a risk not entirely mitigated by aspiration—can result in severe LAST. This clinical concern is supported by the pharmacokinetic data from Joshi et al., who reported that the maximum plasma concentration of bupivacaine is achieved within 5–15 min following intravascular injection of liposomal bupivacaine in dogs [ 14 ]. The study further established a much lower safety threshold for intra-arterial (1.5 mg/kg) compared to intravenous (4.5 mg/kg) administration. These findings indicate that intravascular injection may have compromised the intended sustained-release kinetics of the liposomal formulation, leading to a rapid influx of free bupivacaine into the systemic circulation, thereby precipitating toxicity. A key limitation of this report is the absence of serum bupivacaine concentration measurements, which are considered the gold standard for diagnosing LAST. In neither of the two presented cases was blood concentration monitoring performed. Consequently, we are unable to determine the actual systemic exposure levels of bupivacaine following administration or to assess the relationship between observed toxic effects and corresponding serum concentrations. Thus, the diagnosis of LAST was based on a combination of well-documented administration of the local anesthetic, clinical signs and symptoms consistent with LAST, and careful exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Future cases would benefit from timely blood concentration sampling upon suspicion of LAST, including serial measurements at multiple time points, to better characterize the relationship between drug levels and clinical manifestations. Since its introduction, reports of toxicity associated with liposomal bupivacaine have been limited. A systematic literature review was performed using the MeSH terms and keywords “liposomal bupivacaine” and “local anesthetic systemic toxicity” across the PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP databases from database inception to April 20, 2026. After screening titles, abstracts, and full texts, only two relevant case reports were identified after excluding irrelevant and incomplete records [ 15 , 16 ]. Notably, both patients had significant predisposing factors for LAST. The first was an elderly individual with concomitant non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. In contrast, the second had experienced substantial weight loss (approximately 20 pounds over 3 months) prior to admission, potentially indicating reduced lean body mass. Fortunately, prompt administration of intravenous lipid emulsion therapy in both cases resulted in successful recovery and subsequent discharge. Given that both reported incidents involved admixtures of liposomal and plain bupivacaine, further investigation into the safety profile of such combination regimens is warranted, particularly in patients at elevated risk for LAST. The recommended regimen consists of an initial bolus of 1.5 mL/kg (ideal body weight) administered over 2–3 min, with a maximum initial bolus of 100 mL for patients ≥ 70 kg, followed by a continuous infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min. The infusion should be maintained for at least 15 min after hemodynamic stability is achieved. If circulatory compromise persists, the initial bolus may be repeated once, or the infusion rate may be doubled to 0.5 mL/kg/min. If epinephrine is required, it should be initiated at low dosage (e.g., < 1 µg/kg) to minimize its potential proarrhythmic effects in the context of LAST [ 11 ]. To prevent LAST, the dosage of local anesthetics must be strictly controlled in all clinical scenarios, especially in patients with risk factors such as advanced age, infancy, pregnancy, hepatic or renal insufficiency, hypoalbuminemia, or cardiac dysfunction, which increase susceptibility to toxicity. Furthermore, the dosage should be reduced when administering blocks in highly vascular areas (e.g., intercostal, paravertebral, intrapleural). Mandatory pre-procedural intravenous access and continuous ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry monitoring for a minimum of 30 minutes post-procedure are essential. This pharmacokinetic ranking explains why a dose of 266 mg, which falls within the manufacturer’s recommended limit for low-vascularity local infiltration, may approach or exceed a safe threshold when administered in the highly vascular thoracic or intercostal region. Therefore, we argue that site-specific dosing guidelines are needed, and clinicians should exercise greater caution when using liposomal bupivacaine for thoracic/intercostal blocks. Crucially, accidental intravascular injection—a risk not entirely mitigated by aspiration—can result in severe LAST. This clinical concern is supported by the pharmacokinetic data from Joshi et al., who reported that the maximum plasma concentration of bupivacaine is achieved within 5–15 min following intravascular injection of liposomal bupivacaine in dogs [ 14 ]. The study further established a much lower safety threshold for intra-arterial (1.5 mg/kg) compared to intravenous (4.5 mg/kg) administration. These findings indicate that intravascular injection may have compromised the intended sustained-release kinetics of the liposomal formulation, leading to a rapid influx of free bupivacaine into the systemic circulation, thereby precipitating toxicity. A key limitation of this report is the absence of serum bupivacaine concentration measurements, which are considered the gold standard for diagnosing LAST. In neither of the two presented cases was blood concentration monitoring performed. Consequently, we are unable to determine the actual systemic exposure levels of bupivacaine following administration or to assess the relationship between observed toxic effects and corresponding serum concentrations. Thus, the diagnosis of LAST was based on a combination of well-documented administration of the local anesthetic, clinical signs and symptoms consistent with LAST, and careful exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Future cases would benefit from timely blood concentration sampling upon suspicion of LAST, including serial measurements at multiple time points, to better characterize the relationship between drug levels and clinical manifestations. Since its introduction, reports of toxicity associated with liposomal bupivacaine have been limited. A systematic literature review was performed using the MeSH terms and keywords “liposomal bupivacaine” and “local anesthetic systemic toxicity” across the PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP databases from database inception to April 20, 2026. After screening titles, abstracts, and full texts, only two relevant case reports were identified after excluding irrelevant and incomplete records [ 15 , 16 ]. The first case involved a 71-year-old male with prostate cancer who underwent robot-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy [ 15 ]. The patient received subcutaneous infiltration with a mixture of 20 mL (266 mg) liposomal bupivacaine and 30 mL of 0.25% (75 mg) plain bupivacaine after skin closure. Fifteen minutes post-extubation, the patient experienced a sudden loss of consciousness and subsequent cardiac arrest. The second case described a 68-year-old male who underwent open sigmoid colectomy with end descending colostomy. Bilateral transversus abdominis plane (TAP) blocks were administered under direct visualization using a combination of 20 mL liposomal bupivacaine, 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine, and epinephrine 1:200,000. Shortly after the TAP block, the patient developed sustained ventricular tachycardia progressing to ventricular fibrillation and subsequently pulseless electrical activity [ 16 ]. Notably, both patients had significant predisposing factors for LAST. The first was an elderly individual with concomitant non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. In contrast, the second had experienced substantial weight loss (approximately 20 pounds over 3 months) prior to admission, potentially indicating reduced lean body mass. Both conditions are known to reduce tolerance to local anesthetics [ 12 ]. Fortunately, prompt administration of intravenous lipid emulsion therapy in both cases resulted in successful recovery and subsequent discharge. Given that both reported incidents involved admixtures of liposomal and plain bupivacaine, further investigation into the safety profile of such combination regimens is warranted, particularly in patients at elevated risk for LAST. Immediate administration of 20% lipid emulsion is critical upon first suspicion of LAST. The recommended regimen consists of an initial bolus of 1.5 mL/kg (ideal body weight) administered over 2–3 min, with a maximum initial bolus of 100 mL for patients ≥ 70 kg, followed by a continuous infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min. The infusion should be maintained for at least 15 min after hemodynamic stability is achieved. If circulatory compromise persists, the initial bolus may be repeated once, or the infusion rate may be doubled to 0.5 mL/kg/min. If epinephrine is required, it should be initiated at low dosage (e.g., < 1 µg/kg) to minimize its potential proarrhythmic effects in the context of LAST [ 11 ]. To prevent LAST, the dosage of local anesthetics must be strictly controlled in all clinical scenarios, especially in patients with risk factors such as advanced age, infancy, pregnancy, hepatic or renal insufficiency, hypoalbuminemia, or cardiac dysfunction, which increase susceptibility to toxicity. Furthermore, the dosage should be reduced when administering blocks in highly vascular areas (e.g., intercostal, paravertebral, intrapleural). Mandatory pre-procedural intravenous access and continuous ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry monitoring for a minimum of 30 minutes post-procedure are essential. title: Inflammation-linked adipokine profiles associate with acute organ dysfunction after severe trauma
abstract: Introduction Polytrauma initiates an abrupt shift in immunometabolic signalling, but the role of circulating adipokines in acute post-traumatic organ dysfunction is not fully understood. Resistin and adiponectin are circulating immune-metabolic markers at the interface of inflammation, metabolic stress, and renal dysfunction, but their dynamic response to trauma and their clinical relevance remain uncertain. We therefore characterised serial changes in circulating adipokines during the first 10 days after severe multiple trauma and evaluated their associations with systemic inflammation, organ-specific dysfunction and clinical outcomes. We additionally explored associations between CT-derived waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), as a marker of body-fat distribution, and adipokine profiles. Methods This study represents a secondary retrospective analysis of prospectively collected plasma samples and clinical data from a longitudinal observational cohort, including 67 patients with Injury Severity Score ≥ 16 and 31 healthy volunteers. Plasma resistin, adiponectin, leptin and retinol-binding protein 4 (RBP4) were measured at admission (D0) and on D1, D5 and D10. Longitudinal changes were analysed using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, BMI and WHR. Associations with inflammatory markers and organ dysfunction were assessed using partial Spearman correlations. Exploratory receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) analyses evaluated adipokine-based classification of hospital length of stay (LOS), ICU LOS, shock severity and 30-day mortality. Results Compared with healthy volunteers, trauma patients showed an altered adipokine profile at admission, characterised by elevated resistin ( p < 0.01) and reduced adiponectin ( p < 0.05). At admission, resistin correlated strongly with IL-6 ( r ≈ 0.75), which remained significant after FDR correction. The resistin-to-adiponectin (R/A) ratio demonstrated the most consistent associations across inflammatory and renal parameters. Most WHR-stratified comparisons showed no clear separation across groups. In exploratory ROC analyses, several adipokine measures showed moderate classification of selected clinical outcomes; however, mortality analyses were limited by few available events at later timepoints. Conclusions Severe trauma was associated with rapid changes in circulating adipokine profiles, characterised by early resistin elevation, lower circulating adiponectin, and an increased R/A ratio. Resistin and the R/A ratio showed the most consistent associations with systemic inflammation and renal dysfunction. WHR-stratified differences for most adipokines were limited. Clinical outcome associations were exploratory and require prospective multicentre validation to establish added value beyond conventional clinical parameters. body: Polytrauma (PT), defined by an Injury Severity Score (ISS) ≥ 16, poses a substantial risk for the development of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), which remains a major driver of mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU) [ 1 – 3 ]. MODS arises from a complex interplay of systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation and is routinely assessed using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score to quantify organ failure and stratify mortality risk [ 2 – 4 ]. Despite advances in trauma care, early identification of patients at risk for MODS remains a clinical challenge. White adipose tissue (WAT) has emerged as a biologically active endocrine and immunomodulatory organ, yet its role in the acute phase after trauma has received limited attention. WAT secretes numerous adipokines, including cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and exosomal microRNAs, that influence systemic inflammation, glucose metabolism, endothelial activation, and inter-organ communication [ 5 – 8 ]. Dysregulation of adipokines is well described in metabolic disorders such as insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus [ 6 , 9 , 10 ]. Acute injury can perturb adipose-tissue metabolism and circulating adipokine concentrations; however, the measured markers have distinct cellular sources and should not be interpreted as a uniform adipose-tissue secretory response. In particular, human resistin is predominantly produced by monocytes and macrophages and is therefore more closely linked to myeloid and innate immune activation than to adipocyte secretion [ 11 – 14 ]. Similarly, circulating RBP4 is predominantly hepatocyte-derived in humans and therefore should not be interpreted as a specific marker of adipose-tissue secretion [ 15 ]. Understanding this broader immune-metabolic interplay is particularly relevant because a substantial proportion of trauma patients present with increased adiposity, altered metabolic profiles, and obesity-associated inflammation [ 8 , 16 – 19 ]. Body fat distribution, particularly visceral adiposity, may further modulate the inflammatory response and susceptibility to organ dysfunction after severe injury [ 20 – 22 ]. However, previous studies investigating individual adipokines in critically ill or trauma patients have reported heterogeneous and sometimes conflicting results [ 16 – 18 , 23 , 24 ]. This highlights the need to define how acute trauma alters adipokine dynamics and whether these changes are associated with subsequent clinical outcomes. Adipokine responses after severe trauma are likely shaped by the intensity of injury and shock, systemic inflammation, central fat distribution, sex, and metabolic factors such as catabolism and nutritional status. Resistin, adiponectin, leptin, and RBP4 therefore represent biologically heterogeneous circulating immune-metabolic and organ-stress signals. Beyond single biomarkers, adipokine ratios such as leptin/adiponectin (L/A) and adiponectin/resistin (A/R) have been investigated in metabolic and cardiometabolic disorders as integrated markers of inflammatory and metabolic state [ 10 , 25 – 32 ]. Whether such composite indices reflect early immunometabolic stress and organ dysfunction trajectories in severe polytrauma remains incompletely defined. We therefore analysed L/A and R/A ratios as exploratory composite indices alongside the individual adipokine trajectories. In this study, we performed longitudinal profiling of resistin, adiponectin, leptin, and RBP4, and their ratios, over the first 10 days after severe trauma. Combining mixed-effects modelling, CT-based assessment of waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), partial correlation analysis, and organ-specific clinical endpoints, we aimed to characterise the early adipokine response, determine its relationship with inflammation and organ dysfunction, and perform exploratory analyses of the relationships between adipokine measures prespecified clinical outcomes in severely injured patients. In this study, we performed a secondary retrospective analysis of prospectively collected samples and clinical data from a longitudinal observational study of severely injured polytrauma patients treated at a Level I Trauma Center, Ulm University Hospital, Ulm, Germany. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ulm University (244/11, 94/14, and 260/22), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal representatives in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Adult patients (≥ 18 years) with severe multiple injuries, defined by an ISS ≥ 16 between 2013 and 2024 were included. Exclusion criteria comprised pregnancy, HIV infection, cardiogenic shock as primary diagnosis, hematologic malignancy, recent cytotoxic therapy, or terminal disease with expected survival < 24 h. Clinical evaluation followed standardized trauma protocols including whole-body CT imaging. Detailed inclusion/exclusion criteria are provided in Supplementary Methods. Peripheral blood was collected at admission (D0), 24 h (D1), day 5 (D5), and day 10 (D10), representing the acute injury, early post-resuscitation inflammatory, subacute organ dysfunction, and early in-hospital follow-up phases, respectively. Complete sampling at all four timepoints was not required for study inclusion. Longitudinal mixed-effects models used all available repeated adipokine measurements among participants with complete data for the covariates included in the respective model; repeated outcome measurements were not imputed. Available adipokine measurements decreased over time because of death, discharge, or unavailable samples: D0 n = 66, D1 n = 60, D5 n = 58, and D10 n = 48. Samples were obtained under emergency and ICU conditions; fasting and nutritional status were not standardized or systematically available for adjustment. Detailed exposure data for nutritional support and medications relevant to adipokine biology, including catecholamines, corticosteroids, and insulin, as well as pre-existing metabolic conditions such as diabetes or metabolic syndrome, were unavailable or incompletely captured and therefore could not be included as covariates. Plasma processing and storage followed standard operating procedures (see Supplementary Methods). Routine laboratory parameters, including IL-6, CRP, lactate, glucose, base excess, bilirubin, platelet counts, and creatinine, were obtained from the hospital’s certified central laboratory. Plasma concentrations were measured using commercially available ELISAs (R&D Systems; for analytical ranges and assay details, see Supplementary Methods). RBP4 was retained within the predefined circulating marker panel but, given its predominantly hepatic origin in humans, was not interpreted as a direct adipose-derived signal. Adipokine concentrations were analysed as measured plasma concentrations and were not normalized to hematocrit or total protein. L/A and resistin/adiponectin (R/A) ratios were calculated at each timepoint. Organ dysfunction was assessed using the SOFA score reconstructed at each sampling timepoint. Organ-specific SOFA sub-scores (renal, cardiovascular, respiratory, hepatic, coagulation) were analysed separately. Details of SOFA reconstruction, including handling of missing data and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale to Glasgow Coma Scale (RASS-to-GCS) conversion, are provided in Supplementary Methods. Hemorrhagic shock (HS) was defined as base excess < -6 mmol/L, lactate ≥ 2.5 mmol/L, or transfusion > 2 units of packed red blood cells within the first 24 h following admission [ 33 ]. This variable was used for clinical characterization rather than as a mechanistic exposure defining the primary adipokine analyses. WHR was measured from admission CT scans, using measurements at the level of the umbilicus for waist circumference and the femoral neck for hip circumference. WHR was used as a CT-derived proxy of central body-fat distribution. WHR categories were defined according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria [ 34 ] and were used for descriptive stratification and visualization. Because these thresholds were developed for cardiometabolic risk assessment and are not validated trauma-specific cutoffs, WHR-stratified analyses were interpreted descriptively. Patients were stratified into three WHR categories. For women, moderate WHR was defined as 0.85 ≤ WHR < 0.95. For men, moderate WHR was defined as 0.90 ≤ WHR < 1.00. Values below these ranges were classified as low WHR, and values equal to or above these ranges as high WHR. Statistical analyses and visualisations were performed in R, with additional figures in GraphPad Prism 9.1.2. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD or median [IQR] as appropriate. Admission group comparisons were conducted using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and BMI. Longitudinal adipokine changes were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for patient ID and fixed effects for time, age, sex, BMI, and WHR, with WHR entered as a continuous covariate; log-transformation was applied where required, with model assumptions verified by residual and Q–Q plots. Post-hoc contrasts were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) within each biomarker-specific contrast set. For partial Spearman correlations, FDR correction was applied separately within two predefined correlation families: adipokines/adipokine ratios with inflammatory-metabolic and renal laboratory markers, and adipokines/adipokine ratios with clinical severity and SOFA-domain scores. Coefficients with |r| < 0.30 were considered weak and were not interpreted as biologically or clinically relevant, even when nominally significant. As sensitivity analyses, partial Spearman correlations between admission (D0) adipokines/adipokine ratios and AIS regional scores were adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and global ISS, with FDR correction across all 36 region–marker comparisons. Selected D0 correlations were also repeated with and without additional adjustment for admission hematocrit to assess potential confounding by resuscitation-related hemodilution. ROC analyses were performed exploratorily for prespecified dichotomized clinical outcomes: shock ratio (> 1), hospital LOS (> 21 days), ICU LOS (> 7 days), and 30-day mortality. For clinical context, routinely available admission variables including ISS, shock ratio, base excess, lactate, IL-6, SOFA, creatinine, GFR, and CRP were evaluated using the same exploratory framework for hospital LOS > 21 days and 30-day mortality. These analyses were descriptive and were not intended as formal head-to-head comparisons of biomarker superiority. AUCs with 95% confidence intervals were estimated using the DeLong method. To assess whether R/A provided greater discrimination than resistin alone, paired AUCs were compared using DeLong tests among participants with both measurements available at the corresponding timepoint. Differences in AUC (ΔAUC = AUC R/A − AUC Resistin ) are reported with 95% confidence intervals (Supplementary Fig. 2 A). Reported p-values were derived from Mann–Whitney U tests comparing biomarker distributions between outcome groups and do not test whether an AUC differs from 0.5. No internal or external validation was performed, and the selected cutoffs were not intended as validated prognostic thresholds. Analyses were based on available observations with complete data for the variables and covariates required by each respective analysis; missing data were not imputed. Linear mixed-effects models therefore included all available repeated measurements meeting these requirements. Their interpretation under incomplete follow-up relies on a missing-at-random assumption conditional on the observed data and covariates included in the model. Because later samples could be unavailable because of death, discharge, or clinical instability, this assumption cannot be verified in the present cohort. Accordingly, the mixed-effects models were used to describe the observed longitudinal patterns rather than to estimate population-wide D5–D10 trajectories. Potential attrition-related selection was characterised descriptively by comparing patients with and without an available D10 adipokine measurement; no inferential testing was performed for this comparison. No formal a priori sample-size calculation was performed for this secondary exploratory analysis. WHR-stratified analyses, WHR × sex interaction models, and ROC analyses were therefore considered exploratory. All tests were two-sided (α = 0.05). Sixty-seven polytrauma patients and 31 healthy volunteers (HV) were enrolled. Baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1 . The trauma cohort had a mean age of 50 years and was predominantly male (78%). Injury severity was high, with a median ISS of 27 (IQR 21–33) and an admission shock ratio of 1.1 (IQR 0.9–1.4). Nine patients died within the first 10 days after trauma; in total, 14 patients died within 30 days. To characterize potential attrition-related selection, baseline characteristics were compared descriptively between patients contributing at least one D10 adipokine measurement ( n = 48) and those without a D10 adipokine measurement ( n = 19; Supplementary Table 1 ). Together, these opposite directional changes produced an early rise in the R/A ratio, most pronounced within the first 24 h ( p < 0.01). The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ulm University (244/11, 94/14, and 260/22), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal representatives in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Adult patients (≥ 18 years) with severe multiple injuries, defined by an ISS ≥ 16 between 2013 and 2024 were included. Exclusion criteria comprised pregnancy, HIV infection, cardiogenic shock as primary diagnosis, hematologic malignancy, recent cytotoxic therapy, or terminal disease with expected survival < 24 h. Clinical evaluation followed standardized trauma protocols including whole-body CT imaging. Detailed inclusion/exclusion criteria are provided in Supplementary Methods. Peripheral blood was collected at admission (D0), 24 h (D1), day 5 (D5), and day 10 (D10), representing the acute injury, early post-resuscitation inflammatory, subacute organ dysfunction, and early in-hospital follow-up phases, respectively. Complete sampling at all four timepoints was not required for study inclusion. Longitudinal mixed-effects models used all available repeated adipokine measurements among participants with complete data for the covariates included in the respective model; repeated outcome measurements were not imputed. Available adipokine measurements decreased over time because of death, discharge, or unavailable samples: D0 n = 66, D1 n = 60, D5 n = 58, and D10 n = 48. Samples were obtained under emergency and ICU conditions; fasting and nutritional status were not standardized or systematically available for adjustment. Detailed exposure data for nutritional support and medications relevant to adipokine biology, including catecholamines, corticosteroids, and insulin, as well as pre-existing metabolic conditions such as diabetes or metabolic syndrome, were unavailable or incompletely captured and therefore could not be included as covariates. Plasma processing and storage followed standard operating procedures (see Supplementary Methods). Routine laboratory parameters, including IL-6, CRP, lactate, glucose, base excess, bilirubin, platelet counts, and creatinine, were obtained from the hospital’s certified central laboratory. Plasma concentrations were measured using commercially available ELISAs (R&D Systems; for analytical ranges and assay details, see Supplementary Methods). RBP4 was retained within the predefined circulating marker panel but, given its predominantly hepatic origin in humans, was not interpreted as a direct adipose-derived signal. Adipokine concentrations were analysed as measured plasma concentrations and were not normalized to hematocrit or total protein. L/A and resistin/adiponectin (R/A) ratios were calculated at each timepoint. Organ dysfunction was assessed using the SOFA score reconstructed at each sampling timepoint. Organ-specific SOFA sub-scores (renal, cardiovascular, respiratory, hepatic, coagulation) were analysed separately. Details of SOFA reconstruction, including handling of missing data and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale to Glasgow Coma Scale (RASS-to-GCS) conversion, are provided in Supplementary Methods. Hemorrhagic shock (HS) was defined as base excess < -6 mmol/L, lactate ≥ 2.5 mmol/L, or transfusion > 2 units of packed red blood cells within the first 24 h following admission [ 33 ]. This variable was used for clinical characterization rather than as a mechanistic exposure defining the primary adipokine analyses. WHR was measured from admission CT scans, using measurements at the level of the umbilicus for waist circumference and the femoral neck for hip circumference. WHR was used as a CT-derived proxy of central body-fat distribution. WHR categories were defined according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria [ 34 ] and were used for descriptive stratification and visualization. Because these thresholds were developed for cardiometabolic risk assessment and are not validated trauma-specific cutoffs, WHR-stratified analyses were interpreted descriptively. Patients were stratified into three WHR categories. For women, moderate WHR was defined as 0.85 ≤ WHR < 0.95. For men, moderate WHR was defined as 0.90 ≤ WHR < 1.00. Values below these ranges were classified as low WHR, and values equal to or above these ranges as high WHR. Statistical analyses and visualisations were performed in R, with additional figures in GraphPad Prism 9.1.2. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD or median [IQR] as appropriate. Admission group comparisons were conducted using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and BMI. Longitudinal adipokine changes were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for patient ID and fixed effects for time, age, sex, BMI, and WHR, with WHR entered as a continuous covariate; log-transformation was applied where required, with model assumptions verified by residual and Q–Q plots. Post-hoc contrasts were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) within each biomarker-specific contrast set. For partial Spearman correlations, FDR correction was applied separately within two predefined correlation families: adipokines/adipokine ratios with inflammatory-metabolic and renal laboratory markers, and adipokines/adipokine ratios with clinical severity and SOFA-domain scores. Coefficients with |r| < 0.30 were considered weak and were not interpreted as biologically or clinically relevant, even when nominally significant. As sensitivity analyses, partial Spearman correlations between admission (D0) adipokines/adipokine ratios and AIS regional scores were adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and global ISS, with FDR correction across all 36 region–marker comparisons. Selected D0 correlations were also repeated with and without additional adjustment for admission hematocrit to assess potential confounding by resuscitation-related hemodilution. ROC analyses were performed exploratorily for prespecified dichotomized clinical outcomes: shock ratio (> 1), hospital LOS (> 21 days), ICU LOS (> 7 days), and 30-day mortality. For clinical context, routinely available admission variables including ISS, shock ratio, base excess, lactate, IL-6, SOFA, creatinine, GFR, and CRP were evaluated using the same exploratory framework for hospital LOS > 21 days and 30-day mortality. These analyses were descriptive and were not intended as formal head-to-head comparisons of biomarker superiority. AUCs with 95% confidence intervals were estimated using the DeLong method. To assess whether R/A provided greater discrimination than resistin alone, paired AUCs were compared using DeLong tests among participants with both measurements available at the corresponding timepoint. Differences in AUC (ΔAUC = AUC R/A − AUC Resistin ) are reported with 95% confidence intervals (Supplementary Fig. 2 A). Reported p-values were derived from Mann–Whitney U tests comparing biomarker distributions between outcome groups and do not test whether an AUC differs from 0.5. No internal or external validation was performed, and the selected cutoffs were not intended as validated prognostic thresholds. Analyses were based on available observations with complete data for the variables and covariates required by each respective analysis; missing data were not imputed. Linear mixed-effects models therefore included all available repeated measurements meeting these requirements. Their interpretation under incomplete follow-up relies on a missing-at-random assumption conditional on the observed data and covariates included in the model. Because later samples could be unavailable because of death, discharge, or clinical instability, this assumption cannot be verified in the present cohort. Accordingly, the mixed-effects models were used to describe the observed longitudinal patterns rather than to estimate population-wide D5–D10 trajectories. Potential attrition-related selection was characterised descriptively by comparing patients with and without an available D10 adipokine measurement; no inferential testing was performed for this comparison. No formal a priori sample-size calculation was performed for this secondary exploratory analysis. WHR-stratified analyses, WHR × sex interaction models, and ROC analyses were therefore considered exploratory. All tests were two-sided (α = 0.05). Sixty-seven polytrauma patients and 31 healthy volunteers (HV) were enrolled. Baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1 . The trauma cohort had a mean age of 50 years and was predominantly male (78%). Injury severity was high, with a median ISS of 27 (IQR 21–33) and an admission shock ratio of 1.1 (IQR 0.9–1.4). Nine patients died within the first 10 days after trauma; in total, 14 patients died within 30 days. These descriptive findings do not establish that missingness was random. Adipokine levels changed rapidly after injury (Fig. 1 ). Resistin was elevated at admission compared with HV ( p < 0.01), increased further to a peak on D1 ( p < 0.01 vs. D0), and declined thereafter. In contrast, adiponectin was already reduced at admission ( p < 0.05), reached its lowest level on D1, and increased gradually thereafter. Together, these opposite directional changes produced an early rise in the R/A ratio, most pronounced within the first 24 h ( p < 0.01). title: The cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose index and its derived indices predict cardiometabolic multimorbidity development and progression in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease individuals: a prospective cohort study
abstract: Background Dysregulation of cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and glucose metabolism is thought to be an important metabolic link between metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), type 2 diabetes (T2D), and cardiovascular disease. Although the cholesterol-high-density lipoprotein-glucose (CHG) index and its adiposity-derived indices have been associated with individual cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), their associations with cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM), stage-specific disease progression, and risk prediction in individuals with MASLD remain unclear. Methods This prospective cohort study included 109,434 UK Biobank participants with MASLD and without T2D, coronary heart disease (CHD), or stroke at baseline. Eight CHG-related indices were evaluated. Incident CMM was defined as the occurrence of at least two of the three CMDs. Cox models estimated associations with incident CMM. Multistate models characterized transitions from a disease-free state to individual CMD and subsequently to CMM. Incremental prediction was assessed using the C-index, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Exploratory mediation analyses evaluated circulating biomarkers related to metabolic, inflammatory, hepatic and renal pathways. Results During a median follow-up of 16.4 years, 4225 participants developed CMM. All CHG-related indices were associated with higher CMM risk, with the strongest associations observed for CHG-waist-to-height ratio (CHG-WHtR; hazard ratio [HR] per 1-standard deviation [SD] increment, 1.61; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.57–1.65) and CHG-waist circumference (CHG-WC; HR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.55–1.63). Adding each index to conventional risk models improved discrimination and risk classification. CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC showed relatively favorable predictive performance, although the absolute differences between indices were modest. In multistate analyses, associations were strongest for disease-free to T2D and CHD-to-CMM transitions. Exploratory biomarker analyses showed that baseline biomarker domains related to glycemic regulation, lipid metabolism, inflammation, and hepatic and renal function were statistically linked to these associations. Conclusions Among individuals with MASLD, CHG-related indices, particularly CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC, were associated with incident CMM and transition-specific disease progression and improved risk prediction. These readily available indices may help refine CMM risk stratification in MASLD. Graphical abstract Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12933-026-03343-5 .

All CHG-related indices were associated with higher incident CMM risk. CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC showed the strongest associations and best prediction. How might this study influence clinical practice? CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC may help identify high-risk individuals with MASLD. CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC may help identify high-risk individuals with MASLD. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is currently the leading form of chronic liver disease globally, with approximately 30–40% of adults affected [ 1 ]. Given the continued rise in metabolic diseases worldwide, MASLD prevalence is projected to surpass 55% by 2040, thereby imposing a considerable socioeconomic burden [ 1 ]. The growing recognition of MASLD as a multisystem disorder has prompted increasing interest in outcomes beyond the liver [ 2 ], especially because cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the predominant cause of mortality in this population [ 1 , 3 ]. Recent studies have further shown that MASLD is accompanied by a markedly increased comorbidity burden [ 4 ], with cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) being of particular concern [ 5 , 6 ]. CMM is generally characterized by the coexistence of at least two cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), most commonly coronary heart disease (CHD), stroke, and type 2 diabetes (T2D) [ 7 ]. Existing longitudinal evidence suggests that the progression from a disease-free state to a first CMD and subsequently to CMM is shaped by partly stage-specific factors. Hypertension, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, and a family history of cardiometabolic disease have been more strongly associated with the development of a first CMD [ 8 ], whereas smoking, physical inactivity, an unhealthy diet, harmful alcohol consumption, and socioeconomic disadvantage have been associated with progression from a first CMD to CMM [ 7 , 8 ]. Central and visceral adiposity may also contribute to both the onset and subsequent accumulation of CMDs [ 9 ]. Importantly, these CMDs are not pathophysiologically independent but share an interconnected network of metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular abnormalities. Beyond insulin resistance (IR), hepatic overproduction of atherogenic lipoproteins, chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, endothelial dysfunction, and a prothrombotic state may link MASLD to vascular injury, atherosclerosis, thrombosis, and deterioration of glucose homeostasis [ 1 , 10 – 13 ]. Because individuals with MASLD frequently exhibit several of these shared abnormalities, they may be particularly susceptible to progression along the CMM continuum. In this context, identifying modifiable metabolic markers associated with the onset and progression of CMM in individuals with MASLD is a key priority for both clinical practice and population health. Because of their low cost, convenience, and ability to integrate information from multiple biological processes, composite indices based on routine blood biomarkers have become increasingly attractive in epidemiological and clinical research. The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a well-established surrogate marker for insulin resistance (IR) and cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) [ 14 – 16 ]. However, in individuals with normal triglyceride (TG) levels, the TyG index may have limited predictive utility, as their atherosclerotic risk may be more closely related to cholesterol–glucose metabolic pathways than to triglyceride-mediated mechanisms [ 17 , 18 ]. In this context, the cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose (CHG) index, comprising total cholesterol (TC), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and glucose, has recently been developed as an economical and accessible composite index with cardiometabolic event prediction comparable to the TyG index [ 19 – 21 ]. Several important knowledge gaps warrant further investigation. First, most available evidence has been based on single CMD endpoints [ 19 – 30 ]. Although recent studies have reported associations of the CHG index with MASLD and with mortality among individuals with MASLD [ 31 – 34 ], whether this index predicts the development of CMM in this vulnerable population remains unknown. Second, CMM typically develops along a progressive continuum rather than occurring abruptly. This trajectory usually begins with no CMD, advances to the first CMD (FCMD), and subsequently progresses to CMM as additional CMDs accumulate [ 7 ]. Because CMM represents a more advanced clinical state than isolated CMDs and is linked to higher risks of functional decline and death [ 35 , 36 ], analyses limited to single endpoints may underestimate or obscure the role of the CHG index across CMM development. Third, given the essential role of obesity in MASLD pathogenesis [ 1 ], CHG-related adiposity-derived indices may provide additional prognostic information. Indeed, several studies have suggested that these indices may outperform the CHG index alone in predicting cardiovascular events [ 23 – 25 ]. However, evidence directly comparing different CHG-related indices for CMM risk prediction among individuals with MASLD is still limited. Thus, a large prospective cohort study is required to systematically examine and compare how the CHG index and related adiposity-derived indices are associated with the onset and progression of CMM in MASLD populations. Moreover, individuals with MASLD often exhibit unfavorable biomarker patterns related to inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and multi-organ impairment [ 1 , 37 ], and the CHG index has been associated with several of these biomarkers [ 33 , 34 , 38 – 40 ]. However, because many of these biomarkers are closely related to cardiometabolic status, it remains unclear whether baseline biomarker profiles are statistically linked to the associations between CHG-related indices and incident CMM in individuals with MASLD. To clarify these knowledge gaps, we conducted a large-scale prospective cohort analysis examining the associations between the CHG index, its adiposity-derived indices, and the incidence and progression of CMM in individuals with MASLD. We further assessed whether these indices improved CMM risk prediction and performed exploratory biomarker analyses to identify baseline biomarker domains statistically related to the observed associations. We used data from the UK Biobank, an ongoing population-based prospective cohort designed to investigate the genetic, environmental, and lifestyle determinants of disease. The cohort enrolled more than 500,000 participants aged 37–73 years from 22 assessment centers across England, Scotland, and Wales between 2006 and 2010. At baseline, participants completed touchscreen questionnaires, underwent standardized physical measurements, and provided biological samples, including blood, urine, and saliva. Additional clinical information was obtained through linkage to medical diagnostic records. Details of the cohort design and baseline assessment procedures have been reported elsewhere [ 41 ]. The UK Biobank received ethical approval from the North West Multi-Centre Research Ethics Committee (reference: 21/NW/0157), and all participants provided written informed consent. The current analysis was conducted under UK Biobank application number 227947. For the present analysis, we excluded participants with missing data required to calculate CHG-related indices ( n = 75,199), those without MASLD at baseline ( n = 291,043), and those with prevalent CMDs ( n = 19,041). We further excluded participants with missing covariate data (n = 7,283), leaving 109,434 participants for the main analysis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Study population flowchart. Given that liver imaging data were only available for a small imaging-enhanced subset of UK Biobank participants and not for the full analytic cohort [ 43 – 45 ], hepatic steatosis was operationalized using a fatty liver index (FLI) score ≥ 60 [ 46 ]. The cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose index and its derived indices predict cardiometabolic multimorbidity development and progression in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease individuals: a prospective cohort study

Background Dysregulation of cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and glucose metabolism is thought to be an important metabolic link between metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), type 2 diabetes (T2D), and cardiovascular disease. Although the cholesterol-high-density lipoprotein-glucose (CHG) index and its adiposity-derived indices have been associated with individual cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), their associations with cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM), stage-specific disease progression, and risk prediction in individuals with MASLD remain unclear. Methods This prospective cohort study included 109,434 UK Biobank participants with MASLD and without T2D, coronary heart disease (CHD), or stroke at baseline. Eight CHG-related indices were evaluated. Incident CMM was defined as the occurrence of at least two of the three CMDs. Cox models estimated associations with incident CMM. Multistate models characterized transitions from a disease-free state to individual CMD and subsequently to CMM. Incremental prediction was assessed using the C-index, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Exploratory mediation analyses evaluated circulating biomarkers related to metabolic, inflammatory, hepatic and renal pathways. Results During a median follow-up of 16.4 years, 4225 participants developed CMM. All CHG-related indices were associated with higher CMM risk, with the strongest associations observed for CHG-waist-to-height ratio (CHG-WHtR; hazard ratio [HR] per 1-standard deviation [SD] increment, 1.61; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.57–1.65) and CHG-waist circumference (CHG-WC; HR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.55–1.63). Adding each index to conventional risk models improved discrimination and risk classification. CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC showed relatively favorable predictive performance, although the absolute differences between indices were modest. In multistate analyses, associations were strongest for disease-free to T2D and CHD-to-CMM transitions. Exploratory biomarker analyses showed that baseline biomarker domains related to glycemic regulation, lipid metabolism, inflammation, and hepatic and renal function were statistically linked to these associations. Conclusions Among individuals with MASLD, CHG-related indices, particularly CHG-WHtR and CHG-WC, were associated with incident CMM and transition-specific disease progression and improved risk prediction. These readily available indices may help refine CMM risk stratification in MASLD. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is currently the leading form of chronic liver disease globally, with approximately 30–40% of adults affected [ 1 ]. Given the continued rise in metabolic diseases worldwide, MASLD prevalence is projected to surpass 55% by 2040, thereby imposing a considerable socioeconomic burden [ 1 ]. The growing recognition of MASLD as a multisystem disorder has prompted increasing interest in outcomes beyond the liver [ 2 ], especially because cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the predominant cause of mortality in this population [ 1 , 3 ]. Recent studies have further shown that MASLD is accompanied by a markedly increased comorbidity burden [ 4 ], with cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) being of particular concern [ 5 , 6 ]. CMM is generally characterized by the coexistence of at least two cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), most commonly coronary heart disease (CHD), stroke, and type 2 diabetes (T2D) [ 7 ]. Existing longitudinal evidence suggests that the progression from a disease-free state to a first CMD and subsequently to CMM is shaped by partly stage-specific factors. Hypertension, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, and a family history of cardiometabolic disease have been more strongly associated with the development of a first CMD [ 8 ], whereas smoking, physical inactivity, an unhealthy diet, harmful alcohol consumption, and socioeconomic disadvantage have been associated with progression from a first CMD to CMM [ 7 , 8 ]. Central and visceral adiposity may also contribute to both the onset and subsequent accumulation of CMDs [ 9 ]. Importantly, these CMDs are not pathophysiologically independent but share an interconnected network of metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular abnormalities. Beyond insulin resistance (IR), hepatic overproduction of atherogenic lipoproteins, chronic low-grade inflammation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, endothelial dysfunction, and a prothrombotic state may link MASLD to vascular injury, atherosclerosis, thrombosis, and deterioration of glucose homeostasis [ 1 , 10 – 13 ]. Because individuals with MASLD frequently exhibit several of these shared abnormalities, they may be particularly susceptible to progression along the CMM continuum. In this context, identifying modifiable metabolic markers associated with the onset and progression of CMM in individuals with MASLD is a key priority for both clinical practice and population health. Because of their low cost, convenience, and ability to integrate information from multiple biological processes, composite indices based on routine blood biomarkers have become increasingly attractive in epidemiological and clinical research. The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a well-established surrogate marker for insulin resistance (IR) and cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) [ 14 – 16 ]. However, in individuals with normal triglyceride (TG) levels, the TyG index may have limited predictive utility, as their atherosclerotic risk may be more closely related to cholesterol–glucose metabolic pathways than to triglyceride-mediated mechanisms [ 17 , 18 ]. In this context, the cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, and glucose (CHG) index, comprising total cholesterol (TC), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and glucose, has recently been developed as an economical and accessible composite index with cardiometabolic event prediction comparable to the TyG index [ 19 – 21 ]. Several important knowledge gaps warrant further investigation. First, most available evidence has been based on single CMD endpoints [ 19 – 30 ]. Although recent studies have reported associations of the CHG index with MASLD and with mortality among individuals with MASLD [ 31 – 34 ], whether this index predicts the development of CMM in this vulnerable population remains unknown. Second, CMM typically develops along a progressive continuum rather than occurring abruptly. This trajectory usually begins with no CMD, advances to the first CMD (FCMD), and subsequently progresses to CMM as additional CMDs accumulate [ 7 ]. Because CMM represents a more advanced clinical state than isolated CMDs and is linked to higher risks of functional decline and death [ 35 , 36 ], analyses limited to single endpoints may underestimate or obscure the role of the CHG index across CMM development. Third, given the essential role of obesity in MASLD pathogenesis [ 1 ], CHG-related adiposity-derived indices may provide additional prognostic information. Indeed, several studies have suggested that these indices may outperform the CHG index alone in predicting cardiovascular events [ 23 – 25 ]. title: Screening effect of phase angle and calf circumference in different stages of sarcopenia in patients with maintenance hemodialysis
abstract: Background Complicated testing procedures, high costs and heavy clinical workloads limit routine sarcopenia screening. Patients with different sarcopenia stages present distinct clinical manifestations, so early screening and timely intervention are essential. This study aimed to explore the screening efficiency of phase angle (PhA) and calf circumference (CC) for staged sarcopenia in maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients and develop a simple scoring tool. Methods This prospective cross-sectional study was conducted from September to December 2023 at the Wenjiang Hemodialysis Center, Department of Nephrology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China. Sarcopenia staging followed the 2019 Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) criteria. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to calculate the area under the curve. A simple scoring tool was established based on the optimal cut-off points of CC and PhA. In addition to sensitivity and specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (LR + ), and negative likelihood ratio (LR − ) were computed for each screening marker to fully characterize diagnostic efficiency. Results For possible sarcopenia, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of PhA was 0.680 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.613–0.747), with a sensitivity of 64.29% and specificity of 66.17% (cut-off value: 5.6 °). The AUC of the simple scoring tool was 0.598 (95%CI: 0.531–0.664), with a sensitivity of 53.57% and specificity of 67.67% (cut-off value: 1 point). For sarcopenia, the AUC of CC was 0.771 (95%CI: 0.605–0.937), with a sensitivity of 66.67% and specificity of 81.36% (cut-off value: 29 cm). The AUC of the simple scoring tool was 0.789 (95%CI: 0.658–0.920), with a sensitivity of 66.67% and specificity of 83.90% (cut-off value: 1 point). For severe sarcopenia, the AUC of CC was 0.880 (95%CI: 0.809–0.950), with a sensitivity of 93.33% and specificity of 73.04% (cut-off value: 30 cm). The AUC of PhA was 0.865 (95%CI: 0.773–0.957), with a sensitivity of 86.67% and specificity of 78.26% (cut-off value: 4.9 °). The AUC of the simple scoring tool was 0.911 (95%CI: 0.865–0.958), with a sensitivity of 80.00% and specificity of 90.00% (cut-off value: 1 point). Conclusions The simple scoring tool showed improved screening performance as sarcopenia severity increased, with a consistent cut-off of 1 point. CC and PhA can be used for staged sarcopenia screening in MHD outpatients. With high negative predictive values, these indicators are suitable for preliminary exclusion screening at the bedside rather than definitive diagnosis. However, given the limited number of sarcopenia cases in this single-center study, this scoring tool should be considered exploratory and requires validation in larger independent cohorts before routine clinical implementation. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2100051111), registered on 2021−09−13.
body: As of 2023, an estimated 788 million individuals aged 20 years and older worldwide were living with chronic kidney disease (CKD), with the highest burdens observed in China (152 million cases) and India (138 million cases) [ 1 ]. MHD represents one of the reliable therapeutic strategies for acute and chronic renal failure, enabling survival for millions of affected patients [ 2 ]. Nevertheless, MHD constitutes a lifelong renal replacement therapy associated with a long and arduous treatment trajectory and abundant complications [ 3 ]. Compared with the general population, patients undergoing MHD face a substantially higher risk of sarcopenia, driven by progressive renal deterioration, persistent systemic microinflammation, and long-term dialysis-induced protein-energy wasting [ 4 , 5 ]. Sarcopenia, also termed skeletal muscle loss syndrome, is a degenerative condition defined by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and reduced muscle strength [ 6 ]. As a common complication in patients receiving MHD, it increases the likelihood of multiple adverse events such as falls, fractures, and worsening physical function [ 7 – 9 ]. The global pooled prevalence of sarcopenia reaches as high as 25% among patients with CKD [ 10 ], and this proportion can range from 20% to 55% in individuals with kidney failure (CKD stage 5) [ 11 ]. Both PhA and CC have promising predictive value for sarcopenia screening among MHD patients [ 12 – 16 ], yet they differ markedly in clinical operability: CC measurement is low-cost, rapid and feasible for routine bedside screening without extra equipment or professional training, while PhA testing relies on standardized bioimpedance calibration and trained operators. Despite increased awareness of sarcopenia, screening and assessment are still infrequently performed in clinical practice. Complex diagnostic procedures, additional examination costs, radiation exposure, and increased clinical workload severely limit the recognition of sarcopenia in clinical settings and place high demands on human, material, and administrative resources. Moreover, the different stages of sarcopenia exhibit varying clinical manifestations, making early assessment and intervention particularly important. Currently, few studies have separately characterized the screening performance of PhA and CC across distinct sarcopenia stages in MHD patients, and no prior work has established a simple scoring tool integrating these two markers for staged sarcopenia screening. This study aims to identify a scientific and feasible screening tool for sarcopenia that can facilitate the rapid screening of high-risk patients at different disease stages, streamline the diagnosis of sarcopenia, reduce clinical staff workload, and thus promote the assessment of sarcopenia. This prospective cross-sectional study was conducted from September to December 2023 at the Wenjiang Hemodialysis Center, Department of Nephrology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China. The inclusion criteria were: (1) clear consciousness and intact cognitive function; (2) receiving MHD for no less than 3 months; (3) age ≥ 18 years; (4) voluntary participation in the survey. The exclusion criteria were: (1) any contraindications to bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), such as having a pacemaker, cardiovascular stent, or artificial joint; (2) pregnancy or lactation; (3) significant health changes in the past three months; (4) limb deformity or amputation; (5) cognitive impairment or psychiatric disorders. Three researchers co-designed and finalized the study protocol, with unified criteria, measurement standards and data validation procedures predefined to ensure rigorous and repeatable research. Two standardized trained researchers completed all on-site measurements and data collection; their training covered questionnaires, BIA testing and anthropometric protocols. Each participant provided written informed consent prior to structured face-to-face interviews for demographic and baseline clinical data acquisition. The questionnaire collected the following information: age, sex, dialysis duration, and history of comorbidities including diabetes and hypertension. These data were used to describe the baseline characteristics of the study population and to adjust for potential confounders in the analyses.
