title: Integrative Transcriptomic and Network Pharmacology Analysis Suggests Potential Mechanisms of Propofol in Early-Onset Preeclampsia
abstract: Purpose To investigate the mechanism of action of propofol in early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE). Patients and Methods Integrated transcriptomics and network approaches were employed to screen disease targets, drug targets, and differentially expressed genes from the GSE74341 training set (7 EOPE, 5 controls) and GSE44711 validation set (8 EOPE, 8 controls). Signature genes were further selected using machine learning algorithms (LASSO, SVM, Boruta). Immune infiltration levels were evaluated via ssGSEA and their correlations with signature genes were analyzed. Molecular docking validation of binding affinity was performed using CB-DOCK2. The expression patterns of signature genes in EOPE patients were ultimately confirmed using RT-qPCR in a clinical cohort of 36 EOPE patients and 36 healthy pregnant women. Results Nineteen potential intersection targets of propofol intervention in the EOPE were identified. Machine learning analysis further pinpointed three signature genes ( CASP1 , FLT1 , and CD68 ). Expression validation and ROC curve analysis confirmed their significant dysregulation, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 1.000, 1.000, and 0.886 in the training set and 0.891, 0.844, and 0.875 in the validation set, respectively, indicating good diagnostic performance. Immunoinfiltration analysis revealed significant alterations in 12 immune cell subsets in EOPE samples, which were closely associated with 3 signature genes. Molecular docking showed negative binding energies (from −5.0 to −5.8 kcal/mol), suggesting that propofol can spontaneously bind to all core targets with weak‑to‑moderate affinity, and the binding energy with CD68 was the lowest (–5.8 kcal/mol). RT-qPCR validation in the clinical cohort confirmed that the expression patterns of the three signature genes were consistent with the bioinformatics predictions. Conclusion This study identifies CASP1 , FLT1 , and CD68 as potential targets through which propofol may modulate EOPE-related pathways. Further mechanistic and in vivo validation studies are required.
body: Preeclampsia (PE) is a severe hypertensive disorder of pregnancy and a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality worldwide. 1 Preeclampsia exhibits two distinct subtypes: EOPE and LOPE. 2 EOPE occurs before 34 weeks of gestation and is typically more severe than the late-onset form, often accompanied by significant placental dysfunction, fetal growth restriction, and multi-organ damage. 2 , 3 Notably, there are significant differences in the underlying molecular mechanisms between early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE) and late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE). EOPE is primarily characterized by defective placentation, inadequate spiral artery remodeling, and severe angiogenic imbalance (elevated sFlt-1 and reduced PlGF). In contrast, LOPE is mainly associated with maternal cardiovascular and metabolic susceptibility. 4 , 5 Specifically, EOPE involves pronounced activation of the HIF-1α pathway, dysregulation of PI3K-Akt signaling, and upregulation of immune-inflammatory pathways (eg, increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines), distinguishing it from LOPE, which predominantly presents with maternal immune-metabolic disorders. 6–8 Currently, the etiology and pathogenesis of EOPE remain not fully elucidated, with placental developmental abnormalities widely recognized as a core signature. 9 , 10 Because of the multifactorial nature of the disease, clinical management strategies for EOPE are extremely limited. Beyond symptomatic treatment, blood pressure control, and timely termination of pregnancy, there is a lack of specific therapies capable of effectively delaying disease progression. 11 Although advances have been made in therapies targeting the sFlt-1/PlGF imbalance (eg, siRNA, ELP‑VEGF fusion protein), the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway, and immune dysregulation (eg, complement system, T cell immune regulation), most of these strategies remain in preclinical or early clinical evaluation stages. 12–14 Consequently, the exploration of novel therapeutic strategies targeting critical pathological pathways in EOPE has emerged as a pressing research priority in perinatal medicine. Propofol is a short-acting anesthetic widely used in clinical practice. 15 In addition to its well-established sedative and hypnotic effects, 16 numerous studies have revealed that propofol also exhibits off-target effects, including significant antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and vasomodulatory properties. 17–19 These pathological processes are core mechanisms in the pathogenesis of PE. 20 , 21 In macrophages, propofol inhibits hypoxia/reoxygenation-induced alveolar macrophage death via the TLR4/NF‑κB/NLRP3 signaling pathway. 22 Additionally, under lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation, propofol reduces the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (eg, TNF‑α , IL‑6 ) and nitric oxide (NO) by suppressing the ROS/Akt/IKKβ/NF‑κB signaling pathway. 23 Furthermore, propofol has been clinically applied in obstetric anesthesia for pregnant women with preeclampsia, where it maintains good hemodynamic stability during cesarean section and exhibits a favorable safety. 24 These unique pharmacological properties suggest that propofol may extend beyond its traditional anesthetic role to play a potential protective role in the pathophysiology of EOPE. Previous studies have demonstrated that propofol promotes the growth, migration, and invasion of human chorionic trophoblast HTR-8/SVneo cells. 25 However, whether propofol can target key molecules in early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE) and its underlying multi-target mechanism remain to be systematically elucidated. As an emerging research method in systems biology, network pharmacology’s “disease-gene-target-drug” interaction network analysis strategy demonstrates high consistency with the holistic principles of traditional Chinese medicine and the multi-target treatment concept for complex diseases. 26 It can integrate public database resources, predict drug targets through bioinformatics methods, and systematically elucidate the potential molecular network mechanisms underlying its intervention in complex diseases. 27 Therefore, in this study, we employed an integrative approach combining transcriptomic analysis, network pharmacology, and bioinformatics to systematically predict and identify the core targets through which propofol may intervene in EOPE. Subsequently, immune cell infiltration and GSEA analysis were performed. Molecular docking analysis confirmed the high binding affinity of propofol toward its core targets. Finally, the expression of signature genes was verified by RT-PCR in a clinical cohort and further validated in a cellular model of EOPE. This hypothesis-driven investigation provides a systematic framework for understanding the multi-target mechanisms of propofol in EOPE and offers a theoretical foundation for its potential repurposing in the management of this severe obstetric condition. Download the EOPE dataset GSE74341 (7 cases and 5 controls, training set) from the GEO database, 28 and simultaneously download dataset GSE44711 (8 cases and 8 controls, validation set). PubChem provides the chemical structures, molecular data, and SMILES strings of propofol. 29 Toxicity was subsequently evaluated using the ADMETLAB 3.0 platform. 29 The processed data were subsequently subjected to analysis using the PharmMapper server, 30 the Similarity Ensemble Approach, and the Swiss Target Prediction database. 31 Additionally, partial data were retrieved using the drug name from the CTD ( ). Finally, the drug targets were obtained by deduplicating and merging the data from these four sources. https://ctdbase.org The disease targets of EOPE were predicted by integrating data from the GeneCards database, 32 the OMIM database, 33 the DisGeNET database, 34 and the DrugBank database. 35 The final target set was obtained by deduplicating and merging the data from these sources. The R package limma (version 3.64.1) was applied to perform differential expression analysis, comparing gene expression profiles between the case and control groups. Differentially expressed mRNAs were identified using thresholds of P.adj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 0.5. The ggplot2 package (version 3.3.5) was employed to generate a volcano plot. The intersection of drug targets, disease targets, and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) was then computed to derive the final differential targets for this study. To better elucidate the potential biological roles of the differentially expressed targets, the “clusterProfiler” package 36 (Version 4.6.2) was utilized to conduct GO and KEGG enrichment analyses, and the Benjamini–Hochberg method was applied for multiple testing correction. Significantly enriched terms were identified with a threshold of P.adj < 0.05 (FDR < 0.05). To elucidate potential interactions among the differentially expressed targets, we constructed a PPI network using the STRING database, 37 with a confidence score threshold set at >0.4. To identify hub targets in the PPI network, we utilized the cytoHubba plugin of Cytoscape 38 (Version 3.9.1), comprehensively applying four topological analysis algorithms: MCC, MNC, Degree, and EPC. The intersection of the top 20 targets ranked by each algorithm yielded 15 common targets, which were defined as key candidate targets. Based on the aforementioned candidate key targets, Boruta, SVM, and LASSO regression were employed to perform signature selection on the candidate hub targets. We employed the Boruta package (Version 8.0.0) to identify signature targets of consistent importance. The final selection was based on their robustness across multiple iterations. Subsequently, the SVM algorithm provided by the R package e1071 (Version 1.7–16) was employed to screen important genes. Finally, LASSO regression was performed using the R package glmnet (version 4.1–7) with family = “binomial” and 10-fold cross-validation for signature targets selection. The screening results from these three algorithms were integrated through Venn diagram analysis, with the intersecting targets identified as signature targets. We incorporated the aforementioned signature targets into the GSE74341 and GSE44711 datasets for expression analysis. Targets that were significantly and consistently dysregulated across both datasets were defined as candidate signature targets. To assess the discriminatory power of the candidate key targets, ROC curves were plotted for both the GSE74341 and GSE44711 datasets, utilizing 39 (Version 1.18.4). To characterize the immune landscape, we applied the ssGSEA algorithm from the “GSVA” package 40 to profile the infiltration of 28 immune cell types across patient groups compared to normal controls. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to assess the P-values for differences in immune cell infiltration proportions between disease samples and control samples. The “corrplot” package (Version 0.92) was employed to evaluate the correlations among differentially expressed immune cells. The “psych” package (Version 2.3.9) was employed to assess the association between differentially expressed immune cells and key targets. For functional annotation of the screened key targets, enrichment analysis against the KEGG pathway database was performed. This analysis leveraged the gene set (c2.cp.kegg_legacy.v2023.2.Hs.symbols.gmt) as the background in the training set. The “psych” R package was employed to perform Spearman correlation analysis between each key target and the remaining genes, yielding correlation coefficients. Subsequently, the genes were ranked based on their correlation coefficients in descending order. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of the ranked results was conducted with the “clusterProfiler” R package. Statistical significance was determined using the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) method to control the false discovery rate (FDR), with a cutoff of P.adj < 0.05. Additionally, only pathways with |Normalized Enrichment Score (NES)| > 1 were considered significantly enriched. The top five representative pathways for each signature gene were selected based on P.adj ranking for visualization. Molecular docking was performed on the CB-DOCK2 platform 41 to assess the binding between propofol and key targets. Protein structures were downloaded from the RCSB PDB, and the propofol structure was acquired from PubChem. The binding free energy was evaluated, and the results were visualized using PyMOL and Discovery Studio. A total of 36 patients diagnosed with EOPE at our hospital were enrolled as the study group, with a mean age of 30.37 ± 4.10 years and a mean gestational age of 28.78 ± 5.03 weeks. Thirty-six healthy pregnant women in the first and second trimesters undergoing routine prenatal examinations during the same period were selected as the control group, with a mean age of 29.40 ± 3.60 years and a mean gestational age of 29.21 ± 4.68 weeks. Sample size calculation was performed using G*Power 3.1 software. Based on preliminary data and published literature, the expected effect size (Cohen’s d) for the three signature genes ( CASP1 , FLT1 , CD68 ) was approximately 0.9. Setting α = 0.05 (two-tailed) and power (1-β) = 0.90, the minimum required sample size was 27 per group. To account for potential dropouts or missing data (10–15%), we enrolled 36 participants per group, yielding an actual power of 0.94. On the first morning after diagnosis of EOPE, 3 mL of fasting peripheral venous blood was obtained from the cases. Simultaneously, 3 mL of fasting venous blood was obtained from the control group during routine health examinations. This research was conducted strictly in accordance with the principles set forth in the Helsinki Declaration. Following approval by the Ethics Committee of Weifang Brain Hospital, all voluntarily enrolled participants provided written informed consent, and all collected samples were stored at −80°C for subsequent analysis. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and cultured in DMEM high-glucose medium (HyClone) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich) under standard conditions at 37°C in a 5% CO2 humidified incubator (Thermo Scientific). For all experiments, cells were harvested during the logarithmic growth phase to ensure optimal metabolic activity. The cell treatment groups were as follows: (1) Control group: Cultured in normal medium; (2) EOPE model group: Treated with medium containing 10 ng/mL TNF-α for 24 h to simulate the inflammatory and endothelial dysfunction associated with EOPE; (3) EOPE model + Propofol intervention group: Co-treated with 100 µM propofol 42 (Sigma-Aldrich) in the presence of 10 ng/mL TNF-α for 24 h. The propofol stock solution was dissolved in DMSO (Sigma-Aldrich). Different cell seeding densities were employed according to the experimental requirements: 1×10 5 cells/well in 6-well plates for RNA extraction and apoptosis analysis, and 5×10 3 cells/well in 96-well plates for CCK-8 assays. Total RNA was isolated from serum and cells using the RNAprep Pure Blood Kit (DP443, Tiangen) and TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen), respectively. Subsequently, RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA with the PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (TaKaRa). Gene expression was quantified by qPCR on an ABI 7900 system using GAPDH for normalization, with relative expression calculated via the 2 −ΔΔCt method. All RT-qPCR experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates, each containing three technical replicates. Independent-sample t -test (normal distribution) or Mann–Whitney U -test (non-normal distribution) was used to compare gene expression differences between groups. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05, and primer sequences are provided in Table 1 . And the experimental procedures strictly followed the kit protocol. For the cell experiments, HUVECs were treated under the following conditions: control group (normal culture medium), EOPE model group (medium containing 10 ng/mL TNF-α for 24 h), and EOPE + propofol group (medium containing both 10 ng/mL TNF-α and 100 μM propofol for 24 h). After treatment, cell culture supernatants from each group were collected and centrifuged at 1,000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C to remove cell debris. The supernatants were then used to quantify sFlt-1 protein levels using the same brand of human sFlt-1 ELISA kit. Each experiment was performed with three independent biological replicates. The absorbance (optical density) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader, and the concentration of sFlt-1 was calculated based on a standard curve. We examined the influence of propofol on TNF-α -driven HUVEC proliferation utilizing a CCK-8 assay kit (Beyotime). After 24 h of treatment as described above, 10 µL of CCK-8 solution was added to each well, followed by incubation at 37°C for 2 h. The optical density (OD) of each well was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek, USA). The apoptosis of cells was analyzed by flow cytometry using Annexin V-FITC/PI double staining (KeyGen Biotech). Following 24-hour treatments, cells were detached with EDTA-free trypsin, washed with PBS, and processed for apoptosis analysis. According to the manufacturer’s protocol, cells were resuspended in 195 µL Binding Buffer and stained with 5 µL Annexin V-FITC plus 10 µL PI in the dark for 15 minutes. Flow cytometric analysis was performed using a BD FACSCanto II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences). The forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) were used to gate the main cell population, excluding debris and doublets. A total of 10,000 events within the viable cell gate were collected for each sample. Apoptosis analysis was then conducted by gating on Annexin V-FITC vs propidium iodide (PI) dot plots, where early apoptotic cells were defined as Annexin V-FITC positive and PI negative (lower right quadrant), late apoptotic cells as Annexin V-FITC positive and PI positive (upper right quadrant), and necrotic cells as Annexin V-FITC negative and PI positive (upper left quadrant). The total apoptotic rate was calculated as the sum of early and late apoptotic cells. All statistical analyses and visualizations in this study were performed using R software (version 4.2.1) and GraphPad Prism 9.0. Continuous variables were tested for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Data conforming to a normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and comparisons between two groups were conducted using the independent-samples t -test. Non-normally distributed data were presented as median (interquartile range, IQR), and the Mann–Whitney U -test was applied for inter-group comparisons. Categorical variables were described as counts or percentages, and the chi-square test was used for group comparisons. For bioinformatics analyses, differential gene expression was determined with thresholds of adjusted P-value (P.adj) < 0.05 and |log2(fold change, FC)| > 0.5. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were considered statistically significant at P.adj < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg correction). The diagnostic performance of signature genes was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated to quantify discriminatory ability. Correlations between immune cell infiltration and signature genes were analyzed using Spearman correlation coefficient. In vitro cell experiments were performed in triplicate, and results were presented as mean ± SD. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was used for comparisons among multiple groups. A two-sided P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant in all analyses. Propofol exhibited high lipophilicity, low bioconcentration potential, and moderate toxicity to microorganisms and specific biological species. These properties collectively indicate its potential behavior and impact in the environment and living organisms. title: Effects of a Nurse-Led Diabetes Perception Intervention Delivered via a Mobile Messaging Platform (LINE) on Glycemic Control and Patient Outcomes Among Adults with Diabetes and Poorly Controlled Glucose: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: Background Suboptimal glycemic control remains a major challenge among adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). Illness perceptions may influence diabetes self-management behaviors and glycemic control. Purpose To evaluate the effects of a nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via a mobile messaging platform (LINE) on glycemic control, illness perceptions, and patient satisfaction among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. Methods A randomized controlled trial was conducted among 102 adults aged 30–59 years with T2D and poorly controlled glucose [HbA1c 7.5–9.0% or FPG ≥130 mg/dL]. Participants were randomly assigned to either a nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE plus standard care (n = 51) or standard care alone (n = 51). HbA1c, FPG, and patient satisfaction were assessed at baseline and week 13, and illness perceptions at baseline, week 6, and week 13. Data were analyzed using analysis of covariance and repeated-measures analysis of variance. Results Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. At week 13, after adjustment for baseline values, the intervention group demonstrated significantly lower HbA1c (7.26% vs 7.91%; mean difference = −0.65%, 95% CI: −1.14 to −0.17; p = 0.008), FPG (123.12 vs 164.36 mg/dL; mean difference = −41.24 mg/dL, 95% CI: −57.37 to −25.11; p <0.001), and illness perception scores (31.90 vs 38.39; mean difference = −6.49, 95% CI: −9.58 to −3.40; p <0.001), together with higher patient satisfaction scores (63.90 vs 58.63; mean difference = 5.27, 95% CI: 2.38 to 8.17; p <0.001), compared with the control group. Conclusion The nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE significantly improved glycemic control, illness perceptions, and patient satisfaction among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. These findings support the potential integration of this accessible and feasible nursing intervention into diabetes self-management support in clinical practice.
body: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) is a growing global health concern, currently affecting an estimated 589 million adults, with projections increasing to 853 million by 2050. 1 , 2 In Thailand, the prevalence of T2D continues to rise, particularly among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. 3 On average, individuals diagnosed with diabetes incur healthcare expenditures that are approximately 2.6 times higher than those without the condition. 4 , 5 Poor glycemic control in individuals with T2D is associated with an increased risk of serious complications, reduced quality of life, and substantial healthcare costs. 6–8 Achieving optimal glycemic control, typically defined as a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level below 7%, requires not only pharmacologic therapy but also sustained lifestyle modifications and effective self-management behaviors. 9 Misconceptions about diabetes—such as perceiving limited control over their condition—can undermine self-care efforts and adversely affect glycemic outcomes. Consequently, adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose often require structured support to modify their illness perceptions and adopt healthier dietary and physical activity behaviors. 10–12 Dietary control plays a central role in glycemic management, 13 yet limited diabetes knowledge, competing work demands, and time constraints frequently lead to inappropriate eating patterns. 14–16 Carbohydrate counting is often perceived as complex and disruptive to daily routines. 17 In Thailand, consumption of high-glycemic rice and sugar-sweetened beverages further contributes to excessive carbohydrate intake and suboptimal glycemic control. 18 , 19 Physical activity is essential for enhancing insulin sensitivity and reducing cardiovascular risk. 20 , 21 However, adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose commonly encounter barriers such as work fatigue, limited motivation, and diabetes-related symptoms. 22–25 Insufficient physical activity remains a key factor contributing to poor glycemic outcomes in this population. Illness perceptions have been shown to significantly influence diabetes self-care behaviors and long-term outcomes. 26 , 27 Guided by the Common-Sense Model of Self-Regulation (CSM) 28 , individuals’ beliefs about their illness affect coping strategies, lifestyle choices, and adherence to treatment recommendations. Adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose frequently hold inaccurate or negative beliefs that hinder self-management, leading to poor dietary control, reduced physical activity, and inadequate glycemic regulation. Addressing and reshaping these perceptions is essential to support behavior changes and improve disease management. 29 , 30 Mobile phone–based interventions show promise in supporting diabetes self-management by providing convenient access to guidance on diet, physical activity, medication adherence, and monitoring. 31 , 32 In addition, previous studies have reported improvements in biochemical outcomes, particularly HbA1c and other metabolic parameters, following digital and mobile health interventions among people with diabetes. 33 , 34 However, their adoption is often hindered by limited digital literacy, preference for free and simple applications, unclear instructions, and time-consuming data entry. 35 , 36 LINE, a widely used mobile messaging platform in Thailand and several Asian countries, provides a practical channel for delivering health interventions. Its widespread use, free access, and familiarity among users may facilitate communication between healthcare providers and patients. In addition, features such as text messaging, video calls, reminders, and multimedia sharing enable the delivery of tailored education and ongoing support, making the platform well suited for implementing nurse-led behavioral interventions. Interventions addressing illness perceptions alongside dietary and physical activity behaviors have demonstrated effectiveness in improving diabetes outcomes. 37 , 38 Nevertheless, many of these interventions rely on face-to-face delivery with limited follow-up, posing challenges related to time, staffing, and cost. 39–43 Given the increasing availability of digital communication platforms, nurse-led interventions that integrate motivational strategies with personalized education may offer a scalable and feasible approach to improving diabetes self-management. Informed by the Common-Sense Model of Self-Regulation, this study implemented a nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via a mobile messaging platform (LINE) designed to improve illness perceptions, promote behavior change, and enhance glycemic outcomes among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose in an urban setting. The intervention incorporated dietary and physical activity guidance as well as motivational support to facilitate sustained self-management. Delivered through the LINE platform, the intervention provided structured behavioral guidance and ongoing motivational support. This study adds to the growing evidence on the effects of nurse-led diabetes perception interventions delivered via LINE in improving both glycemic control and patient-reported outcomes among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. This study employed a two-arm, parallel randomized controlled trial to examine the effects of a nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE on glycemic control, illness perceptions, and patient satisfaction with nursing care. The intervention focused on modifying illness perceptions and supporting behavioral change through personalized dietary and physical activity guidance combined with motivational strategies. The trial was registered with the Thailand Clinical Trial Registry and conducted in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines 44 ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 CONSORT Flow Diagram of Participant Progress Through the Trial. The diagram illustrates the number of participants assessed for eligibility, randomized, allocated to interventions, followed up, and analysis. CONSORT flow diagram illustrating participant progress through a trial. Enrollment starts with 141 assessed for eligibility. 39 are excluded: 32 not meeting criteria and 7 declining participation. 102 are randomized into two groups. Allocation assigns 51 to the intervention group, all receiving the intervention and 51 to the control group, all receiving standard diabetes care. Follow-up shows 1 lost from the intervention group and 2 lost from the control group due to geographical movement. Analysis includes 50 from the intervention group and 49 from the control group, with exclusions due to geographical movement: 1 from the intervention group and 2 from the control group. CONSORT diagram: participant progress in enrollment, allocation, follow-up and analysis stages. Abbreviations : CONSORT, Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials. CONSORT Flow Diagram of Participant Progress Through the Trial. The diagram illustrates the number of participants assessed for eligibility, randomized, allocated to interventions, followed up, and analysis. This study was conducted in the diabetes clinic of the medical outpatient department at a 1200-bed tertiary care hospital located in a metropolitan area of Bangkok, Thailand. The clinic provides routine diabetes assessment, medical follow-up, lifestyle counseling, and laboratory monitoring, serving a large and diverse population of adults with T2D. The clinical environment allowed for consistent delivery of standard care and facilitated the integration of the nurse-led LINE-based intervention within existing service workflows. Adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose were eligible to participate if they met the following criteria: (a) aged 30–59 years; (b) diagnosed with T2D and poorly controlled glucose, defined as HbA1c 7.5–9.0% or fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥130 mg/dL; (c) no changes in insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications for at least 3 months prior to enrollment, with no restrictions on specific drug classes; (d) able to communicate in Thai; and (e) able to use a smartphone with the LINE platform. Participants with severe medical conditions that could interfere with participation were excluded according to the study protocol, including those with active malignancy; chronic kidney disease stage 4–5 (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ); unstable medical conditions; recent acute cardiac events within 6 months (eg, myocardial infarction or hospitalization for heart failure); severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mmHg); or severe psychiatric disorders affecting adherence. Participants were withdrawn if they experienced any of the following during the study period: (a) adjustment of glucose-lowering medications; (b) hospitalization that interfered with study participation; or (c) development of severe conditions such as stroke, severe hypertension, or diabetic ketoacidosis. All participants continued to receive standard diabetes care under routine clinical supervision. No changes in glucose-lowering medications occurred during follow-up, reducing the likelihood that observed HbA1c changes were attributable to pharmacological adjustments. Potential participants attending routine follow-up visits at the diabetes clinic were approached by the research team, provided with study information, and invited to participate. The first participant was recruited on 20 July 2023, and recruitment continued until 5 October 2023 at the hospital. The sample size was calculated based on a previous study by Boonjun and Pongpatanawut, 45 which examined the effects of a carbohydrate-counting program among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. In that study, the mean HbA1c levels in the intervention and control groups were 7.62 (SD = 0.9) and 8.31 (SD = 1.3), respectively. Rosner’s formula 46 for comparing two independent means was applied to estimate the required sample size, as follows: n = (Z 1 –α/ 2 + Z 1 –β) 2 (σ 1 2 + σ 2 2 )/(μ 1 – μ 2 ) 2 Where: μ 1 , μ 2 = means of the two groups σ 1 2 , σ 2 2 = variances of the two groups Z 1 –α/ 2 = 1.96 for a two-sided test Z (1 – β) = 0.842 for 80% power Substitution into the formula produced an estimated sample size of 41.75 participants per group. Based on a significance level of 0.05 and power of 0.80, the minimum required sample was 84 participants. To account for an anticipated 20% dropout rate, the final target sample size was increased to 102 participants, with 51 allocated to the intervention group and 51 to the control group using block randomization. Adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose attending routine follow-up visits were invited to participate after receiving detailed information about the study, and written informed consent was obtained prior to baseline assessment. Participants were randomly allocated using a parallel-group design with a 1:1 allocation ratio. A computer-generated randomization sequence with a block size of four was used to ensure balanced group assignment and reduce allocation bias. Participants were assigned to either the intervention group or the control group. Allocation concealment was maintained using sequentially numbered, sealed, opaque envelopes prepared according to the predetermined randomization sequence. After completion of baseline assessments, participants opened the envelope to reveal their group assignment. Recruitment and randomization continued until the target sample size of 102 participants was achieved, with 51 participants allocated to each group. Due to the nature of the behavioral and educational intervention, blinding of participants and the intervention-delivering nurse was not feasible. However, to minimize potential assessment bias, an outcome assessor was blinded to group allocation throughout the data collection process. Statistical analyses were conducted using coded group labels to further reduce the risk of analytical bias. The nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE was developed to modify illness perceptions and promote sustainable behavior change through personalized education and motivational strategies, thereby improving glycemic control among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. The intervention consisted of four structured educational sessions delivered during weeks 1–4 via face-to-face and video-based communication, followed by two telephone follow-up sessions at weeks 7 and 11 for reinforcement and support. The LINE platform was used to facilitate communication, deliver educational materials, provide reminders, and enable ongoing interaction between nurses and participants. Participants received the intervention during routine clinic visits. Supplementary self-management information and reinforcement materials were subsequently delivered via LINE, allowing participants to access the information repeatedly as needed. Participants could also communicate with the nurse researcher through LINE during working hours for additional questions or clarification. The weekly structure, core contents, duration, and mode of delivery of the nurse-led diabetes perception intervention via LINE are summarized in . Supplementary Table S1 Intervention adherence was assessed using attendance records for the educational sessions, completion of follow-up telephone calls, and LINE-based activity logs, including message interaction and participant engagement throughout the intervention period. Participants in the intervention group were encouraged to attend all four educational sessions and complete scheduled follow-up telephone calls. Those who missed intervention activities were contacted by the researcher to promote continued participation and minimize attrition. Participants in the control group received standard diabetes care, which included routine medical treatment, laboratory testing, regular endocrinologist follow-up visits, and individualized diabetes education provided by the healthcare team at the diabetes clinic. The following questionnaires were used for data collection in this study. A demographic and health information form was used to collect participants’ personal and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, educational level, employment status, duration of diabetes, and relevant health-related characteristics. The Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire (BIPQ) was used to assess diabetes-related illness perceptions. 47 The instrument evaluates patients’ cognitive and emotional representations of illness across key domains, including consequences, timeline, personal control, treatment control, identity, concern, and emotional response. The BIPQ consists of eight scored items rated on an 11-point rating scale ranging from 0 (“never/rarely”) to 10 (“very severely”), as well as one open-ended item assessing perceived causes of diabetes. Scores for items 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7 are summed, while items 3 and 4 are reverse scored, yielding a total score range of 0 to 80. Higher scores indicate more negative illness perceptions associated with maladaptive coping, whereas lower scores reflect more accurate illness perceptions and adaptive coping behaviors. The BIPQ was translated into Thai, followed by back-translation and cultural adaptation by Sowattanangoon. 48 The Thai version employs an 11-point rating scale with a right-triangle visual layout to enhance ease of use. The content validity index was appropriately established among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose, demonstrating good internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.75 in the original version 47 and 0.95 in the current study. Patient Satisfaction with Nursing Care Questionnaire developed by Suwisith and Hanucharurnkul 49 was used to assess patient satisfaction with nursing care in this study. This self-administered instrument evaluates satisfaction across three domains: empathy, service quality, and professional competence. It consisted of 15 items rated on a five-point rating scale ranging from 1 (“highly dissatisfied”) to 5 (“highly satisfied”), with total scores ranging from 15 to 75. Higher scores indicate greater satisfaction with nursing care. The questionnaire demonstrated strong content validity among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose and high internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.94 in the original version 49 and 0.95 in the present study. The nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE was piloted with five individuals resembling the target population of adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose to assess feasibility, including intervention procedures, assessment processes, duration, and timing. Feedback from the pilot phase was used to refine the intervention content and delivery procedures prior to study implementation. To ensure intervention quality and consistency, the principal investigator (PI) was the sole provider of nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE according to a standardized protocol. This approach minimized variability in intervention delivery and supported intervention fidelity throughout the study. Data were collected using validated instruments and standardized procedures to ensure data quality and reliability. The intervention was considered low risk. Participants were encouraged to engage in physical activity appropriate to their individual health status, and guidance emphasized safe exercise practices. Participants were monitored for any concerns related to intervention participation, and no adverse events were reported. Several measures were implemented to ensure participant privacy, confidentiality, and appropriate communication throughout the intervention period. Participants used their own password-protected mobile phones to communicate with the researcher through individual LINE accounts, and no group chats were used. Communication was conducted only between the researcher and participants during working hours. No highly sensitive personal health information or detailed medical records were transmitted through the application. All study data were stored separately in password-protected research files accessible only to authorized research personnel. Eligibility screening was conducted based on predefined inclusion criteria, and written informed consent was obtained from eligible participants prior to data collection. Baseline assessments were then completed by a research assistant who was blinded to group allocation. At baseline, demographic and health information, illness perceptions, and patient satisfaction with nursing care were assessed in both the intervention and control groups before the intervention commenced. A total of 102 participants were enrolled and randomized, with 51 participants assigned to the intervention group and 51 to the control group. Participants in the intervention group received the nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE in addition to standard diabetes care, whereas participants in the control group received standard diabetes care alone. At week 6, illness perceptions were reassessed using an online questionnaire administered via Google Forms and distributed to participants through LINE by a research assistant blinded to group allocation. At week 13, participants again completed the online illness perception assessment. At the same time point, glycemic outcomes, including HbA1c and FPG, were extracted from medical records. Patient satisfaction with nursing care was also assessed at week 13. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 25.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Statistical significance was set at a p value of <0.05. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic and health-related characteristics, including frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, and means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs) …

This study employed a two-arm, parallel randomized controlled trial to examine the effects of a nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE on glycemic control, illness perceptions, and patient satisfaction with nursing care. The intervention focused on modifying illness perceptions and supporting behavioral change through personalized dietary and physical activity guidance combined with motivational strategies. The trial was registered with the Thailand Clinical Trial Registry and conducted in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) guidelines 44 ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 CONSORT Flow Diagram of Participant Progress Through the Trial. The diagram illustrates the number of participants assessed for eligibility, randomized, allocated to interventions, followed up, and analysis. CONSORT flow diagram illustrating participant progress through a trial. Enrollment starts with 141 assessed for eligibility. 39 are excluded: 32 not meeting criteria and 7 declining participation. 102 are randomized into two groups. Allocation assigns 51 to the intervention group, all receiving the intervention and 51 to the control group, all receiving standard diabetes care. Follow-up shows 1 lost from the intervention group and 2 lost from the control group due to geographical movement. Analysis includes 50 from the intervention group and 49 from the control group, with exclusions due to geographical movement: 1 from the intervention group and 2 from the control group. CONSORT Flow Diagram of Participant Progress Through the Trial. The diagram illustrates the number of participants assessed for eligibility, randomized, allocated to interventions, followed up, and analysis. This study was conducted in the diabetes clinic of the medical outpatient department at a 1200-bed tertiary care hospital located in a metropolitan area of Bangkok, Thailand. The clinic provides routine diabetes assessment, medical follow-up, lifestyle counseling, and laboratory monitoring, serving a large and diverse population of adults with T2D. The clinical environment allowed for consistent delivery of standard care and facilitated the integration of the nurse-led LINE-based intervention within existing service workflows. Adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose were eligible to participate if they met the following criteria: (a) aged 30–59 years; (b) diagnosed with T2D and poorly controlled glucose, defined as HbA1c 7.5–9.0% or fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥130 mg/dL; (c) no changes in insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications for at least 3 months prior to enrollment, with no restrictions on specific drug classes; (d) able to communicate in Thai; and (e) able to use a smartphone with the LINE platform. Participants with severe medical conditions that could interfere with participation were excluded according to the study protocol, including those with active malignancy; chronic kidney disease stage 4–5 (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ); unstable medical conditions; recent acute cardiac events within 6 months (eg, myocardial infarction or hospitalization for heart failure); severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mmHg); or severe psychiatric disorders affecting adherence. Participants were withdrawn if they experienced any of the following during the study period: (a) adjustment of glucose-lowering medications; (b) hospitalization that interfered with study participation; or (c) development of severe conditions such as stroke, severe hypertension, or diabetic ketoacidosis. All participants continued to receive standard diabetes care under routine clinical supervision. No changes in glucose-lowering medications occurred during follow-up, reducing the likelihood that observed HbA1c changes were attributable to pharmacological adjustments. Potential participants attending routine follow-up visits at the diabetes clinic were approached by the research team, provided with study information, and invited to participate. The first participant was recruited on 20 July 2023, and recruitment continued until 5 October 2023 at the hospital. The sample size was calculated based on a previous study by Boonjun and Pongpatanawut, 45 which examined the effects of a carbohydrate-counting program among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. In that study, the mean HbA1c levels in the intervention and control groups were 7.62 (SD = 0.9) and 8.31 (SD = 1.3), respectively. Rosner’s formula 46 for comparing two independent means was applied to estimate the required sample size, as follows: n = (Z 1 –α/ 2 + Z 1 –β) 2 (σ 1 2 + σ 2 2 )/(μ 1 – μ 2 ) 2 Where: μ 1 , μ 2 = means of the two groups σ 1 2 , σ 2 2 = variances of the two groups Z 1 –α/ 2 = 1.96 for a two-sided test Z (1 – β) = 0.842 for 80% power Substitution into the formula produced an estimated sample size of 41.75 participants per group. Based on a significance level of 0.05 and power of 0.80, the minimum required sample was 84 participants. To account for an anticipated 20% dropout rate, the final target sample size was increased to 102 participants, with 51 allocated to the intervention group and 51 to the control group using block randomization. Adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose attending routine follow-up visits were invited to participate after receiving detailed information about the study, and written informed consent was obtained prior to baseline assessment. Participants were randomly allocated using a parallel-group design with a 1:1 allocation ratio. A computer-generated randomization sequence with a block size of four was used to ensure balanced group assignment and reduce allocation bias. Participants were assigned to either the intervention group or the control group. Allocation concealment was maintained using sequentially numbered, sealed, opaque envelopes prepared according to the predetermined randomization sequence. After completion of baseline assessments, participants opened the envelope to reveal their group assignment. Recruitment and randomization continued until the target sample size of 102 participants was achieved, with 51 participants allocated to each group. Due to the nature of the behavioral and educational intervention, blinding of participants and the intervention-delivering nurse was not feasible. However, to minimize potential assessment bias, an outcome assessor was blinded to group allocation throughout the data collection process. Statistical analyses were conducted using coded group labels to further reduce the risk of analytical bias. The nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE was developed to modify illness perceptions and promote sustainable behavior change through personalized education and motivational strategies, thereby improving glycemic control among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose. The intervention consisted of four structured educational sessions delivered during weeks 1–4 via face-to-face and video-based communication, followed by two telephone follow-up sessions at weeks 7 and 11 for reinforcement and support. The LINE platform was used to facilitate communication, deliver educational materials, provide reminders, and enable ongoing interaction between nurses and participants. Participants received the intervention during routine clinic visits. Supplementary self-management information and reinforcement materials were subsequently delivered via LINE, allowing participants to access the information repeatedly as needed. Participants could also communicate with the nurse researcher through LINE during working hours for additional questions or clarification. The weekly structure, core contents, duration, and mode of delivery of the nurse-led diabetes perception intervention via LINE are summarized in . Supplementary Table S1 Intervention adherence was assessed using attendance records for the educational sessions, completion of follow-up telephone calls, and LINE-based activity logs, including message interaction and participant engagement throughout the intervention period. Participants in the intervention group were encouraged to attend all four educational sessions and complete scheduled follow-up telephone calls. Those who missed intervention activities were contacted by the researcher to promote continued participation and minimize attrition. Participants in the control group received standard diabetes care, which included routine medical treatment, laboratory testing, regular endocrinologist follow-up visits, and individualized diabetes education provided by the healthcare team at the diabetes clinic. The following questionnaires were used for data collection in this study. A demographic and health information form was used to collect participants’ personal and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, educational level, employment status, duration of diabetes, and relevant health-related characteristics. The Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire (BIPQ) was used to assess diabetes-related illness perceptions. 47 The instrument evaluates patients’ cognitive and emotional representations of illness across key domains, including consequences, timeline, personal control, treatment control, identity, concern, and emotional response. The BIPQ consists of eight scored items rated on an 11-point rating scale ranging from 0 (“never/rarely”) to 10 (“very severely”), as well as one open-ended item assessing perceived causes of diabetes. Scores for items 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7 are summed, while items 3 and 4 are reverse scored, yielding a total score range of 0 to 80. Higher scores indicate more negative illness perceptions associated with maladaptive coping, whereas lower scores reflect more accurate illness perceptions and adaptive coping behaviors. The BIPQ was translated into Thai, followed by back-translation and cultural adaptation by Sowattanangoon. 48 The Thai version employs an 11-point rating scale with a right-triangle visual layout to enhance ease of use. The content validity index was appropriately established among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose, demonstrating good internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.75 in the original version 47 and 0.95 in the current study. Patient Satisfaction with Nursing Care Questionnaire developed by Suwisith and Hanucharurnkul 49 was used to assess patient satisfaction with nursing care in this study. This self-administered instrument evaluates satisfaction across three domains: empathy, service quality, and professional competence. It consisted of 15 items rated on a five-point rating scale ranging from 1 (“highly dissatisfied”) to 5 (“highly satisfied”), with total scores ranging from 15 to 75. Higher scores indicate greater satisfaction with nursing care. The questionnaire demonstrated strong content validity among adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose and high internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.94 in the original version 49 and 0.95 in the present study. The nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE was piloted with five individuals resembling the target population of adults with T2D and poorly controlled glucose to assess feasibility, including intervention procedures, assessment processes, duration, and timing. Feedback from the pilot phase was used to refine the intervention content and delivery procedures prior to study implementation. To ensure intervention quality and consistency, the principal investigator (PI) was the sole provider of nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE according to a standardized protocol. This approach minimized variability in intervention delivery and supported intervention fidelity throughout the study. Data were collected using validated instruments and standardized procedures to ensure data quality and reliability. The intervention was considered low risk. Participants were encouraged to engage in physical activity appropriate to their individual health status, and guidance emphasized safe exercise practices. Participants were monitored for any concerns related to intervention participation, and no adverse events were reported. Several measures were implemented to ensure participant privacy, confidentiality, and appropriate communication throughout the intervention period. Participants used their own password-protected mobile phones to communicate with the researcher through individual LINE accounts, and no group chats were used. Communication was conducted only between the researcher and participants during working hours. No highly sensitive personal health information or detailed medical records were transmitted through the application. All study data were stored separately in password-protected research files accessible only to authorized research personnel. Eligibility screening was conducted based on predefined inclusion criteria, and written informed consent was obtained from eligible participants prior to data collection. Baseline assessments were then completed by a research assistant who was blinded to group allocation. At baseline, demographic and health information, illness perceptions, and patient satisfaction with nursing care were assessed in both the intervention and control groups before the intervention commenced. A total of 102 participants were enrolled and randomized, with 51 participants assigned to the intervention group and 51 to the control group. Participants in the intervention group received the nurse-led diabetes perception intervention delivered via LINE in addition to standard diabetes care, whereas participants in the control group received standard diabetes care alone. At week 6, illness perceptions were reassessed using an online questionnaire administered via Google Forms and distributed to participants through LINE by a research assistant blinded to group allocation. At week 13, participants again completed the online illness perception assessment. At the same time point, glycemic outcomes, including HbA1c and FPG, were extracted from medical records. Patient satisfaction with nursing care was also assessed at week 13. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 25.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Statistical significance was set at a p value of <0.05. title: Dose-Finding of Alfentanil for Hysteroscopy Under Remimazolam Sedation in Obese and Normal-Weight Patients: An Up-and-Down Trial
abstract: Background Hysteroscopy is a minimally invasive procedure with rapid recovery. However, obesity may alter opioid pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, and optimal alfentanil dosing remains uncertain. This study estimated the median effective dose (ED 50 ) and explored the 95% effective dose (ED 95 ) of alfentanil for suppressing predefined procedural responses during hysteroscopy under remimazolam sedation in obese and normal-weight patients. Methods This was an up-and-down sequential allocation trial. Patients were classified as obese or normal-weight according to body mass index (BMI). Recruitment and dose allocation were conducted independently within each group until seven crossover pairs were obtained. Alfentanil was administered initially at 10 μg/kg, with subsequent doses adjusted using a 1 μg/kg step size according to the preceding patient’s response. Remimazolam was administered as a 0.4 mg/kg bolus followed by infusion at 1 mg/kg/h, titrated to maintain a bispectral index (BIS) of 40–60. The ED50 was initially estimated using the modified Dixon up-and-down method, followed by probit regression to estimate model-derived ED 50 and exploratory ED 95 . Results Sixty patients (31 normal-weight, 29 obese) were enrolled. Probit regression estimated an ED 50 of 9.71 μg/kg (95% confidence interval [CI], 7.81–12.26) in obese patients and 13.67 μg/kg (95% CI, 12.77–15.07) in normal-weight patients (P = 0.001). The corresponding ED 95 estimates were 12.57 μg/kg (95% CI, 10.92–28.28) and 16.24 μg/kg (95% CI, 14.92–21.48), respectively. The wider confidence interval for ED 95 in obese patients indicated limited precision. Conclusion The total-body-weight (TBW)-normalized ED 50 of alfentanil was significantly lower in obese than in normal-weight patients (P = 0.001). The ED 95 estimates are model-based and carry substantial uncertainty; no formal hypothesis test was performed for ED 95 comparisons. Close respiratory monitoring and individualized titration remain necessary.
body: Hysteroscopy is a well-established minimally invasive technique for the diagnosis of intrauterine pathologies. 1 , 2 Given its short procedural duration and rapid recovery profile, short-acting anesthetic regimens that allow for rapid onset while preserving spontaneous respiration are generally preferred. 3 Patient discomfort and anxiety may affect procedural tolerance, highlighting the importance of adequate analgesic and sedative management during hysteroscopy. 4 Obesity is associated with an increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia and polyps, which are common indications for endometrial evaluation and hysteroscopy. 5 , 6 However, obesity poses significant anesthetic challenges, including altered pharmacokinetics, an increased risk of airway obstruction, and heightened susceptibility to hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability. 7 , 8 These physiological changes may influence opioid requirements and complicate dose optimization during procedural sedation. 9 The optimal weight descriptor for opioid dosing in obese patients remains debated. 10 Although total body weight (TBW) is convenient for clinical use, its validity for opioid dose normalization in this population is questionable. 11 We therefore used TBW as the dosing descriptor to characterize the weight-normalized alfentanil dose-response relationship in obese patients undergoing hysteroscopy using an up-and-down sequential design. The effective dose for 50% of patients (ED 50 ) was the primary dose-related endpoint, while the effective dose for 95% of patients (ED 95 ) was explored using probit regression. Alfentanil, a short-acting μ-opioid receptor agonist, exhibits rapid blood-brain equilibration and limited context-sensitive accumulation, allowing accurate dose titration and rapid offset compared with longer-acting opioids such as fentanyl and sufentanil. 9 Remimazolam, an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine metabolized by nonspecific tissue esterases, provides rapid onset and offset of sedation with predictable recovery and can be specifically antagonized by flumazenil. 12 Compared with propofol, remimazolam is associated with greater hemodynamic stability and less injection-related pain. 13 These pharmacological and clinical characteristics make remimazolam attractive for ambulatory procedural sedation. 14 The remimazolam-alfentanil combination has increasingly been investigated in several ambulatory and endoscopic procedures, including gastroscopy, colonoscopic polypectomy, and ERCP. 15–17 However, evidence guiding alfentanil dosing in obese patients undergoing hysteroscopy remains limited. Recent dose-finding studies have evaluated remimazolam- or opioid-based sedation regimens for ambulatory hysteroscopy and other endoscopic procedures. 18 , 19 However, the influence of obesity on alfentanil dose requirements remains unclear. To our knowledge, no prospective dose-finding study has specifically evaluated intravenous alfentanil requirements in obese patients undergoing hysteroscopy under remimazolam sedation. Therefore, using a modified Dixon up-and-down sequential design, this study aimed to estimate the ED 50 and explore the ED 95 of intravenous alfentanil in obese and normal-weight patients undergoing hysteroscopy under remimazolam sedation. The findings may provide pharmacodynamic information to support individualized alfentanil titration in this population. The protocol for this prospective dose-finding study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Peking University People’s Hospital Qingdao Hospital (Approval No. QFELL-KY-2025-03) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The trial was prospectively registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Registration No. ChiCTR2500097312). Data were collected at the Surgical Center of Qingdao Hospital, Peking University People’s Hospital, between September and December 2025. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment. This study was conducted between September and December 2025 at Peking University People’s Hospital Qingdao Hospital. Consecutive patients undergoing elective hysteroscopy during this period were enrolled. The inclusion criteria included women aged 18–50 years with an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status of I-II who were classified as obese (BMI ≥28 kg/m 2 ) or normal weight (18.5 ≤ BMI <24 kg/m 2 ) according to the Working Group on Obesity in China (WGOC) criteria. 20 , 21 Women with intermediate BMI values (24.0–27.9 kg/m 2 ) were prospectively excluded to minimize physiological heterogeneity. Exclusion criteria included contraindication for sedation or anesthesia or a history of sedation/anesthesia adverse events (AEs); preoperative impaired consciousness or chronic pain managed with long-term analgesic use, psychiatric medications, or alcohol abuse; patients with severe hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hepatic and renal dysfunction, abnormal thyroid function, or other diseases that may affect pharmacokinetics; and allergy to any of the study medications. All participants fasted for at least 8 hours for solid food and 2 hours for clear liquids prior to the procedure, and no premedication was administered. Upon arrival in the operating room, peripheral intravenous cannulation was performed, and patients were placed in the lithotomy position. Standard monitoring-including electrocardiography, noninvasive blood pressure, bispectral index (BIS), pulse oximetry, and respiratory rate-was immediately established. 22 Supplemental oxygen was administered via a face mask throughout the procedure, and respiratory status was continuously monitored. Preoxygenation was performed using a face mask with oxygen at 5 L/min for 3–5 minutes before anesthesia induction. Spontaneous ventilation was maintained throughout the procedure. The alfentanil dose for each patient was determined using the modified Dixon up-and-down sequential method. This sequential design is efficient for estimating the median effective dose with relatively few participants. 23 Based on previous literature, the initial alfentanil dose was set at 10 μg/kg, and a fixed step size of 1 μg/kg was used for dose adjustment. 24 During hysteroscopy, a negative response was defined as the absence of coughing, swallowing, and body movement, whereas a positive response was defined as the occurrence of any of these predefined procedural responses. Following a positive response, the alfentanil dose for the subsequent patient was increased by 1 μg/kg; following a negative response, it was decreased by 1 μg/kg. This sequential process continued independently within each group until seven independent crossover points were obtained, with a crossover defined as a change in response status between two consecutive patients (positive response to negative response or negative response to positive response). This stopping rule was selected based on previous methodological and clinical dose-finding studies, which have generally used at least six crossover pairs for stable estimation of ED 50 . 25 , 26 After preoxygenation, the patient first received an intravenous bolus of alfentanil, calculated according to the sequential method described above, administered over 30 seconds, followed by remimazolam at a dose of 0.4 mg/kg infused over 30–60 seconds. Following the bolus, a continuous infusion of remimazolam was initiated at a rate of 1 mg/kg/h via a syringe pump to maintain the target level of sedation. Remimazolam dosing was standardized across patients, whereas alfentanil was the dose-exploration drug. The depth of sedation was assessed using both the Modified Observer’s Assessment of Alertness/Sedation (MOAA/S) scale and the BIS. 18 Following remimazolam administration, MOAA/S scores were recorded at 10-second intervals. Hysteroscopy was initiated once the prespecified sedation criterion was met, defined as an MOAA/S score ≤ 1 and a BIS value < 60. If the MOAA/S score increased to ≥ 2 during the procedure, a prespecified rescue dose of remimazolam (0.05–0.2 mg/kg) was administered intravenously. Rescue dosing was limited to a maximum of five doses within a 15-minute period, with an interval of at least 2 minutes between consecutive doses. Upon completion of hysteroscopy, the remimazolam infusion was discontinued, and flumazenil was administered to reverse remimazolam-induced sedation. 27 Recovery of consciousness was considered achieved when the MOAA/S score was ≥4 and the BIS value was ≥80. Discharge from the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) was permitted when the modified Aldrete score reached ≥9. 28 The primary pharmacodynamic endpoint was the ED 50 of alfentanil required to suppress predefined procedural responses during hysteroscopy under remimazolam sedation. The ED 50 was formally compared between obese and normal-weight groups. The ED 95 was considered an exploratory pharmacodynamic endpoint and was estimated using the probit dose–response model. The ED 95 estimates and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported descriptively, and no formal hypothesis test was performed to compare ED 95 between groups. Secondary outcomes included mean arterial pressure (MAP), heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and BIS values were measured at predefined time points: baseline (T1, 5 min before anesthesia), loss of consciousness (T2, LOC), cervical dilation (T3), end of procedure (T4), and recovery of consciousness (T5, ROC). Additional variables included total remimazolam consumption (mg), TBW-normalized total remimazolam consumption (mg/kg), induction time, duration of anesthesia and procedure, and recovery time, while adverse events were defined as respiratory depression (RR ≤ 8 breaths/min or apnea), hypoxemia (SpO 2 ≤ 90% for ≥ 15s), hypotension (a ≥ 30% decrease in MAP from baseline), tachycardia (HR > 100 beats/min), bradycardia (HR < 50 beats/min), injection pain, postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), intraoperative awareness, and postoperative pain (VAS score > 3 at 30 min after surgery). Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 27.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), GraphPad Prism (version 9.4.1; GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA), and R software (version 4.3.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Continuous variables were tested for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test and are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range [IQR]), as appropriate. Normally distributed continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t test, whereas non-normally distributed variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U -test. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. The ED 50 of alfentanil was initially estimated using the modified Dixon up-and-down method. Probit regression analysis was subsequently performed to characterize the dose–response relationship and to obtain model-derived ED 50 and exploratory ED 95 estimates with 95% CIs. Model adequacy was assessed using the Pearson chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Likelihood ratio tests were performed in R to compare nested probit models. First, a likelihood ratio test was conducted to evaluate whether the dose-response curves were parallel between the obese and normal-weight groups. After confirming parallelism, a second likelihood ratio test under the common-slope probit model was performed to test for equality of the intercepts, thereby providing the formal comparison of ED 50 between groups. The ED 95 estimates were considered exploratory and were reported descriptively with their corresponding 95% CIs; no formal statistical comparison of ED 95 between groups was performed. Sequential allocation plots and dose–response curves were generated using GraphPad Prism. All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Of the 66 patients assessed for eligibility, 60 were enrolled and completed the study ( Figure 1 ). Participants were classified into a normal-weight group (n = 31) and an obese group (n = 29) according to BMI. The demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1 . Compared with the normal-weight group, the obese group had significantly higher body weight (P < 0.001), BMI (P < 0.01), Mallampati (MMP) scores (P < 0.001), and STOP-Bang scores (P < 0.001), with no significant between-group differences in the other baseline characteristics. Flow diagram of included participants. The modified Dixon up-and-down sequences for the two groups are shown in Figure 2 . Using the modified Dixon up-and-down method, the ED 50 of alfentanil was 9.64 μg/kg (95% CI, 8.38–10.90) in the obese group and 12.93 μg/kg (95% CI, 11.67–14.19) in the normal-weight group. The dose-response curves derived from probit regression are shown in Figure 3 . The probit model showed good fit based on the Pearson chi-square test (χ 2 = 5.159, df = 9, P = 0.820). The model-derived ED 50 was 9.71 μg/kg (95% CI, 7.81–12.26) in the obese group and 13.67 μg/kg (95% CI, 12.77–15.07) in the normal-weight group. The corresponding model-derived exploratory ED 95 estimates were 12.57 μg/kg (95% CI, 10.92–28.28) and 16.24 μg/kg (95% CI, 14.92–21.48), respectively. The first likelihood ratio test showed no significant difference in the slopes of the dose–response curves between the two groups (χ 2 = 0.41, df = 1, P = 0.520), supporting the use of a common-slope probit model. Under this model, a second likelihood ratio test demonstrated a significant difference in ED 50 between groups (χ 2 = 10.74, df = 1, P = 0.001), indicating that the ED 50 of alfentanil was significantly lower in obese patients than in normal-weight patients.
