title: Assessing the Discriminative Power of Metabolic Indices for PMOS Detection in Normal-Weight Women
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to investigate the relationship between metabolic indices and Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) in normal-weight women and to evaluate their individual and combined discriminatory performance. Patients and Methods This retrospective case-control study included 86 normal-weight women (BMI <25 kg/m 2 ) with PMOS and 88 healthy controls. Electronic medical records were used to calculate the Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), Triglyceride–Glucose (TyG) index, Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP), and Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance (METS-IR). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to assess discriminatory performance, and optimal cut-off values were determined using the Youden index. Combined analyses were performed according to concordant classification of the component indices relative to their respective cut-off values. Results Fasting glucose, fasting insulin, triglyceride levels, HOMA-IR, TyG, AIP, and METS-IR were significantly higher in women with PMOS (p<0.05). Among individual indices, TyG showed the highest discriminatory performance (AUC=0.775; 95% CI: 0.706–0.843). HOMA-IR and AIP demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance, whereas METS-IR showed lower performance. Among the combined assessments, HOMA-IR and TyG yielded an AUC of 0.830 (95% CI: 0.747–0.913), with 80.8% sensitivity and 85.2% specificity. Conclusion Metabolic indices, particularly TyG, may be useful for identifying metabolic abnormalities in normal-weight women with PMOS. Combined assessment of complementary metabolic indices may provide additional information for metabolic risk evaluation. These findings support further investigation of such indices as practical tools for metabolic assessment and risk stratification, rather than as independent diagnostic criteria for PMOS.
body: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) is one of the most common endocrine disorders affecting women of reproductive age and is a heterogeneous clinical condition characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. 1 , 2 In a recent large-scale review, the prevalence of PMOS is reported to be approximately 12% in the general population, although this figure varies depending on the diagnostic criteria applied. 3 Nowadays, PMOS is recognized not merely as a condition confined to the reproductive system, but also as a systemic syndrome with significant metabolic components. 4 Insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, dyslipidemia, and increased cardiometabolic risk are among its major metabolic features. Insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia promote ovarian androgen production and suppress hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) synthesis, thereby contributing to hyperandrogenism, impaired follicular development, and ovulatory dysfunction. 5–7 These metabolic disturbances may also contribute to atherogenic dyslipidemia, characterized particularly by increased triglyceride levels, and to increased long-term cardiometabolic risk. 8 , 9 Accordingly, early identification of metabolic abnormalities in PMOS is important, particularly for recognizing individuals who may be at increased long-term metabolic risk. PMOS and its metabolic aspects are frequently associated with obesity. 10 However, a significant proportion of women with PMOS have a normal body mass index (BMI). In this patient group, the clinical phenotype is often more heterogeneous, which can lead to metabolic risks being overlooked. However, accumulating evidence from recent studies indicates that insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction may also occur in normal-weight women with PMOS. 11 This suggests that metabolic risk assessment based solely on BMI may be inadequate, and that there is a need for more sensitive biochemical markers capable of identifying metabolic disorders, particularly in women without excess body weight. In recent years, various metabolic indices that can be easily calculated from routine biochemical parameters have increasingly been used to assess insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk. The Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), the Triglyceride–Glucose (TyG) index, the Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP) and the Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance (METS-IR) are among the indices developed for this purpose and which can be used to assess metabolic risk in different populations. 12–14 Although a growing body of evidence suggests that these indices may be useful for assessing insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and metabolic risk, their discriminatory performance in normal-weight women with PMOS has not yet been fully established. 15–18 In particular, evidence regarding whether combining complementary metabolic indices provides additional discriminatory value over individual indices remains limited. In clinical practice, the diagnosis of PMOS is based on the Rotterdam criteria, 19 which primarily reflect reproductive and morphological features and do not directly characterize the metabolic dimension of the syndrome. Therefore, metabolic indices should not be regarded as substitutes for established diagnostic criteria, but rather as potential tools for identifying metabolic abnormalities and stratifying metabolic risk, particularly in normal-weight women with PMOS. 20 , 21 Furthermore, given the multifactorial aetiopathogenesis of PMOS, the combined assessment of metabolic indices reflecting different metabolic pathways may provide additional discriminatory information beyond that obtained from individual indices. 22 In this context, evaluating the diagnostic performance of metabolic indices—both individually and in combination—and determining their potential to predict PMOS and its metabolic profile, particularly in normal-weight women, could provide clinically valuable insights. Examining the discriminatory power of these indices may contribute to the identification of practical and accessible biochemical markers that could be utilized in clinical practice. This study was designed to comprehensively assess the association between HOMA-IR, TyG index, AIP, and METS-IR and PMOS in normal-weight women. In addition, the study evaluates the individual and combined discriminatory performance of these indices and their potential utility in characterizing the metabolic risk profile of the normal-weight PMOS phenotype. By doing so, it aims to clarify whether these readily available metabolic indices may provide complementary information for metabolic assessment and risk stratification alongside established diagnostic criteria. This study was designed as a retrospective, observational case-control study. The data for the study were obtained by retrospectively reviewing the electronic medical records of patients who attended the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Bandırma Onyedi Eylül University Faculty of Medicine Hospital between January 2023 and December 2025. The study included women of reproductive age aged between 18 and 45. The diagnosis of PMOS was established based on the core Rotterdam criteria framework, which serves as the primary diagnostic foundation in both the 2003 consensus and the updated 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline. 1 , 19 Diagnosis requires the presence of at least two of the following three features: Ovulatory dysfunction (oligo- and/or anovulation), Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, Polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasound. Given the retrospective design of our study and the data collection period (January 2023–December 2025) which spanned a transitional phase in clinical guidelines, PCOM was determined based on the standard sonographic evaluations routinely performed at our center at the time of diagnosis. Ovulatory dysfunction (oligo- and/or anovulation), Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, Polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasound. Given the retrospective design of our study and the data collection period (January 2023–December 2025) which spanned a transitional phase in clinical guidelines, PCOM was determined based on the standard sonographic evaluations routinely performed at our center at the time of diagnosis. Women who met at least two of these three criteria constituted the PMOS group. The control group, meanwhile, was selected from women who attended the outpatient clinic during the same period and did not meet any of the PMOS diagnostic criteria. In line with the aim of the study, only normal-weight women were included in the study to exclude the effect of obesity on metabolic indices. For this reason, women with a BMI value of 25 kg/m 2 or higher—calculated using standard formulas defined in the literature based on height and weight measurements—were excluded from both groups. 23 To minimize potential confounding factors that could influence metabolic parameters, patients with a history of diabetes mellitus, thyroid disorders, Cushing’s syndrome or adrenal disorders, those who were pregnant or breastfeeding, and patients taking medication that could affect lipid metabolism or insulin sensitivity were excluded from the study. Convenience sampling was used. As this was a retrospective study, no a priori sample size calculation was performed. All eligible normal-weight women who met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria and had complete clinical and laboratory data during the study period were included. After applying all inclusion and exclusion criteria, 86 women formed the PMOS group and 88 women formed the control group ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 The flowchart of the study design. A flowchart outlines a study process with 1030 patients, splitting into PMOS and Non-PMOS groups. PMOS branch: 386 diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria. 288 excluded for BMI > 25, leaving 98 with BMI < 25. Further exclusions: 12 chronic disease, 14 on medication, 13 pregnant/breastfeeding, 34 missing data. Final PMOS group: 86 patients. Non-PMOS branch: 644 not diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria. 495 excluded for BMI > 25, leaving 149 with BMI < 25. Further exclusions: 61 for same reasons. Final control group: 88 patients. A flowchart splits 1030 patients into PMOS and Non PMOS, filters BMI less than 25, then exclusions to 86 and 88. Abbreviations : PMOS, Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome; BMI, Body Mass Index. The flowchart of the study design. The participants’ demographic characteristics, anthropometric measurements and laboratory parameters were recorded using a structured data collection form prepared by the researchers. The variables collected included age, height, weight, fasting blood glucose (FBG), fasting insulin (FI), TG and HDL-C levels. These laboratory measurements were obtained from routine biochemical analyses performed following a fast of at least 8 hours. Biochemical parameters were measured in serum obtained by centrifugation of blood samples collected in gel-sealed biochemical tubes, using an enzymatic colorimetric method on an automated biochemical analyzer (Cobas 6000, Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany). All analyses were performed in accordance with daily quality control procedures. Based on the recorded laboratory parameters, metabolic indices were calculated using standard formulas reported in the literature to assess the metabolic risk 12–14 ( Figure 2 ). Figure 2 The calculation formulas for indices as defined in literature. Formulas for HOMA-IR, TyG Index, AIP and METS-IR calculations. Abbreviations : HOMA-IR, Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance; FI, Fasting Insulin; FBG, Fasting Blood Glucose; TyG, Triglyceride-Glucose Index; TG, Triglyceride; AIP, Atherogenic Index of Plasma; HDL-C, High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol; METS-IR, Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance; BMI, Body Mass Index. The calculation formulas for indices as defined in literature. For the combined-index analyses, each metabolic index was classified as positive or negative according to its optimal cut-off value determined by the Youden index. Participants in whom all component indices exceeded their respective cut-off values were classified as combination-positive, whereas those in whom all component indices were below their respective cut-off values were classified as combination-negative. Participants with discordant index classifications were excluded from the diagnostic performance analysis of the corresponding combination. The same concordance-based approach was applied to the three-index combination. All data were recorded anonymously, and personal identifiers have been removed from the dataset prior to statistical analysis to ensure patient confidentiality. The data were analyzed using the SPSS 23.0 statistical software package. Descriptive statistics including frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, median and interquartile range were calculated. The suitability of the variables for a normal distribution was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. In comparing demographic and clinical characteristics according to the presence of PMOS, the Pearson chi-square test was used for categorical variables and the Mann–Whitney U -test for continuous variables. In comparing the mean and median values of metabolic indices according to the presence of PMOS, the Student’s t -test and the Mann–Whitney U -test were utilized, depending on whether the distribution conformed to a normal distribution. The Rotterdam criteria are accepted as the gold standard for assessing sensitivity and specificity. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves were plotted for the metabolic indices, and the Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, Positive Likelihood Ratio (LR+), and Negative Likelihood Ratio (LR−) were calculated to assess the ability of these indices to correctly distinguish individuals with PMOS. AUC values were classified as follows: 0.9–1.0 excellent, 0.8–0.89 good, 0.7–0.79 moderate, 0.6–0.69 poor, and values below 0.6 were considered inadequate. 24 The optimal cut-off values of the metabolic indices for predicting PMOS were determined based on the Youden index, with the point yielding the highest Youden index value defined as the optimal cut-off point. Pairwise comparisons of the AUCs were performed using the DeLong test. To assess the agreement of combined metabolic indices in predicting PMOS, Cohen’s Kappa (κ) coefficient was calculated, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The Shrout classification was used to interpret the Kappa (κ) values: 0–0.10 was considered almost no agreement; 0.11–0.40 slight agreement; 0.41–0.60 moderate agreement; 0.61–0.80 good agreement; and 0.81–1.00 excellent agreement. 25 To evaluate whether the associations between metabolic indices and PMOS were independent of the observed age difference between the study groups, additional binary logistic regression analyses were performed for each metabolic index, adjusting for age. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. In all statistical tests, a significance level of p < 0.05 was adopted. Table 1 compares the demographic and clinical characteristics of participants according to their PMOS status. The median age in PMOS (-) women was statistically significantly higher than in PMOS (+) women (p<0.05). No significant differences were found between PMOS-positive and PMOS-negative women in terms of marital status, educational level, number of pregnancies, number of living children, smoking status, alcohol consumption, BMI and median HDL-C levels (p > 0.05). It was determined that the median values for FBG, FI and TG were significantly higher in PMOS-positive women compared to PMOS-negative women (p<0.05, Table 1 ). The median values for HOMA-IR [1.74 (1.27; 2.30)] and AIP [0.15 (0.33; 0.05)], as well as the mean values for the TyG index [8.29±0.49] and METS-IR [30.52 ± 3.96] were found to be significantly higher in women with PMOS compared to those without PMOS (p < 0.05, Table 2 ). Additional age-adjusted binary logistic regression analyses showed that all four metabolic indices remained significantly associated with PMOS. The adjusted odds ratios were 1.829 for HOMA-IR (95% CI: 1.286–2.601, p=0.001), 13.276 for the TyG index (95% CI: 5.006–35.208, p<0.001), 52.864 for AIP (95% CI: 9.114–306.617, p<0.001), and 1.141 for METS-IR (95% CI: 1.050–1.240, p=0.002). Table 3 presents the diagnostic performance of metabolic indices for predicting PMOS. Among the individual indices, the highest discriminatory power was observed for the TyG index (AUC = 0.775; 95% CI: 0.706–0.843; p < 0.001). The optimal cut-off point for the TyG index was 8.191, with a sensitivity of 60.5% and a specificity of 84.1% at this value. The diagnostic performance of the HOMA-IR and AIP indices was found to be similar and of moderate level (AUC 0.735 and 0.738, respectively; p<0.001). The cut-off point for HOMA-IR was 1.243 (sensitivity 76.7%, specificity 59.1%), and for AIP it was 0.036 (sensitivity 79.1%, specificity 58.0%). The discriminatory power of the METS-IR index was found to be lower than that of the other indices (AUC = 0.638; 95% CI: 0.556–0.721; p = 0.002). Pairwise comparison of ROC curves using the DeLong test showed that the AUC of the TyG index was significantly greater than that of METS-IR (ΔAUC=0.136, p=0.006), whereas its differences from HOMA-IR (p=0.410) and AIP (p=0.109) were not statistically significant. AIP also showed a significantly greater AUC than METS-IR (ΔAUC=0.099, p=0.036). No significant differences were observed between HOMA-IR and AIP (p=0.956) or between HOMA-IR and METS-IR (p=0.065). Combined assessment of complementary metabolic indices may provide additional information for metabolic risk evaluation. These findings support further investigation of such indices as practical tools for metabolic assessment and risk stratification, rather than as independent diagnostic criteria for PMOS.

Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) is one of the most common endocrine disorders affecting women of reproductive age and is a heterogeneous clinical condition characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. 1 , 2 In a recent large-scale review, the prevalence of PMOS is reported to be approximately 12% in the general population, although this figure varies depending on the diagnostic criteria applied. 3 Nowadays, PMOS is recognized not merely as a condition confined to the reproductive system, but also as a systemic syndrome with significant metabolic components. 4 Insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, dyslipidemia, and increased cardiometabolic risk are among its major metabolic features. Insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia promote ovarian androgen production and suppress hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) synthesis, thereby contributing to hyperandrogenism, impaired follicular development, and ovulatory dysfunction. 5–7 These metabolic disturbances may also contribute to atherogenic dyslipidemia, characterized particularly by increased triglyceride levels, and to increased long-term cardiometabolic risk. 8 , 9 Accordingly, early identification of metabolic abnormalities in PMOS is important, particularly for recognizing individuals who may be at increased long-term metabolic risk. PMOS and its metabolic aspects are frequently associated with obesity. 10 However, a significant proportion of women with PMOS have a normal body mass index (BMI). In this patient group, the clinical phenotype is often more heterogeneous, which can lead to metabolic risks being overlooked. However, accumulating evidence from recent studies indicates that insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction may also occur in normal-weight women with PMOS. 11 This suggests that metabolic risk assessment based solely on BMI may be inadequate, and that there is a need for more sensitive biochemical markers capable of identifying metabolic disorders, particularly in women without excess body weight. In recent years, various metabolic indices that can be easily calculated from routine biochemical parameters have increasingly been used to assess insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk. The Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), the Triglyceride–Glucose (TyG) index, the Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP) and the Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance (METS-IR) are among the indices developed for this purpose and which can be used to assess metabolic risk in different populations. 12–14 Although a growing body of evidence suggests that these indices may be useful for assessing insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and metabolic risk, their discriminatory performance in normal-weight women with PMOS has not yet been fully established. 15–18 In particular, evidence regarding whether combining complementary metabolic indices provides additional discriminatory value over individual indices remains limited. In clinical practice, the diagnosis of PMOS is based on the Rotterdam criteria, 19 which primarily reflect reproductive and morphological features and do not directly characterize the metabolic dimension of the syndrome. Therefore, metabolic indices should not be regarded as substitutes for established diagnostic criteria, but rather as potential tools for identifying metabolic abnormalities and stratifying metabolic risk, particularly in normal-weight women with PMOS. 20 , 21 Furthermore, given the multifactorial aetiopathogenesis of PMOS, the combined assessment of metabolic indices reflecting different metabolic pathways may provide additional discriminatory information beyond that obtained from individual indices. 22 In this context, evaluating the diagnostic performance of metabolic indices—both individually and in combination—and determining their potential to predict PMOS and its metabolic profile, particularly in normal-weight women, could provide clinically valuable insights. Examining the discriminatory power of these indices may contribute to the identification of practical and accessible biochemical markers that could be utilized in clinical practice. This study was designed to comprehensively assess the association between HOMA-IR, TyG index, AIP, and METS-IR and PMOS in normal-weight women. In addition, the study evaluates the individual and combined discriminatory performance of these indices and their potential utility in characterizing the metabolic risk profile of the normal-weight PMOS phenotype. By doing so, it aims to clarify whether these readily available metabolic indices may provide complementary information for metabolic assessment and risk stratification alongside established diagnostic criteria. This study was designed as a retrospective, observational case-control study. The data for the study were obtained by retrospectively reviewing the electronic medical records of patients who attended the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Bandırma Onyedi Eylül University Faculty of Medicine Hospital between January 2023 and December 2025. The study included women of reproductive age aged between 18 and 45. The diagnosis of PMOS was established based on the core Rotterdam criteria framework, which serves as the primary diagnostic foundation in both the 2003 consensus and the updated 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline. 1 , 19 Diagnosis requires the presence of at least two of the following three features: Ovulatory dysfunction (oligo- and/or anovulation), Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, Polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasound. Given the retrospective design of our study and the data collection period (January 2023–December 2025) which spanned a transitional phase in clinical guidelines, PCOM was determined based on the standard sonographic evaluations routinely performed at our center at the time of diagnosis. Ovulatory dysfunction (oligo- and/or anovulation), Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism, Polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) on ultrasound. Given the retrospective design of our study and the data collection period (January 2023–December 2025) which spanned a transitional phase in clinical guidelines, PCOM was determined based on the standard sonographic evaluations routinely performed at our center at the time of diagnosis. Women who met at least two of these three criteria constituted the PMOS group. The control group, meanwhile, was selected from women who attended the outpatient clinic during the same period and did not meet any of the PMOS diagnostic criteria. In line with the aim of the study, only normal-weight women were included in the study to exclude the effect of obesity on metabolic indices. For this reason, women with a BMI value of 25 kg/m 2 or higher—calculated using standard formulas defined in the literature based on height and weight measurements—were excluded from both groups. 23 To minimize potential confounding factors that could influence metabolic parameters, patients with a history of diabetes mellitus, thyroid disorders, Cushing’s syndrome or adrenal disorders, those who were pregnant or breastfeeding, and patients taking medication that could affect lipid metabolism or insulin sensitivity were excluded from the study. Convenience sampling was used. As this was a retrospective study, no a priori sample size calculation was performed. All eligible normal-weight women who met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria and had complete clinical and laboratory data during the study period were included. After applying all inclusion and exclusion criteria, 86 women formed the PMOS group and 88 women formed the control group ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 The flowchart of the study design. The participants’ demographic characteristics, anthropometric measurements and laboratory parameters were recorded using a structured data collection form prepared by the researchers. The variables collected included age, height, weight, fasting blood glucose (FBG), fasting insulin (FI), TG and HDL-C levels. These laboratory measurements were obtained from routine biochemical analyses performed following a fast of at least 8 hours. Biochemical parameters were measured in serum obtained by centrifugation of blood samples collected in gel-sealed biochemical tubes, using an enzymatic colorimetric method on an automated biochemical analyzer (Cobas 6000, Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany). All analyses were performed in accordance with daily quality control procedures. Based on the recorded laboratory parameters, metabolic indices were calculated using standard formulas reported in the literature to assess the metabolic risk 12–14 ( Figure 2 ). The calculation formulas for indices as defined in literature. For the combined-index analyses, each metabolic index was classified as positive or negative according to its optimal cut-off value determined by the Youden index. Participants in whom all component indices exceeded their respective cut-off values were classified as combination-positive, whereas those in whom all component indices were below their respective cut-off values were classified as combination-negative. Participants with discordant index classifications were excluded from the diagnostic performance analysis of the corresponding combination. The same concordance-based approach was applied to the three-index combination. All data were recorded anonymously, and personal identifiers have been removed from the dataset prior to statistical analysis to ensure patient confidentiality. The data were analyzed using the SPSS 23.0 statistical software package. Descriptive statistics including frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, median and interquartile range were calculated. The suitability of the variables for a normal distribution was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. In comparing demographic and clinical characteristics according to the presence of PMOS, the Pearson chi-square test was used for categorical variables and the Mann–Whitney U -test for continuous variables. In comparing the mean and median values of metabolic indices according to the presence of PMOS, the Student’s t -test and the Mann–Whitney U -test were utilized, depending on whether the distribution conformed to a normal distribution. The Rotterdam criteria are accepted as the gold standard for assessing sensitivity and specificity. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves were plotted for the metabolic indices, and the Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, Positive Likelihood Ratio (LR+), and Negative Likelihood Ratio (LR−) were calculated to assess the ability of these indices to correctly distinguish individuals with PMOS. AUC values were classified as follows: 0.9–1.0 excellent, 0.8–0.89 good, 0.7–0.79 moderate, 0.6–0.69 poor, and values below 0.6 were considered inadequate. 24 The optimal cut-off values of the metabolic indices for predicting PMOS were determined based on the Youden index, with the point yielding the highest Youden index value defined as the optimal cut-off point. Pairwise comparisons of the AUCs were performed using the DeLong test. To assess the agreement of combined metabolic indices in predicting PMOS, Cohen’s Kappa (κ) coefficient was calculated, along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The Shrout classification was used to interpret the Kappa (κ) values: 0–0.10 was considered almost no agreement; 0.11–0.40 slight agreement; 0.41–0.60 moderate agreement; 0.61–0.80 good agreement; and 0.81–1.00 excellent agreement. 25 To evaluate whether the associations between metabolic indices and PMOS were independent of the observed age difference between the study groups, additional binary logistic regression analyses were performed for each metabolic index, adjusting for age. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. In all statistical tests, a significance level of p < 0.05 was adopted. Table 3 presents the diagnostic performance of metabolic indices for predicting PMOS. Among the individual indices, the highest discriminatory power was observed for the TyG index (AUC = 0.775; 95% CI: 0.706–0.843; p < 0.001). The optimal cut-off point for the TyG index was 8.191, with a sensitivity of 60.5% and a specificity of 84.1% at this value. title: Metabolite Profiling and Network Pharmacology of Persimmon Vinegar ( Diospyros kaki ) Compounds, with in silico Validation for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Therapy
abstract: Objective: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent form of lung cancer, with complex mechanisms, drug resistance, and significant side effects from conventional chemotherapy, all of which hinder effective treatment. Diospyros kaki (persimmon) vinegar, produced through spontaneous fermentation, has enhanced flavonoid content that may increase its pharmacological activity; however, its molecular mechanisms against NSCLC remain unclear. This is the first study to map the molecular mechanisms of persimmon vinegar compounds against NSCLC by integrating metabolite profiling, network pharmacology, and molecular docking validation. Methods: Compounds were identified using liquid chromatography--tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and screened for pharmacological properties, followed by network pharmacology and molecular docking to explore potential targets against NSCLC. Result: Twenty-two compounds were identified, with three key compounds benzoyl arginine amine, indoline, and exocarpic acid, implicated in the NSCLC pathway (hsa05223). Twenty-seven target genes were associated with this pathway. Benzoyl arginine amine exhibited a binding affinity of −86.9707 kcal/mol for CDK6 (PDB ID: 8I0M) and −120.017 kcal/mol for HRAS (PDB ID: 3K8Y), greater than their native ligand, suggesting its potential to inhibit CDK6 activity, block the G1/S phase transition, and suppress cancer cell proliferation via the E2F pathway. Its interaction with HRAS may inhibit the MAPK pathway, which is critical for cancer progression. Conclusion: These findings provide preliminary evidence for the potential of persimmon vinegar compounds as leads for NSCLC drug development, warranting further in vitro and in vivo studies.
body: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent form of lung cancer, comprising about 85% of cases [ 1 ]. NSCLC develops from lung epithelial cells and includes subtypes such as adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma [ 2 ]. Globally, it remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths, with an estimated 1.8 million fatalities annually [ 3 ]. Key risk factors, including smoking, air pollution, and radiation exposure, continue to drive its high incidence [ 4 ]. These mutations are linked to drug resistance and side effects, posing challenges for treatment [ 5 -- 7 ]. Despite progress in targeted and immunotherapies, the five-year survival rate for NSCLC is still low, at only 10--20%. While conventional treatments have evolved, drug resistance and significant adverse effects pose significant challenges in NSCLC management [ 5 -- 7 ]. Consequently, developing novel, more effective, and safer therapeutic approaches is urgently needed. Over the past decade, molecular research has unveiled various oncogenic mutations that contribute to NSCLC, including KRAS (20--30%), EGFR (10--40%), and ALK translocations (3--5%), which activate pathways such as MAPK and CDK6, which play crucial roles in cell cycle regulation and proliferation [ 8 , 9 ]. One promising approach to address these challenges is the utilization of natural compounds as adjunctive or alternative therapy. Phytochemicals found in medicinal plants have demonstrated the potential to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and overcome drug resistance [ 10 , 11 ]. However, research on the use of medicinal plants in NSCLC therapy remains limited and warrants further exploration. Natural products have emerged as promising alternatives due to their multi-targeted mechanisms and lower toxicity profiles. In particular, compounds derived from Diospyros kaki (persimmon) from the Ebenaceae family is one such plant that has shown promise as a chemopreventive agent. Persimmon contains secondary metabolites such as proanthocyanidins, epigallocatechin (EGC), epigallocatechin-3-O-gallate (EGCG), terpenoids, and naphthoquinones, which have been proven to possess anticancer activities [ 12 , 13 ]. Flavonoid content from D. kaki have been reported to induce apoptosis in prostate cancer (PC-3) cells by increasing oxidative stress [ 14 ] and activate c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling [ 15 ]. polysaccharides isolated from persimmon have exhibited anticancer potential by suppressing Transforming Growth Factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1)-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in A549 lung cancer cells [ 16 ]. Persimmon vinegar exhibits strong antioxidant potential, as evidenced by its ability to suppress lipid peroxidation and neutralize 2,2′-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radicals, effects primarily attributed to its abundant phenolic compounds [ 15 ]. Spontaneous fermentation enhances its bioactive content, producing persimmon vinegar with higher levels of phenolics, flavonoids, gallic acid, and chlorogenic acid than fresh fruit or other vinegars, alongside stronger antioxidant activity [ 14 , 15 ]. To date, no study has comprehensively characterized the molecular targets of persimmon vinegar against NSCLC using integrated metabolomics and network pharmacology approaches. Therefore, this study aimed to identify the bioactive compounds of persimmon vinegar and evaluate their potential to inhibit NSCLC pathways. The approach involves liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, network pharmacology, and in silico validation. Network pharmacology serves as a valuable tool for predicting biological targets and complex pathways influenced by natural compounds [ 17 , 18 ], enabling the identification of potential synergistic effects between persimmon vinegar and conventional NSCLC therapies. This study is expected to significantly contribute to developing plant-based therapies for NSCLC by integrating these methods. The novelty of this research lies in the fermentation approach to enhance the pharmacological potential of persimmon and the exploration of molecular mechanisms through the analysis of signaling pathways involved in lung cancer cell proliferation and survival and its validation in silico. The overall research design integrating LC-MS/MS metabolite profiling, target prediction, network pharmacology analysis, and molecular docking validation is summarized in Figure 1 . Research Flowchart. Diospyros kaki has been identified under the number 068/567/102.21/2023 and was collected from Tulungagung Regency, East Java, Indonesia at an altitude of 85 meters above sea level. The region has a tropical wet and dry climate (Aw) with two seasons: the rainy season (November--April) and the dry season (May--October). January is the wettest month (rainfall>270 mm), while August is the driest (rainfall<20 mm). The temperature ranges between 21°--32 °C, with an annual rainfall of 1.400--1.800 mm and 90--120 rainy days per year. Persimmon fruits were selected and sorted based on ripeness level. Immature persimmons were washed, quartered, weighed, and placed in a tank for spontaneous fermentation at room temperature for 6 months. Peeled mature Diospyros kaki fruits were steamed, and dried using a hot oven approach before blended with the fermentation liquid from immature persimmons to form a homogeneous mixture. This mixture underwent another spontaneous fermentation for 6 months at room temperature to ensure a more complete alcohol conversion to acetic acid [ 19 ]. Persimmon vinegar compounds were screened for their predicted physicochemical properties, toxicity, and bioactivity using SMILES codes obtained from PubChem. Physicochemical properties were evaluated with pkCSM (https://biosig.lab.uq.edu.au/pkcsm/prediction) to assess their suitability as orally administered drugs [ 20 ]. Screening followed Lipinski's rule of five, which specifies: molecular weight (MW) ≤ 500 g/mol, log P ≤ 5 (indicating hydrophobicity), hydrogen bond donors (HBD) ≤ 5, hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) ≤ 10, polar surface area (PSA) ≤ 140 Å², and fewer than 10 rotatable bonds, reflecting drug permeability and molecular flexibility [ 21 - 23 ]. Compounds violating no more than one rule were considered suitable for oral administration [ 24 ]. Toxicity was assessed using Protox III (https://tox.charite.de/protox3/), which classifies compounds into six toxicity classes based on median lethal dose (LD50). Bioactivity was predicted using PASS Online (https://www.way2drug.com/passonline/predict.php), which generates a probability of activity (Pa) and probability of inactivity (Pi). Compounds with Pa > 0.7 were classified as highly promising anticancer agents, those with 0.5 < Pa < 0.7 as having moderate potential requiring further validation, and those with Pa < 0.5 as having low predicted anticancer activity [ 25 -- 27 ]. The LC-MS/MS analysis was conducted using UPLC-MS systems with QToF analyzer and positive ESI as the ionization source with the Acquity C18 column 1.8 µm; 2.1 × 150 mm. The eluent applied was a mixture of (A) water (HPLC grade)/formic acid (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) 99.9/0.1 [v/v]; (B) acetonitrile (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany)/formic acid 99.9/0.1 [v/v] with gradient elution. The source and desolvation temperatures were set at 100°C and 350°C, respectively. A 10 mg extract was dissolved in a 10 ml absolute methanol, and 5 µL was injected into the UPLC-MS system. The analysis parameters were set using positive ion mode, with spectra acquired over a mass range from m/z 120 to 1000. Data processing and compound identification were conducted using Mass Lynx v4.1 (Waters, Massachusetts, USA) and PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), generate the chromatogram and spectra of each observed peak. Additionally, chemical prediction was performed using the ChemSpider website with compound's confirmation based on MS/MS fragmentation and an inaccuracy of less than 5 ppm [ 18 ]. A crucial aspect of drug research is predicting whether a chemical interacts with the targets. The gene targets of active compounds from persimmon vinegar based on LC-MS/MS analysis were identified using the GeneCards database (https://www.genecards.org/, cut off>0.7). Conversely, NSCLC-related gene targets were retrieved using the DisGeNET database (https://www.disgenet.org). Subsequently, the network pharmacology using Cytoscape software 3.9.1 to visualize interaction between active compound-gene targets and disease-gene target [ 28 ]. Network pharmacology visualization for overlapping target genes was performed using Cytoscape 3.10.1 (https://cytoscape.org/). Protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis was conducted using STRING 12.0 (https://STRING-db.org/) with a minimum required interaction score of 0.400 26. The PPI analysis explored biological phenomena by annotating functional data related to Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways [ 29 ]. GO and KEGG pathway analyses were performed using SRPlot (https://www.bioinformatics.com.cn). The GO analysis covered biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions affected by CLE compounds, while the KEGG analysis identified NSCLC-related signaling pathways. Both analyses were filtered with a p-value ≤ 0.05 and false discovery rate ≤ 0.05 [ 29 ]. The GO results were refined to the top ten terms for each category and visualized as bubble plots. KEGG pathway enrichment focused on signaling pathways relevant to NSCLC. The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) provides integrated insights by linking genomic, chemical, and systems biology data to clarify key pathways involved [ 30 ]. The target genes identified through network pharmacology were validated using molecular docking with Molegro Virtual Docker 6.0 (http://www.molegro.com). Docking of benzoyl arginine amine was performed and visualized using ChemDraw Ultra 12.0 and Chem3D Pro. The two receptors used CDK6 (PDB ID: 8I0M) and HRAS (PDB ID: 3K8Y) were obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (https://www.rcsb.org/). Initial validation involved re-docking each receptor with its native ligand to ensure accuracy, targeting an RMSD value below 2.0 Å. Docking results were assessed based on the rerank score and interactions with amino acid residues, and were compared with the binding of the native ligand [ 31 ]. LC-MS/MS analysis of persimmon vinegar identified 22 known compounds and 2 unknowns. The total ion chromatogram (TIC) obtained from mass spectrometry is presented in Figure 2 , and detailed in Table 1 , along with their respective elemental formulas. Data from mass spectrometry includes the detected and calculated m/z values, molecular formula, error rate in parts per million (ppm), retention time, and MS fragmentation pattern of the identified compounds. Each peak in the chromatogram corresponded to a specific bioactive compound, which was categorized into one of the following classes: fatty acids/lipids and its derivatives, peptides, monosaccharide and its derivatives, flavonoids, phenol, saponin, amines, amides ( Table 1 ). Notably, the primary component were capsaicinoids including capsaicin, dihydrocapsaicin, nordihydrocapsaicin and capsiamide. The Chromatogram of Persimmon Vinegar ( Diospyros kaki fruit) was Analyzed Using the UPLC-QToF-MS/MS Method. A C18 column served as the stationary phase, while the mobile phases were composed of water with formic acid [99.9:0.1 (v/v)] and acetonitrile with formic acid [99.9:0.1 (v/v)]. Each peak observed in the chromatogram corresponds to an individual compound Interpretation of Metabolite Profiling Results of Persimmon Vinegar ( Diospyros kaki Fruit) The physicochemical characteristics of persimmon vinegar compounds were assessed using Lipinski's Rule of Five. This rule outlines that for a compound to exhibit drug-like properties, it should fulfill the following criteria: molecular weight (MW) ≤ 500 g/mol, Log P ≤ 5 (reflecting hydrophobicity), no more than five hydrogen bond donors (HBD), up to 10 hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), polar surface area (PSA) ≤ 140 Å², and fewer than 10 rotatable bonds, which relate to drug permeability and molecular flexibility [ 23 ]. Compounds that violate no more than one of these conditions are deemed viable for oral drug formulations. Metabolite Profiling and Network Pharmacology of Persimmon Vinegar ( Diospyros kaki ) Compounds, with in silico Validation for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Therapy

Objective: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent form of lung cancer, with complex mechanisms, drug resistance, and significant side effects from conventional chemotherapy, all of which hinder effective treatment. Diospyros kaki (persimmon) vinegar, produced through spontaneous fermentation, has enhanced flavonoid content that may increase its pharmacological activity; however, its molecular mechanisms against NSCLC remain unclear. This is the first study to map the molecular mechanisms of persimmon vinegar compounds against NSCLC by integrating metabolite profiling, network pharmacology, and molecular docking validation. Methods: Compounds were identified using liquid chromatography--tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and screened for pharmacological properties, followed by network pharmacology and molecular docking to explore potential targets against NSCLC. Result: Twenty-two compounds were identified, with three key compounds benzoyl arginine amine, indoline, and exocarpic acid, implicated in the NSCLC pathway (hsa05223). Twenty-seven target genes were associated with this pathway. Benzoyl arginine amine exhibited a binding affinity of −86.9707 kcal/mol for CDK6 (PDB ID: 8I0M) and −120.017 kcal/mol for HRAS (PDB ID: 3K8Y), greater than their native ligand, suggesting its potential to inhibit CDK6 activity, block the G1/S phase transition, and suppress cancer cell proliferation via the E2F pathway. Its interaction with HRAS may inhibit the MAPK pathway, which is critical for cancer progression. Conclusion: These findings provide preliminary evidence for the potential of persimmon vinegar compounds as leads for NSCLC drug development, warranting further in vitro and in vivo studies.

Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent form of lung cancer, comprising about 85% of cases [ 1 ]. NSCLC develops from lung epithelial cells and includes subtypes such as adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma [ 2 ]. Globally, it remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths, with an estimated 1.8 million fatalities annually [ 3 ]. Key risk factors, including smoking, air pollution, and radiation exposure, continue to drive its high incidence [ 4 ]. These mutations are linked to drug resistance and side effects, posing challenges for treatment [ 5 -- 7 ]. Despite progress in targeted and immunotherapies, the five-year survival rate for NSCLC is still low, at only 10--20%. While conventional treatments have evolved, drug resistance and significant adverse effects pose significant challenges in NSCLC management [ 5 -- 7 ]. Consequently, developing novel, more effective, and safer therapeutic approaches is urgently needed. Over the past decade, molecular research has unveiled various oncogenic mutations that contribute to NSCLC, including KRAS (20--30%), EGFR (10--40%), and ALK translocations (3--5%), which activate pathways such as MAPK and CDK6, which play crucial roles in cell cycle regulation and proliferation [ 8 , 9 ]. One promising approach to address these challenges is the utilization of natural compounds as adjunctive or alternative therapy. Phytochemicals found in medicinal plants have demonstrated the potential to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and overcome drug resistance [ 10 , 11 ]. However, research on the use of medicinal plants in NSCLC therapy remains limited and warrants further exploration. Natural products have emerged as promising alternatives due to their multi-targeted mechanisms and lower toxicity profiles. In particular, compounds derived from Diospyros kaki (persimmon) from the Ebenaceae family is one such plant that has shown promise as a chemopreventive agent. Persimmon contains secondary metabolites such as proanthocyanidins, epigallocatechin (EGC), epigallocatechin-3-O-gallate (EGCG), terpenoids, and naphthoquinones, which have been proven to possess anticancer activities [ 12 , 13 ]. Flavonoid content from D. kaki have been reported to induce apoptosis in prostate cancer (PC-3) cells by increasing oxidative stress [ 14 ] and activate c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling [ 15 ]. polysaccharides isolated from persimmon have exhibited anticancer potential by suppressing Transforming Growth Factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1)-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in A549 lung cancer cells [ 16 ]. Persimmon vinegar exhibits strong antioxidant potential, as evidenced by its ability to suppress lipid peroxidation and neutralize 2,2′-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radicals, effects primarily attributed to its abundant phenolic compounds [ 15 ]. Spontaneous fermentation enhances its bioactive content, producing persimmon vinegar with higher levels of phenolics, flavonoids, gallic acid, and chlorogenic acid than fresh fruit or other vinegars, alongside stronger antioxidant activity [ 14 , 15 ]. To date, no study has comprehensively characterized the molecular targets of persimmon vinegar against NSCLC using integrated metabolomics and network pharmacology approaches. Therefore, this study aimed to identify the bioactive compounds of persimmon vinegar and evaluate their potential to inhibit NSCLC pathways. The approach involves liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, network pharmacology, and in silico validation. Network pharmacology serves as a valuable tool for predicting biological targets and complex pathways influenced by natural compounds [ 17 , 18 ], enabling the identification of potential synergistic effects between persimmon vinegar and conventional NSCLC therapies. This study is expected to significantly contribute to developing plant-based therapies for NSCLC by integrating these methods. The novelty of this research lies in the fermentation approach to enhance the pharmacological potential of persimmon and the exploration of molecular mechanisms through the analysis of signaling pathways involved in lung cancer cell proliferation and survival and its validation in silico. title: Performance of Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) Risk Assessment Tools in Clinical Practice - Agreement Between Different CVD Risk Scores Among Patients Attending NCD Clinic in a Tertiary Care Setting: A Prospective Observational Study
abstract: Background: We aimed to compare performance of three cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk estimation tools; the World Health Organization/International Society of Hypertension (WHO/ISH) risk prediction tool, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ACC/AHA ASCVD) Risk Estimator, and Framingham risk score (FRS) in estimating the risk of fatal and nonfatal cardiovascular events. Methods: We conducted a prospective, observational, hospital-based study involving 200 high-risk study participants, who visited a non-communicable disease clinic in a tertiary care hospital in eastern India. The 10-year CVD risk was estimated using the ACC/AHA ASCVD Risk Estimator, FRS, and the WHO/ISH risk prediction tool. We used kappa statistics to determine agreement among these CVD risk estimators. Results: The mean (SD) age of study participants was 54.07 (9.15) years, and the majority (63.5%) were males. About 96% of the participants were diabetic, 33.5% were hypertensive, and 16% were current smokers. About 18%, 20.5%, and 0.5% were classified as high-risk using the ACC/AHA ASCVD Risk Estimator, FRS, and WHO/ISH risk tools, respectively. The agreement was moderate between the ASCVD risk estimator and FRS (Kappa 0.541, P < 0.001) and fair between the ASCVD risk Estimator and WHO/ISH (Kappa 0.305, P < 0.001) and between FRS and WHO/ISH (Kappa 0.314, P < 0.001). Conclusions: A higher level of agreement was found between FRS and ASCVD risk scores compared to the WHO-ISH risk score. The WHO-ISH risk score identified most study participants in the lower-risk category, contrary to the FRS and ASCVD risk scores.
body: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) include a range of conditions such as cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases. Four NCDs, namely CVDs, chronic respiratory disease, cancers, and diabetes, contribute to about 82% of all NCD deaths. Further, CVDs such as coronary heart disease, stroke, and hypertension alone contribute to 45% of all NCD deaths and are the major cause of NCD-related mortality.[ 1 ] CVD are the leading cause of death among people of all ages and have been in the same place for the last three decades.[ 2 ] The majority of NCD deaths take place in low and middle-income countries (LMIC), like India, which is experiencing a rapid urbanization model of epidemiological transition.[ 3 ] Individualized CVD prevention is essential and economical to prevent adverse outcomes. An in-depth study of cardiovascular risk variables in India from 1990 to 2016 discovered that dietary patterns and systolic blood pressure (SBP) contributed substantially to CVDs (56.4%). Following these, the most common risk factors for CVDs in the Indian population were reported as elevated total cholesterol (29.4%), tobacco use (18.9%), increased fasting plasma glucose (16.7%), and high body mass index (14.7%).[ 4 ] The research has shown that the annual rate of CVD decreases by 20%–25% for every one millimole per liter reduction in LDL cholesterol by a statin.[ 5 ] Aspirin therapy was also linked to a substantial (21% lower risk) of cardiovascular events, including nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and cardiovascular death, and a 13% lower risk of all-cause mortality.[ 6 ] The World Health Organization (WHO) advises using CVD risk assessment tools to guide evidence-based treatments, such as aspirin and statin therapy, for the primary prevention of asymptomatic individuals based on their specific level of CVD risk. To identify who would benefit from these treatments, it is essential to assess their absolute risk of developing CVD. This paved the way for the development of various CVD risk prediction tools. There are many CVD risk prediction tools available, including Framingham Risk Score, the WHO/ISH risk prediction tool, SCORE (Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation), Reynolds Risk Score, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD) Risk Estimator, QRISK, and so on. The most used are the World Health Organization/International Society of Hypertension (WHO/ISH) guidelines, the Framingham Risk Score (FRS), and the Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD) risk prediction tools. These scores predict the 10-year risk of occurrence of any fatal or non-fatal CVDs. Risk prediction may influence the patient‘s behavior and treatment choices by providing a better understanding of the patient‘s cardiovascular prognosis. A good risk prediction tool should prevent under- and overtreatment, enhancing individual clinical outcomes and resource allocation.[ 7 ] There is no study in the Indian setting comparing the above-mentioned scales. Hence, this study was conducted to determine the agreement between these tools and to identify the tool with the ability to detect a high number of individuals with medium and high risk. Our objective was to compare three cardiovascular disease risk assessment tools in evaluating patients at a tertiary hospital in India. We conducted this hospital-based, prospective, observational study in the NCD Clinic of an institute of national importance in Eastern India from January to March 2024. In this clinic, approximately 30 to 40 patients attend every day, mainly for the treatment of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia. Participants aged 40–74 years, with a lipid profile report from the last 3 months of data collection, were included. The participants having severe comorbidities such as severe heart failure, severe physical disability, or dementia, which are likely to affect their participation in the study, were excluded. Those who already suffered from angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, stroke, transient ischemic attack, or peripheral vascular disease were excluded from the study. The participants with any of the following laboratory parameters where the score cannot be calculated, such as SBP < 90 mm Hg or > 200 mm Hg, DBP < 60 mm Hg or > 130 mm Hg, TC < 130 mg/dL or > 320 mg/dL, HDL < 20 mg/dL or > 100 mg/dL and LDL < 70 mg/dL or > 300 mg/dL were also excluded for score estimation. The beneficiaries fulfilling the above-mentioned criteria were enrolled consecutively in the study. Based on the available literature, we assumed an adequate sample size of 200 for this study. Sociodemographic, physical, and biochemical parameters necessary for calculating risk prediction were collected after obtaining informed consent from the participants. Biochemical parameters were obtained from available reports of the last three months, whichever is the latest. Background: We aimed to compare performance of three cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk estimation tools; the World Health Organization/International Society of Hypertension (WHO/ISH) risk prediction tool, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ACC/AHA ASCVD) Risk Estimator, and Framingham risk score (FRS) in estimating the risk of fatal and nonfatal cardiovascular events. Methods: We conducted a prospective, observational, hospital-based study involving 200 high-risk study participants, who visited a non-communicable disease clinic in a tertiary care hospital in eastern India. The 10-year CVD risk was estimated using the ACC/AHA ASCVD Risk Estimator, FRS, and the WHO/ISH risk prediction tool. We used kappa statistics to determine agreement among these CVD risk estimators. Results: The mean (SD) age of study participants was 54.07 (9.15) years, and the majority (63.5%) were males. About 96% of the participants were diabetic, 33.5% were hypertensive, and 16% were current smokers. About 18%, 20.5%, and 0.5% were classified as high-risk using the ACC/AHA ASCVD Risk Estimator, FRS, and WHO/ISH risk tools, respectively. The agreement was moderate between the ASCVD risk estimator and FRS (Kappa 0.541, P < 0.001) and fair between the ASCVD risk Estimator and WHO/ISH (Kappa 0.305, P < 0.001) and between FRS and WHO/ISH (Kappa 0.314, P < 0.001). Conclusions: A higher level of agreement was found between FRS and ASCVD risk scores compared to the WHO-ISH risk score. The WHO-ISH risk score identified most study participants in the lower-risk category, contrary to the FRS and ASCVD risk scores.

title: Impact of Health Promotion Programs on Incarcerated Individuals in Northern Mexico
abstract: Background: Individuals deprived of liberty exhibit high health vulnerability due to limited access to medical services and insufficient health promotion efforts. Implementing education and self-care programs constitutes an essential strategy to improve their wellbeing. The objective of this study was to evaluate changes in clinical parameters following the implementation of health promotion programs among incarcerated individuals. Methods: A prospective pre–post intervention study was conducted between February 2023 and July 2024 at the Male Social Reintegration Center No. 1 in Aquiles Serdán, Chihuahua, Mexico. Fifteen male inmates with type 2 diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension participated in a structured health promotion program that included educational workshops on nutrition, physical activity, and chronic disease self-management. Anthropometric and biochemical data were collected before and after the intervention. Statistical analysis included paired Student’s t -test and McNemar’s test ( P < 0.05). Results: Significant reductions were observed in blood glucose (174.1 ± 123.2 vs. 111.1 ± 57.4 mg/dL; P = 0.0017), systolic blood pressure (140.7 ± 18.3 vs. 117.3 ± 9.6 mmHg; P < 0.001), diastolic blood pressure (92.0 ± 10.8 vs. 84.0 ± 7.4 mmHg; P = 0.0013), and waist circumference (83.6 ± 37.6 vs. 80.3 ± 35.7 cm; P = 0.0005), with a favorable trend in body mass index ( P = 0.065). Conclusions: Health promotion programs had a positive impact on the control of chronic diseases among the incarcerated population studied. These findings highlight the need to strengthen sustainable interdisciplinary strategies that uphold the right to health in prison settings.
body: Penitentiary environments represent settings with unique health challenges, characterized by the high prevalence of chronic diseases and limited access to adequate medical services. Most individuals entering correctional facilities have a history of social inequality, substance use, lack of education, and limited access to preventive medicine, which increases their vulnerability in terms of health and overall wellbeing.[ 1 ] Health promotion within the prison system remains a scarcely explored area, yet it holds great potential to improve inmates’ living conditions and overall wellbeing. Its implications span multiple dimensions: prevention of infectious diseases, control of chronic diseases, mental health care, addiction management, and access to both basic and specialized medical services. Moreover, it involves aspects related to the physical environment of penitentiary centers, nutrition, physical activity, hygiene, and occupational health.[ 2 ] In Mexico, the penitentiary system is governed by the National Code of Criminal Procedures and the National Law of Criminal Enforcement (LNEP), which establish the stages and provisions applicable when an individual commits a state or federal crime.[ 3 ] Article 9 of the LNEP recognizes that persons deprived of liberty retain the rights established in the Constitution and in international treaties ratified by the Mexican State, except those restricted by sentence.[ 4 ] Among these rights is access to medical care appropriate to their specific age and sex needs, either through medical units within the penitentiary center or, when necessary, through referral to external health services.[ 4 5 6 ] Additionally, Article 74 states that health is a fundamental human right that must be guaranteed through the protection, promotion, and restoration of inmates’ physical and psychological integrity.[ 4 ] Despite this legal framework, the penitentiary reality is characterized by limited coverage and deficiencies in the quality of health services. Factors such as overcrowding, staff shortages, and lack of material resources hinder adequate and timely medical care.[ 7 ] In most penitentiary centers, medical attention is limited to the primary level and often lacks medicines, medical supplies, and basic equipment. This results in difficulties controlling prevalent diseases such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus, which require continuous monitoring to prevent serious outcomes. Moreover, the absence of preventive and health education programs perpetuates unhealthy lifestyles.[ 8 ] This gap not only undermines the right to health of incarcerated individuals but also amplifies social inequalities as inmates are reintegrated into society without adequate treatment or tools for self-care. The implementation of education and health promotion programs in penitentiary settings represents a key strategy to reduce the incidence of new diseases and improve the control of pre-existing conditions. Providing inmates with self-care knowledge encourages the adoption of healthy habits, reduces risk factors, and promotes physical and mental wellbeing. Additionally, these interventions generate indirect benefits for the penitentiary system by reducing the demand for medical services and the costs associated with treating complications. In the long term, health education becomes an essential tool to facilitate social reintegration by equipping inmates with practical skills to maintain their wellbeing beyond incarceration. Despite the legal advances recognizing the right to health for incarcerated individuals, there is a gap in scientific literature regarding the impact of health promotion programs in Mexican prisons. To our knowledge, this is the first study conducted in northern Mexico assessing the impact of structured health promotion programs on chronic disease control within a penitentiary population. This regional focus provides novel evidence regarding health policy implementation in correctional settings, addressing a gap in national and international literature on the health of incarcerated individuals. In this context, the objective of this study was to evaluate changes in clinical parameters following the implementation of health promotion programs among incarcerated individuals. Figure 1 presents the conceptual framework underlying the health promotion intervention. Conceptual framework of the health promotion program in prison settings A prospective cohort study with a pre- and postintervention comparative design was conducted between February 2023 and July 2024 at the Male Social Reintegration Center No. 1, located in Aquiles Serdán, Chihuahua. The intervention consisted of health promotion programs focused on lifestyle modifications, based on the Ministry of Health’s Risk Factor Questionnaire, which was used for data collection and complemented with information from the databases of the Directorate of Social Reintegration. The study population consisted of individuals deprived of liberty diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension. Participants were selected through convenience sampling based on institutional availability. Data were entered in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) SPSS Statistics 25.0, New York, United States.. Measures of central tendency and dispersion were calculated for quantitative variables, and frequencies and proportions for qualitative variables. Pre- and postintervention comparisons were conducted using the paired Student’s t -test for continuous variables and the McNemar test for proportions, with a 5% significance level. A total of 15 male inmates diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension were included, aged between 20 and 57 years (mean: 42.5 years, SD = 10.6). When comparing clinical and anthropometric parameters between 2023 and 2024, statistically significant reductions were observed in most variables evaluated [ Table 1 ]. Results clínica and anthropometric parameters between 2023 and 2024 Blood glucose levels showed a relevant decrease, dropping from a mean of 174.1 mg/dL (SD = 123.2) in 2023 to 111.1 mg/dL (SD = 57.4) in 2024 ( P = 0.0017). Regarding blood pressure, the mean systolic pressure decreased significantly from 140.7 mmHg (SD = 18.3) in 2023 to 117.3 mmHg (SD = 9.6) in 2024 ( P < 0.001), while the diastolic pressure dropped from 92.0 mmHg (SD = 10.8) to 84.0 mmHg (SD = 7.4) ( P = 0.0013). In relation to body weight, a significant variation was recorded (2023: 68.5 ± 37.7 kg vs. 2024: 88.6 ± 37.5 kg; P = 0.026). The waist circumference decreased from 83.6 cm (SD = 37.6) to 80.3 cm (SD = 35.7), showing a significant difference ( P = 0.0005). The body mass index showed a nonsignificant reduction (2023: 46.4 ± 44.4 kg/m² vs. 2024: 37.5 ± 25.4 kg/m²; P = 0.065), although there was a favorable trend toward lower risk. This study evaluated the impact of health promotion programs on chronic disease control among incarcerated individuals in northern Mexico. The results confirmed that structured interventions emphasizing education, lifestyle modification, and continuous medical follow-up can significantly improve clinical parameters such as blood glucose and blood pressure levels. These findings support the initial hypothesis that health promotion strategies foster better self-care and metabolic control, even in restricted environments where health resources are limited. The significant reduction observed in glucose and blood pressure levels reflects the effectiveness of educational programs that empower inmates to understand their conditions, adhere to medical treatment, and adopt healthier behaviors. Similar results have been reported in a study that found that participation in structured health promotion programs improved physical activity and subjective wellbeing among incarcerated adults.[ 2 ] Likewise, an international systematic review showed that prison-based interventions for the management of chronic noncommunicable diseases are feasible and can lead to meaningful improvements when supported by consistent monitoring and institutional engagement.[ 8 ] Comparable evidence from the Diabetes Prevention Program adapted for correctional facilities demonstrated that lifestyle modification initiatives are achievable in prison settings and produce measurable improvements in weight control and glucose regulation.[ 9 ] These observations reinforce the idea that simple, low-cost interventions—when applied consistently—can have a real impact on the health of incarcerated populations. From a policy perspective, the present findings align with the WHO Health in Prisons Programme and the WHO Prison Health Framework, which both emphasize education, equity, and continuity of care as fundamental components of health promotion in closed settings.[ 10 11 ] In Mexico, previous research has highlighted persistent challenges in the management of diabetes and hypertension among prisoners in large urban centers, underscoring the need for standardized and sustained chronic disease care across facilities.[ 12 ] Our results provide complementary evidence supporting the expansion of such programs at regional and national levels. Although the Journal of Education and Health Promotion mainly reports on health education among prison staff rather than inmates, its studies offer relevant insights about institutional climate and the role of personnel engagement in sustaining health initiatives.[ 13 ] This dimension is crucial for maintaining the continuity of preventive actions and fostering an environment that values health as part of rehabilitation. The improvements observed in our cohort may also be explained by enhanced treatment adherence, increased awareness of nutrition and physical activity, and the presence of continuous professional supervision during the intervention period. Beyond their clinical outcomes, such programs promote empowerment, discipline, and autonomy—elements that contribute to the rehabilitation process and the recognition of health as a basic human right within penitentiary systems. Nevertheless, this study has limitations that should be acknowledged. The absence of a control group restricts causal inference, and convenience sampling may have introduced selection bias. Possible confounders such as changes in diet, medication adherence, or environmental factors were not fully controlled. However, the consistency of the improvement across several clinical parameters and the use of standardized measurement procedures strengthen the internal validity of the results. Overall, these findings confirm the feasibility and relevance of implementing structured health promotion programs within correctional institutions. Integrating educational, behavioral, and medical approaches can improve not only inmates’ physical health but also their prospects for successful reintegration into society. Health promotion interventions implemented in the Male Social Reintegration Center No. 1 in Aquiles Serdán, Chihuahua, resulted in measurable improvements in blood glucose, blood pressure, and waist circumference among inmates diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and hypertension. These findings confirm that structured educational and behavioral programs can positively influence chronic disease control even within restricted environments such as correctional facilities. The main strength of this study lies in demonstrating the feasibility of implementing sustained health promotion strategies in a prison context using limited resources. By integrating education, behavioral change, and medical follow-up, it was possible to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes and promote greater awareness of self-care among participants. However, the absence of a control group and the use of convenience sampling represent important limitations that restrict causal inference. Future studies should adopt randomized or multicenter designs to validate these findings and expand the scope to include mental health, nutrition, and rehabilitation outcomes. From a policy standpoint, the results align with the principles of the WHO Health in Prisons Programme and Mexico’s National Health Promotion Strategy, both of which recognize education, equity, and continuity of care as fundamental components of prison health. Strengthening such initiatives at the national level could reduce health inequities and support the fulfilment of the constitutional right to health for all individuals, regardless of their legal status. Future research should explore the sustainability of these programs and their long-term impact on social reintegration, adherence to treatment, and quality of life after release. Expanding interdisciplinary collaboration between the public health and justice systems will be essential to ensure continuity and scalability of health promotion within Mexico’s correctional institutions. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Universidad Autónoma de Chihuahua (Approval ID: CI-003-24). The research was classified as minimal risk and conducted in accordance with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki (2013 revision). All participants were informed of the study objectives, and data collection respected confidentiality and voluntary participation.
