Impact of Health Promotion Programs on Incarcerated Individuals in Northern Mexico

Background: Individuals deprived of liberty exhibit high health vulnerability due to limited access to medical services and insufficient health promotion efforts. Implementing education and self-care programs constitutes an essential strategy to improve their wellbeing. The objective of this study was to evaluate changes in clinical parameters following the implementation of health promotion programs among incarcerated individuals. Methods: A prospective pre–post intervention study was conducted between February 2023 and July 2024 at the Male Social Reintegration Center No. 1 in Aquiles Serdán, Chihuahua, Mexico. Fifteen male inmates with type 2 diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension participated in a structured health promotion program that included educational workshops on nutrition, physical activity, and chronic disease self-management. Anthropometric and biochemical data were collected before and after the intervention. Statistical analysis included paired Student’s t -test and McNemar’s test ( P < 0.05). Results: Significant reductions were observed in blood glucose (174.1 ± 123.2 vs. 111.1 ± 57.4 mg/dL; P = 0.0017), systolic blood pressure (140.7 ± 18.3 vs. 117.3 ± 9.6 mmHg; P < 0.001), diastolic blood pressure (92.0 ± 10.8 vs. 84.0 ± 7.4 mmHg; P = 0.0013), and waist circumference (83.6 ± 37.6 vs. 80.3 ± 35.7 cm; P = 0.0005), with a favorable trend in body mass index ( P = 0.065). Conclusions: Health promotion programs had a positive impact on the control of chronic diseases among the incarcerated population studied. These findings highlight the need to strengthen sustainable interdisciplinary strategies that uphold the right to health in prison settings.

Penitentiary environments represent settings with unique health challenges, characterized by the high prevalence of chronic diseases and limited access to adequate medical services. Most individuals entering correctional facilities have a history of social inequality, substance use, lack of education, and limited access to preventive medicine, which increases their vulnerability in terms of health and overall wellbeing.[ 1 ] Health promotion within the prison system remains a scarcely explored area, yet it holds great potential to improve inmates’ living conditions and overall wellbeing. Its implications span multiple dimensions: prevention of infectious diseases, control of chronic diseases, mental health care, addiction management, and access to both basic and specialized medical services. Moreover, it involves aspects related to the physical environment of penitentiary centers, nutrition, physical activity, hygiene, and occupational health.[ 2 ] In Mexico, the penitentiary system is governed by the National Code of Criminal Procedures and the National Law of Criminal Enforcement (LNEP), which establish the stages and provisions applicable when an individual commits a state or federal crime.[ 3 ] Article 9 of the LNEP recognizes that persons deprived of liberty retain the rights established in the Constitution and in international treaties ratified by the Mexican State, except those restricted by sentence.[ 4 ] Among these rights is access to medical care appropriate to their specific age and sex needs, either through medical units within the penitentiary center or, when necessary, through referral to external health services.[ 4 5 6 ] Additionally, Article 74 states that health is a fundamental human right that must be guaranteed through the protection, promotion, and restoration of inmates’ physical and psychological integrity.[ 4 ] Despite this legal framework, the penitentiary reality is characterized by limited coverage and deficiencies in the quality of health services. Factors such as overcrowding, staff shortages, and lack of material resources hinder adequate and timely medical care.[ 7 ] In most penitentiary centers, medical attention is limited to the primary level and often lacks medicines, medical supplies, and basic equipment. This results in difficulties controlling prevalent diseases such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus, which require continuous monitoring to prevent serious outcomes. Moreover, the absence of preventive and health education programs perpetuates unhealthy lifestyles.[ 8 ] This gap not only undermines the right to health of incarcerated individuals but also amplifies social inequalities as inmates are reintegrated into society without adequate treatment or tools for self-care. The implementation of education and health promotion programs in penitentiary settings represents a key strategy to reduce the incidence of new diseases and improve the control of pre-existing conditions. Providing inmates with self-care knowledge encourages the adoption of healthy habits, reduces risk factors, and promotes physical and mental wellbeing. Additionally, these interventions generate indirect benefits for the penitentiary system by reducing the demand for medical services and the costs associated with treating complications. In the long term, health education becomes an essential tool to facilitate social reintegration by equipping inmates with practical skills to maintain their wellbeing beyond incarceration. Despite the legal advances recognizing the right to health for incarcerated individuals, there is a gap in scientific literature regarding the impact of health promotion programs in Mexican prisons. To our knowledge, this is the first study conducted in northern Mexico assessing the impact of structured health promotion programs on chronic disease control within a penitentiary population. This regional focus provides novel evidence regarding health policy implementation in correctional settings, addressing a gap in national and international literature on the health of incarcerated individuals. In this context, the objective of this study was to evaluate changes in clinical parameters following the implementation of health promotion programs among incarcerated individuals. Figure 1 presents the conceptual framework underlying the health promotion intervention. Conceptual framework of the health promotion program in prison settings A prospective cohort study with a pre- and postintervention comparative design was conducted between February 2023 and July 2024 at the Male Social Reintegration Center No. 1, located in Aquiles Serdán, Chihuahua. The intervention consisted of health promotion programs focused on lifestyle modifications, based on the Ministry of Health’s Risk Factor Questionnaire, which was used for data collection and complemented with information from the databases of the Directorate of Social Reintegration. The study population consisted of individuals deprived of liberty diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension. Participants were selected through convenience sampling based on institutional availability. Data were entered in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) SPSS Statistics 25.0, New York, United States.. Measures of central tendency and dispersion were calculated for quantitative variables, and frequencies and proportions for qualitative variables. Pre- and postintervention comparisons were conducted using the paired Student’s t -test for continuous variables and the McNemar test for proportions, with a 5% significance level. A total of 15 male inmates diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension were included, aged between 20 and 57 years (mean: 42.5 years, SD = 10.6). When comparing clinical and anthropometric parameters between 2023 and 2024, statistically significant reductions were observed in most variables evaluated [ Table 1 ]. Results clínica and anthropometric parameters between 2023 and 2024 Blood glucose levels showed a relevant decrease, dropping from a mean of 174.1 mg/dL (SD = 123.2) in 2023 to 111.1 mg/dL (SD = 57.4) in 2024 ( P = 0.0017). Regarding blood pressure, the mean systolic pressure decreased significantly from 140.7 mmHg (SD = 18.3) in 2023 to 117.3 mmHg (SD = 9.6) in 2024 ( P < 0.001), while the diastolic pressure dropped from 92.0 mmHg (SD = 10.8) to 84.0 mmHg (SD = 7.4) ( P = 0.0013). In relation to body weight, a significant variation was recorded (2023: 68.5 ± 37.7 kg vs. 2024: 88.6 ± 37.5 kg; P = 0.026). The waist circumference decreased from 83.6 cm (SD = 37.6) to 80.3 cm (SD = 35.7), showing a significant difference ( P = 0.0005). The body mass index showed a nonsignificant reduction (2023: 46.4 ± 44.4 kg/m² vs. 2024: 37.5 ± 25.4 kg/m²; P = 0.065), although there was a favorable trend toward lower risk. This study evaluated the impact of health promotion programs on chronic disease control among incarcerated individuals in northern Mexico. The results confirmed that structured interventions emphasizing education, lifestyle modification, and continuous medical follow-up can significantly improve clinical parameters such as blood glucose and blood pressure levels. These findings support the initial hypothesis that health promotion strategies foster better self-care and metabolic control, even in restricted environments where health resources are limited. The significant reduction observed in glucose and blood pressure levels reflects the effectiveness of educational programs that empower inmates to understand their conditions, adhere to medical treatment, and adopt healthier behaviors. Similar results have been reported in a study that found that participation in structured health promotion programs improved physical activity and subjective wellbeing among incarcerated adults.[ 2 ] Likewise, an international systematic review showed that prison-based interventions for the management of chronic noncommunicable diseases are feasible and can lead to meaningful improvements when supported by consistent monitoring and institutional engagement.[ 8 ] Comparable evidence from the Diabetes Prevention Program adapted for correctional facilities demonstrated that lifestyle modification initiatives are achievable in prison settings and produce measurable improvements in weight control and glucose regulation.[ 9 ] These observations reinforce the idea that simple, low-cost interventions—when applied consistently—can have a real impact on the health of incarcerated populations. From a policy perspective, the present findings align with the WHO Health in Prisons Programme and the WHO Prison Health Framework, which both emphasize education, equity, and continuity of care as fundamental components of health promotion in closed settings.[ 10 11 ] In Mexico, previous research has highlighted persistent challenges in the management of diabetes and hypertension among prisoners in large urban centers, underscoring the need for standardized and sustained chronic disease care across facilities.[ 12 ] Our results provide complementary evidence supporting the expansion of such programs at regional and national levels. Although the Journal of Education and Health Promotion mainly reports on health education among prison staff rather than inmates, its studies offer relevant insights about institutional climate and the role of personnel engagement in sustaining health initiatives.[ 13 ] This dimension is crucial for maintaining the continuity of preventive actions and fostering an environment that values health as part of rehabilitation. The improvements observed in our cohort may also be explained by enhanced treatment adherence, increased awareness of nutrition and physical activity, and the presence of continuous professional supervision during the intervention period. Beyond their clinical outcomes, such programs promote empowerment, discipline, and autonomy—elements that contribute to the rehabilitation process and the recognition of health as a basic human right within penitentiary systems. Nevertheless, this study has limitations that should be acknowledged. The absence of a control group restricts causal inference, and convenience sampling may have introduced selection bias. Possible confounders such as changes in diet, medication adherence, or environmental factors were not fully controlled. However, the consistency of the improvement across several clinical parameters and the use of standardized measurement procedures strengthen the internal validity of the results. Overall, these findings confirm the feasibility and relevance of implementing structured health promotion programs within correctional institutions. Integrating educational, behavioral, and medical approaches can improve not only inmates’ physical health but also their prospects for successful reintegration into society. Health promotion interventions implemented in the Male Social Reintegration Center No. 1 in Aquiles Serdán, Chihuahua, resulted in measurable improvements in blood glucose, blood pressure, and waist circumference among inmates diagnosed with diabetes mellitus and hypertension. These findings confirm that structured educational and behavioral programs can positively influence chronic disease control even within restricted environments such as correctional facilities. The main strength of this study lies in demonstrating the feasibility of implementing sustained health promotion strategies in a prison context using limited resources. By integrating education, behavioral change, and medical follow-up, it was possible to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes and promote greater awareness of self-care among participants. However, the absence of a control group and the use of convenience sampling represent important limitations that restrict causal inference. Future studies should adopt randomized or multicenter designs to validate these findings and expand the scope to include mental health, nutrition, and rehabilitation outcomes. From a policy standpoint, the results align with the principles of the WHO Health in Prisons Programme and Mexico’s National Health Promotion Strategy, both of which recognize education, equity, and continuity of care as fundamental components of prison health. Strengthening such initiatives at the national level could reduce health inequities and support the fulfilment of the constitutional right to health for all individuals, regardless of their legal status. Future research should explore the sustainability of these programs and their long-term impact on social reintegration, adherence to treatment, and quality of life after release. Expanding interdisciplinary collaboration between the public health and justice systems will be essential to ensure continuity and scalability of health promotion within Mexico’s correctional institutions. All participants were informed of the study objectives, and data collection respected confidentiality and voluntary participation. title: Impact of Vitamin D Supplementation on Levels of Serum Cholecalciferol and Cytokines in Individuals with Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Relevant Clinical Trials
abstract: Background: This study assesses the impact of vitamin D supplementation on serum cholecalciferol levels and some cytokines in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. Methods: We conducted a thorough search for relevant RCTs in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar using appropriate keywords until December 2024. We calculated weighted mean differences (WMDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) through random-effects analysis. Results: Five studies were included. Combining data from four studies showed a significant increase in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels after supplementation (WMD: 23.72; 95% CI: 12.92, 34.52). However, results from two studies indicated no significant changes in serum CRP (WMD: -2.48; 95% CI: -7.42, 2.46) and IL-6 (WMD: -2.49; 95% CI: -6.89, 1.92) levels. Conversely, TNF-α significantly decreased after administration (WMD: -0.81; 95% CI: -1.18, -0.45). There were no significant changes in anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 levels (WMD: 0.29; 95% CI: -0.43, 1.01). Conclusions: This study demonstrates a significant rise in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol and a significant decrease in TNF-α, with no notable changes in serum CRP, IL-6, and IL-10 levels in CRC patients after vitamin D treatment.
body: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a significant cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, ranking as the second leading cause of cancer mortality globally, with approximately 935,000 annual deaths.[ 1 ] It accounts for about 10% of all cancer cases.[ 2 ] In Germany, over 60,000 new cases and 24,000 deaths are reported each year.[ 3 ] The growing incidence of CRC results in substantial financial burdens on healthcare systems.[ 4 ] Earlier studies have found that vitamin D deficiency is common among CRC patients.[ 5 6 ] Vitamin D deficiency has been linked to the risk of severe CRC,[ 7 ] which might be partially explained by increment in the body inflammation.[ 8 9 10 ] Specific cytokines and inflammatory markers might play crucial roles in tumor development and progression. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) is known to promote cancer cell proliferation by inducing the expression of other proinflammatory cytokines. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is another key player; it facilitates tumor growth by promoting angiogenesis and enhancing the survival of cancer cells, creating a microenvironment conducive to tumor expansion. Similarly, C-reactive protein (CRP), an acute-phase reactant, is indicative of systemic inflammation and has been associated with poorer outcomes in CRC patients.[ 11 ] Due to the association between vitamin D deficiency and increased risk of inflammation, one might suggest that vitamin D supplementation can reduce inflammation and improve clinical symptoms in CRC patients. However, earlier studies reported conflicting results. Some clinical trials reported significant influence of vitamin D supplementation on inflammation,[ 12 13 ] while others found no significant changes in inflammatory biomarkers.[ 14 ] To the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have summarized the effects of vitamin D on inflammation biomarkers, such as cytokines and serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol concentrations in CRC patients. Some studies have examined vitamin D in combination with other substances and highlight the necessity to a comprehensive meta-analysis focusing on RCTs about vitamin D alone. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to explore the impact of vitamin D on the levels of cytokines and serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol in patients with CRC. We searched PubMed, SCOPUS, and EMBASE for relevant studies published until December 2024 using the following MESH and non-MESH keywords: PubMed: ((“Cholecalciferol”[Mesh] OR “Calcitriol”[Mesh] OR “Vitamin D”[Mesh] OR “Ergocalciferols”[Mesh] OR “vitamin D3”[tiab] OR “Vitamin D2”[tiab] OR “25-hydroxyvitamin D”[tiab] OR “25 (OH) D”[tiab] OR “Cholecalciferol”[tiab] OR “Calcitriol”[tiab] OR “Vitamin D”[tiab] OR “Ergocalciferols”[tiab]) AND (“colorectal cancer”[tiab] OR “colorectal neoplasm”[tiab] OR “colorectal”[tiab]) AND (trial[tiab] OR supplement[tiab] OR supplementation[tiab])). Embase: ((“Cholecalciferol”:ab, ti OR “Calcitriol”:ab, ti OR “Vitamin D”:ab, ti OR “Ergocalciferols”:ab, ti OR “25-hydroxyvitamin D”:ab, ti OR “25 (OH) D”:ab, ti) AND (“colorectal cancer”:ab, ti OR “colorectal neoplasm”:ab, ti OR “colorectal”:ab, ti) AND (trial: ab, ti OR supplement: ab, ti OR supplementation: ab, ti)). Scopus: (TITLE-ABS (Cholecalciferol* OR Calcitriol* OR Vitamin D* OR Ergocalciferols* OR 25-hydroxyvitamin D* OR 25 (OH) D*) AND (colorectal cancer* OR colorectal neoplasm* OR colorectal*) We eliminated duplicates and did not impose restrictions on publication time or language. We also examined reference lists of included RCTs to avoid overlooking relevant publications, excluding unpublished information, gray literature, dissertations, or congress articles. Furthermore, the first 20 pages of Goggle Scholar and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for RCTs were also checked to avoid missing any study. We first screened studies based on their title/abstract. At the second stage of screening, we evaluated full text of those studies. The relevant studies were as follows: All randomized clinical trials examining the impact of vitamin D supplementation on serum levels of cholecaciferol or any serum cytokine in CRC patients were included. Studies were excluded if they: 1) were animal studies, focused on pregnant or lactating women, or involved children; 2) lacked random allocation; 3) were observational; 4) examined the impact of additional supplements combined with vitamin D; 5) measured outcomes immediately after supplementation as this may not show the long-term effects of vitamin D on inflammatory biomarkers; 6) lacked a control group; or 7) measured inflammatory cytokines in cell lines or examined gene expression of those cytokines. Specifically, we excluded studies that combined vitamin D supplementation with other substances, such as calcium or omega-3 fatty acids, due to the potential confounding or synergetic effects these substances. In total, 323 records were found in PubMed, 389 in Scopus, and 302 in Embase. After removing duplicates, 408 records were entered to the screening process. In total, 18 articles passed the initial screening stage by the title/abstract, from which five articles were selected for the final analysis after full-text screening. Two independent reviewers collected the following information from included studies: first author, publication year, sample size, participants’ gender, number of participants in each group, age, vitamin D dosage, study duration, outcomes, and mean ± SD outcomes at baseline and after intervention. Other statistics like standard errors (SEs) or 95% CI were converted to SD before analysis. Measurements in various units were standardized to the most widely used unit. We used random-effects analysis to calculate pooled weighted mean differences (WMDs) and 95% CIs between intervention and control groups.[ 15 ] The Cochran’s Q test and I² statistic assessed study heterogeneity. We conducted subgroup analysis based on the intervention dosage (<2000 IU/day vs >200 0IU/day). Stata version 11.2 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX) was used for analyses, with a significance level of P < 0.05. Due to the limited number of available studies, we were unable to do other subgroup analyses. Publication bias was assessed by the visual inspection of funnel plot as well as using Egger regression test. Sensitivity analysis was performed to explore possible effect of any individual study on overall results. Methodological quality of included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for RCTs. Five studies were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis.[ 3 14 16 17 18 ] The PRISMA flowchart of study selection is presented in Figure 1 . In addition, the PRISMA checklist was completed for the study [ Supplementary Table 1 ]. General characteristics of those studies are summarized in Table 1 . Those studies were published between 2010 and 2023, involving 235 CRC patients, 122 patients in the intervention and 113 controls. Studies were done on both genders (79 females and 156 males). Participants’ age varied from 18 to 75 years. Quality assessment of those studies showed that all of them had at least four domains with low risk of bias [ Supplementary Table 2 ]. PRISMA flowchart of study selection PRISMA checklist From: Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM, Boutron I, Hoffmann TC, Mulrow CD, et al . The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ 2021;372:n71. doi: 10.1136/bmj.n71 General characteristics of included studies Quality assessment of the included studies, based on Cochrane assessment method L: Low risk; H: High risk; U: Unclear Vitamin D consumed in doses ranged from 800 IU/day to 50,000 IU/week, and the intervention duration varied from 8 weeks to 6 months. The measured outcomes included serum levels of 25 (OH) cholecalciferol,[ 3 16 17 18 ] C-reactive protein (CRP),[ 14 17 ] tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α),[ 14 17 ] interleukin (IL)-6,[ 14 17 ] and IL-10.[ 14 18 ] Other inflammatory biomarkers were not included in the meta-analysis because they were reported in only one study. Our meta-analysis indicated a significant increase in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels following vitamin D supplementation (WMD: 23.72; 95% CI: 12.92, 34.52) [ Figure 2 ], such that vitamin D supplementation led to an average increase of 23.72 ng/mL in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels in CRC patients. Subgroup analysis by the intervention dose revealed that supplementation with higher doses resulted in a more pronounced increase in serum levels of 25 (OH) cholecalciferol [ Figure 3 ], emphasizing the existence of a dose–response relationship. Reanalysis after excluding one study with the shortest duration revealed a mean increase of 20.69 ng/mL in 25 (OH) cholecalciferol after vitamin D supplementation (WMD: 20.69; 95% CI: 11.73, 29.64) (data did not show). Forest plot for the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol concentrations in patients with colorectal cancer. Diamonds show pooled estimates from random-effects analysis. Horizontal lines show 95% CIs Forest plot for the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol concentrations stratified by the intervention dose (<2000IU/day vs. >2000IU/day) in patients with colorectal cancer. Diamonds show pooled estimates from random-effects analysis. Horizontal lines show 95% CIs Assessment of funnel plot [ Supplementary Figure 1 ] and Egger regression test ( P = 0.12) reveled no evidence for the existence of publication bias. In addition, sensitivity assessment showed that there were no individual studies with great impact on the overall results [ Supplementary Figure 2 ]. Regarding proinflammatory biomarkers, pooling data from two studies showed no significant changes in serum CRP (WMD: -2.48; 95% CI: -7.42, 2.46) and IL-6 (WMD: -2.49; 95% CI: -6.89, 1.92) [ Figure 4a and b ]. However, TNF-α significantly decreased (WMD: -0.81; 95% CI: -1.18, -0.45) by vitamin D administration [ Figure 5 -a]. No significant change was seen in serum concentrations of anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 (WMD: 0.29; 95% CI: -0.43, 1.01) after vitamin D supplementation [ Figure 5 -b]. Forest plot for the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum CRP (a) and IL-6 (b) concentrations in colorectal cancer patients. Diamonds show pooled estimates from random-effects analysis. Horizontal lines show 95% CIs Forest plot for the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum TNF-α (a) and IL-10 (b) concentrations in colorectal cancer patients. Diamonds show pooled estimates from random-effects analysis. Horizontal lines show 95% CIs This systematic review and meta-analysis found a significant increase in serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol and a significant decrease in serum TNF-α levels in CRC patients after receiving vitamin D supplements, with no significant changes in serum CRP, IL-6, and IL-10 levels. Despite the clear findings from observational studies, few RCTs have examined vitamin D supplementation in CRC patients. A recent meta-analysis of observational studies indicated a lower risk of CRC occurrence among individuals with higher vitamin D intake.[ 19 ] The primary limitation of that meta-analysis was the observational design of the study, which makes it impossible to confer a causal relationship. Moreover, observational studies can be confounded by numerous factors; therefore, further RCTs are required to establish a causal association. Two prospective cohort studies found a strong correlation between serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol levels and inflammation in CRC patients.[ 20 ] Our analysis demonstrated a significant rise in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels following vitamin D supplementation in CRC patients, which is consistent with some earlier trials.[ 3 13 18 ] A combined analysis of these RCTs revealed that vitamin D supplementation led to an average increase of 23.72 ng/mL in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels. The clinical significance of this increase becomes clearer when considering that a serum vitamin D level of ≥20 ng/mL is considered adequate.[ 21 22 ] This increment might also be associated to the reduced inflammatory environment in the body which is associated to the cancer progression, treatment response, and overall survival.[ 20 23 ] A cross-sectional study in CRC patients found significant association between serum vitamin D levels and gene expression of some cytokines.[ 24 ] Although our analysis about the impact of vitamin D on inflammatory biomarkers is limited by the number of studies, we found a significant decrease in TNF-α, while CRP and IL-6 levels remained unchanged. This highlights the need for more RCTs to validate these results. The lack of significant alterations in CRP and IL-6 levels among CRC patients receiving vitamin D supplementation might be explained by some reasons. CRC is associated with a complex inflammatory environment, and the tumor microenvironment may modulate cytokine responses.[ 25 ] Tumors can secrete factors that either stimulate or inhibit cytokine production, potentially overshadowing any anti-inflammatory effects of vitamin D. Indeed, future studies should focus on secretary behavior of CRC tumors in different stages of disease. It seems that each tumor stimulates or inhibits secretion of a specific group of proinflammatory cytokines. TNF-α is a proinflammatory cytokine that plays a role in tumor progression, and high levels of it have been reported among patients with CRC.[ 24 ] Reduction in this proinflammatory cytokine is an important finding for the CRC patients, but this finding should be interpret by the tumor secretary behavior. In addition, the dosage and duration of vitamin D supplementation may influence its effectiveness in altering inflammatory markers. Unfortunately, the limited numbers of relevant studies made it impossible to do subgroup analyses to have more discussion in this area. Factors such as genetic polymorphisms, baseline vitamin D levels, and the presence of comorbidities can also affect inflammatory responses to vitamin D supplementation. The specific way in which vitamin D supplementation may impact inflammation in CRC patients is not fully understood. Vitamin D changes gut microbiota, through which it can reduce serum inflammation.[ 12 ] Vitamin D can promote the growth of beneficial bacteria, such as those in the Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium families. These bacteria are known to produce SCFAs, particularly butyrate. Butyrate is a primary energy source for colon cells and has potent anti-inflammatory effects. By encouraging the growth of these SCFA-producing bacteria, vitamin D indirectly reduces inflammation.[ 12 ] In addition, vitamin D might change gene expression of inflammatory cytokines.[ 24 ] For instance, vitamin D supplementation reduced Poly ADP ribose Polymerase (PARP) in inflammatory cascades in an RCT on a cancer line.[ 26 ] Moreover, vitamin D reduces inflammation by inhibiting p38MAPK activation in lamina propria cells.[ 27 ] Furthermore, activation of Vitamin D Receptor (VDR) can lead to apoptosis and inhabitation of cancer cells’ proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastatic potential.[ 28 ] In immune cells like macrophages and T cells, the activated VDR complex can directly suppress the genes that code for key proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α.[ 26 ] The VDR also interacts with a key inflammatory pathway involving a protein complex called NF-κB.[ 28 ] NF-κB is a master regulator of inflammation; when activated, it triggers the expression of numerous proinflammatory genes.[ 25 ] Vitamin D can inhibit NF-κB activation, effectively “turning off” a significant portion of the inflammatory response before it can even begin.[ 28 ] To the best of our understanding, our meta-analysis is the first systematic review and meta-analysis focused on the effects of vitamin D supplementation (alone) on serum cholecalciferol and inflammation among patients with CRC. Nonetheless, it is imperative to know certain limitations of our study. The limited number of included studies is the first concern. Earlier RCTs have focused on medical and herbal treatments for CRC, and less attention has been done for the dietary supplements. This highlights the importance of nutritional assessments and even dietary supplementations in cases of insufficiency. Moreover, dietary supplements might have additional benefits for the patients, even among those with sufficient intakes. Additionally, discrepancies in disease stage among participants across these studies may also be considered as a potential source of bias. A tumor might have different behaviors in different stages of a disease, in particular for secretion of cytokines, so it might show different responses to vitamin D supplementation. Furthermore, differences in the supplement dosage or duration of study can also affect the results. Our study was done exclusively on English-language studies, which may result in missing some relevant researches from non-English sources. Finally, it is crucial to acknowledge the impact of unmeasured confounding factors, such as participants’ initial vitamin D levels, which may also influence inflammatory outcomes. Considering this factor and other important confounding factors such as patients’ weight and physical activity as well as their medical treatments increases the validity of findings. Future RCTs should investigate vitamin D’s effects on various inflammatory markers in CRC patients. Our study showed a significant increase in serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol and a significant decrease in serum TNF-α levels, with no significant changes in serum CRP, IL-6, and IL-10 levels in CRC patients after vitamin D supplementation. The considerable increment in serum vitamin D levels (>23 ng/ml) and the decrement in TNF-α (>0.8 pg/ml) show clinically important impact of vitamin D supplementation among CRC patients, which is worthy of attention particularly among those with vitamin D insufficiency. Future studies using different vitamin D doses and durations on patients with different stages of the disease and measuring a various list of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines are needed to confirm our results. Stratification of participants based on CRC stages or baseline vitamin D status will result in better understanding of how these factors may influence the final outcomes. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a significant cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, ranking as the second leading cause of cancer mortality globally, with approximately 935,000 annual deaths.[ 1 ] It accounts for about 10% of all cancer cases.[ 2 ] In Germany, over 60,000 new cases and 24,000 deaths are reported each year.[ 3 ] The growing incidence of CRC results in substantial financial burdens on healthcare systems.[ 4 ] Earlier studies have found that vitamin D deficiency is common among CRC patients.[ 5 6 ] Vitamin D deficiency has been linked to the risk of severe CRC,[ 7 ] which might be partially explained by increment in the body inflammation.[ 8 9 10 ] Specific cytokines and inflammatory markers might play crucial roles in tumor development and progression. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) is known to promote cancer cell proliferation by inducing the expression of other proinflammatory cytokines. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is another key player; it facilitates tumor growth by promoting angiogenesis and enhancing the survival of cancer cells, creating a microenvironment conducive to tumor expansion. Similarly, C-reactive protein (CRP), an acute-phase reactant, is indicative of systemic inflammation and has been associated with poorer outcomes in CRC patients.[ 11 ] Due to the association between vitamin D deficiency and increased risk of inflammation, one might suggest that vitamin D supplementation can reduce inflammation and improve clinical symptoms in CRC patients. However, earlier studies reported conflicting results. Some clinical trials reported significant influence of vitamin D supplementation on inflammation,[ 12 13 ] while others found no significant changes in inflammatory biomarkers.[ 14 ] To the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have summarized the effects of vitamin D on inflammation biomarkers, such as cytokines and serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol concentrations in CRC patients. Some studies have examined vitamin D in combination with other substances and highlight the necessity to a comprehensive meta-analysis focusing on RCTs about vitamin D alone. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to explore the impact of vitamin D on the levels of cytokines and serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol in patients with CRC. We searched PubMed, SCOPUS, and EMBASE for relevant studies published until December 2024 using the following MESH and non-MESH keywords: PubMed: ((“Cholecalciferol”[Mesh] OR “Calcitriol”[Mesh] OR “Vitamin D”[Mesh] OR “Ergocalciferols”[Mesh] OR “vitamin D3”[tiab] OR “Vitamin D2”[tiab] OR “25-hydroxyvitamin D”[tiab] OR “25 (OH) D”[tiab] OR “Cholecalciferol”[tiab] OR “Calcitriol”[tiab] OR “Vitamin D”[tiab] OR “Ergocalciferols”[tiab]) AND (“colorectal cancer”[tiab] OR “colorectal neoplasm”[tiab] OR “colorectal”[tiab]) AND (trial[tiab] OR supplement[tiab] OR supplementation[tiab])). Embase: ((“Cholecalciferol”:ab, ti OR “Calcitriol”:ab, ti OR “Vitamin D”:ab, ti OR “Ergocalciferols”:ab, ti OR “25-hydroxyvitamin D”:ab, ti OR “25 (OH) D”:ab, ti) AND (“colorectal cancer”:ab, ti OR “colorectal neoplasm”:ab, ti OR “colorectal”:ab, ti) AND (trial: ab, ti OR supplement: ab, ti OR supplementation: ab, ti)). Scopus: (TITLE-ABS (Cholecalciferol* OR Calcitriol* OR Vitamin D* OR Ergocalciferols* OR 25-hydroxyvitamin D* OR 25 (OH) D*) AND (colorectal cancer* OR colorectal neoplasm* OR colorectal*) We eliminated duplicates and did not impose restrictions on publication time or language. We also examined reference lists of included RCTs to avoid overlooking relevant publications, excluding unpublished information, gray literature, dissertations, or congress articles. Furthermore, the first 20 pages of Goggle Scholar and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for RCTs were also checked to avoid missing any study. We first screened studies based on their title/abstract. At the second stage of screening, we evaluated full text of those studies. The relevant studies were as follows: All randomized clinical trials examining the impact of vitamin D supplementation on serum levels of cholecaciferol or any serum cytokine in CRC patients were included. Studies were excluded if they: 1) were animal studies, focused on pregnant or lactating women, or involved children; 2) lacked random allocation; 3) were observational; 4) examined the impact of additional supplements combined with vitamin D; 5) measured outcomes immediately after supplementation as this may not show the long-term effects of vitamin D on inflammatory biomarkers; 6) lacked a control group; or 7) measured inflammatory cytokines in cell lines or examined gene expression of those cytokines. Specifically, we excluded studies that combined vitamin D supplementation with other substances, such as calcium or omega-3 fatty acids, due to the potential confounding or synergetic effects these substances. In total, 323 records were found in PubMed, 389 in Scopus, and 302 in Embase. After removing duplicates, 408 records were entered to the screening process. In total, 18 articles passed the initial screening stage by the title/abstract, from which five articles were selected for the final analysis after full-text screening. Two independent reviewers collected the following information from included studies: first author, publication year, sample size, participants’ gender, number of participants in each group, age, vitamin D dosage, study duration, outcomes, and mean ± SD outcomes at baseline and after intervention. Other statistics like standard errors (SEs) or 95% CI were converted to SD before analysis. Measurements in various units were standardized to the most widely used unit. We used random-effects analysis to calculate pooled weighted mean differences (WMDs) and 95% CIs between intervention and control groups.[ 15 ] The Cochran’s Q test and I² statistic assessed study heterogeneity. We conducted subgroup analysis based on the intervention dosage (<2000 IU/day vs >200 0IU/day). Stata version 11.2 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX) was used for analyses, with a significance level of P < 0.05. Due to the limited number of available studies, we were unable to do other subgroup analyses. Publication bias was assessed by the visual inspection of funnel plot as well as using Egger regression test. Sensitivity analysis was performed to explore possible effect of any individual study on overall results. Methodological quality of included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for RCTs. Five studies were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis.[ 3 14 16 17 18 ] The PRISMA flowchart of study selection is presented in Figure 1 . In addition, the PRISMA checklist was completed for the study [ Supplementary Table 1 ]. General characteristics of those studies are summarized in Table 1 . Those studies were published between 2010 and 2023, involving 235 CRC patients, 122 patients in the intervention and 113 controls. Studies were done on both genders (79 females and 156 males). Participants’ age varied from 18 to 75 years. Quality assessment of those studies showed that all of them had at least four domains with low risk of bias [ Supplementary Table 2 ]. The measured outcomes included serum levels of 25 (OH) cholecalciferol,[ 3 16 17 18 ] C-reactive protein (CRP),[ 14 17 ] tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α),[ 14 17 ] interleukin (IL)-6,[ 14 17 ] and IL-10.[ 14 18 ] Other inflammatory biomarkers were not included in the meta-analysis because they were reported in only one study. Our meta-analysis indicated a significant increase in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels following vitamin D supplementation (WMD: 23.72; 95% CI: 12.92, 34.52) [ Figure 2 ], such that vitamin D supplementation led to an average increase of 23.72 ng/mL in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels in CRC patients. Subgroup analysis by the intervention dose revealed that supplementation with higher doses resulted in a more pronounced increase in serum levels of 25 (OH) cholecalciferol [ Figure 3 ], emphasizing the existence of a dose–response relationship. Reanalysis after excluding one study with the shortest duration revealed a mean increase of 20.69 ng/mL in 25 (OH) cholecalciferol after vitamin D supplementation (WMD: 20.69; 95% CI: 11.73, 29.64) (data did not show). Diamonds show pooled estimates from random-effects analysis. Horizontal lines show 95% CIs Assessment of funnel plot [ Supplementary Figure 1 ] and Egger regression test ( P = 0.12) reveled no evidence for the existence of publication bias. In addition, sensitivity assessment showed that there were no individual studies with great impact on the overall results [ Supplementary Figure 2 ]. Regarding proinflammatory biomarkers, pooling data from two studies showed no significant changes in serum CRP (WMD: -2.48; 95% CI: -7.42, 2.46) and IL-6 (WMD: -2.49; 95% CI: -6.89, 1.92) [ Figure 4a and b ]. However, TNF-α significantly decreased (WMD: -0.81; 95% CI: -1.18, -0.45) by vitamin D administration [ Figure 5 -a]. No significant change was seen in serum concentrations of anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 (WMD: 0.29; 95% CI: -0.43, 1.01) after vitamin D supplementation [ Figure 5 -b]. Diamonds show pooled estimates from random-effects analysis. Horizontal lines show 95% CIs This systematic review and meta-analysis found a significant increase in serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol and a significant decrease in serum TNF-α levels in CRC patients after receiving vitamin D supplements, with no significant changes in serum CRP, IL-6, and IL-10 levels. Despite the clear findings from observational studies, few RCTs have examined vitamin D supplementation in CRC patients. A recent meta-analysis of observational studies indicated a lower risk of CRC occurrence among individuals with higher vitamin D intake.[ 19 ] The primary limitation of that meta-analysis was the observational design of the study, which makes it impossible to confer a causal relationship. Moreover, observational studies can be confounded by numerous factors; therefore, further RCTs are required to establish a causal association. Two prospective cohort studies found a strong correlation between serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol levels and inflammation in CRC patients.[ 20 ] Our analysis demonstrated a significant rise in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels following vitamin D supplementation in CRC patients, which is consistent with some earlier trials.[ 3 13 18 ] A combined analysis of these RCTs revealed that vitamin D supplementation led to an average increase of 23.72 ng/mL in serum 25 (OH) cholecalciferol levels. The clinical significance of this increase becomes clearer when considering that a serum vitamin D level of ≥20 ng/mL is considered adequate.[ 21 22 ] This increment might also be associated to the reduced inflammatory environment in the body which is associated to the cancer progression, treatment response, and overall survival.[ 20 23 ] A cross-sectional study in CRC patients found significant association between serum vitamin D levels and gene expression of some cytokines.[ 24 ] Although our analysis about the impact of vitamin D on inflammatory biomarkers is limited by the number of studies, we found a significant decrease in TNF-α, while CRP and IL-6 levels remained unchanged. This highlights the need for more RCTs to validate these results. The lack of significant alterations in CRP and IL-6 levels among CRC patients receiving vitamin D supplementation might be explained by some reasons. CRC is associated with a complex inflammatory environment, and the tumor microenvironment may modulate cytokine responses.[ 25 ] Tumors can secrete factors that either stimulate or inhibit cytokine production, potentially overshadowing any anti-inflammatory effects of vitamin D. Indeed, future studies should focus on secretary behavior of CRC tumors in different stages of disease. It seems that each tumor stimulates or inhibits secretion of a specific group of proinflammatory cytokines. TNF-α is a proinflammatory cytokine that plays a role in tumor progression, and high levels of it have been reported among patients with CRC.[ 24 ] Reduction in this proinflammatory cytokine is an important finding for the CRC patients, but this finding should be interpret by the tumor secretary behavior. In addition, the dosage and duration of vitamin D supplementation may influence its effectiveness in altering inflammatory markers. Unfortunately, the limited numbers of relevant studies made it impossible to do subgroup analyses to have more discussion in this area. Factors such as genetic polymorphisms, baseline vitamin D levels, and the presence of comorbidities can also affect inflammatory responses to vitamin D supplementation. The specific way in which vitamin D supplementation may impact inflammation in CRC patients is not fully understood. Vitamin D changes gut microbiota, through which it can reduce serum inflammation.[ 12 ] Vitamin D can promote the growth of beneficial bacteria, such as those in the Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium families. These bacteria are known to produce SCFAs, particularly butyrate. Butyrate is a primary energy source for colon cells and has potent anti-inflammatory effects. By encouraging the growth of these SCFA-producing bacteria, vitamin D indirectly reduces inflammation.[ 12 ] In addition, vitamin D might change gene expression of inflammatory cytokines.[ 24 ] For instance, vitamin D supplementation reduced Poly ADP ribose Polymerase (PARP) in inflammatory cascades in an RCT on a cancer line.[ 26 ] Moreover, vitamin D reduces inflammation by inhibiting p38MAPK activation in lamina propria cells.[ 27 ] Furthermore, activation of Vitamin D Receptor (VDR) can lead to apoptosis and inhabitation of cancer cells’ proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastatic potential.[ 28 ] In immune cells like macrophages and T cells, the activated VDR complex can directly suppress the genes that code for key proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α.[ 26 ] The VDR also interacts with a key inflammatory pathway involving a protein complex called NF-κB.[ 28 ] NF-κB is a master regulator of inflammation; when activated, it triggers the expression of numerous proinflammatory genes.[ 25 ] Vitamin D can inhibit NF-κB activation, effectively “turning off” a significant portion of the inflammatory response before it can even begin.[ 28 ] To the best of our understanding, our meta-analysis is the first systematic review and meta-analysis focused on the effects of vitamin D supplementation (alone) on serum cholecalciferol and inflammation among patients with CRC. Nonetheless, it is imperative to know certain limitations of our study. The limited number of included studies is the first concern. Earlier RCTs have focused on medical and herbal treatments for CRC, and less attention has been done for the dietary supplements. This highlights the importance of nutritional assessments and even dietary supplementations in cases of insufficiency. Moreover, dietary supplements might have additional benefits for the patients, even among those with sufficient intakes. Additionally, discrepancies in disease stage among participants across these studies may also be considered as a potential source of bias. A tumor might have different behaviors in different stages of a disease, in particular for secretion of cytokines, so it might show different responses to vitamin D supplementation. Furthermore, differences in the supplement dosage or duration of study can also affect the results. Our study was done exclusively on English-language studies, which may result in missing some relevant researches from non-English sources. Finally, it is crucial to acknowledge the impact of unmeasured confounding factors, such as participants’ initial vitamin D levels, which may also influence inflammatory outcomes. Considering this factor and other important confounding factors such as patients’ weight and physical activity as well as their medical treatments increases the validity of findings. Future RCTs should investigate vitamin D’s effects on various inflammatory markers in CRC patients. Our study showed a significant increase in serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol and a significant decrease in serum TNF-α levels, with no significant changes in serum CRP, IL-6, and IL-10 levels in CRC patients after vitamin D supplementation. The considerable increment in serum vitamin D levels (>23 ng/ml) and the decrement in TNF-α (>0.8 pg/ml) show clinically important impact of vitamin D supplementation among CRC patients, which is worthy of attention particularly among those with vitamin D insufficiency. Future studies using different vitamin D doses and durations on patients with different stages of the disease and measuring a various list of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines are needed to confirm our results. Stratification of participants based on CRC stages or baseline vitamin D status will result in better understanding of how these factors may influence the final outcomes. title: Navigating Therapeutic Frontiers: A Meta-review and Meta-analysis of COVID-19 Treatment Options
abstract: To assess the efficacy and safety of each therapeutic options in the treatment of COVID-19 by assessing the evidence from existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and to carry out an umbrella meta-analysis of all meta-analysis studies to assess the efficacy of each drug. A comprehensive search was carried out in electronic databases for systematic reviews and meta-analyses which compared the efficacy and/or safety of therapeutic options in the treatment of COVID-19. Findings from the reviews were synthesized using tables and forest plots and the pooled estimate of effect size using the DerSimonian and Laird method was used for the updated meta-analysis. The main outcome was mortality. 285 reviews with 152 meta-analyses were included, The analysis of systematic reviews contents indicated that most reviewed drugs were as follows: chroquine/hydroxychloroquine ( n = 48), tocilizumab ( n = 39), remdesivir ( n = 25), corticosteroids ( n = 25), JAK inhibitors ( n = 12), colchicine ( n = 11), ivermectin ( n = 8), anakinra ( n = 7), favipravir ( n = 7), lopinavir/ritonavir ( n = 6), ACEI/ARB ( n = 6), azithromycin ( n = 4), sofosbuvir ( n = 4), and Vitamin D ( n = 4). Findings from the included reviews suggested that tocilizumab, remdesivir, corticosteroids, JAKI, anakinra, colchicine, ivermectin, and sofosbuvir decreased the rate of mortality significantly in those taking the drugs; otherwise hydroxylchroquine increased the risk of mortality significantly, while Lopinavir/Ritonavir had no benefit and ACEI and azithromycin decreased mortality rate not significantly. lower requirement for mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit admission and a shorter hospital length of stay was observed with the tocilizumab, JAKIs, anakinra, corticosteroids and sofosbuvir Only one third of the included reviews had 70% quality based on the AMSTAR scale assessment. The results of this study have the potential to be a useful tool for the translation of health evidence and for designing the decision support systems for evidence synthesis.
body: In December 2019, several cases of unexplained pneumonia with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) were first reported in Wuhan, China. A novel coronavirus, later identified as SARS-CoV-2, was determined to be the causative agent and subsequently designated as COVID-19 by the World Health Organization (WHO). As of January 18, 2022, over 326 million confirmed cases and 5.54 million deaths had been reported globally.[ 1 ] Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in Iran (March 2019), approximately 7 million individuals have been infected, and 140,000 have lost their lives.[ 2 ] The widespread availability of vaccines has played a significant role in controlling the disease globally. However, vaccination rates have been slower in low-and middle-income countries, and the morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 are expected to continue increasing, driven by successive waves of SARS-CoV-2 variants impacting many countries.[ 3 ] This persistent rise in COVID-19-related morbidity and mortality underscores the need for effective therapeutic interventions. Efforts are ongoing to identify drugs with proven efficacy in the treatment of COVID-19. Currently, Remdesivir is the only drug approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of COVID-19.[ 4 ] Other treatments that have received emergency use authorization include Molnupiravir, Paxlovid, and certain monoclonal antibodies, such as Bebtelovimab. In addition, the use of interferons, ivermectin, chloroquine, azithromycin, and lopinavir/ritonavir is not recommended.[ 5 ] The approval of drugs for use or nonuse is often based on clinical studies, including clinical trials, which are reviewed and categorized in evidence-based medicine. Evidence-based medicine involves identifying a well-defined question, searching for relevant evidence, critically appraising it, applying the findings, and measuring the associated outcomes, similar to the process of conducting a systematic review. As a result, high-quality evidence often originates from systematic reviews that synthesize clinical trials.[ 6 7 ] Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, numerous antiviral and anti-inflammatory drugs were proposed and entered clinical trials for COVID-19 treatment. Several systematic reviews have been conducted to evaluate these drugs, producing some evidence, although significant uncertainties remain. Like primary studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses have presented contradictory results. Reviews of systematic reviews are particularly valuable in evidence-based healthcare decision-making. This era has been termed the “age of evidence-based everything,” in which healthcare decision-makers are encouraged to create an environment conducive to peer-to-peer evidence sharing. Reviews of systematic reviews are particularly useful for translating health evidence into decision-making, and they serve as important resources for policy briefs and decision support systems. By synthesizing evidence from multiple systematic reviews, these umbrella reviews provide comprehensive summaries that are often preferred by healthcare decision-makers.[ 8 ] In this context, we conducted this umbrella review with two main objectives: (1) to assess the efficacy and safety of various therapeutic options for COVID-19 by evaluating evidence from existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses and (2) to conduct an umbrella meta-analysis of all available meta-analytic studies to assess the efficacy of each drug. These secondary studies are instrumental in developing treatment guidelines, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to internationally approved drugs may be restricted. This study comprises two main components: An overview of all existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and an umbrella meta-analysis of these meta-analyses to assess the efficacy of each drug in the treatment of COVID-19, as determined by mortality rates. The design of this overview followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Systematic Reviews (PRISMA) guidelines, while the updated meta-analysis adhered to the PRISMA standards.[ 9 ] We conducted a comprehensive search across several databases, including Cochrane, PubMed, Scopus, LITCOVID, and Web of Science, using both Keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms specific to each database from 2019 through September 2023. The search terms included: Coronavirus COVID-19 SARS-CoV-2 Systematic review Meta-analysis Treatment Drug Therapy Pharmacotherapy Medicine Management Efficacy Safety Clinical trials. The full electronic search strategy can be found in Appendix 1 [Supplementary File 1]. We included systematic reviews and meta-analyses that compared the efficacy and/or safety of therapeutic options in the treatment of COVID-19. Only articles published in English were considered. Studies were included regardless of the severity of disease in participants or the setting (e.g., hospital-based, community-based, or both). We excluded narrative and literature reviews, reviews focusing on herbal treatments, stem cell therapy, interferons, and alternative medicine. The primary outcome of this review was mortality. We performed a meta-analysis on the pooled mortality estimates reported in the included meta-analyses. The title and abstract of each article were screened by the authors, and data extraction was carried out based on the PICOT framework (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time). Information extracted from each study included details on the population (patients), intervention (drug/therapy), comparison, outcome measures, and type of study. Two researchers (SM, MB) independently extracted data using a predefined data extraction form. Any discrepancies were resolved by rechecking the data and discussing with a third investigator (AF). Key information extracted from the systematic reviews included: Author(s) and year of publication, drug(s) studied, study population (outpatient or inpatient), study purpose (treatment or prevention), number of studies included, types of studies (randomized controlled trial [RCT], observational, etc.), final sample size, and outcomes assessed. Outcomes assessed included efficacy and safety of each drug, measured through all-cause mortality, disease exacerbation, virological cure, adverse events, need for mechanical ventilation, ICU admission, length of hospitalization, and clinical improvement, with mortality as the primary outcome. The quality of each systematic review and meta-analysis was independently assessed by two authors (SM, MB) using the AMSTAR 2 tool.[ 10 ] AMSTAR 2 (A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews) is an updated, widely used tool for evaluating the methodological quality of systematic reviews, particularly those related to interventions. It includes 16 items that assess various aspects of the review process, such as study selection, risk of bias, data extraction methods, and meta-analysis techniques. AMSTAR 2 emphasizes transparency, precision, and up-to-date standards in the evaluation of review methodologies and results. This tool is crucial for ensuring that systematic reviews are methodologically rigorous and their findings are reliable. Each review was scored using the AMSTAR 2 tool, with a maximum score of 16. Higher scores reflect better methodological quality. Disagreements between authors were resolved through discussion. For clarity, the maximum score is determined based on the relevant items for each review, and the scores for specific drugs or interventions may vary. For all included meta-analyses, we evaluated the effect of each drug on mortality compared to controls. Risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for RR were calculated as pooled effect sizes using the DerSimonian and Laird method.[ 11 ] Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochran Q Chi-squared test and I 2 statistic. Heterogeneity levels were categorized as low (25%), moderate (50%), and high (75%).[ 12 ] To assess publication bias, funnel plots, as well as Egger’s and Beg’s tests, were employed. A significant publication bias was indicated when the P value from these tests was <0.05 and asymmetry was evident in the funnel plot.[ 13 ] Sensitivity analyses and meta-regression were performed to identify sources of heterogeneity, considering the number of studies and the total sample size across meta-analyses. In addition, sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the influence of individual meta-analyses on the overall pooled effect estimate (RR). All statistical analyses were performed using STATA Version 11 (Stata Corp., College Station, TX, USA). P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. In this review, we retrieved a total of 3575 articles from the initial database search. After the removal of duplication and screening, 285 studies were selected for inclusion in this review. Figure 1 shows the PRISMA diagram. The Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Systematic Reviews diagram The analysis of the contents of systematic reviews indicated that most evaluated drugs were distributed as follows: chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine ( n = 48), tocilizumab ( n = 39), remdesivir ( n = 25), corticosteroids ( n = 25), JAK inhibitors ( n = 12), colchicine ( n = 11), ivermectin ( n = 8), anakinra ( n = 7), favipiravir ( n = 7), lopinavir/ritonavir ( n = 6), ACEI/ARB ( n = 6), azithromycin ( n = 4), sofosbuvir ( n = 4), and Vitamin D ( n = 4). The characteristics of the included reviews and quality assessment of them are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-16. Supplementary Tables 1-16 summarized data based on the PICOT. A total of 48 systematic reviews assessed the efficacy and safety of Chloroquine (CQ) and Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) in the treatment of COVID-19, with 36 of these being meta-analyses [Supplementary Table 1]. Most of the included reviews scored above 20 points on the AMSTAR scale, with Deng et al .[ 14 ] achieving the highest score of 35 points, which was based on 51 studies involving 61,221 patients. Among the systematic reviews without meta-analysis, Barzkar et al .[ 15 ] and Das et al .[ 16 ] each scored 21 points on the AMSTAR scale. Overall, 37.5% of the included reviews demonstrated 70% quality, with scores ranging from 18 to 35 for systematic reviews with meta-analyses and 6–21 for reviews without meta-analyses. In total, 28 meta-analyses were included in our umbrella meta-analysis. The analysis revealed that Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine significantly increased the mortality rate (RR: 1.02, CI: 1.00–1.04, P = 0.011, I 2 = 63.4%, P < 0.001) [ Figure 2 ]. Meta-regression analysis did not provide evidence for the confounding effects of sample size ( P = 0.875) or the number of studies included in each meta-analysis ( P = 0.535) on the pooled estimated effect size of Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine on mortality rate. Although no publication bias was detected based on the visual inspection of the funnel plot and the Begg test ( P = 0.73), some evidence of publication bias was identified through Egger’s regression test ( P = 0.028). In response, a trim-and-fill analysis was conducted to adjust for publication bias, but the results remained unchanged. Sensitivity analysis indicated that the exclusion of any individual meta-analysis did not significantly affect the estimated pooled effect size. Ivermectin i. sofosbuvir j. ACE1 and ARB k. Azithromycin l. Lopinavir m. Chloroquine & Hydroxychloroquine Safety Regarding the safety of Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), seven reviews specifically assessed its safety as the sole outcome. In comparison with the control group, HCQ significantly increased the risk of adverse effects (RR: 2.23, CI: 0.84–3.63, P = 0.011, I 2 = 76.7%, P < 0.001), although it caused fewer side effects when compared to standard treatments. The most notable adverse effect was an increase in QT prolongation, which was rare and only observed in patients who received HCQ in combination with azithromycin or those with severe COVID-19. No significant differences were observed in other outcomes, such as virological cure, mortality, clinical worsening, hospitalization rates, length of hospital stay, or the need for mechanical ventilation when HCQ was compared with the control or conventional treatment. A total of 26 reviews evaluated both the efficacy and safety of Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ). The risk of any adverse effects was significantly higher in the HCQ group compared to the control group, but no significant difference was found for serious adverse effects. Cardiac toxicity, including arrhythmias, was more prevalent in patients with severe COVID-19 and those receiving HCQ in combination with azithromycin. A total of 39 systematic reviews assessed the efficacy and safety of Tocilizumab in the treatment of COVID-19, with 36 of these being meta-analyses [Supplementary Table 2]. Most of the included reviews scored above 20 points on the AMSTAR scale, with Conti et al .[ 17 ] achieving the highest quality score of 35 points, based on 47 articles involving 9,640 patients. Among the systematic reviews without meta-analysis, Cortegian et al .[ 18 ] scored 19 points on the AMSTAR scale, based on 9 articles involving 64,289 patients. Approximately 33.3% of the included reviews demonstrated 70% quality based on the AMSTAR scale assessment, with scores ranging from 18 to 35 for systematic reviews with meta-analysis and 15–19 for those without meta-analysis. A total of 35 meta-analyses were included in the umbrella meta-analysis. The analysis indicated that Tocilizumab significantly reduced the mortality rate (RR: 0.9, CI: 0.88–0.92, P < 0.001, I 2 = 76.6%, P < 0.001) [ Figure 2 ]. Meta-regression analysis found no evidence of confounding effects related to sample size ( P = 0.88); however, there was some evidence of confounding due to the number of studies included in each meta-analysis ( P = 0.02) on the estimated effect of Tocilizumab on the mortality rate. Publication bias was detected based on visual inspection of the funnel plot and formal tests, including Egger’s regression test ( P < 0.001) and Begg’s test ( P < 0.001). However, a trim-and-fill analysis did not alter the previous results. Sensitivity analysis showed that excluding any of the included meta-analyses did not significantly affect the pooled estimated effect size. In terms of the safety profile, 20 reviews reported the safety outcomes of Tocilizumab. Overall, Tocilizumab did not significantly increase the risk of adverse events or secondary infections. However, some reviews indicated a significantly increased risk of neutropenia in RCTs. In addition, Tocilizumab was found to reduce the risk of requiring mechanical ventilation in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, but it had no effect on ICU admission rates or length of hospitalization. A total of 25 systematic reviews assessed the efficacy and safety of Remdesivir in the treatment of COVID-19, with 20 of these being meta-analyses [Supplementary Table 3]. Most of the included reviews scored above 24 points on the AMSTAR scale, with Bansal et al .[ 19 ] (including 9 studies with 1,895 patients) and Piscoya et al .[ 20 ] (including 6 studies with 2,324 patients) achieving the highest quality score of 31. Among the systematic reviews without meta-analysis, Roshanshad et al .[ 21 ] scored 19 points on the AMSTAR scale. Approximately 28% of the included reviews demonstrated 70% quality based on the AMSTAR scale assessment, with scores ranging from 14 to 31 for systematic reviews with meta-analysis and 5–19 for those without meta-analysis. A total of 18 meta-analyses were included in the umbrella meta-analysis. The analysis showed that Remdesivir significantly reduced the mortality rate (RR: 0.9, CI: 0.87–0.94, P < 0.001, I 2 = 69.9%, P < 0.001) [ Figure 2 ]. Navigating Therapeutic Frontiers: A Meta-review and Meta-analysis of COVID-19 Treatment Options

To assess the efficacy and safety of each therapeutic options in the treatment of COVID-19 by assessing the evidence from existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and to carry out an umbrella meta-analysis of all meta-analysis studies to assess the efficacy of each drug. A comprehensive search was carried out in electronic databases for systematic reviews and meta-analyses which compared the efficacy and/or safety of therapeutic options in the treatment of COVID-19. Findings from the reviews were synthesized using tables and forest plots and the pooled estimate of effect size using the DerSimonian and Laird method was used for the updated meta-analysis. The main outcome was mortality. 285 reviews with 152 meta-analyses were included, The analysis of systematic reviews contents indicated that most reviewed drugs were as follows: chroquine/hydroxychloroquine ( n = 48), tocilizumab ( n = 39), remdesivir ( n = 25), corticosteroids ( n = 25), JAK inhibitors ( n = 12), colchicine ( n = 11), ivermectin ( n = 8), anakinra ( n = 7), favipravir ( n = 7), lopinavir/ritonavir ( n = 6), ACEI/ARB ( n = 6), azithromycin ( n = 4), sofosbuvir ( n = 4), and Vitamin D ( n = 4). Findings from the included reviews suggested that tocilizumab, remdesivir, corticosteroids, JAKI, anakinra, colchicine, ivermectin, and sofosbuvir decreased the rate of mortality significantly in those taking the drugs; otherwise hydroxylchroquine increased the risk of mortality significantly, while Lopinavir/Ritonavir had no benefit and ACEI and azithromycin decreased mortality rate not significantly. lower requirement for mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit admission and a shorter hospital length of stay was observed with the tocilizumab, JAKIs, anakinra, corticosteroids and sofosbuvir Only one third of the included reviews had 70% quality based on the AMSTAR scale assessment. The results of this study have the potential to be a useful tool for the translation of health evidence and for designing the decision support systems for evidence synthesis.

In December 2019, several cases of unexplained pneumonia with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) were first reported in Wuhan, China. A novel coronavirus, later identified as SARS-CoV-2, was determined to be the causative agent and subsequently designated as COVID-19 by the World Health Organization (WHO). As of January 18, 2022, over 326 million confirmed cases and 5.54 million deaths had been reported globally.[ 1 ] Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in Iran (March 2019), approximately 7 million individuals have been infected, and 140,000 have lost their lives.[ 2 ] The widespread availability of vaccines has played a significant role in controlling the disease globally. However, vaccination rates have been slower in low-and middle-income countries, and the morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 are expected to continue increasing, driven by successive waves of SARS-CoV-2 variants impacting many countries.[ 3 ] This persistent rise in COVID-19-related morbidity and mortality underscores the need for effective therapeutic interventions. Efforts are ongoing to identify drugs with proven efficacy in the treatment of COVID-19. Currently, Remdesivir is the only drug approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of COVID-19.[ 4 ] Other treatments that have received emergency use authorization include Molnupiravir, Paxlovid, and certain monoclonal antibodies, such as Bebtelovimab. In addition, the use of interferons, ivermectin, chloroquine, azithromycin, and lopinavir/ritonavir is not recommended.[ 5 ] The approval of drugs for use or nonuse is often based on clinical studies, including clinical trials, which are reviewed and categorized in evidence-based medicine. Evidence-based medicine involves identifying a well-defined question, searching for relevant evidence, critically appraising it, applying the findings, and measuring the associated outcomes, similar to the process of conducting a systematic review. As a result, high-quality evidence often originates from systematic reviews that synthesize clinical trials.[ 6 7 ] Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, numerous antiviral and anti-inflammatory drugs were proposed and entered clinical trials for COVID-19 treatment. Several systematic reviews have been conducted to evaluate these drugs, producing some evidence, although significant uncertainties remain. Like primary studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses have presented contradictory results. Reviews of systematic reviews are particularly valuable in evidence-based healthcare decision-making. This era has been termed the “age of evidence-based everything,” in which healthcare decision-makers are encouraged to create an environment conducive to peer-to-peer evidence sharing. Reviews of systematic reviews are particularly useful for translating health evidence into decision-making, and they serve as important resources for policy briefs and decision support systems. By synthesizing evidence from multiple systematic reviews, these umbrella reviews provide comprehensive summaries that are often preferred by healthcare decision-makers.[ 8 ] In this context, we conducted this umbrella review with two main objectives: (1) to assess the efficacy and safety of various therapeutic options for COVID-19 by evaluating evidence from existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses and (2) to conduct an umbrella meta-analysis of all available meta-analytic studies to assess the efficacy of each drug. These secondary studies are instrumental in developing treatment guidelines, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to internationally approved drugs may be restricted. This study comprises two main components: An overview of all existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and an umbrella meta-analysis of these meta-analyses to assess the efficacy of each drug in the treatment of COVID-19, as determined by mortality rates. The design of this overview followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Overviews of Systematic Reviews (PRISMA) guidelines, while the updated meta-analysis adhered to the PRISMA standards.[ 9 ] We conducted a comprehensive search across several databases, including Cochrane, PubMed, Scopus, LITCOVID, and Web of Science, using both Keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms specific to each database from 2019 through September 2023. The search terms included: Coronavirus COVID-19 SARS-CoV-2 Systematic review Meta-analysis Treatment Drug Therapy Pharmacotherapy Medicine Management Efficacy Safety Clinical trials. The full electronic search strategy can be found in Appendix 1 [Supplementary File 1]. We included systematic reviews and meta-analyses that compared the efficacy and/or safety of therapeutic options in the treatment of COVID-19. Only articles published in English were considered. Studies were included regardless of the severity of disease in participants or the setting (e.g., hospital-based, community-based, or both). We excluded narrative and literature reviews, reviews focusing on herbal treatments, stem cell therapy, interferons, and alternative medicine. The primary outcome of this review was mortality. We performed a meta-analysis on the pooled mortality estimates reported in the included meta-analyses. The title and abstract of each article were screened by the authors, and data extraction was carried out based on the PICOT framework (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time). Information extracted from each study included details on the population (patients), intervention (drug/therapy), comparison, outcome measures, and type of study. Two researchers (SM, MB) independently extracted data using a predefined data extraction form. Any discrepancies were resolved by rechecking the data and discussing with a third investigator (AF). Key information extracted from the systematic reviews included: Author(s) and year of publication, drug(s) studied, study population (outpatient or inpatient), study purpose (treatment or prevention), number of studies included, types of studies (randomized controlled trial [RCT], observational, etc.), final sample size, and outcomes assessed. Outcomes assessed included efficacy and safety of each drug, measured through all-cause mortality, disease exacerbation, virological cure, adverse events, need for mechanical ventilation, ICU admission, length of hospitalization, and clinical improvement, with mortality as the primary outcome. The quality of each systematic review and meta-analysis was independently assessed by two authors (SM, MB) using the AMSTAR 2 tool.[ 10 ] AMSTAR 2 (A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews) is an updated, widely used tool for evaluating the methodological quality of systematic reviews, particularly those related to interventions. It includes 16 items that assess various aspects of the review process, such as study selection, risk of bias, data extraction methods, and meta-analysis techniques. AMSTAR 2 emphasizes transparency, precision, and up-to-date standards in the evaluation of review methodologies and results. This tool is crucial for ensuring that systematic reviews are methodologically rigorous and their findings are reliable. Each review was scored using the AMSTAR 2 tool, with a maximum score of 16. Higher scores reflect better methodological quality. Disagreements between authors were resolved through discussion. For clarity, the maximum score is determined based on the relevant items for each review, and the scores for specific drugs or interventions may vary. For all included meta-analyses, we evaluated the effect of each drug on mortality compared to controls.
